And the Letter of Intent is where you're going to kind of break out the most significant aspects of,
like the purchase price, who the parties are, how the purchase price is going to be paid,
what the contingencies on Closing are going to be, what kind of post-closing transition the
seller is going to give to you to help you step into the business and operate it. Things like
that. So the Letter of Intent is usually where I get really heavily involved. (I have a timeline
on the next slide). Once the Letter of Intent has been signed, then you usually are going to have,
the searcher is going to have, about 60 days. You know, I've seen 30-day Due Diligence periods,
but 60, I think, is reasonable. I've seen as many as 90. If I can, you know, if we're at 30 and the
seller is adamant that it's only going to be 30, I'll try and get 45. Give me a little something,
right? But that's going to be an opportunity for the searcher to come into the business
and kick the tires, see everything: the books, the tax returns, ask questions, walk the site,
walk the location, learn the process, all these things. Part of the Letter of Intent. One of the
important things about the Letter of Intent as well is that there's an exclusivity aspect to it,
and that's binding on both parties. Basically, that gives the searcher, the buyer, the comfort
that they're not going to get into a bidding war, that essentially, the seller is going to take the
business off the market until we get to a certain milestone. So, we want the business. Sometimes,
in my Letters of Intent ,I try and get them, if it's listed somewhere on the internet, to de-list
it as well, but I get a lot of pressure not to, you know. I get a lot of a kickback on that.
But essentially, we want that exclusivity, because we're going to spend money and invest in Due
Diligence and in looking for funding and things like that. Due Diligence. There's a financial
side to Due Diligence, and generally, I tell my Searchers, hey, get your financial Due Diligence
done first, because there's no sense spending any money on a lawyer if the financial stuff doesn't
work out, right? Because if you know right away that the finances look terrible, and I've seen
that happen where you know information wasn't shared in the CIM at the evaluate and analyze
level, and it comes out as we dig deeper into the books, and we call the deal off. And we never get,
that way we’ve never even gotten to legal Due Diligence. Legal Due Diligence is part of the
Due Diligence process where I'm, as the attorney, coming in and looking at all the contracts. Can
they be transferred? or are there conditions that have to be met in order to transfer them? We live
in an area where there's, there are a lot of defense contractors and federal government
contracts cannot be transferred in an asset sale, they're not. So, you have to structure
the deal differently. You have to structure it as an equity purchase, and even in those instances,
you may have to go to the government agency and get their permission. But these are the kinds
of things that I'm looking for in the legal Due Diligence. You're also, during the Due Diligence
period, you're looking for money to pay the purchase price. And so typically, right now,
SBA 7A loans are super hot. Before 2017, I think I closed in my whole career, maybe three to five
SBA loans. Since 2017, since ETA has heated up so much, I've probably closed 100 SBA loans,
and there are a couple reasons for that. SBA 7A . The lenders have gotten very good at doing the
SBA loans. There are specialty lenders out there who all they do is SBA 7A loans. And so, I know
who those lenders are. They're great to work with. They do a really good job. All these SBA lenders
are cash flow lenders. They're not collateral based lenders. In other words, they don't want
to take, they don't want to make sure that you have a lot of collateral, like hard assets and
real estate as collateral for the loan. What they want to make sure is that you have really good
cash flow so that you can service the debt. That's what they're looking for. They're not going to
lend that if you come out with a lot of collateral and say, “Hey, I have all these assets that you
can take a lien in.” They're not that interested in that. But if you come at them and say, “Look
at the cash flow that this business throws off, we can totally service your debt.” And they're very
excited about that, and they've gotten very good at it. But that's part of what you'll be doing
during Due Diligence as well. You'll be going to these lenders, you'll be giving them applications.
They'll be looking at considering your applications and giving you commitment letters,
and you'll be securing or putting that funding in place so that when you're ready to close, the
money's there. After Due Diligence, you've decided everything's going great, the company looks great,
the lender is happy, they're going to loan you the money. Then that's when you really start to
spend a lot of time with me, because I'm going to draft all the documents: the Purchase Agreement,
there's probably about another 15 Closing documents that have to be drafted, the Bill of
Sale, the Assignment of Intellectual Property, the Assignment of Contracts, the Assignment of Leases,
the Non-competition Agreement, all these types of agreements get drafted as part,
but we're going to spend a huge amount of time on the Purchase Agreement. There's
going to be some back and forth between me and the seller's attorney. Now, I've done this a
lot. There are some very kind of customary and standard ways to draft these agreements. So,
we're typically drafting more middle of the road so that we don't have to spend a lot of time
butting heads over negotiating the Purchase Agreement, there's still going to be negotiation,
but depending on who the attorneys are on the other side, if they're experienced in ETA,
everybody's going to kind of know that we're going to end up in the middle, and we're going to know
what the middle is. I'm doing a negotiation right now, I spent two hours on the phone yesterday, and
I'm just hitting my head on the brick wall because the attorney on the other side. I just feel like
that person has never negotiated one of these kind of deals, and we're negotiating things that are
like, a seller is an LLC and I want the owner of that LLC, the founder, to sign a non-competition
agreement. That's only fair, right? Because why would I let that guy sell the business to me and
then be able to just walk out? He said, “Well, I’ll have my LLC sign the non-compete but not
me.” And I'm like, that doesn't work. I don't care about your LLC. I care about you. You're
the guy who's going to go out and compete. Once we get through that, we'll close. Closing is simply
an exercise where all the documents are going to get signed, the money is going to flow, and then
you're going to walk into the business, and it's yours. Last year, I had a client who was an MBA
student at Georgetown University. On Friday, he walked across the stage and got his MBA,
and on Monday, he walked into his business as the CEO of the business because he had during his last
semester of MBA school, he did his search. He did a self-funded search. We went through this
whole process of analyzing and doing the Due Diligence. We drafted and negotiated all the
Purchase Agreements. The Monday after he graduated we signed everything in the morning, and he was on
site and walked in and introduced as the president of the company. About 35 employees, I think it was
about two and a half million in EBITDA each year. And yeah, and thrilled. And then six months later,
we were at the Southeastern Entrepreneur Through Acquisition conference, and he was on a panel
speaking about his experience of walking in and buying the business and becoming an operator. Now,
after that, there are some different approaches to ETA. One of the approaches is kind of a flip
approach, where you might hold the company for five to seven years and then exit it, or use the
company you first buy as leverage to buy your next business. There are people who have strategies
where they create, like a holding company, and they're going to roll up, like every landscaping
business in the southeast, or something like that. That's pretty ambitious. We were at Wharton last
year, and there was a guy on the panel. He and his buddy from business school decided in business
school that they were going to buy funeral homes. And they, I don't remember how long it was they
had, after a couple of years, maybe five or seven years, they had rolled up 40 funeral homes. And so
that's an approach. But, another approach, which is more typical, is that you just hold and grow,
you just operate and grow, and then you know when you're ready to retire, perhaps you exit out.
Okay, let's talk quickly about timeline. This is a question that Searchers always ask me. How long
is this going to take? The Search itself could take years. I've got some clients who have signed
five or six Letters of Intent, and we've passed on every one of those businesses when we've got
into Due Diligence. And, you can see that even if Due Diligence is 60 days, that's two months
right there, in and of itself. If you sign five Letters of Intent, and go through sequentially,
and you go through five Due Diligence experiences, you've easily gotten to a year at that point. The
LOI goes very quickly, maybe a week, once you decide you want to do it. Due Diligence could
be 30, 45, 60, 90-days. The Purchase Agreement. The Closing documents, and the Closing. Really,
what I tell people is between Letter of Intent and Closing to budget or plan on about four to six
months. Most of the transactions that I'm closing are in the four-month period. Six months is on the
outer edge if things kind of get kind of wonky. I've closed deals faster, but I really don't like
it. I hate to be rushed. We closed a deal last year in 60 days from Letter of Intent to Closing,
because the other side, I was on the seller side, and the buyer was a private equity firm, and they
just pushed and pushed and pushed us hard. But we did it. So that's kind of the timeline.
That's what to expect. Costs. We’ll go quickly. Search, it really can be whatever you make of it.
If you're able to find investors to back your search, then you might be able, that three to
$400,000 that people invest are to pay a salary for you. So you may be able to pay yourself about
$100,000-$130,000 a year as a salary and then that money is also used for you to travel. And you
don't really need to hire a lot of professionals during that time, but if you do, that's what the
money is there for. Where do people get the money? Well, their savings, their retirement accounts,
ROBS is a rollover business startup. So, you take your 401K, and you roll it over, and you,
instead of investing in public market stock, you invest in your own corporation. You buy the stock
of your corporation, and you bring that money from your retirement account into your new business,
and you use it that way. It's the same thing with an IRA. It's called a self-directed IRA, where
you're able to take your IRA, and you have to set it up a certain way to satisfy the IRS. Capital
Raise. You might go out and find investors to help you, and there are investors out there. There are
investment funds that look for Searchers. They're actively looking for Searchers that they can back.
But you also might get money. One of the first deals I ever did when I was a young attorney was
to help somebody buy a Cinnabon franchise. Almost, probably 25 more or more years ago, and he raised
his money from his father-in-law and from four of his college buddies. At the time, he only
needed $250,000 that seems like not much right now, but that's all he needed. And, man, I mean,
it was like, it's like owning the Chick-fil-A franchise. It's like printing money, you know. So,
what kind of professional fees are you going to pay? You’ve got to have a lawyer. You’ve got to
have a CPA. There may be a broker involved, if you have a buyer side broker, otherwise,
if there's a broker that's representing the seller, the seller is going to pay that brokers
commission. You don't have to worry about that. Lawyer Fees. Kind of the conventional wisdom is
it can range anywhere between like a half percent to one and a half percent of the purchase price.
There are attorneys out there right now, I'm still a little bit more traditional, where I just charge
by the hour, but I've done so many deals that I can give you a budget. You know, for a deal that's
in the one to $3 million purchase price range, I would probably tell you to budget about $15,000
in attorney’s fees. You can see that if I told you that I wanted one and a half percent, that would
be more if it was a $3 million deal. CPAs and the broker are always going to take somewhere between
six and 10%, but again, if you're the buyer and the broker’s on the seller side, you don't have to
worry about that. That comes out of the seller's cash. You're going to need to form an entity,
typically an LLC, that's what everybody's using. And there's some money involved in that, but it
shouldn’t be a lot. And then you need post-closing working capital. This is a really big issue. One
of the you're going to learn as you Search is that you may buy a company that has a collection
cycle of 30, 60, or 90 days. So, you may walk into that company… like I’ve helped people buy and sell
health care practices, and you may walk into that company and not be able, the work you do on day
one when you own it is not going to be collected until 90 days later, at the earliest. So,
what are you going to do during that gap? You need some working capital. It could come from your SBA
loan. You could get a line of credit where you get an extra $100,000-$150,000 on top. Or, what's
kind of become more traditional now, is that we essentially buy working capital from the seller.
So, we tell the seller, hey, you got to leave $100,000 in cash in the business, or transfer
it over to us. 25 years ago, that would have been, never, people would have just said, “You're crazy,
we're not doing that,” but now sellers are realizing that they may need to do that in order
to make the sale happen. The other thing we didn't talk about in funding. We talked about the loan;
I've mentioned SBA loans, but seller financing is a big, hot issue right now too. The SBA may loan
you up to 90% of the purchase price. You’ll have to come up with the other 10%. You may not have
that money. And so, if you can convince the seller to take a promissory note for 5% then that's going
to help you get over the finish line. So, seller financing is big. You're going to see a lot of
stuff online if you dig deep into this about how to buy a business with $0 down. If you ask me,
have I done that? Yes, I have. I have represented buyers who have bought businesses with zero money
down, giving a promissory note to the seller for the entire purchase price. But in 25 years,
I've probably done it three times, and those times have all been when there's been some sort
of personal relationship with the seller. Like it's a key employee who's buying the business,
or something like that. All right. If you want to dig deeper into this, this is what I would do.
I would go to LinkedIn. There's lots of talk on LinkedIn, Twitter as well. I put one guy up here,
Samuil Jariwala. He's one of my very favorites. He has a fund called the FETA fund. But,
he puts something up on LinkedIn almost every day that's geared towards Searchers. Like tips
on how to make your Search good, how to evaluate businesses, things like that. Saumil is great.
The other thing I would do is, I mean, you can network, you can talk to there's tons of people
to talk to, and you can meet them online. So, meeting Saumil, following him is a great way
to get started. There are books out there. That's my book [Here’s the Deal: Everything
You Wish a Lawyer Would Tell You about Buying a Small Business]. That's a plug, but really,
you don't need to read my book until you get close to a deal. The other two books are, “Buy Then
Build” and the “Harvard Business Review: Buying a Small Business.” They're kind of like the Bibles
of this ETA movement from a business perspective. My book complements them from a legal perspective.
The other thing that you really should think about doing is, if you're really interested in this,
go to one of these ETA conferences. There's one coming up at UVA in September. September 5-6th.
There's a consortium between UVA University, North Carolina, Georgetown, and Duke University,
and they put on this thing called the Southeast Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition conference.
We've been to it twice now. It's really good. It's in the mid-Atlantic, and you're going to see,
essentially, the people who come speak at these are kind of like circuit riders that you'll see a
lot of the same, attorneys, investors, Searchers. If you are really serious about finding investors,
these ETA conferences are a good place to network and connect with investors as well. And a lot of
times, the investors will have dedicated rooms where you can sign up for a 20-minute consult
and go in and talk to them. So you know, SEETA is probably the most accessible thing for us. Harvard
is a huge one, Booth-Kellog up at the University of Chicago is massive. And yeah, I mean,
if you're interested in learning more about this, they're usually two or three days long,
and they have all these panels and opportunities for you to connect with people and things like
that. So great stuff. All right, I'm done. I think. What questions can I answer for you? Yes.
[Inaudible]. When you do the offer, the Letter of Intent, is there some sort of deposit? No,
no, don't pay a deposit. I'm just telling you right now. If they tell you that they want to,
if you're buying a business that's priced under $5,000,00, $5-$6 million and they're telling
you they want a deposit, don't do it. It's a red flag. Will they take it off the market?
Yes. So, there's a lot of what I would call creep into ETA lately, what I've observed
over the last seven or eight years. Brokers who aren't experienced in buying and selling small
businesses, they may be really well experienced in commercial real estate or residential real estate.
They're coming into the space, and they're trying to bring those types of concepts into the space,
but those, that doesn't work. I had a broker in Florida. He wanted not only a deposit,
but a non-refundable deposit, and he wanted the Purchase Agreement drafted and approved within
five days after signing the Letter of Intent. We didn't sign. We told him, he's crazy. We're not.
Nobody's doing that, right? It is ridiculous! But what I see, I do see people starting to ask for
deposits. I have a deal right now that I'm working on where they ask for a deposit. I told my client,
don't do it, but he did it anyway. I told him, if you're going to do it, do it at about 10% of what
they're asking for. He didn't. He did, he did it all. I don't know why, right? But no, if they're
asking for deposit, that's a concept from a different type of transaction, and that's not the
way we do it. So, it's a great question. They'll take it off, they should take it off the market.
Brokers come in different flavors. Let's, talk about that. [Inaudible]. Yeah,
the marketing expense. [Inaudible]. Yeah, well, but okay, so I'm going to argue back against that,
because my guy is expending money as well. I hear the seller argument all the time. We're spending
money, blah, blah, blah. My guy's spending a lot of money too. He's already spent a lot of money
to get here. Hopefully you guys have vetted my guy well enough, or girl, so that that you're
comfortable enough to move forward with the Letter of Intent. If you're not, if you think that the
deal is not serious enough by the Letter of Intent phase, or they're not comfortable enough that you
have to have money for a small deal. Now, a bigger deal is a different story, but a small deal is,
you know, it's just not. The other reason, I see it done a lot more. And I'm going to speak,
I'm going to tell you why I think you should get a deposit. That's because it is the wild, wild west,
and so you're probably getting hundreds and hundreds of inquiries about businesses from
people who are submitting, Searchers who are submitting, 100 inquiries to brokers every
day. They've got a bot set up or something like that, and you're having to spend your time wading
through all that, trying to figure out what's real, who's serious, who's got the resources to
do it. And I feel you on that, because I'm getting those too. I'm getting people who want to talk to
me for an hour, hour and a half, about they want to buy a business, but they don't have any money,
and can I walk them through the process, and will I cut my fees and all that stuff? It's rough out
there. [Inaudible]. Listing active? Yeah, and I'm cool with that. I mean, I'll ask for
it to be delisted, but if you tell me, No, we're going to leave it up there, that's fine. And you
can even take offers you just can't act on them. [Inaudible]. Yeah, some businesses have critical
dependency on subcontractors, maybe key employees. And, you know, they could even be family related,
so you can't be sure that they're going to stay in place. In some cases,
you might want to acquire the subcontractor at the same time. Oh, that's interesting idea.
How would you deal with a situation like that? Well, typically, I mean, absolutely,
that's an issue in almost every transaction. Like, are we going to be able to transition
the business in a way that we're not going to lose revenue, that we're not going to lose customers,
things like that. And that, maybe, we might make it a contingency on Closing, that we get
satisfactory employment agreements with the five key employees, or that we get the subcontractors
to agree that they're going to stay on with us. But those discussions typically would happen just
prior to Closing and would be a contingency to Closing so that if we didn't get those,
we wouldn't close. So how do you ensure that you identify those dependencies? Yeah, that's going
to happen during Due Diligence. I hope you know that's if you're a good searcher that it should
be happening during Due Diligence. So, I want to go, can I go back to the broker real quickly? Only
because there's another aspect that I think people should know about. You may ask for deposits,
but you may also see buyers asking for what they call breakage fees. Are you seeing that now? Yeah,
yeah. So that's a mid-market creep. So in mid-market deals, and we're talking deals like,
you know, $20 to $50 million, it wouldn't be uncommon for a buyer to say, hey,
if I find something during Due Diligence that you didn't tell me about, and I break the deal,
you have to reimburse me for my legal fees, and my attorney, my CPA fees. And sometimes they may just
put a number in, $15,000, $20,000, and so I have buyers now, when we're doing Letters of Intent,
ask me if we can put a breakage fee in. And my advice is, don't. It's like asking for a deposit,
like we just don't do it. And they say, “Well, I'm going to spend money.” Well,
so is the seller. Everybody's going to carry their own water until we get this deal done. You know,
that's just, we have to kind of trust each other. If we don't, that's not a great way to start out.
What is the maximum amount of an SBA loan? Well, it depends. Yeah, it depends. If you're
going to get a loan from the SBA under the SBA 7A program, $5 million is the limit. That's as much
as you're going to get. That doesn't mean that the purchase price has to be $5 million or less,
it just means you're going to get $5 million. So, if you can come up with the other I mean,
I'm about to help somebody buy a company for six and a half million, and the five is going
to come from the SBA, but the other one and a half is going to come from seller financing,
from investors, and from their own cash. Just one quick question. I think it kind of piggybacks on
the last. Can you just characterize some of the businesses that you have helped people buy? Like,
what are the types of businesses that people are buying? That's a great question,
but it's really just about anything. So trades are really popular, right? Like plumbing businesses,
landscaping, roofing, gutter businesses. They're real popular right now, although some are kind
of going out of favor. You should ask the broker too. But landscaping, people are kind of soured on
landscaping businesses and HVAC too, a little bit as well. I've helped people buy and sell wellness
businesses, like yoga, coaching businesses, I helped somebody sell a YouTube channel,
manufacturing businesses, small manufacturing businesses, like specialty automotive parts,
healthcare businesses, dentist office, podiatrist, veterinaries, veterinarians. I'm just trying to
think marketing businesses, online marketing agencies, brick and mortar marketing agencies.
I mean, as I keep thinking, I can keep going, but I'm running out of time. Okay.
I'll stick around if anybody wants to talk afterwards. Thank you very much.

videos.full_text: A different pathway to entrepreneurship that comes through acquiring a business. So with that, I will welcome Joel, thanks for being here. All right, so, okay, I even got it off mute. Graham basically told you everything I'm already going to talk about. So, I'm excited to be here, because I was talking to Stephanie earlier, I think. And this is a topic that is, it's not just a topic, it's a hot topic, and I'm really excited that it's the first topic of the semester, because it is a different approach, a different path to entrepreneurship than a more traditional start from scratch approach. It's being talked about all over the place, and this is the first time that anybody has invited us to talk about it in Virginia. We've talked about it at University of Illinois, Columbia Business School. We've been to conferences at Duke, Georgetown and the University of Pennsylvania. We're going to go to Darden, UVA in a couple of weeks. So, we're really excited that people in Virginia are starting to talk about Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition. It's a lot to say, so we're just going to use the acronym ETA. So let's, let's kind of jump into it real quickly. Graham already talked to you a little bit. He asked, everybody keeps asking me if I brought a copy of my book. I didn't. I'm not prepared. I went to my office yesterday and I realized I didn't have any copies, but we'll send some up in a week or so when they come in. So if you're interested, you can take a look. The book has been a lot of fun. It's introduced us to the ETA ecosystem, and we've been in that ecosystem, doing legal work for about seven years now. We did this work before, we just didn't know that it was called ETA. I've been helping people buy and sell businesses for over 25 years, but there's this community, and we'll talk more at the very end about how you can learn more about the ETA ecosystem and maybe even get plugged into that as well. So, one of the reasons why it's a hot topic is because there's something called, everybody calls it, the Silver Tsunami. Sometimes it's called the Gray Wave. Basically, there is a massive wealth transfer that's occurring and will be occurring for the next 10 to 15 years. People age 55 and plus. You can see the stats. I'm not going to read it, but they make up a big part of, and they own a lot of small businesses. I saw an article the other day that said that there's approximately seven to $10 trillion in small businesses that will be transferred or, shut down. That's the other thing that's happening is that approximately 1,500 businesses are either shutting themselves down or getting transferred every day. That's the statistic. I'm not a stats guy, so I look at that and I think that can't be real. But anyway, I guess it averages all out, if you look at all the numbers. So that's why it's hot. People have realized that, and I love the way Graham put it, that the barrier or the hurdle to getting into ETA is perhaps lower than the barrier or the hurdle of starting a business from scratch. So, this is the traditional startup model. I have a client that I had, when he was in business school, he and his friend decided that there needed to be a solution for students. And they ended up developing this company while they were in business school, and then when they graduated with their MBAs, they just kept going with this business. And they ran this business for 11 years, and they eventually got acquired. So he exited the business. So they went through that traditional: came up with an idea, did the research and development, created the minimally viable product, got their funding, you know all their different capital raises and things like that, built their product and their brand, launched, operate, grew, and then it took them about 11 years from the start to the finish to exit. So that's the traditional role, or the traditional model, and that's great. I've spent a lot of time also in my career, helping people do this type of thing. Several years ago, one of my best friends worked in a large like a fortune 100 company. There was a huge merger/change in management. He literally was moved from close to the C suite all the way down to the basement of the of the building. And so he came to me, and he said, You know, I think I've got an idea. We're going to start a business. He was a very early adopter of data analytics for sales forces, and creating software to help apply that concept to companies that had large sales forces that were selling large catalogs of products like medical supply businesses and veterinary supply businesses and things like that. So I helped him start his LLC, contract with coders, protect his intellectual property, things like that. And then approximately 25 years later he exited and he sold to a much larger company. So, I've seen that happen. It's a great path to entrepreneurship. I want to back up, though. I want to tell you one other quick thing, because I want to make sure I get you all…I want to entice you. I'm going to tell you at the end about some, if you're interested, some places where you can go look, some resources you can go look at. Stanford Business School has been in the ETA, they’re kind of the grandfather of ETA, and they have about 40 years of resources and data that they've been crunching. And one of the things that you're going to read, if you go read some of the Stanford information, is that people are excited about ETA because of the potential or the average return on investment. So, from what I understand, the average return on investment, if you invest in the stock market, is about nine or 10%. But Stanford crunches their data and tells us that the average return on investment in the ETA ecosystem is 34%. So again, you can see why people get really interested in this, not just people who want to actually acquire and operate the businesses, but also investors who want to invest in something that's going to bring them a pretty significant return on their investment. In other words, the upside for the investors is a lot more attractive in the ETA space than the upside in the traditional model. All right, here's the ETA model. The ETA model is Search. And business people are like, when I talk to business schools like MBA programs, this is what they're focused on, Search. How do I find the business that I want to acquire? and how long is that going to take? There are a lot of different approaches to Search, and frankly, as a lawyer, I don't get involved typically in the Search process. They usually come to me right about in this phase right here [LOI]. But I do spend a lot of time talking to people and learning about their experiences. Search is kind of like the wild, wild west right now, especially because it's such a hot area. You'll find lots of people: brokers, buyer side brokers, finders, you'll find websites like bizbuysell, you'll find other websites that list businesses for sale, brokers who have their own websites that list businesses for sale. There are seller side brokers. You'll find lots of coaches out there who are willing to coach people on how to not only find, like doing cold calls, that's a big part of finding and searching is doing cold calls. And what do you say when you email somebody, or Search somebody, or contact somebody, call them, who's maybe in their mid 60s, and they own a business that's throwing off about one to $2 million in EBITDA each year? How do you approach them and convince them that you're the person that they want to sell to? So, Search is a topic in and of itself that we could spend, and it wouldn't really be me, you would want somebody from the business school perhaps, to talk about Search, or somebody who's actually gone through the Search process. But, I have seen people go through Search for many years, and I have clients, for example, who have found 5, 6, 7 companies that we've gotten down the road on and then we've passed on them for one reason or another. So, Search can be lengthy, it can be challenging, it can be difficult. It is the wild, wild west. There are a lot of people out there that you'll see who are willing to sell you an online course about how to search, or will want to sell you coaching services about how to search, or something like that. I mean, it's, it's kind of crazy out there right now. But, that's where it starts, a traditional search, and this is an ETA kind of term of art. Traditional Search is something that the Stanford Business School created. When somebody says, “I'm a traditional searcher, I'm going to do a traditional search,” what they're telling you is that they're going to create a Limited Liability Company. They're going to go look for some investors who are going to give them some money so that they can, usually it's about maybe three to $400,000, so that they can spend the next two years as a full time, that's their full time job, is searching for a company. And what they're going to do is they're going to bring whatever companies they find. They're going to have a Search thesis. They're going to have written out an approach to what industries are they going to search in? What amount of gross revenue? or EBITDA? or what kind of factors are they going to apply to their search? And that's when they pitch that to their investors and they pitch their experience to their investors. Then their investors will give them this money and allow them to go out and do a Search for a year or two, it's usually two years. As they find companies that meet those Search parameters, they will come back and present to the investors. If the investors give the thumbs up and say, yes, we want you to acquire this company, then the investors have a choice. They can either put more money in and get a preferred return on investment, or they could just stay where they're at. Usually, they put more money in. And who are these investors? I have seen lots of family offices invest in this type of investment. In fact, I helped sell a business recently in the Virginia Beach area, where the buyer on the other side was a family office that was owned by the family that owns the Kansas City Chiefs. So that's where the money came from. I did another sale a couple of years ago where the buyer, the searcher, was a 31-year-old MBA graduate. He had 13 family offices who invested about, no, I think it was 23 family offices that invested about $13 million to help him purchase the business, and he coupled that with an SBA loan, and with some of his own money, very little of his own money, frankly, and bought a very nice business and walked in as a 31-year-old as the CEO of this business. So, once you find the Search, that's what traditional search. Most of the clients that I deal with are self-funded. In other words, they're doing the Search using their own money, money that they've saved up or they've got a full-time job that they're using to supplement, and theySearchat night or part time or something like that. That's what self-funded means. It just means you don't have any investors behind you who are helping support you in your Search. Once you find a business, you're going to go to the next step. You're going to evaluate and analyze the business, you're going to sign an NDA/Non-disclosure Agreement. I've been seeing some conversations online the last couple of days about the most ridiculous things some attorneys have been seeing in recent NDAs. You should have somebody take a look at it. If you're going to sign an NDA, take a look at it. I had somebody want my client to sign an NDA a couple of weeks ago that said if the buyer, I'm sorry, if the seller didn't pay the broker's commission, that the buyer would agree to pay the broker's commission. We're like, no, that's not. We're not doing that, that’s silly. The CIM acronym stands for Confidential Information Memorandum, and that's a document that if you are dealing, if the seller is represented by a broker, you're going to get some sort of what they call the CIM. You'll get the CIM, and that'll have a lot of the basic information to help you decide whether you want to go to the next step. And, the next step is actually to give them a Letter of Intent. And now this is a non-, part of it, most of it nonbinding, but there are some binding legal aspects to it as well. A Letter of Intent is not required by law. Before seven years ago, I was hardly ever using a Letter of Intent, but since then, I've probably closed 150 deals where we've used Letters of Intent. One of the reasons why is because lenders want them and brokers want them. They want to see these Letters of Intent. And the Letter of Intent is where you're going to kind of break out the most significant aspects of, like the purchase price, who the parties are, how the purchase price is going to be paid, what the contingencies on Closing are going to be, what kind of post-closing transition the seller is going to give to you to help you step into the business and operate it. Things like that. So the Letter of Intent is usually where I get really heavily involved. (I have a timeline on the next slide). Once the Letter of Intent has been signed, then you usually are going to have, the searcher is going to have, about 60 days. You know, I've seen 30-day Due Diligence periods, but 60, I think, is reasonable. I've seen as many as 90. If I can, you know, if we're at 30 and the seller is adamant that it's only going to be 30, I'll try and get 45. Give me a little something, right? But that's going to be an opportunity for the searcher to come into the business and kick the tires, see everything: the books, the tax returns, ask questions, walk the site, walk the location, learn the process, all these things. Part of the Letter of Intent. One of the important things about the Letter of Intent as well is that there's an exclusivity aspect to it, and that's binding on both parties. Basically, that gives the searcher, the buyer, the comfort that they're not going to get into a bidding war, that essentially, the seller is going to take the business off the market until we get to a certain milestone. So, we want the business. Sometimes, in my Letters of Intent ,I try and get them, if it's listed somewhere on the internet, to de-list it as well, but I get a lot of pressure not to, you know. I get a lot of a kickback on that. But essentially, we want that exclusivity, because we're going to spend money and invest in Due Diligence and in looking for funding and things like that. Due Diligence. There's a financial side to Due Diligence, and generally, I tell my Searchers, hey, get your financial Due Diligence done first, because there's no sense spending any money on a lawyer if the financial stuff doesn't work out, right? Because if you know right away that the finances look terrible, and I've seen that happen where you know information wasn't shared in the CIM at the evaluate and analyze level, and it comes out as we dig deeper into the books, and we call the deal off. And we never get, that way we’ve never even gotten to legal Due Diligence. Legal Due Diligence is part of the Due Diligence process where I'm, as the attorney, coming in and looking at all the contracts. Can they be transferred? or are there conditions that have to be met in order to transfer them? We live in an area where there's, there are a lot of defense contractors and federal government contracts cannot be transferred in an asset sale, they're not. So, you have to structure the deal differently. You have to structure it as an equity purchase, and even in those instances, you may have to go to the government agency and get their permission. But these are the kinds of things that I'm looking for in the legal Due Diligence. You're also, during the Due Diligence period, you're looking for money to pay the purchase price. And so typically, right now, SBA 7A loans are super hot. Before 2017, I think I closed in my whole career, maybe three to five SBA loans. Since 2017, since ETA has heated up so much, I've probably closed 100 SBA loans, and there are a couple reasons for that. SBA 7A . The lenders have gotten very good at doing the SBA loans. There are specialty lenders out there who all they do is SBA 7A loans. And so, I know who those lenders are. They're great to work with. They do a really good job. All these SBA lenders are cash flow lenders. They're not collateral based lenders. In other words, they don't want to take, they don't want to make sure that you have a lot of collateral, like hard assets and real estate as collateral for the loan. What they want to make sure is that you have really good cash flow so that you can service the debt. That's what they're looking for. They're not going to lend that if you come out with a lot of collateral and say, “Hey, I have all these assets that you can take a lien in.” They're not that interested in that. But if you come at them and say, “Look at the cash flow that this business throws off, we can totally service your debt.” And they're very excited about that, and they've gotten very good at it. But that's part of what you'll be doing during Due Diligence as well. You'll be going to these lenders, you'll be giving them applications. They'll be looking at considering your applications and giving you commitment letters, and you'll be securing or putting that funding in place so that when you're ready to close, the money's there. After Due Diligence, you've decided everything's going great, the company looks great, the lender is happy, they're going to loan you the money. Then that's when you really start to spend a lot of time with me, because I'm going to draft all the documents: the Purchase Agreement, there's probably about another 15 Closing documents that have to be drafted, the Bill of Sale, the Assignment of Intellectual Property, the Assignment of Contracts, the Assignment of Leases, the Non-competition Agreement, all these types of agreements get drafted as part, but we're going to spend a huge amount of time on the Purchase Agreement. There's going to be some back and forth between me and the seller's attorney. Now, I've done this a lot. There are some very kind of customary and standard ways to draft these agreements. So, we're typically drafting more middle of the road so that we don't have to spend a lot of time butting heads over negotiating the Purchase Agreement, there's still going to be negotiation, but depending on who the attorneys are on the other side, if they're experienced in ETA, everybody's going to kind of know that we're going to end up in the middle, and we're going to know what the middle is. I'm doing a negotiation right now, I spent two hours on the phone yesterday, and I'm just hitting my head on the brick wall because the attorney on the other side. I just feel like that person has never negotiated one of these kind of deals, and we're negotiating things that are like, a seller is an LLC and I want the owner of that LLC, the founder, to sign a non-competition agreement. That's only fair, right? Because why would I let that guy sell the business to me and then be able to just walk out? He said, “Well, I’ll have my LLC sign the non-compete but not me.” And I'm like, that doesn't work. I don't care about your LLC. I care about you. You're the guy who's going to go out and compete. Once we get through that, we'll close. Closing is simply an exercise where all the documents are going to get signed, the money is going to flow, and then you're going to walk into the business, and it's yours. Last year, I had a client who was an MBA student at Georgetown University. On Friday, he walked across the stage and got his MBA, and on Monday, he walked into his business as the CEO of the business because he had during his last semester of MBA school, he did his search. He did a self-funded search. We went through this whole process of analyzing and doing the Due Diligence. We drafted and negotiated all the Purchase Agreements. The Monday after he graduated we signed everything in the morning, and he was on site and walked in and introduced as the president of the company. About 35 employees, I think it was about two and a half million in EBITDA each year. And yeah, and thrilled. And then six months later, we were at the Southeastern Entrepreneur Through Acquisition conference, and he was on a panel speaking about his experience of walking in and buying the business and becoming an operator. Now, after that, there are some different approaches to ETA. One of the approaches is kind of a flip approach, where you might hold the company for five to seven years and then exit it, or use the company you first buy as leverage to buy your next business. There are people who have strategies where they create, like a holding company, and they're going to roll up, like every landscaping business in the southeast, or something like that. That's pretty ambitious. We were at Wharton last year, and there was a guy on the panel. He and his buddy from business school decided in business school that they were going to buy funeral homes. And they, I don't remember how long it was they had, after a couple of years, maybe five or seven years, they had rolled up 40 funeral homes. And so that's an approach. But, another approach, which is more typical, is that you just hold and grow, you just operate and grow, and then you know when you're ready to retire, perhaps you exit out. Okay, let's talk quickly about timeline. This is a question that Searchers always ask me. How long is this going to take? The Search itself could take years. I've got some clients who have signed five or six Letters of Intent, and we've passed on every one of those businesses when we've got into Due Diligence. And, you can see that even if Due Diligence is 60 days, that's two months right there, in and of itself. If you sign five Letters of Intent, and go through sequentially, and you go through five Due Diligence experiences, you've easily gotten to a year at that point. The LOI goes very quickly, maybe a week, once you decide you want to do it. Due Diligence could be 30, 45, 60, 90-days. The Purchase Agreement. The Closing documents, and the Closing. Really, what I tell people is between Letter of Intent and Closing to budget or plan on about four to six months. Most of the transactions that I'm closing are in the four-month period. Six months is on the outer edge if things kind of get kind of wonky. I've closed deals faster, but I really don't like it. I hate to be rushed. We closed a deal last year in 60 days from Letter of Intent to Closing, because the other side, I was on the seller side, and the buyer was a private equity firm, and they just pushed and pushed and pushed us hard. But we did it. So that's kind of the timeline. That's what to expect. Costs. We’ll go quickly. Search, it really can be whatever you make of it. If you're able to find investors to back your search, then you might be able, that three to $400,000 that people invest are to pay a salary for you. So you may be able to pay yourself about $100,000-$130,000 a year as a salary and then that money is also used for you to travel. And you don't really need to hire a lot of professionals during that time, but if you do, that's what the money is there for. Where do people get the money? Well, their savings, their retirement accounts, ROBS is a rollover business startup. So, you take your 401K, and you roll it over, and you, instead of investing in public market stock, you invest in your own corporation. You buy the stock of your corporation, and you bring that money from your retirement account into your new business, and you use it that way. It's the same thing with an IRA. It's called a self-directed IRA, where you're able to take your IRA, and you have to set it up a certain way to satisfy the IRS. Capital Raise. You might go out and find investors to help you, and there are investors out there. There are investment funds that look for Searchers. They're actively looking for Searchers that they can back. But you also might get money. One of the first deals I ever did when I was a young attorney was to help somebody buy a Cinnabon franchise. Almost, probably 25 more or more years ago, and he raised his money from his father-in-law and from four of his college buddies. At the time, he only needed $250,000 that seems like not much right now, but that's all he needed. And, man, I mean, it was like, it's like owning the Chick-fil-A franchise. It's like printing money, you know. So, what kind of professional fees are you going to pay? You’ve got to have a lawyer. You’ve got to have a CPA. There may be a broker involved, if you have a buyer side broker, otherwise, if there's a broker that's representing the seller, the seller is going to pay that brokers commission. You don't have to worry about that. Lawyer Fees. Kind of the conventional wisdom is it can range anywhere between like a half percent to one and a half percent of the purchase price. There are attorneys out there right now, I'm still a little bit more traditional, where I just charge by the hour, but I've done so many deals that I can give you a budget. You know, for a deal that's in the one to $3 million purchase price range, I would probably tell you to budget about $15,000 in attorney’s fees. You can see that if I told you that I wanted one and a half percent, that would be more if it was a $3 million deal. CPAs and the broker are always going to take somewhere between six and 10%, but again, if you're the buyer and the broker’s on the seller side, you don't have to worry about that. That comes out of the seller's cash. You're going to need to form an entity, typically an LLC, that's what everybody's using. And there's some money involved in that, but it shouldn’t be a lot. And then you need post-closing working capital. This is a really big issue. One of the you're going to learn as you Search is that you may buy a company that has a collection cycle of 30, 60, or 90 days. So, you may walk into that company… like I’ve helped people buy and sell health care practices, and you may walk into that company and not be able, the work you do on day one when you own it is not going to be collected until 90 days later, at the earliest. So, what are you going to do during that gap? You need some working capital. It could come from your SBA loan. You could get a line of credit where you get an extra $100,000-$150,000 on top. Or, what's kind of become more traditional now, is that we essentially buy working capital from the seller. So, we tell the seller, hey, you got to leave $100,000 in cash in the business, or transfer it over to us. 25 years ago, that would have been, never, people would have just said, “You're crazy, we're not doing that,” but now sellers are realizing that they may need to do that in order to make the sale happen. The other thing we didn't talk about in funding. We talked about the loan; I've mentioned SBA loans, but seller financing is a big, hot issue right now too. The SBA may loan you up to 90% of the purchase price. You’ll have to come up with the other 10%. You may not have that money. And so, if you can convince the seller to take a promissory note for 5% then that's going to help you get over the finish line. So, seller financing is big. You're going to see a lot of stuff online if you dig deep into this about how to buy a business with $0 down. If you ask me, have I done that? Yes, I have. I have represented buyers who have bought businesses with zero money down, giving a promissory note to the seller for the entire purchase price. But in 25 years, I've probably done it three times, and those times have all been when there's been some sort of personal relationship with the seller. Like it's a key employee who's buying the business, or something like that. All right. If you want to dig deeper into this, this is what I would do. I would go to LinkedIn. There's lots of talk on LinkedIn, Twitter as well. I put one guy up here, Samuil Jariwala. He's one of my very favorites. He has a fund called the FETA fund. But, he puts something up on LinkedIn almost every day that's geared towards Searchers. Like tips on how to make your Search good, how to evaluate businesses, things like that. Saumil is great. The other thing I would do is, I mean, you can network, you can talk to there's tons of people to talk to, and you can meet them online. So, meeting Saumil, following him is a great way to get started. There are books out there. That's my book [Here’s the Deal: Everything You Wish a Lawyer Would Tell You about Buying a Small Business]. That's a plug, but really, you don't need to read my book until you get close to a deal. The other two books are, “Buy Then Build” and the “Harvard Business Review: Buying a Small Business.” They're kind of like the Bibles of this ETA movement from a business perspective. My book complements them from a legal perspective. The other thing that you really should think about doing is, if you're really interested in this, go to one of these ETA conferences. There's one coming up at UVA in September. September 5-6th. There's a consortium between UVA University, North Carolina, Georgetown, and Duke University, and they put on this thing called the Southeast Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition conference. We've been to it twice now. It's really good. It's in the mid-Atlantic, and you're going to see, essentially, the people who come speak at these are kind of like circuit riders that you'll see a lot of the same, attorneys, investors, Searchers. If you are really serious about finding investors, these ETA conferences are a good place to network and connect with investors as well. And a lot of times, the investors will have dedicated rooms where you can sign up for a 20-minute consult and go in and talk to them. So you know, SEETA is probably the most accessible thing for us. Harvard is a huge one, Booth-Kellog up at the University of Chicago is massive. And yeah, I mean, if you're interested in learning more about this, they're usually two or three days long, and they have all these panels and opportunities for you to connect with people and things like that. So great stuff. All right, I'm done. I think. What questions can I answer for you? Yes. [Inaudible]. When you do the offer, the Letter of Intent, is there some sort of deposit? No, no, don't pay a deposit. I'm just telling you right now. If they tell you that they want to, if you're buying a business that's priced under $5,000,00, $5-$6 million and they're telling you they want a deposit, don't do it. It's a red flag. Will they take it off the market? Yes. So, there's a lot of what I would call creep into ETA lately, what I've observed over the last seven or eight years. Brokers who aren't experienced in buying and selling small businesses, they may be really well experienced in commercial real estate or residential real estate. They're coming into the space, and they're trying to bring those types of concepts into the space, but those, that doesn't work. I had a broker in Florida. He wanted not only a deposit, but a non-refundable deposit, and he wanted the Purchase Agreement drafted and approved within five days after signing the Letter of Intent. We didn't sign. We told him, he's crazy. We're not. Nobody's doing that, right? It is ridiculous! But what I see, I do see people starting to ask for deposits. I have a deal right now that I'm working on where they ask for a deposit. I told my client, don't do it, but he did it anyway. I told him, if you're going to do it, do it at about 10% of what they're asking for. He didn't. He did, he did it all. I don't know why, right? But no, if they're asking for deposit, that's a concept from a different type of transaction, and that's not the way we do it. So, it's a great question. They'll take it off, they should take it off the market. Brokers come in different flavors. Let's, talk about that. [Inaudible]. Yeah, the marketing expense. [Inaudible]. Yeah, well, but okay, so I'm going to argue back against that, because my guy is expending money as well. I hear the seller argument all the time. We're spending money, blah, blah, blah. My guy's spending a lot of money too. He's already spent a lot of money to get here. Hopefully you guys have vetted my guy well enough, or girl, so that that you're comfortable enough to move forward with the Letter of Intent. If you're not, if you think that the deal is not serious enough by the Letter of Intent phase, or they're not comfortable enough that you have to have money for a small deal. Now, a bigger deal is a different story, but a small deal is, you know, it's just not. The other reason, I see it done a lot more. And I'm going to speak, I'm going to tell you why I think you should get a deposit. That's because it is the wild, wild west, and so you're probably getting hundreds and hundreds of inquiries about businesses from people who are submitting, Searchers who are submitting, 100 inquiries to brokers every day. They've got a bot set up or something like that, and you're having to spend your time wading through all that, trying to figure out what's real, who's serious, who's got the resources to do it. And I feel you on that, because I'm getting those too. I'm getting people who want to talk to me for an hour, hour and a half, about they want to buy a business, but they don't have any money, and can I walk them through the process, and will I cut my fees and all that stuff? It's rough out there. [Inaudible]. Listing active? Yeah, and I'm cool with that. I mean, I'll ask for it to be delisted, but if you tell me, No, we're going to leave it up there, that's fine. And you can even take offers you just can't act on them. [Inaudible]. Yeah, some businesses have critical dependency on subcontractors, maybe key employees. And, you know, they could even be family related, so you can't be sure that they're going to stay in place. In some cases, you might want to acquire the subcontractor at the same time. Oh, that's interesting idea. How would you deal with a situation like that? Well, typically, I mean, absolutely, that's an issue in almost every transaction. Like, are we going to be able to transition the business in a way that we're not going to lose revenue, that we're not going to lose customers, things like that. And that, maybe, we might make it a contingency on Closing, that we get satisfactory employment agreements with the five key employees, or that we get the subcontractors to agree that they're going to stay on with us. But those discussions typically would happen just prior to Closing and would be a contingency to Closing so that if we didn't get those, we wouldn't close. So how do you ensure that you identify those dependencies? Yeah, that's going to happen during Due Diligence. I hope you know that's if you're a good searcher that it should be happening during Due Diligence. So, I want to go, can I go back to the broker real quickly? Only because there's another aspect that I think people should know about. You may ask for deposits, but you may also see buyers asking for what they call breakage fees. Are you seeing that now? Yeah, yeah. So that's a mid-market creep. So in mid-market deals, and we're talking deals like, you know, $20 to $50 million, it wouldn't be uncommon for a buyer to say, hey, if I find something during Due Diligence that you didn't tell me about, and I break the deal, you have to reimburse me for my legal fees, and my attorney, my CPA fees. And sometimes they may just put a number in, $15,000, $20,000, and so I have buyers now, when we're doing Letters of Intent, ask me if we can put a breakage fee in. And my advice is, don't. It's like asking for a deposit, like we just don't do it. And they say, “Well, I'm going to spend money.” Well, so is the seller. Everybody's going to carry their own water until we get this deal done. You know, that's just, we have to kind of trust each other. If we don't, that's not a great way to start out. What is the maximum amount of an SBA loan? Well, it depends. Yeah, it depends. If you're going to get a loan from the SBA under the SBA 7A program, $5 million is the limit. That's as much as you're going to get. That doesn't mean that the purchase price has to be $5 million or less, it just means you're going to get $5 million. So, if you can come up with the other I mean, I'm about to help somebody buy a company for six and a half million, and the five is going to come from the SBA, but the other one and a half is going to come from seller financing, from investors, and from their own cash. Just one quick question. I think it kind of piggybacks on the last. Can you just characterize some of the businesses that you have helped people buy? Like, what are the types of businesses that people are buying? That's a great question, but it's really just about anything. So trades are really popular, right? Like plumbing businesses, landscaping, roofing, gutter businesses. They're real popular right now, although some are kind of going out of favor. You should ask the broker too. But landscaping, people are kind of soured on landscaping businesses and HVAC too, a little bit as well. I've helped people buy and sell wellness businesses, like yoga, coaching businesses, I helped somebody sell a YouTube channel, manufacturing businesses, small manufacturing businesses, like specialty automotive parts, healthcare businesses, dentist office, podiatrist, veterinaries, veterinarians. I'm just trying to think marketing businesses, online marketing agencies, brick and mortar marketing agencies. I mean, as I keep thinking, I can keep going, but I'm running out of time. Okay. I'll stick around if anybody wants to talk afterwards. Thank you very much.

metadata.title: Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition 101
metadata.author: The Wall Street Skinny
metadata.shortDescription:
Join us as we dive deep into the world of Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) with our guest, Jesse Safir, President of ABG Print. In this episode, finance enthusiasts and budding entrepreneurs will find a treasure trove of insights about search funds, self-funded searches, and the nitty-gritty of buying and operating a small business. Jesse shares his journey from being an investment analyst to becoming the President of a printing company, shedding light on the decision-making process, the importance of due diligence, and the challenges encountered along the way.

Discover the intricacies of financing acquisitions, including the roles of bank debt, seller debt, and SBA loans in structuring deals. Jesse's firsthand experience with navigating these financial tools provides a practical guide for anyone looking to understand the financial frameworks that support entrepreneurship through acquisition. He explains the nuances of asset versus stock purchase deals and the critical considerations for evaluating a business's financial health and growth potential.

Financial listeners will also hear about the impact of external market shocks, like the COVID-19 pandemic, on small businesses and the strategies employed to navigate these turbulent times. Jesse offers a candid look at operational pivots, cash conservation techniques, and the resilience required to not only survive but thrive through unprecedented challenges. This episode is a must-listen for anyone interested in the intersection of finance and entrepreneurship, offering a masterclass in business acquisition, management, and recovery.

Follow Jesse on LinkedIn here:  https://www.linkedin.com/in/jessesafir/

Follow ABG Print on LinkedIn here: https://www.linkedin.com/company/abgprint/

metadata.title: Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition: The Smarter Way to Become a CEO?
metadata.author: The Explainer USA - Business & Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
What is ETA, also known as Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition?

In this video, we explain the ETA model in simple words and break down why many entrepreneurs are choosing to buy an existing business instead of starting a new company from zero.

Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition is a business strategy where an entrepreneur searches for, buys, manages, and grows an existing company. Instead of building a startup from scratch, ETA allows a person to acquire a business that already has customers, revenue, employees, operations, and market presence.

But how does ETA actually work?

Why are investors, MBA graduates, entrepreneurs, and future CEOs interested in this model?

And is buying a small business really better than launching a startup?

In this explainer video, we cover the full concept of Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition, including search funds, acquisition entrepreneurship, business buying, small business ownership, private equity-style investing, and the risks and opportunities of becoming an entrepreneur by acquisition.

This video is useful for anyone interested in business, finance, startups, entrepreneurship, investing, management, search funds, acquisitions, mergers and acquisitions, and business ownership.

Why investors like ETA

I went on a platform called Flipper, which is basically a marketplace for buying and selling online businesses. And there I started looking around. I found some interesting businesses. And when I did so, I scheduled calls with the sellers. My plan was not necessarily to buy a business immediately. I just wanted to find out how the processes work. Besides that, I also consumed a ton of content online mainly from Cody Sanchez who is a YouTuber very big in this space and offline mainly from reading books. Cody Sanchez herself has published a book which is really good which I can really recommend. It's called Main Street Millionaire. Over time I also signed up for an M&A newsletter and I always get notifications once a local business is up for sale. And here's the truth. I deeply believe if you only do those little steps, then you get ahead of lots and lots of people and you understand ETA better than most people do. But enough from me. Let's talk about you. Now, if you are starting in ETA, these are the steps you can take right now. First, educate yourself. Consume content from people like Cody Sanchez or also from me. Read and listen to case studies and learn how deals are structured. Knowledge actually compounds. Second, browse marketplaces. There are websites like Flippa or Bis by Cell which is a bit more American or also just other M&A websites. Even if you don't want to buy a business right away, it's really helpful to see what's out there. Third, talk to sellers. Don't be afraid to schedule a call with them. You'll learn the language. you'll learn to negotiate with them and also you understand what their motivations are for the sale. Fourth and really important, join newsletters. Many brokers have mailing lists and there you can see once a new business is up for sale. And fifth is obviously networking. Go to business events. Get to know people who are in the ETA space, especially because lots of deals are going through word of mouth. None of these steps cost you much, but they'll position you as someone who's already in the game. Entrepreneurship through acquisition is not for everyone. But if you want to create wealth, if you want to own a business, and if you don't really want to reinvent the wheel, then ETA is probably the best thing you can do right now. You don't have to have it all figured out today. Start small, educate yourself, browse deals, talk to sellers, build relationships, and so on and so forth. And that's exactly what I did half a year ago and it has already opened me a bunch of doors. For example, I already have one deal in due diligence. So the choice is yours. Either you build something from scratch and potentially waste years of doing this or you buy an existing system and you build upon that. If you want to see more about my ETA journey and how you can start yours, hit subscribe.

metadata.title: INSEAD Explains Entrepreneurship: Becoming an Entrepreneur by Acquisition
metadata.author: INSEAD
metadata.shortDescription:
Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) presents a compelling proposition for those who want to lead a business with a foundation already in place, says Ivana Naumovska, Associate Professor of Entrepreneurship and Family Enterprise at INSEAD, in this episode of INSEAD Explains Entrepreneurship*. 

Contrary to the conventional wisdom that high returns can only be born from high risk, search fund investments have both lower risk and higher returns compared to venture capital, according to recent research. The question then is how to get there. 

When entrepreneurs step into businesses with proven demand, as well as an established business model, cash flow and operations, the challenge shifts from survival to operational excellence, innovation and growth. 

Naumovska highlights three main ETA approaches and discusses what it takes to succeed as an entrepreneur through acquisition.

Chapters:
00:00 - Why is entrepreneurship so important today?
00:53 - How does entrepreneurship through acquisition differ from traditional entrepreneurship?
02:00 - What are the top entrepreneurship through acquisition approaches?
04:11 - What does it take to succeed as an entrepreneur through acquisition?
07:07 - How do search funds compare with venture capital investments?

*See all episodes of INSEAD Explain Entrepreneurship on INSEAD Knowledge here: https://knowledge.insead.edu/insead-explains-entrepreneurship

metadata.title: Navigating Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition | Ep. 43 Part 1 | Before You Buy or Sell a Business
metadata.author: Before You Buy or Sell a Business Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
In this two-part episode of the @beforeyoubuyorsellabusiness I sit down with my borrowers, Peter Hucal and Garrett Johnson, two dynamic entrepreneurs from Wharton who embarked on a journey of Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA). 

Their diverse backgrounds across engineering, project management, social impact, and consultancy have uniquely positioned them for success in the acquisition space. Tune in as they share authentic insights into their professional path and elaborate on the intricacies of navigating such an acquisition in today's market.

Embarking upon a 13-month journey, Peter and Garrett discuss their extensive search for the right business, sharing the trials, errors, and eventual triumphs they encountered along the way. By focusing on core business fundamentals rather than specific industries, they outline how their open mindset towards geographical and sector-based opportunities guided their success. Alongside key strategies for maintaining broker relationships and insights on necessary interpersonal skills, the duo candidly dissects the realities of acquisition, dispelling myths of ease perpetuated by various online narratives.

Stay tuned for part two of this episode for what business Peter and Garrett settled on and the strategic partners they sought out.

Episode Highlights
✅Adopting a flexible strategy in ETA, being open to any industry or geography, can enhance the success rate.
✅Building strong relationships with brokers is crucial and can lead to greater success in finding suitable deals.
✅The process of finding and acquiring a business is complex and often requires resilience in face of numerous setbacks.

metadata.shortDescription:
Jared Johnson takes a different seat in this episode as he gets interviewed and answers real questions from buyers and sellers about entrepreneurship through acquisition. The conversation cuts straight through the hype and focuses on what it actually takes to buy and run a business.

Jared explains why ETA has become so popular in recent years and why much of what people see online does not match reality. He talks through what lenders are really looking for, including experience, liquidity, and consistent cash flow, and why those factors matter so much when getting a deal approved.

The episode also covers the most common reasons deals fall apart. Jared walks through red flags like inconsistent financials, customer concentration, and buyers trying to operate businesses remotely. He shares where buyers go wrong, especially when they skip due diligence, rush into deals, or rely too heavily on brokers and sellers without verifying the numbers.

There is also a personal story from Jared’s first acquisition that shows how expensive mistakes can be when diligence is limited. It is a clear reminder that even deals that look solid on the surface can carry real risk.
This is a practical, honest look at ETA for anyone considering buying a business or currently in the process.

Main Takeaways:
- ETA is real, but it is much harder than it is often presented online
- You cannot treat buying a business like passive income, it requires real involvement
- Lenders focus heavily on buyer experience, available cash, and stable cash flow
- Deals often fail early due to weak financials or lack of buyer preparation
- Customer concentration and inconsistent revenue create major risk
- Skipping due diligence or hiring the wrong advisors can be costly mistakes
- Asking why the seller is selling can reveal important issues
- The best deals match the buyer’s experience with the business they are buying
- Investors can help, but not all investor relationships are good ones
- Patience matters, buying the wrong business is worse than waiting

metadata.title: SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: The New Rules for Buying a Business (Effective Oct 1, 2026)
metadata.author: Pioneer Capital Advisory LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
On August 26 I sat down with Chris Barrett of Midwest CPA and went through SOP 50 10 8.1 the way we'd go through a live deal. It takes effect October 1, 2026, and it reshapes how nearly every 7(a) business acquisition gets structured.

The headline items: a dedicated Appendix 15 now governs every change of ownership, quality of earnings becomes mandatory at $3MM and up, the minimum DSCR moves off a single 1.15x to category-specific floors starting at 1.25x, and the 51% real estate shortcut is gone in favor of a blended amortization formula.

We walk through the four transaction categories and how a lender documents its way into the favorable one. We get into what actually counts toward your 10% equity injection now that sourcing rules tightened, what an outside investor gives up to qualify as non-controlling, and the new cap on total debt against the business valuation.

Chris covers the QoE change from the CPA side, including the part that caught a lot of people flat-footed: the buyer is no longer the client of the report.

About 20 minutes of this is live Q&A from the 132 people on the call, so if you're mid-deal right now, the back half is probably the useful half.

CHAPTERS

0:00 Intro
0:05 Welcome: why SOP 50 10 8.1 matters
0:41 Who we are
3:48 What we're covering
4:03 Why 8.1 is more than a technical update
5:19 The four transaction categories
6:30 DSCR moves from 1.15x to 1.25x
7:41 Seller transition goes from 12 to 24 months
10:17 Initial acquisition: the default lane
11:50 Business expansion: the five tests
17:42 Owner buyouts and partial changes of ownership
21:19 Quality of earnings becomes mandatory at $3MM
21:40 The buyer is no longer the QoE client
30:56 Q&A: do deal costs count toward the injection?
34:54 Equity injection and the new 5% sourcing rule
36:37 Worked example: a $4MM acquisition
39:03 Outside investors: what qualifies and what it costs
42:35 Profit vs tax-only distributions
45:09 The 51% real estate rule is gone
46:23 Term and blended amortization, old vs new
49:43 The new cap on total debt
52:16 Seller transition and consulting agreements
53:23 Seller note refinance
57:03 Closing Q&A
59:44 Wrap up

WHO'S TALKING

Matthias Smith, Founder and President of Pioneer Capital Advisory, a commercial loan brokerage in Madison, Wisconsin. We've worked with 150+ buyers on more than $340 million of acquisitions since 2022. On SBA deals the bank pays us after closing, so there's no cost to the buyer.
matthias@pioneercap.com
pioneercapitaladvisory.com

Chris Barrett, CPA, Managing Director and Owner of Midwest CPA in Janesville, Wisconsin. Midwest CPA works with acquisition entrepreneurs on quality of earnings and post-close accounting and tax.
chris@midwest.cpa
midwest.cpa

Send us the deal and we'll tell you which lane it's in, what the QoE and equity stack look like, and whether the DSCR works, before you spend money on diligence.

DISCLAIMER

This webinar summarizes SOP 50 10 8 (effective June 1, 2025) and SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective October 1, 2026). It is not a substitute for the controlling SOP, 13 CFR Part 120, or any lender's credit policy. Confirm transaction-specific eligibility against the governing requirements. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.
