metadata.title: The New SBA Rules are LIVE: How to Plan Business Acquisition in 2026
metadata.author: Matthias Smith
metadata.shortDescription:
The SBA’s new 7(a) loan rules are now in effect. If you’re planning to buy a business in the next 12 months, these changes could affect your down payment, qualifying cash flow, due diligence costs, loan structure, and closing timeline.

In this video, Matthias Smith of Pioneer Capital Advisory breaks down the new SBA acquisition guidelines and explains how business buyers can plan ahead, evaluate deals, and prepare for financing under the updated rules.

In this video, we cover:
• The four SBA acquisition categories and what they mean for buyers
• How the 10% minimum equity injection works under the new rules
• A real-dollar example of the cash needed to purchase a $3 million business
• Why the debt service coverage requirement increased from 1.15x to 1.25x
• New Quality of Earnings requirements for deals of $3 million and above
• What independent valuations mean for purchase prices and equity requirements
• How changes to real estate financing can affect loan terms and payments
• Why business expansion and add-on acquisitions may have an advantage
• Practical steps to take before signing a Letter of Intent (LOI)

Planning a business acquisition? Start by pressure-testing the company’s historical cash flow, understanding your available equity, and building additional diligence costs and time into your plan.

📊 Get the free guide comparing the old and new SBA rules: https://www.pioneercapitaladvisory.com/sba-sop-50-10-8-1-vs-50-10-8-acquisition-rules
📅 Schedule a call with Pioneer Capital Advisory: https://www.pioneercapitaladvisory.com/contact 
▶️ Watch our webinar on the new SBA guidelines: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WF2-6ODNQms

Pioneer Capital Advisory helps business buyers navigate acquisition financing, evaluate lending options, and move from LOI to closing with a clear financing strategy.

This video is for educational purposes only. SBA lending requirements and lender underwriting criteria may vary. Consult qualified advisors regarding your specific transaction.

How to buy a business with an SBA loan, with real math: the 10% equity injection on the whole project, how a seller note on full standby can cover half of it, and what the monthly payment looks like. SBA 7(a) loan rules explained for 2026 (SOP 50 10 8.1, effective October 1, 2026).

Example: a $1 million business plus $150,000 of working capital and costs is a $1.15 million project. 10% is $115,000; a seller note on full standby can cover up to half, so the buyer brings about $57,500 in cash. We also cover the personal guarantee, the new rule for veteran buyers, and why clean books decide whether an SBA deal closes.

metadata.title: SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: What Changed for Business Acquisitions, and What Didn’t
metadata.author: Lion Business Advisors
metadata.shortDescription:
SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 is effective October 1, 2026. For some SBA 7(a)-financed business acquisitions, it adds more defined financial diligence. It does not change every business sale or mean an owner-operated business is no longer financeable.

In this episode of The Texas Business Broker Podcast, Josh Carnes and guest:

- Which acquisitions are covered by Appendix 15
- Why the $3 million quality of earnings (QoE) threshold is based on the business purchase price, not the SBA loan amount
- What cash proof and verified add-backs mean for a seller’s financial records
- How buyer equity, seller financing, 7(a) Small, and SBA Express fit into the updated rules
- When a seller may consult with the buyer for up to 24 months after closing

For sellers, the practical question is whether a buyer’s financing plan is supported by verifiable earnings and a workable ownership transition.

SBA sources:
SOP 50 10 8.1: https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs
September 25 technical update: https://www.sba.gov/document/information-notice-5000-882227-issuance-technical-updates-sop-50-10-81

This episode features AI-generated hosts and voices discussing the SBA’s published guidance. It is an educational conversation, not a recorded interview with an acquisition lender.

segments.text: Two reactions to the October SBA lending
update are making the rounds. One is
every business sale now needs a quality
of earnings report.
The other is no more seller financing to
bridge valuation gaps. Neither helps an
owner evaluate an offer that depends on
SBA financing. The useful questions are
what type of transaction is this? What's
the business purchase price? and will
the earnings a lender can verify support
the debt? Let's break down what the SBA
actually changed. Welcome to the Texas
Business Broker. I am your host, Josh
KS. Today we look at the decisions
behind a business sale, value, buyer
selection, financing, diligence, and
getting from an offer to a closing.
Today we're discussing the latest SBA
updates and its effect on business
acquisitions. And let's separate what
the SBA actually wrote from what a
particular bank may choose to require in
its own underwriting.
>> A seller shouldn't hear new SOP and
assume the market shut down. At the same
time, someone with an SBA dependent deal
should understand the new diligence
before promising a closing date. The
focus today is appendix 15, which
addresses 7A, changes of ownership.
We'll explain the rules and the seller
decisions that follow from them.
Specific transactions still have to be
assessed by the buyer's lender and deal
advisers. Start with the date. What did
October 1st mean and what do sellers
misunderstand about it?
>> The SBA issued an updated version of SOP
510 with an October 1st, 2026 effective
date. Its September 25 information
notice says this version applies to
applications received by SBA on or after
October 1, while applications submitted
through September 30 continue under
SOP8. This updated SOP supersedes the
earlier published 8.1 version. And the
September notice uses a different
effective date description from the
August notice, a listing date, an LOI
date, or the day a buyer first calls a
bank does not decide which instructions
apply. The lender needs to confirm the
actual application status.
>> So, if a seller signed an LOI in
September, saying we're grandfathered
in, would be a pretty dangerous
assumption.
Yes, rushing an incomplete financing
package to meet a calendar date can
create its own problems. The lender
still needs a financable transaction and
a complete credit case. For a deal
already moving, the seller and buyer
should ask which SOP the lender is
applying and whether any open conditions
changed the timet.
>> What else should we understand about
this release? Some people talk as if
every provision was invented on October
1st.
>> It wasn't. The SBA notice says 8.1
builds on 8.0, incorporates earlier
policy and procedural notices and places
change of ownership lending in appendix
15. Business valuation, tax
verification, equity, and debt service
analysis were already part of SBA
acquisition lending. There are
meaningful new or revised instructions,
including the specified quality of
earnings requirement, but SBA lenders
just started looking at the financials
would be false.
>> Let's draw the boundary. An owner
operated business in Texas might attract
an SBA buyer, a conventional borrower,
or a strategic acquirer. Who should pay
close attention? Anyone structuring a
change of ownership with 7A financing
should pay attention to appendix 15. It
covers more than a first-time buyer
purchasing a company outright. The SOP
distinguishes an initial acquisition, a
business expansion, an owner buyout, and
an ESOP or cooperative transaction.
Those categories can carry different
rules. The general QoE requirement is
narrower. It applies to initial
acquisitions and business expansions
when the defined business purchase price
is $3 million or more. Owner buyouts and
ESOP or cooperative transactions are
excluded from that mandatory QoE
provision. The technical updates also
include a narrow exception for an
acquisition involving an owner occupied
special purpose property. None of those
exceptions removes the rest of the
lender's financial diligence.
>> Here's the practical version for an
owner. If your likely buyer is a
firsttime operator with SBA financing,
you want to understand this. Now, if a
strategic buyer is paying with its
balance sheet and a conventional credit
facility, appendix 15 doesn't govern
that financing. The strategic buyer may
still order its own QOE, of course, for
different reasons,
>> right? Also, a sale price over $5
million does not automatically mean SBA
is impossible. A standard 7A loan has a
$5 million loan limit, which is a loan
limit, not a universal cap on the total
transaction value. It depends on the
rest of the capital structure and
eligibility. But SBA is usually more
relevant to the smaller end of the
market than to a larger lower middle
market transaction funded without SBA
support.
>> And a small purchase price doesn't mean
no rules. It means we should stop
confusing the broad appendix 15
requirements with this one $3 million QE
trigger. Exactly. The appendix calls for
financial due diligence on all seven of
changes of ownership. The threshold
decides whether that due diligence must
include the specified independent QOE
for the two categories we just
discussed.
>> Why did SBA put this into appendix 15?
Are we supposed to read the move itself
as a warning about acquisitions?
>> The published notice says change of
ownership guidance is now in appendix
15. The practical benefit is having one
place that defines transaction types and
lays out the valuation, diligence,
equity, and credit analysis that go with
them. Appendix 15 also says its rules
govern a change of ownership if another
part of the SOP conflicts with it. That
matters when someone finds a more
general 7A rule and assumes it overrides
the acquisition specific one.
>> Give me a real world category
distinction.
>> A buyer who's never owned or worked in
the target is generally an initial
acquisition. An existing operating
business buying another company in the
same four-digit NAICS industry group
with the other qualifying conditions met
may be a business expansion. A remaining
partner buying out an owner is an owner
buyout. You can't simply call a first
time acquisition an expansion because
the buyer would prefer the expansion
rules. The lender has to document the
right category.
>> That's a good warning for brokers, too.
Deal labels in a teaser or LOI aren't
the lender's eligibility decision.
Before we talk about a clever structure,
we'd better know how the bank will
classify it.
>> And ask early. The category affects much
more than which form goes in a file.
>> Here's the point that will matter to a
lot of sellers. The $3 million threshold
is not simply the SBA loan amount. Walk
us through it.
>> Appendix 15 uses the business purchase
price. For this purpose, you start with
the price in the purchase and sale
agreement and remove the appraised value
of any owner occupied commercial real
estate included in the acquisition. The
threshold is tested before buyer equity,
seller debt, or other financing sources
reduce the requested 7A loan. It is also
separate from total project costs, which
can include working capital and other
uses.
>> Let's make up a clean example with an
ordinary office or shop building, not a
specialurpose property. The contract
price is $4.2 million, including the
building appraised at $1 million. The
business component is $3.2 million. Say
the buyer puts in equity and requests a
$2.7 million 7A loan. Is that above the
QE line?
>> For a qualifying initial acquisition or
business expansion, generally yes. The
business purchase price in that example
is $3.2 million. The smaller loan
request does not move it below the $3
million threshold. The lender would
generally need both a business valuation
and a QE. One technical exception
involves acquisition of an owner
occupied special purpose property where
the updated SOP says a QE is not
required even above the threshold.
That's a defined limited category, not
an exception for every transaction that
includes real estate.
>> Reverse it. If the business purchase
price is $2.8 $8 million, but the
overall project is more than $3 million
after working capital and other costs.
Does crossing $3 million in total
project costs alone require this
particular QE?
>> No, not from this specific threshold.
The lender still performs financial
diligence and may independently require
deeper work based on the deal's risks or
its own policy. That's the distinction
between SBA requires a QE under this
paragraph and the lender wants one
>> and exactly $3 million counts. The
language says equal to or greater than
>> correct exactly $3 million is in another
nuance. An owner buyout or ESOP or
cooperative transaction isn't subject to
this particular mandatory QoE provision.
Even when its price crosses $3 million,
it still has its own underwriting and
valuation requirements. Who can
commission a QoE that the lender will
actually use? An owner might say, "I'll
order one myself and give every buyer
the PDF." A seller can organize records,
reconcile the books, and have an
accountant do preparatory work. That may
expose issues early, but a QoE prepared
by or for the seller cannot satisfy the
SOP. The report must be performed by an
independent, experienced financial
professional for the lender's benefit.
There is a useful distinction in the
September technical updates. If the
buyer commissioned an independent QoE
for its own diligence before engaging
the bank, the lender may use that report
after an approved vendor reviews it and
the lender retains both reports. The
lender cannot simply rely on another
party's report without that review.
Costs can be passed to the borrower and
certain applicant spending on financial
due diligence can count toward the
required equity injection subject to
lender treatment. How early should the
possibility of a QOE be identified at
listing, at LOI, or once underwriting is
underway?
>> Identify the trigger while you're
assessing financing before people build
a closing calendar around assumptions.
Discuss record availability and scope
before or during LOI diligence. Under
delegated PLP processing, appendix 15
allows the valuation and applicable QOE
to finish after the SBA loan number is
issued and before closing, but they must
already be formally engaged when that
number is issued. The lender then
updates its credit analysis for the
actual findings. That's a scheduling
rule, not permission to treat the result
as a formality.
>> One phrase owners may hear for the first
time is cash proof. What does that mean
in ordinary language? It's a required
part of the specified QOE. The analyst
reconstructs cash coming in and cash
going out and reconciles bank statement
activity to the income statement and tax
return. The SOP calls for work over the
trailing 12 months and the last two
fiscal years. If the acquired business
has operated for less than 2 years, the
updated SOP allows the scope to be
reduced to its operating history. The
purpose is to identify differences in
reported revenue or expenses. A seller
needs to explain why bank deposits, book
revenue, and taxable income may not line
up neatly
>> in a trades company. That might be
several operating accounts, merchant
processor deposits, loan proceeds that
are not revenue, owner transfers,
customer deposits, maybe payroll running
through a separate account. A mismatch
on day one isn't automatically a
scandal. But saying my accountant has
the taxes doesn't give the analyst a
bridge from bank cash to the P and L.
>> Exactly. Timing differences and
legitimate accounting treatments exist.
The point is to document them. A bank
deposit may include sales tax collected
for the state, an intercomp transfer, or
a draw on a credit line. A sale booked
in December may be collected in January.
The analyst has to separate those from
operating revenue and show the tie out.
If nobody can explain material
differences, the lender has to
underwrite what it can support, and that
can delay or change the transaction.
>> What should an owner get together before
a buyer applies? Give me a usable list,
not clean up your books. Three years of
business tax returns and the underlying
annual financials. Recent monthly profit
and loss and balance sheets with a
comparative prior year period. Bank
statements for all operating and deposit
accounts covering the two fiscal years
and trailing 12 months. General ledger
detail, payroll and owner compensation
records, debt schedule, and a list of
proposed adjustments with invoices or
other backup. Also, make sure the
accountant can explain differences
between tax basis, cash basis, and
acrruel basis reporting. The exact
request list depends on the lender and
the business. The key is being able to
trace major numbers, not creating a
polished folder full of unreconciled
spreadsheets.
>> A practical owner point, do this under a
controlled process with your CPA and
advisor. You don't need to broadcast raw
account level data to every person who
expresses interest. But once you've
selected a credible buyer and lender,
the records have to exist and be
available securely. Let's talk about the
earnings number. Sellers often hear a
broker say, "We'll add that back." Then
the lender's analysis is lower. What
happens if an adback can't be verified?
>> It may not be included in the earnings
used for underwriting. The SOP requires
the QoE to identify and document
adjustments, including non-recurring
items, owner compensation above or below
market, related party transactions,
deferred maintenance, and cash versus
acrruel differences. It separately
requires the lender to justify its own
cash flow adjustments. An expense isn't
an adback merely because the owner calls
it personal. The questions are, was it
actually incurred? Will it disappear
after the sale? Will the buyer need to
replace it with another cost? Is there a
record to support the amount?
>> Take a founder HVAC company. The owner
runs sales relationships, oversees the
service managers, and pays himself
He says the new owner can add that all
back. If the buyer isn't going to
perform that work, there may be a real
replacement salary. The historical
owner's pay was cash out, but the
ongoing business still needs somebody
accountable for those functions.
>> That's the right question. A buyer may
personally take over some tasks, but the
lender has to assess management capacity
and what that owner will need to live
on. An adjusted earnings figure has to
make economic sense after closing.
Similarly, a one-time legal bill may be
a valid adjustment if it really is
non-recurring and documented. Deferred
maintenance isn't free cash flow just
because it wasn't paid last year. A
buyer might need to fund it.
>> Let's put numbers around debt coverage
without pretending every deal has the
same math. Suppose the proposed

metadata.title: The SBA Does It Again: More Changes to the New SBA SOP
metadata.author: Commercial Lending X
metadata.shortDescription:
Just days before the new SBA SOP takes effect, the SBA released another round of updates—and many of the changes are good news for business buyers.

In this video, Brad Hettich, Founder & President of Commercial Lending X, breaks down the most important Technical Updates to SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 and what they could mean for SBA-financed transactions beginning October 1, 2026.

Brad covers key changes affecting business acquisitions, employee buyouts, Quality of Earnings reports, working capital, loan amortization, SBA 7(a) and Express loans, SBA 504 financing, special-use properties, equity injections, and more.

If you’re buying a business or considering SBA financing and want to understand how the new rules could affect your transaction, reach out to Commercial Lending X to discuss your financing options.

#SBALoans #SBA7a #SBA504 #BusinessAcquisition #CommercialLendingX

Understanding Seller Notes in SBA Loans is critical if you’re buying or selling a business using SBA 7(a) financing. In this video, we break down the official SBA rules for seller financing, how standby periods work, and what lenders look for when structuring deals.

✅ Learn how to use seller notes to reduce your equity injection
✅ Find out when seller notes can count toward your down payment
✅ Avoid the most common SBA compliance mistakes that delay approvals
✅ Understand the latest 2025 SBA loan rule updates affecting seller financing

Whether you’re a buyer, seller, or business broker, this video gives you the insider knowledge to structure your SBA deal the right way and get approved faster.

metadata.title: What a Perfect Business Acquisition Application Looks Like | SBA Loans
metadata.author: SBA University
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to SBA University! 🎓
I’m Glenn Giro, and in this episode, we’re breaking down what a perfect SBA 7(a) loan application for a business acquisition looks like—so you can aim high and get as close as possible to checking all the right boxes. You don’t need to be perfect to get approved, but knowing what makes a strong application can put you in the best position for success.

Here’s what you’ll learn:
1️⃣ Cash Flow & Trends – Why year-over-year growth in revenue and profitability is key—and what to watch for in financials.
2️⃣ Industry & Management Experience – How your background plays a role and what makes experience “applicable” to lenders.
3️⃣ Credit Profile – What lenders are looking for in your credit history (and why it goes beyond just your score).
4️⃣ Equity Injection – Understanding the down payment range (from 5% to 20%) and how seller financing fits in.
5️⃣ Collateral Strength – From business assets to your personal property, how collateral factors into SBA approval.

I’ll walk you through each of these five categories so you know what lenders love to see—and how to improve your chances of approval.

💡 Questions? Drop them in the comments! I’d love to help.
📝 Don’t forget to subscribe to SBA University for more weekly lessons to simplify SBA lending.

👉 Contact me directly: ggiro@tbank.com
👉 Subscribe for more insights!

metadata.title: New SBA Rules 2027: What Changed for Buying a Business
metadata.author: Michael S Glaspie
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying or selling a business? 

We can stress-test your numbers, show whether a lender will support the purchase, and estimate what a buyer might pay on exit: 

https://www.g2businesssolutions.com/calendar

As of October 1, 2026, the SBA rewrote where your down payment can come from, who's allowed to own the business, and what happens if the seller wants to stay. In this video I walk through exactly what changed under SOP 50 10 8.1, what it means for you at closing, and the tax side of year one that most buyers never plan for.

CHAPTERS
00:00 - 00:40 The SBA rules just changed
00:40 - 01:10 When the new rules apply
01:10 - 01:43 The 10% equity injection
01:43 - 02:52 How seller financing used to work
02:52 - 04:07 New cap on seller notes and minority investors
04:07 - 05:07 Partial buyouts: if the seller keeps a stake
05:07 - 05:51 Buying control means the seller exits
05:51 - 06:25 Why this matters as owners retire
06:25 - 06:59 Who can own it: the citizenship rule
06:59 - 07:46 The tax side: equipment and bonus depreciation
07:46 - 08:59 Goodwill: amortized over 15 years
08:59 - 10:07 Where SBA buyers get hurt: cash flow
10:07 - 10:40 Buying or selling? We can help

#SBALoan #BuyingABusiness #SmallBusiness

metadata.title: SBA Loan Changes 2026: What Business Sellers Need to Know
metadata.author: Ed Weeks Jr. MBA
metadata.shortDescription:
The SBA loan changes that took effect October 1, 2026 (SOP 50 10 8.1) change how much an SBA buyer can borrow to buy your business. For a buyer taking over a company for the first time, lenders now need 1.25x debt service coverage on your actual history, not the buyer's projections, and a purchase price of $3 million or more needs an independent quality of earnings report.

The lender measures that coverage on your last fiscal year or the average of your last two. A seller note only counts toward the buyer's down payment if it sits on full standby, with no principal or interest paid for the life of the SBA loan. I explain what that means for owners of established companies, how the Fed's September 16 rate hike fits in, and five things to get on paper before you talk price. I call it paper before price.

Chapters:
0:00 What changed
0:29 Three changes
1:41 Why they matter
2:35 Five things to do
3:16 Paper before price

If you want to see where your company stands today, take the Business Optionality Assessment. It takes about 3 minutes: https://edweeksjr.com/assessment/

https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs

segments.text: A company can report record profits and
still be worth far less than it appears.
The difference often hides inside a
quality of earnings analysis.
A quality of earnings review is not just
an accounting exercise. It asks a more
practical question. How much of the
company's reported profit is real,
repeatable, and transferable to a new
owner?
Quality of earnings, often shortened to
QOE, tests the reliability of profit. A
company may show strong earnings because
of a temporary contract, aggressive
timing, or unusual savings, and the
analysis brings those effects into the
open.
A strong review answers five core
questions.
It checks whether profits can continue,
whether proposed adjustments deserve
credit, and whether revenue, costs, and
risks support the valuation being
discussed. Normalization means removing
distortions from the past, so the
numbers better represent a normal
operating period. For example, a
one-time legal settlement may be
removed, but an ongoing maintenance cost
should remain. Typical adjustments
include owner pay that will change after
a sale, isolated legal costs, and
restructuring charges.
But analysts also look for the reverse
problem. Costs that management left out,
even though the buyer will continue
paying them. Now, we move beneath the
headline profit number. The most
important work is testing whether
revenue quality and cost behavior can
support the earnings being presented.
Revenue analysis goes well beyond the
total sales figure. You want to know
whether a few customers drive the
result, whether customers stay, whether
growth comes from price or volume, and
whether reported sales landed in the
correct period. Looking across roughly
three to five years helps separate a
trend from a lucky period. It also shows
how the business performed through
different customer cycles, cost levels,
and operating conditions.
On the cost side, determine which
expenses move with revenue and which
stay fixed.
Then look for owner-related pay, vendor
changes, missing costs, or future
pressures that could make the current
margin look better than it really is.
A buyer can agree on sustainable
earnings and still face a bad deal if
debt, working capital, or hidden
obligations are misunderstood.
This chapter connects operating
performance to transaction mechanics.
Net debt is not limited to the obvious
bank loan.
Leases, accrued interest, seller
obligations, and unfunded commitments
may also reduce the value delivered to
equity holders, depending on the deal
definition.
A debt-like item may sit outside
traditional borrowings, but still
represent a cash claim on the business.
The key question is whether the buyer
will effectively fund it after closing.
Picture the diligence room. One person
traces revenue to contracts, another
challenges an add-back, and a third
reconciles the balance sheet.
The best conclusions come from
connecting management explanations to
independent evidence.
The final stage is about communication.
A quality of earnings report should make
the earnings bridge clear, show the
risks, and explain exactly how the
findings affect price or deal
protections.
These warning signs deserve immediate
follow-up. A sudden customer spike,
aggressive cut-off, or unsupported
add-back can make earnings look
stronger, while missing recurring
expenses can quietly inflate margins.
In an interview, organize your answer
around the earnings base, the evidence
behind adjustments, revenue quality,
working capital, and valuation impact.
That structure shows commercial judgment
instead of just accounting vocabulary.
Once you can separate repeatable
earnings from temporary noise, deals,
valuations, and interview cases become
much easier.
Follow Candy Mentor for more finance
concepts made clear.
Thank you for watching. Please like and
subscribe for more content.

metadata.title: Qualifying EBITDA Add-Backs - Separating Fact From Fiction | Masterclass
metadata.author: growthink
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re prepping for a sale, buying a company, or just EBITDA-curious, this session breaks down EBITDA add-backs (aka adjustments): what qualifies, what gets rejected, and how buyers, PE firms, and QoE providers treat them in diligence. We define EBITDA vs Adjusted EBITDA, show how owner discretionary expenses, one-time or non-recurring costs, rent normalization, and above-market owner compensation roll up into a defensible Adjusted EBITDA, and how that can move enterprise value dollar-for-dollar at deal multiples. We cover Quality of Earnings (QoE), working capital, LOI structures tied to post-QoE EBITDA, financial vs strategic buyer perspectives, and the line between add-backs and synergies. Real-world examples show what the market will and will not accept, how to document and track adjustments monthly, and why clean, conservative, well-evidenced add-backs protect valuation and deal certainty.

What you’ll learn
- Definitions: EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA (AEBITDA), add-backs/adjustments
- Common categories: non-recurring, non-operational, owner discretionary, rent normalization, above-market compensation, services-for-equity
- Market reality: which add-backs pass, which need strong defense, which die in QoE
-QoE 101: what firms test (revenue quality, retention, concentration, working capital, sustainability)
- Buyer lens: financial vs strategic; add-backs vs synergies; impact on debt sizing and covenants
- How to bake Adjusted EBITDA into your model and avoid retrades
- Case studies across multiple industries

Why it matters:
At a 6x multiple, a 250,000 dollar accepted add-back can add 1.5 million dollars to enterprise value. Clean books, documented adjustments, and a pre-market QoE can be the difference between closing at price vs deal fatigue and a haircut.

Pro tips:
- Track add-backs monthly with receipts and memos; use one card for pass-throughs
- Be conservative; credibility beats wishful thinking
- Build your M&A team early (CPA, tax, banker); align on working capital and QoE scope
- Know your audience: PE prioritizes durable cash flow; strategics price in synergies (but rarely pay you for them)

02:20 - Guest intros and session focus

metadata.title: Quality of Earnings Report
metadata.author: Edspira
metadata.shortDescription:
A Quality of Earnings Report (QoE) is part of the due diligence in an acquisition or a merger. 

When you acquire a company, you want confidence in their financial figures.  Their financials affect the amount you’re willing to pay, and whether you want to go through with the deal.   

Thus, the buyer (and in some cases the seller) can hire a third party to inspect the financial statements of the company selling its business.

The goal is to understand:
• The extent to which earnings are cash or noncash
• The extent to which earnings are recurring or nonrecurring
• The extent to which earnings are the result of aggressive accounting

The buyer wants to know the seller’s adjusted EBITDA, because valuation is often expressed as a multiple of EBITDA.  

To determine the adjusted EBITDA, a QoE analysis would look for:
• Improper revenue recognition
• Improper capitalization of expenses
• Unsupported changes to allowance accounts
• Non-GAAP accounting
• Changes in accounting methods, principles, policies, or procedures
• Overstated inventory
• The loss of key customers
• Contingent liabilities that have not been reported
• Related-party transactions

The QoE report makes adjustments to the seller’s EBITDA based on these factors.

If the QoE report finds a significant discrepancy between the EBITDA reported by the seller and the actual EBITDA, this could result in (1) a renegotiation of the purchase price or (2) the buyer walking away from the deal.  

While a QoE analysis usually focuses on earnings, it can also analyze topics such a free cash flow, customer retention, and working capital.

Remember, the management team of the seller has an incentive to make the company look as good as possible, because they’re trying to sell the business.  

A QoE report tells you whether the financial situation is as good as the seller says it is.

Thus, getting a QoE report is like having a mechanic inspect a used car before you buy it.

and still have weak earnings underneath.

Before comparing these terms, we need to
understand what each one is designed to
answer.
One measures operating performance,
while the other tests whether that
performance is genuinely sustainable.
EBITDA is a performance measure built
from operating earnings.
It removes financing, tax, and certain
non-cash accounting effects so analysts
can compare businesses more easily.
The calculation starts with net income
and adds back interest, taxes,
depreciation, and amortization.
That gives you a rough view of operating
performance before those specific items
affect profit. Quality of earnings is
not just a number on the income
statement. It is an investigation into
how repeatable, cash generating, and
economically real those earnings
actually are.
EBITDA is a metric you calculate usually
for a specific period. Quality of
earnings is a broader assessment that
asks whether the metric deserves to be
trusted and used in a transaction.
Analysts like EBITDA because it creates
a more comparable operating lens.
It can help compare companies with
different debt levels, tax situations,
or depreciation policies, especially
when applying valuation multiples.
A quality of earnings review goes behind
the headline metric.
It looks for unusual revenue, temporary
costs, aggressive adjustments, and other
items that could make future performance
look weaker than the current
presentation suggests. Now we can see
where the confusion starts. The same
company may present several versions of

The calculation starts with net income and adds back interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. That gives you a rough view of operating performance before those specific items affect profit. Quality of earnings is not just a number on the income statement. It is an investigation into how repeatable, cash generating, and economically real those earnings actually are. EBITDA is a metric you calculate usually for a specific period. Quality of earnings is a broader assessment that asks whether the metric deserves to be trusted and used in a transaction. Analysts like EBITDA because it creates a more comparable operating lens. It can help compare companies with different debt levels, tax situations, or depreciation policies, especially when applying valuation multiples. A quality of earnings review goes behind the headline metric. It looks for unusual revenue, temporary costs, aggressive adjustments, and other items that could make future performance look weaker than the current presentation suggests. ►EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1) SELLERS LIE ABOUT EBITDA — EVEN THE HONORABLE ONES: When a seller knows the exit is priced at 3–5x EBITDA, every dollar of fiction in that number pays them three to five times over. That's the moment even the most honorable people start hiding things between data sets you don't have time to reconcile.

2) YOU'RE ABOUT TO PAY $4M FOR A NUMBER NOBODY CHECKED: The CIM says $1M EBITDA, you presume a 4x multiple, and congratulations — you've "valued" the company at $4M. The real number could be $800K, $1.2M, $500K, or zero. You can't value what you can't verify.

3) SMALL-BUSINESS BOOKS HAVE NO STANDARD. NONE.: 16 years of deals, and Elliott has seen cash-ish and accrual-ish — never straight either one. If you can't read their revenue recognition, you can't read their financials, period.

4) THE QoE IS THE AUDIT BEFORE YOU WIRE: An outsourced, audit-like validation of the EBITDA you're putting a multiple on — run while you're busy raising capital, courting lenders, and visiting the seller. The reason is simple: you can't overpay for an asset and win.

In this Acquira Accelerator Program (AP Call), we break down Quality of Earnings (QOE) and why it can make or break a business acquisition. You’ll learn how financial due diligence impacts purchase price, negotiation leverage, and post-close outcomes, especially in lower middle-market deals.

We cover proof of cash, adjusted EBITDA, working capital traps, deferred revenue issues, customer concentration risk, and real transaction war stories that nearly killed deals. If you’re buying a small business, this episode gives you a practical diligence framework to avoid expensive mistakes.

Topics covered:

What a QOE report actually tells buyers
QOE vs audit: key differences
Working capital and EBITDA adjustments
Revenue recognition and deferred revenue red flags
Real-life diligence failures and lessons learned
Best practices for acquisition entrepreneurs

metadata.title: One Wrong Move, Scary Result: Asset Purchase vs Share Purchase
metadata.author: Martin Godfrey Legido
metadata.shortDescription:
When buying a business, the way you structure the deal matters more than you might think.

Choose the wrong approach, and you could face unexpected liabilities, additional costs, complicated paperwork and unnecessary disruption.

In this episode, Martin Godfrey Legido explains the key differences between an asset purchase and a share purchase, including:

🔹 Why buying shares can offer a smoother transition when acquiring an established company.
🔹 When an asset purchase may be the better option.
🔹 The importance of understanding liabilities, valuations, legal requirements and tax implications before committing.
🔹 Why the right structure depends on the business and the circumstances of the deal.

There is no one-size-fits-all answer. Understanding your options before signing can help you make a more informed acquisition decision.

Thinking about buying a business? Book a free 1-to-1 Acquisition Roadmap Call with Martin to discuss your acquisition plans.

[https://tinyurl.com/ms9wcxuj](https://tinyurl.com/ms9wcxuj)

#BusinessAcquisition #MergersAndAcquisitions #SharePurchase #AssetPurchase #AcquisitionAssist

HMRC are very can be very hot on this. >> [snorts] >> And you know, they're very careful about manipulations. So um there's not a great deal without get getting into immense detail. You'll see it's online, and we'll be very happy to help you. Many thanks.

metadata.title: Asset Sale vs Stock Sale
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
One of the biggest conflicts that exist within transactions is the type of deal you’re doing – asset sale or stock sale.  Buyers typically prefer assets and sellers prefer stock sales. The key for any acquisition entrepreneur is understanding the big differences between both these types of sales. 

In this piece, I’ll help you navigate through those differences and elaborate on the benefits associated with both so that you can make the best decision. 

You may also read the blog here: https://buythenbuild.com/asset-sale-and-stock-sale-definitions-differences-and-advantages/

Join us and accelerate your acquisition with our “do-it-with-you” buy-side advisory service. Our collaborative approach blends graduate-level instruction with hands-on buy-side consulting. Together we will master the skills needed to identify, evaluate, and acquire the right business for you.

Don't forget to like and subscribe to be updated with new vlogs and learn more about business acquisition!

VISIT OUR WEBSITE: http://acquisitionlab.com
DOWNLOAD BUY THEN BUILD SAMPLE CHAPTER DOWNLOAD: https://acquisitionlab.com/free-chapter
LEARN FROM OUR BLOGS: https://acquisitionlab.com/blog/
MORE BLOGS AT BUY THEN BUILD: https://buythenbuild.com/blog/
CLIENTS' TESTIMONIALS: https://acquisitionlab.com/testimonials/
JOIN THE LAB: https://acquisitionlab.com/application/
SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/buythenbuild
 

*********

Walker is a serial acquisition entrepreneur, bestselling author, and M&A advisor. He acquired seven companies over ten years and co-founded several startups. His bestselling book, Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game, released to critical acclaim including being recognized by Forbes as “one of the top 7 books all entrepreneurs must read,” and is currently being used in many universities. The Acquisition Lab, offers buy-side M&A services for first-time financial buyers in a do-it-with-you service, providing information, coaching, tools, and community. Read more here: https://acquisitionlab.com/meet-the-team/

segments.text: Hey gang! It’s Walker Deibel, author of Buy Then Build and creator of the Acquisition Lab. During my many years of buying
companies and now I spend the majority of my time advising buyers and sellers.
Sometimes, it'll come up on the buy-side in regards to how I think about these certain
liabilities that the seller has on their on their balance sheet? And then I come to
figure out that it's really sort of a question around asset sale versus stock sale.
Once you understand the structure, I think a lot of it starts to make sense. So, let's
understand what the difference is between an asset sale and a stock sale. Why you would
want to do certain things in them? Or make certain decisions around them.
So the selling entity… The selling business is a legal entity. This legal entity
is liable for any sort of legal things and it's
the legal entity that pays taxes and reflects ownership
of the companies’ stock in this legal entity, is owned. But this legal
entity owns a bunch of assets inside of it. Now these assets can be tangible or they can be
intangible. What I mean by that is a tangible asset might be a printing press or
a powder coat oven, or some big physical industrial piece of equipment.
Intangible is going to be the brand, the logo. Frankly, the culture of the
people, the sort of standard operating procedures the intellectual property, the website,
all of these kinds of things. And the truth is that the legal entity in and of itself,
doesn't actually generate any cash, does it? It's the assets. It's the assets that generate
the cash, right? So, it's ultimately the cash flow and the assets that you're after
whether or not you want this blue legal entity is usually dependent on just
a couple of things. But let me say it like this… Almost all lower middle market and
main street transactions are going to be an asset sale and not a stock sale. An asset sale
is where you form your own legal entity. And then we're going to move all of these
assets and all of this cash over into your legal entity, leaving this one hollow.
In other words, we would have this cash flow that of course is coming from these assets.
Don't make fun of my drawings, I know you're thinking about it.
What we did was we moved them from here to there, so this of course is now
a hollow legal entity and that's it. Sometimes it could be
this legal entity over here, maybe there was a building
or something like that… It is owned and that
was an asset that this company didn't want. Something like that in which case
this building should be black. Maybe this legal entity still owns a building
or a separate online business it had or something like that. More common
or not, it's actually left empty, and then this is a shell of an entity that this the seller.
They might accept a seller's note or something like that. They might leave it open to start a new
business. Often times they'll kind of shut it down. And then that legal entity is
gone. You've moved all of the assets and all of the cash flow things that generate cash flow
over here, that includes employees and all the rest of it. Usually, you have to
terminate them from this legal entity and hire them on that legal entity. Usually done
in the days following the transaction. Listen, the reason this is
beneficial, it's a cash-free debt-free transaction. Let's write that down, cash-free.
What does that mean Walker? It means that any cash that was in that original entity is not is
retained by the owner. So, any cash that was in here and any cash balance is retained by the
owner. That would be… I had a million dollars in cash, I'm going
to take that cash and then I'm going to sell you these assets, so cash does not move over.
The other thing would be liabilities. It’s debt-free, okay? Debt-free, if you made
fun of my drawings, you'll also be making fun of my handwriting. I had a million dollars in
cash and I had 250 000 in debt. I keep my debt, if I'm the seller and
you, as the buyer, don't accept any of the cash or any of the debt. Why does this happen?
Well, it really is to the benefit of the buyer, because it limits the sort of
historical risk of the original legal asset. Let's say, you buy this…
You buy the stock of this company and you as the owner, are
liable for the entire history of this entity. You buy Whiteboard
Manufacturing Corporation, you buy the stock, okay?
And then four years after you buy it, a bunch of toxic waste, barrels show up
in the Pacific Ocean, with Whiteboard Corporations printed on them
or there was a bunch of bad products that failed. You're now liable because
you are the owner of this legal entity. When you buy the assets and not the legal entity, you
are not liable for anything that did not happen on your watch. A huge benefit to a buyer and
the core reason why most of them happen that way. It is the default setting. The other reason…
I'm sorry, let me see it differently. The reason why you would do a stock sale typically, because of
there's some kind of contract. A supplier contract or a customer contract,
or some kind of license that is non-transferable. That is essential
to the business, okay? That's probably number one. Number two would be…
Obviously, if you are investing in a minority role, like say a startup or something like
that, you're buying Equity. And the third would be… Once you get into a sort of larger deals,
it becomes easier and calmer, slightly more common in a stock sale. But it might
be like if the seller is going to stay on and continue to retain. Let's
make it up 20% of the business and you're gonna buy 80% of the company in sort of a
private equity situation there might be a reason in this structure to do a stock sale.
If you, as the buyer decide to buy it as a stock sale it has tremendous tax benefits to the seller
and so as a result, what almost always happens is that the purchase price… If I'm
going to buy a purchase price on assets, it's usually higher than if you buy it with stock.
The reason why is that the cost of the purchase price tends to be worth more
to the seller. So a bad example but just to make an example. Let's say, I'm going
to buy a company for a hundred dollars and after taxes, this person is going to
get sixty-five dollars. If I buy his company for a hundred dollars as a
stock sale then this person might get seventy-five dollars.
By the way, if you buy a Canadian company or an Australian company or anything
like that. These have drastically different impacts, to the point that a lot of them
say at first that…It’s gotta be a stock sale, right? And so in essence, this gap
between the 75 and the 65 is not lost on the buyer, ever. They know that this is
worth more to a seller. And so they will very often say well look… If I spend
a hundred dollars here or if I spend I came to that mouth in my head but let's just
say ninety dollars, if I spent a hundred dollars as an asset sale or ninety dollars as a stock
sale, it ends up being worth the same to you. So that doesn't exactly transfer.
The only other thing that I want to add is that when you do an asset sale, you might say…
Well, I bought Whiteboard Corporation but LLC is called Walker Deibel Corporation.
How on Earth does that, I can't name it the same thing, right? Legally. And so all that
happens is that this new asset that you buy, has a doing business as you file a DVA
with your state government and it's just that simple. You file it online, it's like
ten dollars then you have to re-up it. I think every three years something like that. Listen,
thank you so much. When I first went out and tried to buy a business in 2004
I failed. There was no good information, there was no good instruction, it was an opaque
private marketplace that I had to navigate, very fragmented. And along the way, I ended
up acquiring seven companies. I've acquired 16.5 million dollars in revenue over a 10 year
period. I ultimately wrote Buy Then Build as sort of like what I learned
walking that path and it was always sort of my dream to ultimately create some kind
of world-class instruction around this, and it wasn't until readers started asking me to
help them find and buy a business. I was like… That's crazy! I can't do that. I can't charge
you enough, it's way too hard and I can't guarantee results. And so, what we did was I recognized that
there was… You could sort of do it yourself, like buy a copy of Buy
Then Build, go out, and buy a copy of the Harvard Business review guide to buying a small business
and sort of go out there. Do it yourself or you can hire a buy-side advisor for
five thousand dollars a month, plus a double Lehman success formula, which would be about
on average of 150 000 extra expenses to a buyer. Well, if you're an acquisition
entrepreneur, why would you increase the cost of your transaction like 15% to bring
on someone that's not doing anything that you can't do? A lot of us search is full-time or
heavy part-time, right? So ultimately, I created the Acquisition Lab. The point here
was to build world-class instruction, a suite of tools, and ongoing coaching, so that we could
provide assistance on the subject you needed when you needed it. Rather than just having a pre-recorded
online course. They had to go back and dive into it. I wanted to do all this. Just a vetted
community, that we made sure that everyone was accepted would actually be able to acquire
a business. They've got this sort of like business sophistication or they kind of drive to
do so and also just has access to at least a little bit of capital in order to get that done.
We did that, it's called the Acquisition Lab and what I didn't expect was that the vetted
community would take off in the way that it has. It's such an impressive group of people, it's such
a thriving community. And if you are looking to buy a business in the next 6 to 18 months,
we created the acquisition lab as a do it with you, buy-side advisory service and it's
offered all at the cost of less than one month of a buy-side advisor, with lifetime access to you.
If you have an interest in joining us, we run cohorts every so often. Please go to
acquisitionlab.com and apply. I look forward to working with you soon. Thanks!

metadata.title: Working Capital Adjustment: Common Issues in M&A Transactions
metadata.author: Morse
metadata.shortDescription:
M&A Deal Tips #6: M&A Attorney Scott Bleier explains why working capital is a vital piece of the M&A transaction. What is working capital? In its simplest definition, working capital is current assets over current liabilities. Buyers want to buy a business with enough working capital to keep this going without an immediate need for a cash infusion. Sellers, conversely, don't want to sell the business with too much working capital or cash — as they want to realize as much profit as possible. So how do you negotiate a target working capital amount for 2 or 3 months? And what happens when disputes arise over the working capital post-closing? Drafting and negotiating a proper working capital adjustment is an important component of the M&A deal, and one Morse, Barnes-Brown & Pendleton attorneys have the experience to provide their clients.

https://www.morse.law/practice/corporate/mergers-acquisitions/

Top Ten Issues in M&A Transactions

metadata.title: M&A Deal Structures: Working Capital Adjustments vs. Locked Box Closing Approach
metadata.author: Brett Cenkus
metadata.shortDescription:
Have questions? Book a call, and talk to Brett today: 
https://rebrand.ly/clarity-brettcenkus67

_______________________________________________


You can reach Brett through:
 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/brettcenkus
https://twitter.com/BCenkus
https://cenkuslaw.com
https://braatenwoods.com
https://merger-resources.com


_______________________________________________



Brett A. Cenkus has 20+ years of experience in business law, finance, and entrepreneurship. Through Cenkus Law, PC, he provides advice and services for mergers & acquisitions (M&A), securities offerings, founders’ agreements, and other general business law issues.
 
Through Braaten Woods, LLC, Brett helps business owners in the lower middle market ($2MM - $25MM) position themselves for sale, find buyers, negotiate, and close M&A deals. 

Brett also maintains merger-resources.com, a site packed with free articles, videos, checklists, deal diagrams, template contracts, and other tools to help pass M&A knowledge to others. 

Brett regularly consults with entrepreneurs and invests his own capital as an angel investor. 

From 2010-2013, Brett served as Chief Legal Counsel of a publicly-traded international oilfield services company. From 2001 to 2006, he and a partner founded and built Paragon Residential Mortgage. Bridge Investments acquired Paragon in 2006. 

Brett holds a Juris Doctorate from Harvard Law School and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics from Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania.

Brett lives in Austin with his wife, Cathryn, and two children. He enjoys reading, squash, classic movies, great food and wine, and the New England Patriots.

working capital in an M&A deal. So working capital is current assets minus
current liabilities. So most businesses that's cash and accounts receivable
minus accounts payable. There can be inventory which would be
added to the assets side of the equation but in a service business you wouldn't
have that, of course. There could be deferred revenue; which is like prepaid
revenue would be over on the liability side, short-term loans and stuff like
that, but a lot of times in M&A the debts all gonna be paid off at the closing
table. So when we're talking working capital, we're often talking accounts
receivable plus cash minus accounts payable. That net is your working capital
and in the US we typically use what's called the Closing Accounts Approach. And
we're going to distinguish between that and the Locked Box Approach; which is
what they generally use over in Europe. And we're gonna talk about pros and cons of
those. In the Closing Accounts Approach, what happens is the buyer and the seller
come up with reach an agreement on a headline price-of a purchase price for
the business. Often they'll do that at the time that they sign a Letter of
Intent or Term Sheet, which is non-binding except for user exclusivity
and maybe confidentiality. The exclusivity is it stops the seller from
shopping the deal around. Now, the buyer comes in and spends 30 60 90 days
doing due diligence- kicking the tires, looking at everything. That's when they
get their auditors and accountants in there to look at the accounts. They'll
come up with a target working capital number that's fair for the business.
Sometimes it's not as important as Letter of Intent is signed, other times it's
sort of that can is kicked, and along the way the parties come up with what they
believe it ought to be. So, between signing that Letter of Intent and
closing, the diligence is being done We've got our set purchase price and
then we've got a target working capital number. So right before closing sometimes
there's other adjustments on the, you know, day before closing. On the day of
closing the seller will usually prepare a balance sheet that shows how what they
believe working capital is as of the day of closing or will be as of the day of
closing. Now, it's not a hundred percent accurate or rarely is, because most
businesses are in flux- at any point in time there's money coming in and out and
you can't really know exactly what what what it is. Sometimes there's more
complicated mechanisms for dealing with bad accounts receivable and stuff like
that so it's like it can be a little bit messy and it's hard to know exactly what
it is on the day of closing. So we've got the purchase price, a target working
capital number. We don't know exactly what it is. But at the closing, the parties
have an idea, and then typically the purchase price is adjusted a little bit
to take into account the shortfall, or the excess above or under the working
capital target number. So let's say it was the business sells for five million
dollars. The target working capital number of the parties decide on is five
hundred thousand and on the day of closing the the seller believes it's six
hundred thousand working capital; the buyer will pay an extra one hundred
thousand dollars to the seller. The purchase price is going up a little bit.
But that's not the end of the story it's just beginning from the standpoint of
working capital, because after the buyer- remember on the day of closing we don't
know exactly what it is. We have a we we have an idea, and we know what the target
is. What we need it-what it's supposed to be, we know approximately what it is. We
don't know exactly. The buyer gets the business, gets the keys, gets in there and
once they understand the business and the books and all that, the buyer will
generate its own the calculation of working capital as of the day of closing.
The buyer will say "okay, I know what it was supposed to be, I know
what you think it was, here's what it was". Now, in the "here's what it was" there's a
lot of opportunity for disagreement. Number one: even though all of this will
generally be covered by them- the way the books are done will be according to GAAP
which is Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. GAAP isn't perfect science
it's it's it's it's standards. It's not always exactly "do this, do that". So how
the buyer might do things and how their accountants might do things, it may be a
little bit different than how the seller does it. You've got an inherent sort of
misalignment of interests: maybe the buyer is going to have a desire
obviously in minimizing the working capital number as of the day of closing
because it means they might be due a refund. Or you know, they're looking
obviously they want to have negotiated for the highest working capital numbers
possible, but then in terms of save what it was, the lower the better because then
they were just gonna check from the seller. so there's a little bit of a
conflict there, and it's not done collaboratively usually. And then when it
starts to get complicated- distilling the business deal- as a lawyer that we take
the business deal we put it on paper; it can be really challenging and there
could be a disconnect and you don't always know, are you really about are the
other principles really understanding what this says using the account and
start looking at it. So it's like taking their deal, getting it clear
getting it on paper, and then with the misalignment interest there's a lot of
opportunity for profits to occur. So there's a lot of litigation around that.
Now, the alternative is what they do in Europe mainly; which is the Locked Box
Approach. So back to with the U.S. the party set a a headline purchase price
number. Somewhere along the line they get a working capital target number and then
they close. Along the way it doesn't matter what the sellers doing. Now
contractually, the seller may be prohibited from taking money out of the business or
doing different things, but like, usually the buyer doesn't really care. Doesn't
matter, because ultimately the buyer knows "I've got to get it with X amount
of working capital anyway", so you take all the cash out of the business
sometimes you know, that's the we're doing that on purpose- but it doesn't
matter because the buyers gonna get what the buyer expects. In Europe
with the Locked Box Approach, that point between signing and closing adjustments
in the working capital are for the benefit or you know, detriment of the
buyer. So the buyer and the seller agree on a five million dollar price and the
balance sheet as of today: we just agree on the deal, and it doesn't matter what
happens between now and closing from a working capital perspective. The buyer
doesn't have to be worried about the seller "riding the trade", which is where
the seller just doesn't pay its payables and collects really aggressively out its
receivables. They don't have to be worried about that because all of the
benefit and the detriment of the receivables and all that action goes to
the buyer. Now, that means that the buyer has to do a lot more work upfront before
they even get to a purchase price. Before they even decide on the deal they accept
the balance sheet, they meaning the buyer needs their auditors and counts in
there really aggressively understanding the business. That's more time and money
spent upfront, but it's less on the backside and upfront anything that the
buyer's seeing, they're gonna bounce off the seller. They're going to talk about it
going to reach an agreement, they're both going to feel good, and they're gonna
cement it and that's the end of story. Okay whereas in the U.S. to get deals to
a table quickly, we kick this problem kind of and it's sort of front-loaded in
Europe and that works better if what you're concerned about is more
minimizing disputes and disagreements the Locked Box Approach could be much much
better. It's not perfect and again you're shifting cost in time upfront but it
works it works well for that. There's a concept called Permitted Leakage, which
allows the seller to take some money out of business or do different things, but
again, you're pretty much freezing the working capital in effect at the time

metadata.title: Net Working Capital Peg for Business Owners
metadata.author: Kirk Michie
metadata.shortDescription:
When business owners think about selling their company, they usually focus on valuation and purchase price. But one overlooked deal term can have a direct impact on how much money you actually receive at closing: the net working capital peg.

In this video, M&A Advisor Kirk Michie explains what a net working capital peg is, how it’s calculated, and why buyers insist on including it in virtually every acquisition. He also discusses how working capital adjustments work, why they frequently lead to post-closing disputes, and what founders should understand before signing a letter of intent.

You’ll learn:

• What a net working capital peg is
• How net working capital is calculated in an M&A transaction
• What “cash-free, debt-free” means
• How working capital adjustments affect purchase price
• Why buyers require a working capital target
• Common causes of post-closing disputes
• What founders should review before signing an LOI

Many founders spend months negotiating valuation but overlook the deal terms that can ultimately affect their proceeds. Understanding the working capital provisions upfront can help avoid surprises and protect the value you’ve spent years building.

If you’re considering selling your business, this is one deal term you don’t want to ignore.

#BusinessSale #MergersAndAcquisitions #SellingABusiness #BusinessExit #WorkingCapital #NetWorkingCapital #LOI #BusinessBroker #PrivateEquity #Founder

networking capital formula and negotiate it as a separate point and what you want to do is you want to determine the percentage of that deposit that either gets held back and left behind for the buyer metadata.title: SPECIAL EPISODE - Structuring the Deal: Letters of Intent Explained
metadata.author: Letters of Intent
metadata.shortDescription:
It’s the document that inspired the name of our show, and today, we are dedicating an entire episode to it. In this episode of Letters of Intent, Pankaj Raval and Sahil Chaudhary break down the critical importance of getting your LOI right before you ever look at a Purchase and Sale Agreement (PSA).


They explore how a well-crafted LOI acts as a "movie trailer" for a deal, surfacing major disagreements and dealbreakers before either party spends thousands of dollars on legal fees or due diligence. Whether you are buying commercial real estate, selling a growing business, or bringing on new partners, Pankaj and Sahil walk you through the 10 essential terms every LOI needs, the dangers of seller financing, and the critical difference between binding and non-binding provisions.


Takeaways

  •  Don't Negotiate on a Handshake: Proceeding with due diligence without an LOI in place leaves you completely exposed. You can spend thousands of dollars inspecting a business or property, only for the seller to walk away with zero consequences.
  •  The 10 Essential Terms: Price is just one factor. Your LOI must outline the deposit, due diligence period, closing date, exclusivity, financing contingencies, deal structure (asset vs. stock), key economic terms, closing conditions, and confidentiality.
  •  Binding vs. Non-Binding: While the core economic terms of an LOI are generally non-binding, you must ensure that clauses protecting your process—like exclusivity, confidentiality, and breakup fees—are strictly binding.
  •  Beware of Seller Financing: If a buyer is asking for seller financing, it often means a bank won't lend to them. Unless you are fully prepared to act as a bank and navigate a complex foreclosure process, proceed with extreme caution.
  •  Bring Counsel in Early: The biggest mistake business owners make is handing their attorney an already-signed LOI. By bringing counsel in before signing, you can identify blind spots, secure leverage, and avoid being locked into unfavorable terms.

Soundbites

  •  "Three weeks of momentum and $8,000 gone, an LOI would have cost them an afternoon."
  •  "Is an LOI kind of like a movie trailer? It gives you the highlights. It tells you, do you want to watch this movie?"
  •  "Unless you're prepared to be the bank and try to foreclose and try to deal with the property and take back the property, you do not want that headache."
  •  "The price is only one factor of a deal and you have to weigh that against many other factors."
  •  "If there's one takeaway... you can't read the other person's mind. The biggest protection you have against making assumptions is the LOI."

Keywords


Letter of Intent, LOI, Mergers and Acquisitions, Commercial Real Estate, Business Acquisition, Term Sheet, Exclusivity, Due Diligence, Seller Financing, Carbon Law Group

metadata.title: Key Terms to Know When Negotiating a Letter of Intent
metadata.author: PCE Investment Bankers - M&A | ESOP | Valuation
metadata.shortDescription:
The letter of intent (LOI) in an M&A deal declares a commitment between the buyer and the seller to enter a transaction. It outlines the key terms of the transaction agreement. By defining binding and nonbinding terms of the agreement, the LOI provides protection to all parties involved. In this video, we define the most important terms you need to know for a well-executed LOI.

Non-Binding Terms: Purchase price, deal structure, earnouts, seller notes, contingencies, due diligence, working capital.
Binding Terms: Exclusivity, disclosure & confidentiality, governing law.
Strategic Balance: Focus on core deal points while leaving room for further negotiation in the definitive agreement.
Benefits of an Investment Banker: Expert guidance on prioritizing critical terms and navigating the M&A process.

Learn more: https://hubs.ly/Q0383Lt20
Contact us: https://hubs.ly/Q0383Lw50
Visit PCEs M&A University: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLeCr7_FWVaHnk3DDg6T2lG-BtxU3TPbsC

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:24 What is a Letter of Intent?
0:43 Non-Binding Terms in an LOI - purchase price, structure, earnout, contingencies, due diligence, working capital
1:45 Binding Terms in an LOI - exclusivity, disclosure & confidentiality, governing law
2:31 How to negotiate an LOI

segments.text: For my money, the letter of intent is one of the most critical negotiations you will
enter when you decide to sell your company.
You need to get it right since it is the blueprint for your sale.
My name is Mike Rosendahl with PCE Investment Bankers and today I'll discuss the terms you will negotiate
in the LOI that create the framework, or roadmap, for closing the deal.
The letter of intent is the first document that is negotiated between the buyer and the
seller and outlines the key terms of the deal.
This agreement marks the basic understanding of the transaction and confirms there are
no dealbreakers between the buyer and the seller.
As you work through the LOI, it is important that you are clear to which terms will be
binding and which terms will be non-binding.
Examples of non-binding terms include the purchase price, structure, potential earnout
or seller note, contingencies, the due diligence process, and working capital.
The purchase price is the enterprise value for the company and will include the cash
component plus an earnout or seller note if they are part of the transaction.
Structure describes whether or not the transaction is a stock or asset deal which will impact
the taxes paid by the seller.
The potential earnout or seller note is only included if there will be a contingent payment
or you're helping to finance a portion of the transaction.
Contingencies are such things as do we need board or lender approval; conversations with
certain employees, customers or suppliers that will need to take place prior to the close.
The due diligence process will outline the specific parts of the business the buyer would
like to review, who will be part of the process, and how long it should take.
Working capital is a critical piece that makes sure that the seller operates the business
in the normal course from the time you sign a letter of intent until closing.
Examples of binding terms include exclusivity, disclosure and confidentiality, and governing law.
Exclusivity is when you grant the buyer a period of time where you will not negotiate
with another buyer.
The reason you provide the buyer exclusivity is due to the time, money and effort the buyer
will devote to the due diligence process and definitive agreement negotiations.
The buyer wants to make sure the deal isn't being shopped and increase the likelihood
of closing the deal under the terms of the letter of intent.
Disclosure & confidentiality- well that's just to make sure the information that's being
shared won't be shared with other parties as well as the fact that the transaction is
taking place won't be shared with other parties.
Governing law is the law that will govern the agreement and in case there's an issue,
you know where you'll be going to court and which laws will be overseeing the LOI.
As you develop your letter of intent, remember that you don't have to negotiate all the deal terms.
Work to find a balance of the most significant points and leave the rest for later.
An investment banker can be a great ally to help you prioritize the most important deal terms.
Thanks for joining me today.
If you like this video, please subscribe to our channel so you'll be notified whenever
new content is posted.

metadata.title: M&A Letters of Intent: Are They Really Necessary?
metadata.author: Brett Cenkus
metadata.shortDescription:
Letters of intent are commonly used in mergers and acquisitions to lay out the key terms of the deal. But, what are they, and do you even need one?

Good question! In this video, you'll find out the 3 situations in which Brett finds LOIs most useful.

_____________________________________________


Have questions? Book a call, and talk to Brett today: 
https://rebrand.ly/clarity-brettcenkus34

_______________________________________________


You can reach Brett through:
 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/brettcenkus
https://twitter.com/BCenkus
https://cenkuslaw.com
https://braatenwoods.com
https://merger-resources.com


_______________________________________________



Brett A. Cenkus has 20+ years of experience in business law, finance, and entrepreneurship. Through Cenkus Law, PC, he provides advice and services for mergers & acquisitions (M&A), securities offerings, founders’ agreements, and other general business law issues.
 
Through Braaten Woods, LLC, Brett helps business owners in the lower middle market ($2MM - $25MM) position themselves for sale, find buyers, negotiate, and close M&A deals. 

Brett also maintains merger-resources.com, a site packed with free articles, videos, checklists, deal diagrams, template contracts, and other tools to help pass M&A knowledge to others. 

Brett regularly consults with entrepreneurs and invests his own capital as an angel investor. 

From 2010-2013, Brett served as Chief Legal Counsel of a publicly-traded international oilfield services company. From 2001 to 2006, he and a partner founded and built Paragon Residential Mortgage. Bridge Investments acquired Paragon in 2006. 

Brett holds a Juris Doctorate from Harvard Law School and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics from Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania.

Brett lives in Austin with his wife, Cathryn, and two children. He enjoys reading, squash, classic movies, great food and wine, and the New England Patriots.

general provisions or terms in a in a letter of intent - almost entirely
non-binding which means that most of those terms are just intent.

Generally, I use them in three situations. One is we want to be

always want to use a letter of intent. I'm curious, if you've been involved in

Greetings, everyone! Thank you for being a part of our informative series on the Eight Milestones of Mergers and Acquisitions. I'm Jacob, your host, and in today's episode, we're unveiling a significant step in your M&A journey – the Letter of Intent document, or simply, the LOI.

This is an exciting phase because it means that we have a buyer who genuinely values your company and is submitting their best offer to acquire your business. We call for LOI submissions after the management meetings, aiming to collect them all at once for your review.

The LOI is a formal document signifying the buyer's interest in exclusively engaging your company for a specified period, during which they can conduct a comprehensive due diligence process. An essential point to remember is that once you accept the LOI, you are generally prohibited from speaking with other potential buyers. This is a crucial aspect to emphasize.

The LOI is the phase where, as the seller, you begin to cede some control over the process. Why is this understanding important? Because the LOI should encompass a summary description of all the material deal terms that will later appear in the purchase agreement. From our seasoned perspective as an experienced Investment Bank, it's better to cover more details in the LOI than to defer them to the final purchase agreement. This allows you to negotiate from a position of strength.

The LOI typically spans around 10 pages and can cover various items, which we will work closely with you to fully understand before you make a final decision. It's important to note that the LOI is generally non-binding, meaning the buyer is 100% committed but not 100% bound to purchasing your company. However, there may be binding aspects included at this stage.

In an ideal scenario, we'll create a comparison chart, similar to the one pictured here, to enable you to efficiently compare various offers and find the best one aligned with your goals. Keep in mind that the results from the management meetings will also factor into your decision-making.

Once a decision is reached, you'll sign the best LOI, setting the stage for working towards the final purchase agreement, a topic we'll explore in our next video.

Don't miss the next installment of our series on the 8 Milestones of M&A, presented by Transact Capital.
