metadata.title: Letter of Intent Terms to Settle Before Due Diligence
metadata.author: Escamilla Law Office
metadata.shortDescription:
A $5 million offer can mean very different things. M&A attorney Rick Escamilla explains what a letter of intent should settle before buyers and sellers spend weeks on due diligence.

A letter of intent, or LOI, is often treated as a quick step on the way to the real agreement. Rick Escamilla of Escamilla Law Office sees it differently. In many deals, some of the most important negotiations happen before the purchase agreement is even drafted. The LOI sets the basic economics, the proposed structure, and the process for getting to a final agreement. If those terms stay vague, the parties can spend weeks and real money on diligence, only to learn they never agreed on the deal.

This video is for owners, buyers, and advisors working on the sale of a privately held business. Rick walks through the purchase price, working capital, asset or equity structure, exclusivity, diligence, bank and SBA financing, and which LOI terms are binding. He then puts it all together with a Texas service business example, where the buyer and seller agree on $5 million and still find out they did not agree on much else.

In this episode:
- Why two $5 million offers can carry very different risk for the seller.
- What to ask about cash at closing, seller notes, and payments tied to future performance.
- Why working capital should come up in the LOI, even without a full formula.
- How asset or equity structure affects contracts, licenses, taxes, and liabilities.
- Why exclusivity is a real concession for a seller and not just boilerplate.
- How lender rules and third-party consents can affect the closing timeline.
- Which LOI terms are often binding and which usually are not.

Questions this episode answers:
What should a letter of intent resolve before due diligence?
Rick says it should set the essential economic and structural terms of the deal. It should also name the material risks and conditions that could affect closing, and set a reasonable process for diligence and negotiation. It does not need to settle every legal detail.

Is a letter of intent legally binding?
It depends on the language of the document. In many private company deals, the main business terms are meant to be non-binding, while terms like exclusivity and confidentiality are often meant to be enforceable. The LOI should clearly say which is which.

Why does exclusivity matter so much to a seller?
Once a seller agrees to exclusivity, the business may be off the market for a set time. Other buyers may move on, and the seller may lose negotiating power. Rick looks at how much time the buyer actually needs and whether the buyer has the ability to close.

Does a longer LOI mean a better LOI?
No. A short LOI is not better because it is simple, and a long one is not better because it is comprehensive. Rick says what matters is whether the document resolves the issues that are material to that particular deal.

Watch this if you are buying or selling a privately held business and want to understand the deal before you sign a letter of intent.

Chapters
00:00 Why the LOI and price terms matter
03:48 Working capital
05:56 Deal structure: what is being bought
08:18 Exclusivity and what sellers give up
10:52 Diligence, financing, path to closing
13:29 What in an LOI is actually binding
16:21 Example: same price, different deal
18:49 What makes an LOI effective

Read the full article: https://escamillalawoffice.com/blog/letter-of-intent-before-due-diligence/
Discuss a transaction: https://escamillalawoffice.com/contact/ | (210) 997-0025

Escamilla Law Office advises buyers, sellers and privately held companies on mergers and acquisitions throughout Texas, including Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio.

Attorney advertising. This video is for general informational purposes only and is not legal advice. Viewing it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Escamilla Law Office, 7550 I-10, Ste 800-863, San Antonio, TX 78229.

segments.text: What should an LOI resolve before due diligence begins?
When someone is buying or selling a privately held business, one of the first documents they'll
encounter is a letter of intent, commonly referred to as an LOI. And I think there's a fairly common
misconception about what this document is supposed to accomplish. A lot of people
approach the LOI as a preliminary agreement, but think uh they think the buyer and the seller just
need to agree on a purchase price, sign some confirming something confirming their general
intentions and let the attorneys work through the details later. But that's not really uh how
you know I look at it as the as a transaction attorney. Uh in many transactions, some of
the most consequential negotiations take place before the purchase agreement is even drafted.
The letter of intent establishes the framework for the transaction. It outlines the basic economics
uh the proposed structure, the conditions under which the parties intend to proceed
and the process for getting to a definitive agreement. Now that doesn't mean the LOI needs
to address every legal issue that might arise during the acquisition. In fact,
I think trying to negotiate every detail at this stage can be counterproductive. But there are
certain issues that need to be resolved early. Otherwise, uh the buyer and seller may spend
several weeks conducting due diligence, engaging attorneys and accountants, negotiating agreements,
and incurring significant expenses only to discover that they never really agreed on the
fundamental terms of the deal. Uh so that's what I want to discuss now. Uh what should the parties
actually negotiate in the LOI? Which provisions deserve the most attention? And what issues can
reasonably reasonably be left for the definitive purchase agreement? ICS. Let's start with
something that sounds obvious, the purchase price. Often the buyer earns $5 million to purchase a
privately held business. The seller agrees. Both parties believe they've reached an understanding
and they ready to move forward. But what exactly uh does that $5 million represent? Is it $5
million at cash at closing? Is the buyer assuming certain liabilities? Does the seller have to leave
a particular amount of working capital in the business? Is part of the purchase price contingent
upon the company's future performance? Will the seller finance a portion of the transaction? Uh,
these aren't minor details and can fundamentally change the economics of the transaction. So, let
me give you an example. Imagine two buyers each offer $5 million for the same company. The first
buyer offers uh the full purchase price in cash at closing, assuming certain customary adjustments.
The second buyer uh offers $4 million at closing, a $500,000 seller note, and an additional $500,000
uh contingent upon the business achieving specific financial targets over the next 2 years. Both
buyers have the headline purchase price of $5 million, but they're clearly not equal. Uh in
the second transaction, the seller is accepting additional credit risk and performance risk.
the seller must have to wait years to receive a full amount and some of that consideration
may never become payable. Uh that doesn't m necessarily uh make the second offer a bad
offer. But there can be legitimate reasons for structuring a transaction that way. A buyer may
need to bridge a valuation gap, preserve cash, or uh address uncertainty about the company's
future performance. But those terms need to be understood before the parties begin spending
significant time and money negotiating the transaction. From an attorney's perspect,
I want the LOI to establish the economic bargain with enough specificity uh that we understand
what each party is actually agreeing to. We can work through the detailed mechanics later. Uh
but we shouldn't be discovering the basic payment structure for the first time when we're drafting
the purchase agreement. Another issue that I think deserves attention early is working capital. This
comes up frequently in acquisitions of operating businesses. When a buyer purchases a company,
the buyer generally wants to receive a business that has significant operating assets and the
liquidity to continue functioning after closing. Depending on the transaction, those assets may
include accounts receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses, and other working capital components.
The problem is that buyers and sellers don't always have the same expectations about what
should be delivered. For example, let's say a seller agrees to sell a business for $5 million.
The seller might believe that all cash belongs to the seller, that existing accounts receivable will
be collected for the seller's benefit, and that certain liabilities will remain with the seller.
Meanwhile, the buyer might believe that the $5 million purchase price includes a normal level of
operating working capital, including receivables and inventory subject to an agreed calculation.
Those are very different economic understandings, and the disagreement becomes even more significant
when the business has substantial receivables, inventory, and working capital requirements. Now,
I don't necessarily believe that parties need a fully developed working capital formula in
the LOI. That formula may require financial diligence, historical balance sheet analysis
and input from other parties like accountants. But I do think the LOI should address the fundamental
understanding. Is the business being sold on a free cash debtree basis? Will the seller
developer sorry will the de will the seller deliver a normalized amount of working capital?
uh what categories of assets and liabilities are expected to be included or excluded and will the
final purchase price be subject to a post-closing adjustment? Those are all questions I would want
the parties discussing early on because if the seller thinks $5 million means one thing
and the buyer thinks it means something completely different, then the parties don't actually have an
agreement on the economics. They have an agreement on the number, but those are two different things.
Uh the next issue is transaction structure. At a basic level, most private company acquisitions
are structured as either an asset purchase or an equity purchase, although there are
variations and more complex structures. And the distinction matters. In an asset acquisition,
the buyer generally purchases specifically identified assets and assumes liabilities
as agreed in the transaction documents subject to applicable law. In the equity acquisition,
the buyer purchases ownership interest in the company itself. That means the legal entity
generally continues to exist along with the assets, contracts, liabilities subject to the
terms of those arrangements in and applicable law. Neither structure is automatically better
in every situation. Buyers often prefer asset acquisitions because they can negotiate which
assets they acquire and which liabilities they assume. But an asset purchase does not necessarily
eliminate every potential exposure to historical liabilities. Sellers, on the other hand,
may prefer an equity transaction for tax reasons, simplicity, or other commercial considerations.
There are also practical issues. For example, suppose the target company has several valuable
customer contracts. In an asset purchase, the buyer may need those contracts assigned to the
acquired entity. Depending on the contractual language, customer consent may be required.
In an equity purchase, the contracting entity may remain the same, but change of control provisions
could still trigger consent consent requirements or other consequences. Licenses, permits, leases,
employees, and financing arrangements can also be affected by the structure. Uh, this is why I don't
like treating transaction structure as something the lawyers can simply figure out in the end.
uh the structure can influence the price, the allocation of liabilities, the tax consequences
and whether the transaction is practical in the first place. Uh now the parties may enter into
the LOI with a proposed structure that changes after diligence or tax analysis. That's perfectly
reasonable, but they should have an initial understanding of what is being purchased and
why. And if one party has a strong preference or a requirement concerning the structure that
should be discussed before the other party invests substantial resources moving forward.
Let's talk about exclusivity. This is one of the most important provisions that I think sellers
sometimes underestimate. Most buyers are going to want some period of exclusivity after signing
an LOI. In practical terms, the buyer wants the seller to stop negotiating with other potential
purchasers while the buyer completes diligence, arranges finances, and negotiates the definitive
agreements. From the buyer perspective, that request makes sense. An acquisition requires
time and money. Buyers may engage attorneys, accountants, lenders, and other professionals.
They may spend significant resources evaluating a business. A buyer generally doesn't want to
undertake the process while the seller continues shopping the company to competing biders. Uh but
we also need to appreciate that what the seller is giving up. Once the seller agrees to exclusivity,
the seller may be taking the business off the market for a spec specified period.
Other interested buyers may move on. The seller may lose negotiating leverage with them. And if
the transaction ultimately falls apart and the seller may have to restart the process. That's
why I view exclusivity as a meaningful commercial concession. It's not simply boilerplate. When I'm
looking at an exclusivity provision, I want to know how much time the buyer actually needs
and why. Is the buyer paying cash or does the transaction require third party financing? Does
the buyer already uh reviewed meaningful financial information? Are there complicated regulatory,
licensing, or third-party consent issues? How quickly can the buyer complete diligence? I
also want to know whether the buyer has the ability to close a transaction. For example,
a buyer requesting a lengthy exclusivity period without having made meaningful progress on
financing presents a different risk profile than a buyer with committed capital and an established
diligence process. That doesn't mean the seller should refuse exclusivity. In many acquisitions,
a reasonable exclusivity period is necessary to move the deal deal forward, but I believe
its duration and any extension rights should be negotiated in relation to the circumstances of the
transaction. From the seller's perspective, I generally prefer defined deadlines,
a clear end to the exclusivity obligation, and careful consideration on whether extensions are
justified by the buyer's progress. The goal is to give a serious buyer sufficient time to
complete the transaction without unnecessarily restricting the seller for an indefinite period.
Another important function of the LOI is establishing the process for getting from
preliminary agreement to closing. This is where due diligence and financing become particularly
important. Due diligence is the buyer's opportunity to investigate the business.
The buyer may review financial statements, tax returns, customer contracts, employment
agreements, corporate records, liabilities, litigation, licenses, and numerous other
matters. And depending on the transaction, that process may be fairly straightforward
or quite extensive. What I want to avoid is an LOI that establishes an aggressive closing
deadline without considering what actually needs to happen before the deal can close. For example,
if the acquisition is bank financed, the lender may have its own underwriting requirements,
collateral requirements, documentation, and approval process. These requirements may
affect the transaction structure. The purchase agreement, any seller financing agreements,
and ultimately the closing date. In an SBA financed acquisition, seller financing can
represent additional issues uh because the lender may impose restrictions concerning payments,
subordination, and other terms of the seller note depending on the applicable loan requirements. And
the lender isn't necessarily going to approve every term that the buyer and seller have have
negotiated. They have their own requirements. That can become a significant problem if the parties
wait until late in the transaction to address the lender requirements preliminary. Similarly,
if the buyer needs the consent of a landlord, a major customer or another third party,
that process is affect may affect the timeline. The LOI doesn't need to resolve every diligence
issue. In fact, it can't. That's the purpose of conducting due diligence. But I think it should
establish realist realistic expectations like how long will the buyer have to conduct due diligence?
What access to information will the buyer receive? Is financing a condition to completing
the transaction? Are there material third party approvals that the parties need already know will
be required? And what is the anticipated timeline for negotiating and executing the definitive
agreement? I also think there is value in being transparent about potential problems early.
If a seller knows that a major customer contract cannot be assigned without consent,
that is generally better addressed early than discovered just before closing. A goal should
be to establish a credible path to closing rather than simply agreeing on optimistic closing dates.
Now, let's talk about an important legal distinction. One of the most common questions
concerning letters of intent is whether they are legally binding. And the answer is that it
depends on the language of the document and the obligations the parties intend to create. In many
private company acquisitions, the principal commercial terms of an LOI are intended to be
non-binding. In other words, the buyer and the seller are expressing their current intentions
concerning the proposed transaction, but they are not necessarily entering into an enforcable
obligation to complete the acquisition. Typically, the parties contemplate negotiating and executing
a definitive purchase agreement before becoming obligated to consummate the transaction. But
that doesn't mean every provision in the LOI is non-binding. Certain pro provisions are frequently
intended to be enforceable. Exclusivity is one example. Confidentiality obligations are another,
although the parties may already have a separate non-disclosure agreement.
Other provisions may address transaction expenses, public announcements, access to information,
or how certain disputes will be handled. The important point is that the document should
clearly distinguish the provisions intended to be binding from those intended to be non-binding. I
also believe the LOI should be explicit about whether the parties intend to any obligation
to complete the transaction before the definitive agreement is signed. This is not something I would
leave to implication. A poorly drafted LOI can create uncertainty about the party's obligations
and that uncertainty can become a dispute in the if the transaction falls apart. But
there's another issue here that I think is just as important. Even when the principal business terms
are expressly non-binding, they can still have a substantial practical effect on negotiation.
Let's say a seller signs an LOI providing for a particular purchase price and payment structure.
Averal after several weeks of diligence, the seller decides that those terms are no longer
attractive and wants to renegotiate. The seller may have the contractual flexibility to propose
different terms depending on the document, but the buyer may reasonably respond to th that those were
the terms on which the buyer agreed to spend time, money, and and effort investigating the business.
The relationship can become strained and the parties may end up renegotiating issues they
believe they had already settled. So, I think it's important to distinguish legal enforcability from
commercial expectations. An LOI can be largely non-binding and still have a significant effect
on the direction of a transaction. That's why I don't recommend it treating it casually.
Let me put these issues together in a hypothetical example. Suppose a buyer and
a seller are negotiating the the acquisition of a Texas service business for $5 million. The seller
has operated the business for many years and is ready to exit. The buyer believes the business
is attractive and wants to move quickly. They agree on $5 million purchase price and sign a
relatively short LOI. The buyer receives a 90-day exclusivity period. Both parties are optimistic.
But once diligence begins, several issues emerge. First, the buyer expects the business
to be delivered with approximately $300,000 of normalized working capital. The seller however
believed that the accounts receivable in cash would remain with the seller. Second, the buyer
intended the finance part of the purchase price through a seller promisary note. The
seller believed the entire purchase price would be paid in cash at closing. Third, the buyer needs
bank financing and discovers that the lender has requirements affecting the seller note and other
aspects of the transaction. Fourth, the buyer learns that a major customer contract requires
consent before it can be assigned. And finally, the buyer's proposed purchase agreement includes
indemnification obligations that the seller considers substantially broader than expected. At
that point, both parties may become frustrated. The seller believes the buyer is changing the
deal. The buyer believes that they are customary requirements for acquiring an operating business.
In any case, both parties believe the other side is being unreasonable. Now, some of these issues
may have been impossible to resolve fully before diligence, and that's understandable, but several
of them could have been identified and addressed in the LOI. The parties could have established
their expl their expectations concerning working capital. They could have identified whether seller
financing was part of the proposed consideration. They could have discussed the intended transaction
structure and they could have considered whether the proposed closing timeline was realistic given
the financing and consent requirements. That doesn't guarantee the deal will close. Diligence
may still uncover issues that neither party anticipated, but it substantially reduces the
likelihood that the parties are spending time and money pursuing two different understandings of the
same transaction. And that's really the value of a well-negotiated LOI.
I want to finish by emphasizing that the buyer and seller are naturally going to
approach the LOI from different perspectives. A buyer generally wants flexibility. The buyer
hasn't completed diligence and may not yet know everything about the business. The buyer wants
enough time to access the buyer wants enough time and access to investigate the company,
assess the risk, arrange financing if necessary, and negotiate the definitive agreements. The
seller has different priorities. Seller wants certainty concerning the economics, confidence
that the buyer can complete the acquisition, and protection against spending months pursuing
a transaction that ultimately falls apart. Neither perspective is inherently unreasonable,
just different. The the purpose of negotiating the LOI is to establish a framework that reasonably
accommodates both both interests. And I think one of the mistakes parties can make is measuring the
quality of an LOI by its length. A short LOI isn't necessarily better because it's simple
and a long LOI isn't necessarily better because it's comprehensive. What matters is whether the
document resolves the issues that were material to the particular transaction. For some acquisitions,
the structure may be relatively straightforward and a concise LOI may be entirely appropriate. for
other transactions, particularly those involving collect payment arrangements, seller financing,
retained ownership, regulatory issues, or significant third-party consents. The parties
may need to address additional terms before moving forward. The important question isn't how many
pages the LOI contains, it's whether the parties understand the transaction they're proposing to
undertake. From my perspective as an M&A attorney, I want the LOI to establish three things. First,
establish the essential economic and structural terms of the proposed transaction. Second,
identify the material risks, conditions, and requirements that could affect whether
the transaction can close. And third, establish a reasonable process for diligence and negotiation
while clearly distinguishing between binding and non-binding obligations. If we've accomplished
those things, we've given the parties a much stronger foundation for negotiating the definitive
agreement. Ultimately, the goal isn't to win every point in the LOI. It's to establish a commercially
reasonable framework that allows the parties to move forward with a shared understanding of the
transaction. And in my view, that's what an effective letter of intent should accomplish.

That's perfectly reasonable, but they should have an initial understanding of what is being purchased and why. And if one party has a strong preference or a requirement concerning the structure that should be discussed before the other party invests substantial resources moving forward. Let's talk about exclusivity. This is one of the most important provisions that I think sellers sometimes underestimate. Most buyers are going to want some period of exclusivity after signing an LOI. In practical terms, the buyer wants the seller to stop negotiating with other potential purchasers while the buyer completes diligence, arranges finances, and negotiates the definitive agreements. From the buyer perspective, that request makes sense. An acquisition requires time and money. Buyers may engage attorneys, accountants, lenders, and other professionals. They may spend significant resources evaluating a business. A buyer generally doesn't want to undertake the process while the seller continues shopping the company to competing biders. Uh but we also need to appreciate that what the seller is giving up. Once the seller agrees to exclusivity, the seller may be taking the business off the market for a spec specified period. Other interested buyers may move on. The seller may lose negotiating leverage with them. And if the transaction ultimately falls apart and the seller may have to restart the process. That's why I view exclusivity as a meaningful commercial concession. It's not simply boilerplate. When I'm looking at an exclusivity provision, I want to know how much time the buyer actually needs and why. Is the buyer paying cash or does the transaction require third party financing? Does the buyer already uh reviewed meaningful financial information? Are there complicated regulatory, licensing, or third-party consent issues? How quickly can the buyer complete diligence? I also want to know whether the buyer has the ability to close a transaction. For example, a buyer requesting a lengthy exclusivity period without having made meaningful progress on financing presents a different risk profile than a buyer with committed capital and an established diligence process. That doesn't mean the seller should refuse exclusivity. In many acquisitions, a reasonable exclusivity period is necessary to move the deal deal forward, but I believe its duration and any extension rights should be negotiated in relation to the circumstances of the transaction. From the seller's perspective, I generally prefer defined deadlines, a clear end to the exclusivity obligation, and careful consideration on whether extensions are justified by the buyer's progress. The goal is to give a serious buyer sufficient time to complete the transaction without unnecessarily restricting the seller for an indefinite period. Another important function of the LOI is establishing the process for getting from preliminary agreement to closing. This is where due diligence and financing become particularly important. Due diligence is the buyer's opportunity to investigate the business. The buyer may review financial statements, tax returns, customer contracts, employment agreements, corporate records, liabilities, litigation, licenses, and numerous other matters. And depending on the transaction, that process may be fairly straightforward or quite extensive. What I want to avoid is an LOI that establishes an aggressive closing deadline without considering what actually needs to happen before the deal can close. For example, if the acquisition is bank financed, the lender may have its own underwriting requirements, collateral requirements, documentation, and approval process. These requirements may affect the transaction structure. The purchase agreement, any seller financing agreements, and ultimately the closing date. In an SBA financed acquisition, seller financing can represent additional issues uh because the lender may impose restrictions concerning payments, subordination, and other terms of the seller note depending on the applicable loan requirements. And the lender isn't necessarily going to approve every term that the buyer and seller have have negotiated. They have their own requirements. That can become a significant problem if the parties wait until late in the transaction to address the lender requirements preliminary. Similarly, if the buyer needs the consent of a landlord, a major customer or another third party, that process is affect may affect the timeline. The LOI doesn't need to resolve every diligence issue. In fact, it can't. That's the purpose of conducting due diligence. But I think it should establish realist realistic expectations like how long will the buyer have to conduct due diligence? What access to information will the buyer receive? Is financing a condition to completing the transaction? Are there material third party approvals that the parties need already know will be required? And what is the anticipated timeline for negotiating and executing the definitive agreement? I also think there is value in being transparent about potential problems early. If a seller knows that a major customer contract cannot be assigned without consent, that is generally better addressed early than discovered just before closing. A goal should be to establish a credible path to closing rather than simply agreeing on optimistic closing dates. Now, let's talk about an important legal distinction. One of the most common questions concerning letters of intent is whether they are legally binding. And the answer is that it depends on the language of the document and the obligations the parties intend to create. In many private company acquisitions, the principal commercial terms of an LOI are intended to be non-binding. In other words, the buyer and the seller are expressing their current intentions concerning the proposed transaction, but they are not necessarily entering into an enforcable obligation to complete the acquisition. Typically, the parties contemplate negotiating and executing a definitive purchase agreement before becoming obligated to consummate the transaction. But that doesn't mean every provision in the LOI is non-binding. Certain pro provisions are frequently intended to be enforceable. Exclusivity is one example. Confidentiality obligations are another, although the parties may already have a separate non-disclosure agreement. Other provisions may address transaction expenses, public announcements, access to information, or how certain disputes will be handled. The important point is that the document should clearly distinguish the provisions intended to be binding from those intended to be non-binding. I also believe the LOI should be explicit about whether the parties intend to any obligation to complete the transaction before the definitive agreement is signed. This is not something I would leave to implication. A poorly drafted LOI can create uncertainty about the party's obligations and that uncertainty can become a dispute in the if the transaction falls apart. But there's another issue here that I think is just as important. Even when the principal business terms are expressly non-binding, they can still have a substantial practical effect on negotiation. Let's say a seller signs an LOI providing for a particular purchase price and payment structure. Averal after several weeks of diligence, the seller decides that those terms are no longer attractive and wants to renegotiate. The seller may have the contractual flexibility to propose different terms depending on the document, but the buyer may reasonably respond to th that those were the terms on which the buyer agreed to spend time, money, and and effort investigating the business. The relationship can become strained and the parties may end up renegotiating issues they believe they had already settled. So, I think it's important to distinguish legal enforcability from commercial expectations. An LOI can be largely non-binding and still have a significant effect on the direction of a transaction. That's why I don't recommend it treating it casually. Let me put these issues together in a hypothetical example. Suppose a buyer and a seller are negotiating the the acquisition of a Texas service business for $5 million. The seller has operated the business for many years and is ready to exit. The buyer believes the business is attractive and wants to move quickly. They agree on $5 million purchase price and sign a relatively short LOI. The buyer receives a 90-day exclusivity period. Both parties are optimistic. But once diligence begins, several issues emerge. First, the buyer expects the business to be delivered with approximately $300,000 of normalized working capital. The seller however believed that the accounts receivable in cash would remain with the seller. Second, the buyer intended the finance part of the purchase price through a seller promisary note. The seller believed the entire purchase price would be paid in cash at closing. Third, the buyer needs bank financing and discovers that the lender has requirements affecting the seller note and other aspects of the transaction. Fourth, the buyer learns that a major customer contract requires consent before it can be assigned. And finally, the buyer's proposed purchase agreement includes indemnification obligations that the seller considers substantially broader than expected. At that point, both parties may become frustrated. The seller believes the buyer is changing the deal. The buyer believes that they are customary requirements for acquiring an operating business. In any case, both parties believe the other side is being unreasonable. Now, some of these issues may have been impossible to resolve fully before diligence, and that's understandable, but several of them could have been identified and addressed in the LOI. The parties could have established their expl their expectations concerning working capital. They could have identified whether seller financing was part of the proposed consideration. They could have discussed the intended transaction structure and they could have considered whether the proposed closing timeline was realistic given the financing and consent requirements. That doesn't guarantee the deal will close. Diligence may still uncover issues that neither party anticipated, but it substantially reduces the likelihood that the parties are spending time and money pursuing two different understandings of the same transaction. And that's really the value of a well-negotiated LOI. I want to finish by emphasizing that the buyer and seller are naturally going to approach the LOI from different perspectives. A buyer generally wants flexibility. The buyer hasn't completed diligence and may not yet know everything about the business. The buyer wants enough time to access the buyer wants enough time and access to investigate the company, assess the risk, arrange financing if necessary, and negotiate the definitive agreements. The seller has different priorities. Seller wants certainty concerning the economics, confidence that the buyer can complete the acquisition, and protection against spending months pursuing a transaction that ultimately falls apart. Neither perspective is inherently unreasonable, just different. The the purpose of negotiating the LOI is to establish a framework that reasonably accommodates both both interests. And I think one of the mistakes parties can make is measuring the quality of an LOI by its length. A short LOI isn't necessarily better because it's simple and a long LOI isn't necessarily better because it's comprehensive. What matters is whether the document resolves the issues that were material to the particular transaction. For some acquisitions, the structure may be relatively straightforward and a concise LOI may be entirely appropriate. for other transactions, particularly those involving collect payment arrangements, seller financing, retained ownership, regulatory issues, or significant third-party consents. The parties may need to address additional terms before moving forward. The important question isn't how many pages the LOI contains, it's whether the parties understand the transaction they're proposing to undertake. From my perspective as an M&A attorney, I want the LOI to establish three things. First, establish the essential economic and structural terms of the proposed transaction. Second, identify the material risks, conditions, and requirements that could affect whether the transaction can close. And third, establish a reasonable process for diligence and negotiation while clearly distinguishing between binding and non-binding obligations. If we've accomplished those things, we've given the parties a much stronger foundation for negotiating the definitive agreement. Ultimately, the goal isn't to win every point in the LOI. It's to establish a commercially reasonable framework that allows the parties to move forward with a shared understanding of the transaction. And in my view, that's what an effective letter of intent should accomplish.

metadata.title: Why a Letter of Intent Is Critical to the Sale of a Business
metadata.author: Oberman Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
If you are buying or selling a business, which document matters most?

Stuart Oberman says the Letter of Intent may be the most important piece of the whole puzzle. His firm handles roughly 100 business purchase and sale transactions a year, and the LOI remains one of the most important provisions in every one of them.

In this podcast you will learn:
• What an LOI does before due diligence and definitive agreements begin
• Which key principles it establishes: price, structure, timelines and exclusivity
• Why it protects everyone in the negotiation

Before you sign anything, hear it from an attorney who sees these deals every week.

🔗 http://obermanlaw.com/business-law

Listen to the full podcast here: https://www.buzzsprout.com/2184162/episodes/20073568

#StuartOberman #ObermanLawFirm #LOI #MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessLaw #BusinessOwners

What Really Happens When You Sign a Letter of Intent to Buy a Business?

Are you a real estate investor or business owner looking to expand? Book a discovery call with Beau to learn all the ways he can help you - http://bookwithbeau.com/
Join my new Business Ownership Academy community on Skool - http://businessownershipacademy.com/

Q: I've signed a letter of intent (LOI) to buy a business. I have the seller's P&L and my financials together. I went to my local bank; they don't seem interested in helping me finance this acquisition. The business, by the way, is a landscape business that does landscaping and builds outdoor patios. What happens now? Thanks!

Paul 

Timestamps:
(00:01) Paul asks about the letter of intent to buy a business.
(00:25) Explanation about traditional bankers and the importance of working with a bank specialized in SBA loans and being a PLP (preferred lender).

(01:26) Beau's fee structure, commitment to quick feedback, and responsiveness compared to traditional bankers.
(02:04) The common misconception about local banks and the national footprint of most SBA lenders.

If you'd like to ask me a question about real estate, do it here -- https://investorfinancingpodcast.com/ask

💥 Thanks for watching 💥
#Finance #BusinessAcquisition #SBALoan

🎥 The video interviews we do on IFP will help you scale your real estate business and learn how to finance all your projects. 

About the Channel: Want to structure your investments in the right and secure way?

metadata.title: Why a Letter of Intent Is Critical to the Sale of a Business
metadata.author: Oberman Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
If you are buying or selling a business, which document matters most?


Stuart Oberman says the Letter of Intent may be the most important piece of the whole puzzle. His firm handles roughly 100 business purchase and sale transactions a year, and the LOI remains one of the most important provisions in every one of them.


In this podcast you will learn:


• What an LOI does before due diligence and definitive agreements begin


• Which key principles it establishes: price, structure, timelines and exclusivity


• Why it protects everyone in the negotiation


Before you sign anything, hear it from an attorney who sees these deals every week.


🔗 http://obermanlaw.com/business-law


#StuartOberman #ObermanLawFirm #LOI #MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessLaw #BusinessOwners

metadata.title: The Anatomy of an LOI
metadata.author: Lockaby PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
A Letter of Intent, or LOI, helps set the framework for an M&A transaction before the parties move toward a final purchase agreement.

In this video, Matt Lockaby breaks down what typically goes into an LOI, including the proposed purchase price, deal structure, timelines, confidentiality and exclusivity provisions, conditions to closing, and common issues buyers and sellers should watch for.

Learn more about the M&A process and explore our M&A Lifecycle series: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLv-HqV0cc2XSYjQ06kh7-FkTe1LzKaCIl&si=EVN9eM5nMS56zSsY

Lockaby PLLC advises buyers and sellers throughout mergers and acquisitions, from initial negotiations and due diligence through closing.

Follow us on socials! 

Facebook: facebook.com/lockabypllc 
Instagram: instagram.com/lockaby_pllc 
LinkedIn: linkedin.com/lockaby-pllc 
Website: https://LockabyLaw.com 
Subscribe to our newsletter! http://eepurl.com/hOJJNz

metadata.title: Walker Deibel | Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game
metadata.author: Darius Mirshahzadeh
metadata.shortDescription:
Most entrepreneurs are taught that the path to success starts with a blank page, a new idea, a startup, a grind from zero. But what if the real opportunity is in what's already built? 

Walker Deibel, Wall Street Journal bestselling author of “Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game,” has spent over a decade proving that acquiring existing businesses is one of the most powerful and overlooked paths to entrepreneurial wealth. He has bought roughly 10 companies outright, been inside over 100 deals, and helped hundreds of entrepreneurs acquire more than a billion dollars in small businesses. And his message is simple: you don't have to build from scratch to build something great.

In this episode of The Greatness Machine, Darius sits down with Walker Deibel to explore the acquisition entrepreneur mindset, why high margins matter more than almost anything else, and where the biggest opportunities in private markets exist right now.

In this episode, Darius and Walker will discuss:
(00:00) Introduction and Excitement for the Episode
(02:53) The Power of Alignment and Purpose
(05:46) The Journey of Writing and Publishing a Book
(08:38) The Entrepreneurial Journey: Successes and Failures
(11:33) Walker Deibel's Background and Business Philosophy
(14:21) The Importance of Acquisitions in Entrepreneurship
(17:16) The Intersection of Old and New Economies
(20:21) Investing in Boring Businesses for Stability
(23:48) Identifying High-Potential Companies
(29:11) The Importance of Margins in Business
(37:31) Investing in Businesses vs. Running Them
(46:25) Overcoming Barriers to Greatness

Walker Deibel is a serial acquisition entrepreneur, WSJ and USA Today bestselling author, Emmy-nominated film producer, and award-winning M&A advisor. He is the creator of Acquisition Lab, the elite business buying accelerator, and founder of Build Wealth, an alternative investment firm offering private market opportunities he personally invests in. His bestselling book, Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game, was recognized by Forbes as one of the top 7 books all entrepreneurs must read and is now used in university programs across the country. Walker has participated in over 100 private transactions, acquired seven companies over ten years, and his writing has been featured in Inc, Entrepreneur, Forbes, Fast Company, and Harvard Business Review.

metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying a business is one of the fastest ways to build real wealth—but it’s also one of the easiest ways to lose it if you make rookie mistakes. Too many first-time buyers go in unprepared, take high salaries too soon, or try to change everything overnight.

In this video, I break down the most common mistakes first-time business buyers make—and how to avoid costly missteps that could sink your acquisition before it even gets off the ground.

You'll learn:
✅ Why taking a high salary right away is a major mistake
✅ How to navigate deal negotiations without walking away empty-handed
✅ The right time to start making changes after acquisition
✅ Why business ownership is an emotional rollercoaster—and how to handle it

I share lessons from my own acquisitions, including why integration timing is critical, how to avoid the emotional traps of ownership, and the number one thing you need to do to set yourself up for success.

If you’re serious about building real wealth and buying back your freedom, this 80-minute masterclass is for you. Right now, millions of profitable “boring” businesses are quietly changing hands as owners retire, creating the biggest wealth transfer of our generation.

This isn’t about chasing flashy startups or gambling on the stock market. It’s about learning how to spot cash-flowing businesses, buy them without millions in the bank, and turn them into wealth-generating machines.

I’ve done it myself, going from a burned-out employee to owning businesses that generate tens of millions in revenue. And now I’m giving you the exact playbook: how to find, buy, and scale businesses that pay you from day one.

We're taking back Main Street.

metadata.shortDescription:
Buy Then Build, written by Walker Deibel, presents a compelling alternative to the traditional, high-risk startup model. Most startups fail because they attempt to build complex infrastructure from scratch while simultaneously hunting for product-market fit and revenue, leading to a precarious cash-burning cycle. Deibel advocates for "acquisition entrepreneurship," a strategy that bypasses these volatile early stages. Instead of starting from zero, aspiring entrepreneurs purchase existing, profitable businesses, allowing them to step into the role of CEO with established revenue, customers, and infrastructure already in place.

This approach reframes business ownership as a form of active financial engineering rather than just pure innovation. By utilizing the company’s ongoing cash flow and strategic financing—such as SBA-backed loans—entrepreneurs can leverage ownership to generate significant wealth while minimizing risk. The "buy then build" system emphasizes shifting one’s mindset from a technical worker to an investor and visionary leader, focusing on operational improvements to unlock hidden value. Ultimately, it provides a more predictable and sustainable roadmap for achieving autonomy and long-term success compared to the speculative nature of traditional venture-backed startups.

segments.text: We have all heard that nine out of 10
startups do not survive their early
years. Data indicates that at best only
half of all startups survive past the
launch phase. Out of those that do
manage to survive, the vast majority
remain extremely small. Only 4% of all
companies in the United States ever
exceed $1 million in revenue.
When we examine these numbers on a
structural level, we are left with the
stark fact that well over 99% of all
startups either fail completely or never
achieve meaningful financial or
impactful scale. The startup phase is
quite literally a company killer.
It is odd that despite the growing
global obsession with entrepreneurship,
society has not engineered a more
predictable way to bypass this highly
volatile launch phase and build
sustainability from the beginning.
Startups force founders to build a
complex business infrastructure while
simultaneously hunting for revenue to
support it. Often leading to a fatal
crash when the capital run out before
product market fit is achieved.
Fortunately, an alternative path exists.
An entrepreneurship hack that allows
ambitious individuals to skip the
startup runway altogether. This path is
called acquisition entrepreneurship.
Instead of starting from scratch and
building an infrastructure from zero,
the acquisition entrepreneur begins by
purchasing an existing profitable
business. This allows them to step into
the role of chief executive officer from
day one, inheriting a sustainable
infrastructure that already has
customers, brand awareness, experienced
employees, and most importantly,
established revenue and profits. By
combining the sustainable foundation of
an existing small business with the
drive, energy, and innovation of a new
entrepreneur,
a highly potent recipe for value
creation is formed.
Practicing acquisition entrepreneurship
flips the traditional startup model on
its head. While startups build
infrastructure in the hope of finding
revenue, acquisition entrepreneurship
buys profitable revenue first, then
builds from there. This immediate
profitability eliminates the extreme
survival stress of managing a cash
negative burn rate, allowing the new CEO
to focus on managing, innovating, and
scaling an already successful
enterprise.
Walker Dybo's own career is a perfect
testament to the transformative power of
this approach. Following the collapse of
Viewpoint, an adviser who had assisted
him in a previous transaction identified
an established print management and
distribution company for sale. The
business was generating several million
dollars in revenue and possessed a
handful of highly respected corporate
clients.
Upon analyzing the business, Walker Dyel
and his team realized that although
print management was valuable to its
customers, the company's real
underutilized core competency lay in its
supply chain inventory management and
fulfillment capabilities.
They recognized an opportunity to build
a sophisticated business-to- business
fulfillment platform providing a private
customized Amazon-like experience for
corporate clients with multiple national
locations.
Walker Dyel acquired the company in
early 2015 with a low six-f figureure
personal equity investment and a bank
loan. Utilizing the company's existing
cash flow, his team hired software
engineers, built a proprietary
e-commerce storefront, and rolled it out
to tens of thousands of users
nationwide,
achieving the exact goal they had spent
months trying and failing to reach at
Viewpoint.
The results were immediate. Within the
first 11 months, his team more than
