risks they are taking on. This is
completely normal. The buyer must lean
on their prep work and process to
maintain their composure and push the
deal across the finish line.
To ensure a highly successful transition
in the first 90 days, the new CEO must
establish a systematic assess then
execute routine.
The first 30 days must be spent entirely
on assessment,
learning the existing processes,
building rapport with employees, and
meeting key customers and suppliers.
The CEO should avoid making any
significant operational or personnel
changes during this period as rapid
changes can create extreme anxiety and
disrupt productivity.
In the second month, the CEO turns their
attention to learning how the money
flows, putting together a 13-week cash
flow projection to understand the
company's liquidity demands.
By the third month, the CEO can
confidently implement strategic
optimizations,
launching growth initiatives and setting
clear expectations for their team,
driving the company to new heights of
success.
The entrepreneurial landscape is on the
cusp of an unprecedented revolution.
Over the next two decades, retiring baby
boomers will transition ownership of
millions of small businesses, triggering
what Walker Dybel calls the largest
transfer of wealth in human history.
This is not merely a macroeconomic
statistic. It is a profound invitation
to ambitious individuals who refuse to
be bound by the traditional corporate
ladder. For those who possess the
courage to act, this transition
represents the ultimate gateway to
financial independence, self-direction,
and lasting legacy. Throughout this
book, the foundational principles of
acquisition entrepreneurship have shown
that the most reliable path to business
ownership does not require starting from
zero.
Starting from scratch forces the
entrepreneur to navigate a perilous road
where the odds of failure are
overwhelmingly stacked against them. In
contrast, by choosing to buy an existing
profitable enterprise, the acquisition
entrepreneur begins their journey with
an established customer base, trained
employees, a proven product or service,
and immediate cash flow. As Walker Dybel
famously notes, buy then build is a
scalable model that allows you to buy a
profitable infrastructure and then layer
growth on top.
The existing company is not a static
asset. It is a high-powered engine that
is ready to be optimized and scaled. To
seize this historic opportunity, one
must let go of the romanticized startup
myth and embrace the cold analytical
reality of the market. Success in this
field belongs to those who think like
investors and act like leaders. It
belongs to those who align their
personal strengths, secure reliable
adviserss, and execute their searches
with relentless systematic focus.
As Walker Dybo reminds us, true autonomy
is not about starting from scratch. It
is about taking control of an existing
engine and driving it forward.

videos.full_text: We have all heard that nine out of 10 startups do not survive their early years. Data indicates that at best only half of all startups survive past the launch phase. Out of those that do manage to survive, the vast majority remain extremely small. Only 4% of all companies in the United States ever exceed $1 million in revenue. When we examine these numbers on a structural level, we are left with the stark fact that well over 99% of all startups either fail completely or never achieve meaningful financial or impactful scale. The startup phase is quite literally a company killer. It is odd that despite the growing global obsession with entrepreneurship, society has not engineered a more predictable way to bypass this highly volatile launch phase and build sustainability from the beginning. Startups force founders to build a complex business infrastructure while simultaneously hunting for revenue to support it. Often leading to a fatal crash when the capital run out before product market fit is achieved. Fortunately, an alternative path exists. An entrepreneurship hack that allows ambitious individuals to skip the startup runway altogether. This path is called acquisition entrepreneurship. Instead of starting from scratch and building an infrastructure from zero, the acquisition entrepreneur begins by purchasing an existing profitable business. This allows them to step into the role of chief executive officer from day one, inheriting a sustainable infrastructure that already has customers, brand awareness, experienced employees, and most importantly, established revenue and profits. By combining the sustainable foundation of an existing small business with the drive, energy, and innovation of a new entrepreneur, a highly potent recipe for value creation is formed. Practicing acquisition entrepreneurship flips the traditional startup model on its head. While startups build infrastructure in the hope of finding revenue, acquisition entrepreneurship buys profitable revenue first, then builds from there. This immediate profitability eliminates the extreme survival stress of managing a cash negative burn rate, allowing the new CEO to focus on managing, innovating, and scaling an already successful enterprise. Walker Dybo's own career is a perfect testament to the transformative power of this approach. Following the collapse of Viewpoint, an adviser who had assisted him in a previous transaction identified an established print management and distribution company for sale. The business was generating several million dollars in revenue and possessed a handful of highly respected corporate clients. Upon analyzing the business, Walker Dyel and his team realized that although print management was valuable to its customers, the company's real underutilized core competency lay in its supply chain inventory management and fulfillment capabilities. They recognized an opportunity to build a sophisticated business-to- business fulfillment platform providing a private customized Amazon-like experience for corporate clients with multiple national locations. Walker Dyel acquired the company in early 2015 with a low six-f figureure personal equity investment and a bank loan. Utilizing the company's existing cash flow, his team hired software engineers, built a proprietary e-commerce storefront, and rolled it out to tens of thousands of users nationwide, achieving the exact goal they had spent months trying and failing to reach at Viewpoint. The results were immediate. Within the first 11 months, his team more than doubled the company's value. To accelerate this growth further, Walker Dyel acquired a local promotional product and corporate apparel business the following year and merged it into the fulfillment platform. This strategic acquisition immediately boosted the company's revenue by 20% and added 500 existing customers funded entirely by the cash flow of the original business. Over the next 10 years, Walker Dyel went on to acquire seven different companies and make minority investments in many others. These acquisitions spanned book printing, online distribution, promotional products, e-commerce, education, and metal fabrication. In almost every case, he successfully made these businesses far more valuable than they were at the time of purchase, eventually experiencing highly profitable exits, the ultimate crown jewel achievement that startups rarely reach. Buying an existing business is a proven system masterfully executed by veteran entrepreneurs and it is increasingly taking hold in top tier business schools. By shifting the order of mastery, starting as a CEO of an existing company and then bringing innovation, acquisition entrepreneurs bypass the startup trap and engineer highly predictable wealth. To appreciate the sheer scale of the opportunity, one must examine the psychological toll of the startup journey. Founders are often trapped in a cycle of constant raising of capital, delilution of ownership, and pivoting products based on speculative assumptions. They burn through millions of investor cash to build a brand only to realize that the market does not want what they are selling. When viewpoint failed, Walker Dybel did not merely lose a business. He lost a piece of his identity. a common trauma for starting from scratch entrepreneurs. In sharp contrast, buying an existing business grounds your entrepreneurial spirit in a proven reality. The cash flow from an established printing, manufacturing, or distribution company is an active living buffer that absorbs strategic mistakes. When Walker Dyel purchased Corly Printing, he did not need to hope that customers would buy his digital books. The order books were already full. He simply had to implement modern digital print technologies and optimize operations, converting a legacy business into one of the top 2% printing companies in the nation. This active optimization is the heart of what Walker Dyel terms the buy then build system. [clears throat] It allows the new CEO to focus their creative energy on high-level strategy and innovation rather than survival. Starting from scratch is like swimming against a heavy current where the majority of your energy is spent simply trying not to drown. Buying an existing company is like jumping on a high-speed train that is already moving in the right direction. Your only job is to guide the train, upgrade the engine, and add new cars. The sustainable infrastructure of a small business is a powerful shield against economic volatility. It provides the necessary resources to hire specialized developers, acquire complimentary competitors, and expand into new geographic territories. The combination of an established business's historical success with the vision of a growthminded CEO creates a powerful unstoppable engine of value creation. [clears throat] This is the book Buy Then Build. A strategic road map for anyone with the ambition and courage to step off the traditional path and seize control of their destiny. The economics of acquisition versus starting from scratch. To understand the power of acquisition entrepreneurship, we must examine why the venture capital model is fundamentally flawed for the individual entrepreneur. Elite venturebacked startups enjoy immense media attention, celebrating the tiny fraction of companies that achieve the coveted unicorn status. >> [gasps] >> Startups aim to become the next massive disruptor raising millions from venture capital funds to aggressively capture market share. However, Shakar Goch, a prominent Harvard Business Review lecturer, revealed through his research that even venture capital funded startups, which have the backing of the best investment teams and raise an average of $41 million per launch, suffer from a 75% failure rate. This means that despite raising astronomical sums of money, three out of four venture-backed companies still fail to achieve sustainability. For a venture capital fund, this model makes perfect sense. They manage massive portfolios, typically averaging $350 million per fund, which allows them to invest in 10 to 14 companies. A single massive home run is enough to pay for the fund's losses and deliver exceptional returns to the passive investors. [gasps] The venture capitalist is perfectly comfortable with a 75% failure rate because they are diversified. The individual entrepreneur, however, is not diversified. They do not own a portfolio of 14 startups. they own one. [gasps] The economic advantages of portfolio diversification do not extend to the founder, meaning they are making a highly concentrated bet in a game where the odds of failure are overwhelmingly stacked against them. For the entrepreneur, accepting venture capital is often a reckless gamble that results in losing equity, losing control, and statistically losing everything. Starting a VCbacked company believing you will be the next cover success story is a highly risky proposition. It is often a punishment for failing to understand basic probability. In sharp contrast, acquisition entrepreneurship offers an asymmetrical risk profile that favors the individual. When an entrepreneur acquires an existing company, typically one generating over $1 million in revenue, [gasps] they inherit a profitable infrastructure from day one. They do not have to spend months raising capital, selling off company stock, and trying to build a market from scratch. They begin with established cash flow, a loyal customer list, and experienced employees, completely eliminating the startup runway. Furthermore, the macroeconomic landscape of the United States has created a massive historic opportunity for acquisition entrepreneurs. >> [gasps] >> The baby boomer generation owns more small businesses than any other generation in history. In 2013, baby boomers owned approximately 12 million small businesses, representing a staggering 43% of all small businesses in the country. That same year, baby boomers began retiring at a rate of 9,000 per day, a number that expanded to 11,000 per day by 2021. Between 2013 and 2029, almost 77 million people representing roughly 20% of the entire United States population will enter retirement. As a result, it is estimated that over $10 trillion in existing business value will need to change hands. The boomers are already selling off their established, highly successful companies at record rates. Because the supply of available small businesses is increasing so rapidly, it is creating an unprecedented buyers market. The infrastructure built by the hard work of generations past is now available for purchase at the most affordable levels ever experienced, allowing a new generation of leaders to step into ownership. Most people remain completely blind to this historic wealth transfer because they believe that buying a business requires millions of personal wealth. This is a common misconception. >> [clears throat] >> In reality, buying an existing business is far more affordable than starting a business or buying a residential home. According to statistics from Babson College and the Wall Street Journal, the average startup in the United States launches with approximately $65,000 in invested capital. Similarly, the average down payment on a home for millennials in the fastest growing counties is roughly $66,000. Because privately held businesses under $10 million in revenue sell for lower multiples than middle market or publicly traded corporations. A $65,000 personal equity investment can be leveraged. By partnering with a bank that offers a loan backed by the Small Business Administration, SBA, the entrepreneur can secure a 90% loan to purchase a business for $650,000. A company of this size typically sells at a multiple of three times its adjusted earnings. This means the company is generating over $216,000 in discretionary earnings and assuming a 15% margin is generating over $1.4 million in revenue. To further appreciate the contrast between acquisition and venture capital, one must look at how ownership and control are structured. In a traditional VCbacked startup, the founder is forced to sell significant portions of their equity in multiple funding rounds. By the time the company reaches a liquidity event, the founder often owns less than 10% of their own creation. Furthermore, venture capital comes with intense board oversight where outside investors can veto strategic decisions, push for premature scaling, or even terminate the founder from their role as CEO. [sighs] The acquisition entrepreneur, on the other hand, utilizes bank debt rather than equity partners to fund the transaction. Because the Small Business Administration guarantees up to 75% of the loan to the lending bank, the buyer is able to secure a 90% leveraged position while retaining 100% of the company's stock. This means the buyer enjoys absolute autonomy and complete control over their corporate strategy. They do not have to report to a board of directors or appease impatient venture capitalists. They are the undisputed master of their own business. This structural autonomy allows the acquisition entrepreneur to prioritize long-term sustainable value creation over short-term speculative growth. VCbacked startups are under intense pressure to achieve rapid exponential scale, often forcing them to make highly risky strategic decisions. Small businesses, however, can grow organically and profitably at their own pace. By utilizing the company's ongoing cash flow to reinvest in operational efficiency and marketing, the CEO builds a highly stable cashgenerating asset that can withstand economic downturns. This stability is why small business acquisition holds an incredibly low default rate of roughly 2% according to statistics from the Small Business Administration. In comparison, three out of four venture-backed startups fail to return their investors [clears throat] capital. When an entrepreneur chooses acquisition over starting from scratch, they are choosing a proven statistical pathway to success. They are refusing to participate in a broken startup game and instead leveraging the macroeconomic force of the retiring baby boomer wealth transfer to build an enduring legacy. To think like an acquisition entrepreneur, one must first learn to think like an investor. Traditional startups focus entirely on the appreciation lever, attempting to create value out of nothing. Acquisition entrepreneurship, however, is a model of active financial engineering. It borrows the highly successful leveraged buyout LBO business model of the private equity industry and applies it to small business speculation. To understand business ownership as an investment vehicle, we can look at the empirical research surrounding wealth creation in the United States. In their landmark best-selling book, The Millionaire Next Door, Thomas Stanley and William Dano established that effectively 100% of non-retired millionaires in the United States own their own businesses. Out of this group, roughly 20% are professionals running service or medical practices, while the remaining 80% are small business owners and entrepreneurs. John Bowen, the CEO of CEG Worldwide and co-author of the state of the affluent, similarly concluded that 80% of the affluent are either retired or business owners and an astounding 91% of individuals with a net worth over $5 million own their own company. These statistics demonstrate a powerful macroeconomic truth. [gasps] Owning your own business is the single best way for most people to build real generational wealth. But to maximize wealth creation while managing risk, the entrepreneur must evaluate three core investment fundamentals. return on investment, margin of safety, and upside potential. The concept of return on investment, ROI, is simple. If an investor injects $100 into an asset and it generates $6 in cash back every year, they receive an annual cash flow ROI of 6%. If they sell the asset after 7 years for $120, they realize a total return of $62 on their initial $100, resulting in an annual compounded ROI of 8.9%. When evaluating a potential business acquisition, the cash flow the company generates is the single most important factor. It is the driver behind the valuation and ultimately what the buyer is paying for. While safe United States Treasury bonds return 2.5 to 3% and real estate cap rates average around 9%. A small business with under $5 million in revenue typically trades at a multiple of 2.5 to six times its annual cash flow. This low multiple translates into an extraordinarily high return on investment. To see how this financial engineering operates in a realworld business over a longer horizon, let us look at a more detailed model of NY's journey. Suppose Nancy identifies an established business generating $216,000 in annual sellers discretionary earnings SDE on $1.44 million of revenue. At a multiple of 3.2 times SDE, the purchase price is set at $691,200. To ensure a smooth transition, Nancy adds $200,000 for inventory and working capital and $50,000 for closing costs and professional fees, bringing the total cash requirement to $941,200. Working with an SBA preferred lender to secure a 90% leveraged position, [clears throat] she injects a 10% personal down payment of $94,120 out of pocket with the bank providing the remaining $847,080 as an SBA loan at a 6% interest rate. Because the bank loan is fully amortized over 10 years, the monthly debt service payments will require approximately $9,400 out of the business's $18,000 in monthly SDE, leaving over $8,600 in monthly pre-tax cash flow to Nancy. This means that despite paying off a major bank loan, she receives over $100,000 in annual cash flow, a cash oncash annual ROI of over 100% on her initial $94,120 investment. The power of active value creation becomes clear when we project these numbers over a 10-year horizon. Suppose Nancy uses her CEO skill set to grow the business's revenue by a healthy, modest rate of 10% every year. The business will exceed $2 million in revenue in year 4 and reach over $3.6 million in annual revenue by year 10. Assuming the SDE margin remains constant at 15%. NY's annual SDE will expand to over $540,000. At this point, the 10-year bank loan is fully paid off, meaning the $9,400 in monthly debt payments now flows directly to her as additional cash flow. Furthermore, Nancy has built up significant equity. In year 11, she agrees to exit the business at a multiple of four times SDE, selling the company for $2.16 million and receiving an additional $300,000 for working capital and inventory, resulting in a total exit price of $2.46 million. NY's total pre-tax compensation over the 11 years less the bank debt payments is a staggering 5,747,934. This represents an astronomical 45% compounded annual growth rate on her original 94,120 down payment. In comparison, the same $94,120 invested in a balanced stock portfolio generating 8% would have appreciated to only $219,000. Furthermore, NY's debt payments are actively building equity in her business. Every monthly payment of $9,400 consists of both interest and principal. The principal portion of the payment directly reduces the outstanding balance of the bank loan, effectively acting as a forced savings account that builds her personal net worth. Over the 10-year life of the loan, NY's monthly payments will systematically pay off the entire $847,080 principle, leaving her with a highly valuable debtfree asset. This equity buildup is a critical component of wealth creation that passive stock portfolios or real estate investments cannot match. In real estate, the property's value is heavily tied to market appreciation, which is entirely outside the investor's control. In a small business, however, Nancy can actively build value by implementing operational improvements, expanding sales channels, and growing SDE. By combining the wealth generating power of active management with the compounding effects of financial leverage, acquisition entrepreneurs can engineer an extraordinary level of personal wealth. The CEO mindset shifting from technical worker to visionary leader. Operating a successful business as its CEO from day one requires a powerful mental realignment. Walker Dybel conceptualizes the successful entrepreneur as a three-legged stool requiring all three legs of attitude, aptitude, and action to function in perfect harmony. The first leg attitude is the single largest predictor of long-term entrepreneurial success. It is heavily determined by possessing a growth mindset. Carol Dwek, a world-renowned Stanford University psychologist and author of Mindset: How We Can Learn to Fulfill Our Potential, pioneered the study of fixed versus growth mindsets. A person with a dominant fixed mindset views their intelligence and talents as innate permanent gifts. They believe that effortless success is the hallmark of true talent and that having to exert enormous effort is a sign of weakness. [gasps] Fixed mindset individuals are highly risk averse. They fear failure because they perceive a setback as a permanent reflection of their lack of ability. In contrast, a growth mindset views intelligence and talents as malleable qualities that can be developed and expanded through dedication, strategies, and learning. Growthminded individuals view effort as the natural path to mastery, embrace challenges, and are inspired by the success of others. For an acquisition entrepreneur, cultivating a growth mindset is an enormous psychological advantage. The belief that things are malleable creates an immediate interest in solving market problems, re-engineering outdated business practices, and implementing ongoing improvements. Dwek's research indicates that organizations have collective mindsets as well. And as the leader of a newly acquired company, the CEO must model a growthoriented attitude. This mindset can be actively cultivated. The first step is identifying when your internal thoughts take on a fixed defensive framework, the voice that arises during setbacks, criticism, or challenges. By recognizing that you have a choice in how you interpret these difficulties, you can actively talk back to the fixed voice with a growthminded response, taking responsibility for the outcome. Seligman's perma formula, positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and achievement, further aligns the entrepreneurs's personal well-being with their professional goals. Most entrepreneurs are highly achievement-driven, motivated by the deep personal satisfaction of accomplishing difficult complex goals. Achievement rather than praise or financial reward is the primary driver that pushes them to persist through obstacles. The second leg of the stool is aptitude, which comprises both raw intelligence and competencies. High intellectual ability is a powerful predictor of entrepreneurial performance, but raw IQ is fixed by adulthood. Fortunately, emerging data supports that emotional intelligence, EQ, is an even more powerful driver of leadership success than IQ. And many key competencies can be actively learned. Walker Dybel tested this by evaluating a list of character traits commonly associated with successful CEOs of companies generating between 1 million and $20 million in revenue. ratios and assessments show that being organized, methodical, and laser focused actually holds zero correlation with CEO success. In business, ambiguity reigns supreme and being laser focused can be a major liability if the market landscape is shifting. Successful entrepreneurs must possess strategic thinking skills, strategic agility, and a high tolerance for managing ambiguity. They must be decisive, self-confident, and extremely thick skinned. Perfectionism, too, is a clear negative. In entrepreneurship, rapid action is consistently rewarded over perfection. Calculating risk is essential. While entrepreneurs are publicly perceived as high-risk gamblers, the most successful ones are highly calculated and view themselves as risk averse. The third leg of the stool is action, which requires the entrepreneur to define what their daily activities will look like. Business activities are typically divided into two core overarching functions. Revenue generation, sales and marketing, and operational execution, accounting and profit management. Gino Wickman, the creator of the EOS system and author of traction, defines two distinct types of business owners, visionaries and integrators. Visionaries are the creative force of the company, running 60 m an hour to push the business into the future, while integrators organize, coordinate, and profitably execute those ideas. In smaller businesses, the CEO must initially play both roles. To identify the right acquisition target, the entrepreneur must complete a personal SWAT analysis and build a comprehensive resume using action verbs to quantify their past achievements. By defining the activities they excel at and the tasks they wish to avoid, the buyer identifies their sweet spot. They avoid the fatal mistake described by Michael Gerber in the E-Myth of assuming that understanding the technical work of a business qualifies a person to run a business that does that technical work. The three A's provide a powerful target framework to cultivate a highly effective CEO mindset. The entrepreneur must learn to actively manage their own psychological and emotional energy. Seligman's perma model reveals that human flourishing requires positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and achievement. For a business leader, engagement is achieved when they are working within their sweet spot, performing tasks that align with their natural strengths and interests. If a CEO is naturally an operational integrator, forcing themselves to spend 80 hours a week on cold calling and outbound sales will quickly lead to burnout. Conversely, if a visionary revenue generator is bogged down in the minutia of inventory counting and bookkeeping, they will stifle the company's growth. The acquisition entrepreneur must have the self-awareness to recognize their weaknesses and build a team that shores up those gaps. Strategic hiring is not a sign of weakness. It is the hallmark of strategic leadership. Furthermore, the transition from employee to CEO requires letting go of the need for immediate approval. In a corporate career, employees are rewarded for following rules and pleasing their superiors. As the CEO of your own company, you are the final authority. There is no boss to give you a gold star or validate your decisions. The market is your only judge and the market is completely impartial. This absolute autonomy can be terrifying for individuals with a fixed mindset who rely on external validation to confirm their intelligence. The growthminded leader, however, views the market's feedback as data to learn from. If a growth initiative fails, they do not perceive themselves as a failure. They simply analyze what went wrong, pivot their strategy, and try again. This absolute resilience and grit are what allow successful CEOs to navigate the extreme ambiguity and volatility of the business world, guiding their company to long-term sustainability. Mapping the target, the four acquisition profiles and core filters. With a clear understanding of their personal strengths, the entrepreneur must outline what their target company will look like. This begins by mapping the potential business's opportunity profile to the buyer's strengths and goals. Walker Dyel developed the acquisition opportunity profiles matrix which segments growth opportunities into four distinct quadrants eternally profitable turnaround high growth and platform. The first profile, eternally profitable, describes established, mature businesses that serve a perpetual market need that is highly unlikely to go away. A classic example was profiled in the New York Times where three former venture capitalists purchased a snow removal and landscaping company. Although snow plowing is a mature slow growth industry, it is highly geographic and completely insulated from technological disruption. As long as the service is excellent, customers rarely switch, protecting the company from new market entrance. These stable cash cows provide safe, dependable economics, making them ideal for consolidation plays. The second profile is the turnaround which describes the acquisition of a company that has fallen on hard times. Turnarounds are the business equivalent of a fixeruppper and represent an exceptional place to create value for buyers who possess strong operational, financial, and cash flow management expertise. Because these companies are underperforming, they are typically valued at a steep discount, often close to liquidation or book value. The turnaround process is highly demanding and requires a series of difficult, uncomfortable decisions. Overhead must be reduced immediately, which often requires layoffs on day one. The key to a successful turnaround is ensuring the company possesses a strong underlying product market fit and ongoing market demand. The upside potential lives in the operational improvements while the risk is tied to the buyer's ability to execute. The third profile is high growth which is exciting and attractive but introduces significant risk. A company experiencing rapid revenue growth is highly desirable. But because growth drives value, the buyer will pay a higher multiple of earnings for that prior performance. If the growth rate does not materialize under the new owner's leadership, the high monthly debt service payments can quickly become a devastating overhead expense, crushing the business's margins and reducing its margin of safety. Furthermore, rapid growth typically translates into extremely tight cash flow because the company must constantly reinvest its earnings into inventory and infrastructure. High growth acquisitions introduce risk by increasing the variance of results. It is essentially the opposite of a turnaround. Instead of the risk of a company in trouble, it is the risk of a company in high demand. The fourth profile is the platform which represents the ideal target for most acquisition entrepreneurs. In private equity, a platform refers to the first company a firm acquires in a specific industry which they intend to grow organically or through add-on acquisitions. In acquisition entrepreneurship, a platform company is a stable, profitable business where the buyer operates directly as the active CEO. The main driver of a platform is that the company's growth opportunity matches the buyer's unique aptitude and daily activity goals. For example, an online marketing expert can acquire a traditional distributor with zero web presence and scale sales exponentially. A business-to business sales expert can acquire an operationally sound manufacturer that lacks a dedicated sales team. This model is at work at the highest levels of innovation. Peter Teal and Elon Musk leveraged the platform of PayPal. And Gary Veaynerchuk used his parents' retail liquor store as a platform to scale revenues from 3 million to $60 million. The platform company provides a secure foundation of profitable revenue while allowing the entrepreneurs's innovation to drive the business to new heights. To further appreciate the nuances of the acquisition opportunity profiles matrix, we must examine how the choice of quadrant dictates the buyer's transition plan. In an eternally profitable business, the primary goal of the new CEO is preservation because the company's value lies in its stable recurring revenue and established customer relationships. The buyer must avoid making any rapid disruptive changes. They must focus on learning the existing processes, building trust with the employees, and maintaining the highest level of customer service. In a turnaround, however, the buyer must act with extreme urgency and decisiveness. Because the company is actively losing money, the new leader must cut costs, renegotiate supplier contracts and restructure operations within the first 30 days. This high pressure environment is not suitable for everyone. It requires a highly analytical fix-kinned leader who is comfortable making unpopular decisions. Similarly, the high growth and platform quadrants require highly distinct leadership skill sets. High growth acquisitions require a CEO who is exceptionally skilled at managing working capital and scaling operations to keep up with surging demand. >> [sighs and gasps] >> They must closely monitor their operating cash cycle, ensuring that receivables are collected quickly and inventory is managed efficiently to prevent a fatal cash squeeze. In a platform company, the CEO acts as a visionary growth engine, identifying underutilized assets and introducing modern innovation to unlock hidden value. This could mean acquiring a local competitor to expand geographic reach or investing in digital marketing to scale sales channels. By aligning their personal strengths with the specific demands of their chosen quadrant, the acquisition entrepreneur ensures a smooth transition and maximizes their chances of building significant long-term value. To run a successful timebound search, the entrepreneur must translate their platform goals into a precise target statement. This requires filtering opportunities based on size, industry type, and limiters. First, size must be measured not by topline revenue, but by sellers discretionary earnings, SDE. Revenue is a highly deceptive metric. A software as a service company with 70% net income and a scrap metal trading business with 1% net margins are completely different beasts. SDE represents the total pre-tax cash flow benefit to an active owner. It is calculated by taking pre-tax earnings and adding back interest, non-cash expenses like depreciation and amortization and discretionary owner perks such as salary, personal health insurance, personal vehicles, and one-time expenses. In the middle market, this number is referred to as adjusted EBITDA, reflecting passive ownership. Privately held companies under $700,000 in SDE typically trade at multiples of 2.5 to 3.5 times. While larger middle market companies attract institutional private equity firms driving multiples significantly higher. The most affordable and stable sweet spot for firsttime buyers is the $250,000 to $700,000 SDE range. Second, the entrepreneur must define their target industry by general type rather than a narrow niche. Cast a wide net by categorizing businesses into three broad types: product, distributor, or service. By maintaining a broad industry definition, the buyer avoids artificial constraints and reviews more opportunities. Product companies such as traditional manufacturers often possess legacy systems and outdated marketing practices. An online marketing expert can back into a manufacturing target simply because they recognize an opportunity to apply digital marketing to an established product. Service companies, on the other hand, often enjoy highly stable recurring subscription models, similar to the software as a service model, such as commercial landscaping, plumbing, or preschools. If a buyer has spent a decade in a specific industry and possesses genuine, deeply rooted customer relationships, they should certainly look there. However, customers are highly loyal to the company itself. When a salesperson moves to a competitor, the vast majority of clients stay with the original business. Therefore, keep your industry definition wide to maximize deal flow. Third, the entrepreneur must identify their limiters, non-negotiable variables that immediately rule out a potential company. The top limiter is geographic preference. Does the buyer's personal life require them to stay in their current city or are they willing to commute? Are they open to relocating anywhere in the country for the absolute best opportunity or are they targeting an online business that is completely relocatable? Once size, industry type, and limiters are defined, the entrepreneur pulls all of these variables together to construct their target statement. This is the ultimate compass of the search. Examples include, I am looking for a distribution company with strong sales and marketing processes, but needing operational excellence generating 300,000 to $400,000 in SDE in or around the Chicago area. or I am looking for a manufacturing company with no current e-commerce presence generating $250,000 to $300,000 in SDE. Submitting this target statement to brokers immediately communicates that the buyer is a serious focused professional who is ready to execute. To build a robust target statement, the entrepreneur must also understand the tax implications of different size ranges. In smaller acquisitions under $1 million in transaction value, the deal is almost always valued on a multiple of SDE. Because these businesses are actively operated by the owner, SDE includes the owner's personal salary and perks which are fully deductible from corporate taxes. In larger transactions, however, the target is valued on a multiple of adjusted EBITDA because these companies are often managed by professional non-owner executives. EBIDA represents the company's earnings before taking out interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, providing a standardized metric for passive investors. The acquisition entrepreneur must discuss with their accountant how the transition from SDE to adjusted Ebida impacts their personal tax liability, ensuring they choose a size range that aligns with their financial goals. Furthermore, the choice of industry type, product, distributor, or service will heavily impact the company's working capital requirements. Product-based manufacturing businesses are highly capital inensive, requiring significant investment in machinery, raw materials, and warehouse space. Distribution businesses require managing massive inventories and complex supply chain logistics which can tie up significant capital in the cash conversion cycle. Service-based businesses, however, are highly asset light, requiring minimal inventory or capital equipment. >> [snorts] >> These businesses enjoy high margins and predictable recurring revenues, but they are heavily reliant on human capital. If a key manager leaves, the quality of service can quickly decline, risking customer attrition. The buyer must analyze these industry specific dynamics carefully, ensuring they have the financial resources and the leadership skill set to manage the unique demands of their target business. The hunt, direct outreach, broker relations, and building your deal flow. Only 10% of potential buyers who start looking for a business ever succeed in acquiring one. The reason for this dismal success rate is that most buyers follow a deeply flawed search process. They begin by hitting public online marketplaces like biz by sell, spending hours of their leisure time passively scrolling through listings. Walker Dybel warns that this is a fatal trap. Active search requires absolute professional commitment and a strict timeline. A prepared, motivated buyer must commit to finding and acquiring a company within 6 months. This sense of urgency is critical because the transaction process, including due diligence, bank underwriting, and legal drafting, takes months. Passive scrolling must be replaced with an organized database-driven routine. Furthermore, the best, most lucrative businesses are rarely listed on the public internet. Online marketplaces are heavily populated with lowgrowth lifestyle businesses, laundromats, or junk deals. Highquality, scalable platform companies are highly coveted and typically sell long before they ever hit a public website. To find a great company, the entrepreneur must get upstream. In the investment banking and private equity world, success is driven by deal flow. [sighs and gasps] The top firms always get the first look at the best opportunities because they have built deep trusted relationships with the intermediaries who represent the sellers. The entrepreneur must replicate this strategy by networking directly with business brokers, Ammon advisers and local investment bankers in their target city. Steven Levitt and Steven Dubner, the authors of freconomics, explored how brokers are compensated. Intermediaries make 90 to 100% of their compensation when a transaction occurs, receiving a commission of two to 8% of the sale price. Because of this, they are highly motivated to work with capable vetted buyers who have the financial means and the psychological commitment to close. Firsttime buyers have a terrible reputation among brokers because they are typically tire kickers who lack capital, do not know what they want, and cannot pull the trigger. To gain the trust of brokers, and get first looks at private listings, the buyer must present themselves as a professional. The first meeting with a broker is a critical two-way screening interview. The buyer must show up on time, dress professionally, and demonstrate their preparedness. They should explain that they have spent months getting smart on the process, have arranged access to capital, and are committed to buying a business within 6 months. Presenting a personal balance sheet and a professional resume immediately thrills brokers who are used to wasting time on unprepared tire kickers. When the broker asks what type of business the buyer is looking for, the buyer must hit them with their prepared target statement, explaining that they define their target by SDE and growth opportunity rather than narrow industry codes. This communication immediately sets the buyer apart as an elite candidate. To generate continuous deal flow, the buyer must meet with every broker in their city, get on their private email lists, and maintain regular contact. They can also initiate direct outreach to companies they admire, using an intermediary to approach the owner confidentially, a strategy that often unlocks exceptional unlisted opportunities. To build a highly effective search strategy, the entrepreneur must also learn to navigate the high level of confidentiality that surrounds small business transactions. When an owner decides to sell their company, they are extremely concerned that their employees, customers, or competitors will learn about the impending sale. If the staff finds out, morale can plummet and key managers may start looking for other jobs. If customers find out, they may lose confidence in the company's long-term stability and switch to a competitor. To protect the seller, brokers require potential buyers to sign a strict non-disclosure agreement, NDA, before releasing any detailed information. The acquisition entrepreneur must respect this confidentiality completely, treating the seller's information with the highest level of care. This professionalism builds immediate trust with the broker and the seller, positioning the buyer as a highly desirable candidate. Furthermore, the buyer must understand how to navigate the complex world of business brokers and M&A advisors. Intermediaries range from small local main street brokers who transact laundromats and retail shops to highly sophisticated middle market investment bankers who manage multi-million dollar corporate acquisitions. The buyer must research the broker landscape carefully, identifying the firms that specialize in transacting businesses within their target SDE range. By focusing their networking efforts on the top performing intermediaries, the entrepreneur ensures a steady stream of highquality prevetted opportunities. They should also leverage LinkedIn and local business registries to identify unlisted companies that match their target statement, initiating direct confidential outreach. This proactive strategy allows the buyer to bypass broker competition altogether, negotiating a proprietary deal that is customized to their mutual goals. Under the hood, due diligence, financial decryption, and the team of adviserss. Acquiring a company is not a linear step-by-step process. It is a complex negotiation that requires managing a web of independent players, each with their own distinct financial incentives. The buyer must build a world-class acquisition team long before they secure a signed letter of intent. The first critical team member is the banker. The entrepreneur must start meeting with banks as soon as they initiate their search, preparing their personal balance sheet, credit reports, and tax returns. The banker's business model is driven entirely by making loans. However, they want to turn down deals that do not fit their internal criteria. The entrepreneur must seek out local and regional banks that are actively executing growth strategies and are hungry for loans. Specifically, they must find banks with preferred lenders program PLP status with the SBA. Preferred lenders can underwrite, process, and approve loans inhouse, completely bypassing the slow external government processing that can delay a closing by 6 to 8 weeks. Because SBA rates are typically floating, having multiple banks bidding on a deal ensures the buyer gets the best possible interest rate, maximizing their future cash flow. The second team member is a transactions certified public accountant, CPA. Traditional CPAs who focus exclusively on filing corporate tax returns are not suitable for M&A due diligence. The buyer needs a CPA who has extensive experience representing buyers and sellers in small business transactions. A skilled CPA can read the history of a business through its financial statements, identify where snakes can hide in the recast P&L, and help structure the purchase price allocation for maximum tax benefit. The third and most sensitive team member is the lawyer. Walker Dybel warns that lawyers are the number one source of deals that fail to close. This is because a lawyer's natural incentive is to protect their client from all risks at all costs. During the redline phase, lawyers often complicate agreements beyond what is necessary, rewriting clauses in a highly defensive win lose manner that offends the other party. The entrepreneur must actively manage their legal counsel. They must remind the attorney that the goal is to reach a fair win-win agreement between two responsible adults who trust each other by negotiating a not to exceed budget and utilizing boilerplate documents. The buyer keeps legal fees under control. To protect themselves and secure the loan, the bank will require the buyer to carry keyman life insurance for the uncolateralized portion of the debt. The entrepreneur should arrange this medical checkup and underwriting early in the process, treating the premium as a deductible business expense. Furthermore, if the buyer owns a home, they should secure a home equity line of credit, H E LC, prior to closing on their SBA loan. Once an SBA loan is in place, the bank will place a lean on the buyer's personal assets, making it almost impossible to secure a heliloc later. This home equity serves as a critical emergency reserve. CPAs and lawyers are also excellent sources of unlisted deal flow. By sharing their target statement with these professionals, the entrepreneur taps into their private networks of business owners who may be considering retirement. Managing the team with clear roles, written budgets, and constant communication is the hallmark of a successful CEO. Dealm is the art of creating something out of nothing. And the strength of your team determines your success. To successfully manage the acquisition team, the entrepreneur must understand the unique psychological dynamics and incentives of each professional. CPAs and lawyers are paid on an hourly basis, meaning they have a natural incentive to extend negotiations and write extremely complex contracts to bill more hours. While these professionals provide invaluable protection, the buyer must remember that they are the CEO. They are the final decision maker. They must not allow their adviserss to run the deal or make strategic decisions on their behalf. The buyer must establish clear written guidelines and hourly budgets for their CPA and lawyer, ensuring that their work remains focused on key risks rather than trivial clauses. By taking a hands-on, proactive approach, the entrepreneur keeps transaction costs manageable and ensures the deal moves forward with momentum. Furthermore, the buyer must build a close personal relationship with their SBA lender. SBA backed loans require a highly rigorous underwriting process where the bank deeply investigates the buyer's credit history, tax returns, personal balance sheet, and management experience. To secure the loan, the buyer must prove that they possess the necessary skills and education to successfully run the target business. Preferred SBA lenders have a dedicated in-house team of underwriters and closers who are highly experienced in transacting small business loans. By partnering with a PLP lender and supplying all requested documentation in a highly organized, timely manner, the buyer accelerates the underwriting process and ensures that financing is committed well before the due diligence period ends. This financial preparation is what separates elite acquisition entrepreneurs from ordinary tire kickers, winning them great favor with brokers and sellers alike. In a small business transaction, the financial statements tell the ultimate story of the company's operational health. To evaluate a potential platform, the entrepreneur must understand how cash flows through a business. Most small businesses internally keep acrruel basis accounting where revenues and expenses are matched and recorded when the transaction occurs. However, for tax purposes, they file on a cash basis model where transactions are recorded only when cash changes hands. This results in internal statements and tax returns often telling time differently. This mismatch requires careful reconciliation. To see how cash moves, suppose a business purchases raw materials in December, pays for them in January, delivers the finished product in February, and collects the payment from the customer in March. Under cash accounting, the expense is recorded in January and the revenue in March, making the business appear highly volatile. Under acrual accounting, the transaction is cleanly matched in February, providing a true picture of operational margins. Acrrual basis accounting is highly superior because it provides visibility into accounts receivable and accounts payable. The income statement or profit and loss statement, P&L, reports the company's financial performance over a specific period showing revenue, cost of goods sold, COGS, gross margin, operating expenses, and net income. While public corporations are valued on net income, small private businesses are valued on sellers discretionary earnings SDE or adjusted EBIDA. SDE represents the total pre-tax cash flow benefit to an active owner. The recast process begins with net income and systematically adds back interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and discretionary owner perks. Discretionary perks include the owner's salary, health insurance, personal vehicles, travel, cell phones, and any one-time nonrecurring business expenses. The buyer must go line by line through the recast statements to verify the legitimacy of these adbacks, ensuring that the broker has not artificially inflated the cash flow. Recreating these statements in a personal spreadsheet allows the buyer to analyze yearover-year revenue trends, identify seasonality blips, and project the cash conversion cycle with precision. The balance sheet is a snapshot of the company's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity on a specific date following the formula assets equals liabilities plus owner's equity. Ratios like return on equity, ROE, debt to equity, and the current ratio help measure the company's leverage and short-term liquidity. However, the balance sheet can be highly misleading because assets are depreciated linearly over time on the books, which does not match their real market value. >> [sighs] >> A three-year-old computer may be valued at zero on the books but remain fully functional while specialized manufacturing equipment depreciates exponentially. During valuation, the buyer must focus on assetbased versus cash flowbased methods. Book value, fair market value, and liquidation value are helpful academic benchmarks. But for a profitable platform, the buyer is paying for future cash flow, not hard assets. Nonrevenuegenerating intellectual property or custom software should be heavily devalued. Sizable middle market acquisitions use adjusted EBITD DA to represent passive cash flow while smaller transactions rely on SDE to represent active owner benefit. To truly master financial due diligence, the entrepreneur must learn to identify where financial skeletons can hide in a small business's books. One common area of manipulation is cost of goods sold, COGS. Some sellers will misclassify operating expenses as COGS to artificially inflate their gross margins or vice versa. The buyer must verify the exact cost of all raw materials, shipping, and direct labor, ensuring that gross margins are calculated accurately. Another common area of concern is customer concentration. If a business generates 40% of its revenue from a single customer, the loss of that client following the transition can quickly push the business into financial distress. The buyer must analyze the customer list carefully, ensuring that no single client represents more than 10% of sales. If concentration exists, the deal must be structured with significant earnouts or seller notes to protect the buyer from customer attrition. Furthermore, the buyer must analyze the company's balance sheet liabilities in detail. They must ensure that all accounts payable are current, all tax filings are fully paid, and there are no pending or threatened lawsuits against the company. The recast balance sheet must reflect the true fair market value of all machinery and equipment. The buyer should hire a professional appraiser to inspect the condition of all hard assets, estimating their remaining useful life and replacement costs. This physical due diligence ensures the buyer is not inheriting worn out machinery that will require massive capital expenditure immediately after closing. By conducting a highly thorough line by line financial and physical audit, the acquisition entrepreneur builds a highly accurate company portrait, ensuring they pay a fair price that is grounded strictly in past performance. Closing the deal and leading day one, valuation, negotiation, and smooth transition. Most inexperienced buyers go into their first meeting with a seller filled with caution and suspicion. They expect to be pitched and they look for hidden traps. Walker Dyel argues that this adversarial approach is entirely wrong. In a small business transaction, the first meeting is a first date. It is a deeply emotional process for the seller who has poured their life, sweat, and identity into building their business. The business is their baby. To win the deal, the buyer's first job is to convince the seller that they are the right person to take over their legacy. During the first meeting, the buyer must build immediate rapport by being polite, respectful, and highly professional. They must present themselves as an interested, capable entrepreneur who is willing and able to close. Rather than acting like a cold venture capitalist, the buyer should treat the meeting like a job interview for the role of CEO. They should compliment the seller on their success, explain their background, and share their target statement. By getting the seller comfortable, the buyer unlocks access to critical, confidential information. Research consistently shows that a proactive, problem-solving, and cooperative approach yields the best outcomes. The buyer should negotiate qualitative goals first, such as employee retention or the transition timeline, which are highly emotional to the seller, but cost the buyer nothing. This win-win approach positions the buyer as a partner rather than an adversary. During the meeting, the buyer must actively listen and download the seller's brain, identifying whether the business's success is tied to the seller's personal relationships or if it is built on a highly transferable operational infrastructure. Understanding the seller's true motivation for exit, whether it is retirement, burnout, or a liquidity event, is essential to evaluating the business's future stability. If the seller is selling because they are bored, the buyer must investigate whether the entire staff is bored and if the company is sliding into obsolescence. Following the first meeting, the buyer must get a comprehensive tour of the facility. Cleanliness, orderliness, and the attitude of the employees tell a powerful story about the company's culture. Culture is the single most overlooked aspect of an acquisition target. Yet, it is essential to the buyer's plan for how to manage the company from day one. John Bllye, the author of Cracking the Code, starts every acquisition by go to lunch with the seller. If they do not establish a strong personal connection, he walks away from the deal immediately. Furthermore, the buyer must understand that once the transaction is complete and the cash is in the bank, the seller will be mentally and spiritually ready to leave as fast as possible. their emotional connection is gone. The transition period should be structured to last only one to four weeks on site with a few months of availability by phone. Keeping the seller around for too long after closing prevents the new CEO from establishing full control and can create confusion among the employees. The transition must be clean and decisive. To successfully build trust with the seller during the transition period, the new CEO must practice exceptional emotional intelligence and active listening. The seller is going through a major life transition, often experiencing a profound sense of loss and anxiety about the future. They have spent decades building this company and they view the employees as their family. The new CEO must validate these emotions, assuring the seller that they will protect their legacy and treat the employees with the highest level of care. By showing genuine gratitude and respect for the seller's accomplishments, the buyer builds an unbreakable personal bond that ensures the seller's full cooperation during the transition phase. This human connection is far more valuable than any legal warranty or contract clause. Furthermore, the transition period must be planned with extreme precision. The new CEO must work with the seller to outline a detailed day-by-day training schedule for the first 30 days. This schedule should cover all taskoriented execution items such as introducing the buyer to key suppliers, setting up banking codes, transferring software licenses, and training the buyer on proprietary machinery. By structuring this transition to be short and intensive, the buyer quickly gains the necessary operational knowledge while allowing the seller to depart the business gracefully. Keeping the seller around for too long can create a dual authority environment where employees are confused about who the real leader is. The transition must be decisive, establishing the new CEO as the undisputed final authority of the organization from day one. Once a target business has passed the initial screening, the entrepreneur must zoom out and analyze the industry at large. They must understand the underlying business model and build a robust strategic business plan to guide their future leadership. Michael Porter's five forces model, first introduced in the Harvard Business Review in 1979, is a cornerstone of corporate strategy. The five forces provide a powerful framework for identifying where power lies in the supply chain. The threat of new entrance, the company's moat, the threat of substitutes, buyer power, the risk of commoditization, supplier power, and competitive rivalry. The threat of new entrance is kept at bay by high switching costs, brand equity, and proprietary distribution channels. The threat of substitutes analyzed at a high level reveals the true value the product delivers. If a business serves a few large buyers, those buyers possess significant power to drive prices down. Conversely, if a business relies on a single unique supplier, that supplier can squeeze gross margins. Applying these forces allows the buyer to identify the core risks of the company. The entrepreneur must also evaluate where the industry sits in its life cycle, introduction, growth, maturity, or decline. Startups thrive in adolescent high-growth markets. But these markets are highly volatile, capital and prone to rapid consolidation. Acquisition entrepreneurs heavily favor mature fragmented industries. These stable, unsexy industries make up the bulk of the economy and are highly insulated from rapid disruption. Mature industries are ripe for consolidation plays. An established company generating $8 million in revenue can acquire a competitor of the same size at a much lower multiple than a growth startup would command, providing a highly predictable path to rapid scale. Jim Collins in-depth research in his best-selling book, Good to Great, introduced the hedgehog concept, the sweet spot, where an organization's passion, its ability to be the best in the world, and its economic driver intersect. Collins proved that companies that align their strategies with this concept generate superior economic returns even in mature or declining industries. The buyer must apply this concept to identify the single metric that drives the business's economic engine. To communicate this vision to banks and equity backers, the entrepreneur must translate their research into a concise business plan. Walker Dyel argues that writing a 100page academic business plan is a wasted effort. Instead, the buyer should construct a short executive summary and a highly focused pitch deck based on Guy Kawasaki's legendary 10 slide template from the art of the start. >> [gasps] >> The deck must address the core strategy clearly defining the problem, the pain or luxury, the value proposition, the solution, the underlying magic, the moat or core competency, the go-to market plan, a competitive analysis, and a three-year financial forecast by utilizing Seem Isma's exponential organization. framework. The new CEO can leverage existing assets and scale the company rapidly, proving that high growth is not reserved exclusively for tech startups. To build a robust go-to market plan for their business plan, the entrepreneur must deeply understand how to leverage modern digital technologies in a mature industry. Many established small businesses have been operated by the same owner for decades, meaning they have completely ignored online sales, social media marketing, and search engine optimization. The acquisition entrepreneur can capitalize on this digital gap using their modern skill set to scale sales channels rapidly by implementing a highly targeted digital marketing campaign, building a userfriendly e-commerce storefront or optimized search ads. The new CEO can attract an entirely new generation of customers, driving rapid topline growth. This digital transformation is a highly predictable low-risk growth strategy. Furthermore, the entrepreneur must analyze the competitive landscape using Porter's five forces to identify their strategic positioning. They must determine what makes their company different from competitors, focusing on unique geographic advantages, proprietary supplier relationships, or exceptional customer service rather than trying to compete on price in a race to the bottom. The CEO must focus on high margin differentiated value propositions. Jim Collins hedgehog concept guides the leader to focus their energy exclusively on what they can be the best in the world at aligning all operational and marketing efforts around this core strength. By combining this strategic focus with a robust three-year financial forecast, [gasps] the entrepreneur builds a highly professional business plan that wins the confidence of banks and investors alike. With a strategic business plan in place, the entrepreneur is ready to make a formal non-binding offer by submitting a letter of intent LOI. Because the LOI is non-binding, the buyer must get comfortable taking this pivotal step. Too many potential buyers get stuck in analysis paralysis, using endless research as an excuse to avoid making an offer. Submitting an LOI communicates seriousness and secures an exclusive negotiating window, typically 45 to 60 days, during which the seller cannot market the business to other buyers. The LOI must outline the core terms of the proposal, including the purchase price, deal structure, closing date, and contingencies. The deal structure typically involves a combination of all cash, earnouts, and seller notes. Carrying a seller note is highly advantageous. A note of 10 to 20% of the purchase price paid over 2 to 5 years keeps the seller's skin in the game and aligns their incentives with the buyer's success. Before proposing a purchase price, the buyer must stress test their financial model. They must calculate the annual debt service payments on their SBA loan and determine how much revenue could decline in a downturn before the business fails to cover its obligations. To successfully negotiate a letter of intent, the entrepreneur must also understand the mechanics of the purchase consideration and escrow deposits. When the buyer submits an LOI, they typically propose a good faith escrow deposit, usually $10,000 to $50,000, to be held by a neutral third-party escrow agent. This deposit proves the buyer's commitment and is fully refundable if the buyer walks away due to unsatisfactory due diligence findings. If the transaction proceeds to closing, the escrow deposit is applied directly to the purchase price. The LOI must also specify how transaction expenses will be allocated with each party typically responsible for paying their own legal and accounting representation. This clear structure prevents lastminute disputes. Furthermore, the buyer must understand how to handle the seller's counter offer. A counter offer is the most common response to an initial LOI with the seller typically pushing for a higher purchase price, a smaller seller note, or a shorter exclusive negotiation window. The buyer must analyze the counter offer carefully, maintaining a calm, objective mindset. They must negotiate everything they can other than price first, giving the seller easy wins on qualitative goals while picking their battles on key risk protections. By overcommunicating with the listing broker and explaining the financial reasoning behind their pricing, the buyer coaches the broker to help convince the seller to accept a fair win-win deal. This collaborative negotiation is the hallmark of a professional dealmaker. Once the LOI is signed, the transaction enters the high stakes acquisition phase. This is an intense roller coaster period where multiple tasks must be performed simultaneously. The buyer must immediately form a new legal entity, typically an LLC filing as an SC corporation, get bank underwriting underway, and initiate legal, financial, and operational due diligence. Due diligence is the permission to enter the verify phase where every assumption, financial statement, and seller claim is rigorously investigated. Operational due diligence involves walking an order through the building, tracking its path from sales to production, delivery, and invoicing. This process reveals the company's internal flow, identifies key employees, and surfaces inefficiencies. >> [sighs and gasps] >> A powerful underutilized strategy during this phase is the nonowner advantage. Because the buyer does not yet own the business, they can reach out to potential customers and industry owners in other geographic regions with zero sales pressure, gathering invaluable market insights, and building a customer pipeline. As closing approaches, buyers often experience the 11th hour freakout, a sudden heightened anxiety about the risks they are taking on. This is completely normal. The buyer must lean on their prep work and process to maintain their composure and push the deal across the finish line. To ensure a highly successful transition in the first 90 days, the new CEO must establish a systematic assess then execute routine. The first 30 days must be spent entirely on assessment, learning the existing processes, building rapport with employees, and meeting key customers and suppliers. The CEO should avoid making any significant operational or personnel changes during this period as rapid changes can create extreme anxiety and disrupt productivity. In the second month, the CEO turns their attention to learning how the money flows, putting together a 13-week cash flow projection to understand the company's liquidity demands. By the third month, the CEO can confidently implement strategic optimizations, launching growth initiatives and setting clear expectations for their team, driving the company to new heights of success. The entrepreneurial landscape is on the cusp of an unprecedented revolution. Over the next two decades, retiring baby boomers will transition ownership of millions of small businesses, triggering what Walker Dybel calls the largest transfer of wealth in human history. This is not merely a macroeconomic statistic. It is a profound invitation to ambitious individuals who refuse to be bound by the traditional corporate ladder. For those who possess the courage to act, this transition represents the ultimate gateway to financial independence, self-direction, and lasting legacy. Throughout this book, the foundational principles of acquisition entrepreneurship have shown that the most reliable path to business ownership does not require starting from zero. Starting from scratch forces the entrepreneur to navigate a perilous road where the odds of failure are overwhelmingly stacked against them. In contrast, by choosing to buy an existing profitable enterprise, the acquisition entrepreneur begins their journey with an established customer base, trained employees, a proven product or service, and immediate cash flow. As Walker Dybel famously notes, buy then build is a scalable model that allows you to buy a profitable infrastructure and then layer growth on top. The existing company is not a static asset. It is a high-powered engine that is ready to be optimized and scaled. To seize this historic opportunity, one must let go of the romanticized startup myth and embrace the cold analytical reality of the market. Success in this field belongs to those who think like investors and act like leaders. It belongs to those who align their personal strengths, secure reliable adviserss, and execute their searches with relentless systematic focus. As Walker Dybo reminds us, true autonomy is not about starting from scratch. It is about taking control of an existing engine and driving it forward.

metadata.title: Acquiring a Company vs. Innovating an Industry
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Walker discusses how acquiring small to mid-sized businesses is more affordable and, over time, gains market share. But innovation in an industry can also be a huge game changer and business opportunity. The key here is that innovation and acquisition are equally important.

Timestamps:
0:00 Intro
0:15 Acquisition is equally important as innovation
0:17 When do you know when to start a business from scratch or whether to acquire one?
0:43 Understanding the industry landscape is critical
01:07 Research from MacKenzie Consulting report
02:05 Those who acquire many small and medium-sized businesses are "winners."
04:59 Consolidation curve - 4 parts
07:29 Alternative consolidation curve
11:13 A.T. Kearney's graph - Who drives?
16:05 Conclusions

Join us and accelerate your acquisition with our "do-it-with-you" buy-side advisory service. Our collaborative approach blends graduate-level instruction with hands-on buy-side consulting. Together we will master the skills needed to identify, evaluate, and acquire the right business for you. Check out acquisitionlab.com and see you on the inside.

Remember to like, subscribe, and click the bell to be updated when we have a new video and learn more about business acquisition with Acquisition Lab. Do you have any questions, tips, or ideas about managing risk in business acquisition? Let us know in the comments section below!

VISIT OUR WEBSITE: http://acquisitionlab.com
DOWNLOAD BUY THEN BUILD SAMPLE CHAPTER DOWNLOAD: https://acquisitionlab.com/free-chapter
LEARN FROM OUR BLOGS: https://acquisitionlab.com/blog/
MORE BLOGS AT BUY THEN BUILD: https://buythenbuild.com/blog/
CLIENTS' TESTIMONIALS: https://acquisitionlab.com/testimonials/
JOIN THE LAB: https://acquisitionlab.com/application/
SUBSCRIBE: youtube.com/buythenbuild 


********

Walker Deibel has practiced acquisition entrepreneurship since 2006, amassing $16.5 million in revenue through acquisitions. He has co-founded three startups, acquired seven companies outright, and has consulted (or participated in) over $200,000,000 in business transactions.

Walker holds an MBA from the Olin School of Business at Washington University in St. Louis, where he was awarded the Declaration of Accomplishment in Entrepreneurship. 

He is a Certified M&A Advisor, Certified M&A Professional, M&A Master Intermediary, Certified Exit Planning Advisor, and former SEC-licensed stockbroker. He was awarded the Platinum Award from M&A Source and Thought Leader of the Year by The Alliance of M&A Advisors and Axial.com. Forbes, Entrepreneur, Fast Company, Inc, and the Harvard Business Review have featured his work.

Find out more about the team here https://acquisitionlab.com/meet-the-team/

metadata.title: Master the 'Moneyball' of Business: Unveiling Acquisition Entrepreneurship with Walker Deibel
metadata.author: Jake & Gino
metadata.shortDescription:
In this high-energy episode, Jake Stenziano and Gino Barbaro invite best-selling author and seasoned entrepreneur Walker Deibel onto the show. Walker, who is the creator of Acquisition Lab, has an impressive background in acquisition entrepreneurship, amassing over 16.5 million in revenue since 2006.

Join us as we dive into Walker's journey from the Olin School of Business to becoming an acquisition entrepreneur. He shares some hard-earned wisdom about the high failure rate of startups, the challenges of scaling a business, and the statistical truths of entrepreneurship.

We also discuss the concept of acquisition entrepreneurship and how it contrasts with typical startup culture. Walker dives into how acquisition is just as important and effective as innovation and explains why buying businesses is the "moneyball of entrepreneurship".

Gino and Jake share insights from their experiences in the multifamily industry, discussing market cycles, cost of capital, and how they've managed to continue growing despite the frothy market of the past few years. We also touch upon the fascinating idea of buying for the future while paying for the past.

Whether you're a startup entrepreneur or an established business owner, this episode is filled with priceless advice and perspectives that can help you understand the world of business from different angles. Watch this episode to get a deep dive into the world of acquisition entrepreneurship, business valuations, and much more!

Buy Walker's Book - https://amzn.to/45akZWJ
The Acquisition Lab - https://acquisitionlab.com/
Buy Then Build Program - https://buythenbuild.com/

Don't forget to hit the like button, share, and subscribe to our channel for more enlightening content.

Jake & Gino are multifamily investors, operators, and mentors who have created a vertically integrated real estate company. They control over $250M in assets under management.
