metadata.title: The Self Funded Search Model | Robert Graham & Jordan carter
metadata.author: Acquiring Minds
metadata.shortDescription:
Key findings from SIG's new study on self-funded search: financial outcomes, deal costs & terms, search lengths & more.

❤️ Enjoy this interview? SUBSCRIBE for more: https://bit.ly/42hLnN0 ❤️

About 

I’ve been an entrepreneur for most of my career, primarily building online media brands. I sold a few of those businesses, but I’ve never been on the buyer's side of the table. Recently I became curious about buying a business.

I found myself browsing the for-sale business marketplaces, imagining the possibilities. And while there were plenty of listings to explore, I couldn’t find much information to guide me through the process of acquiring a business. Unlike start-a-business entrepreneurship, there are not countless channels and podcasts devoted to buy-a-business entrepreneurship.
There are still fewer public stories about entrepreneurs who have taken the plunge to buy a business and done well — though I knew such successes are plentiful.

Acquiring Minds is a channel to both correct that, and educate me on the journey toward buying a business. Business acquisition is an exciting prospect, and I intend for Acquiring Minds to make the path more accessible to myself and others.

💡 Get the #1 Private Equity recruiting course, which comes with 3-statement LBO model tests, mega fund case studies, and headhunter coverage: https://bit.ly/PF-PrivateEquity
📚 Free recruiting resources: https://peakframeworks.com
** Stanford GSB's Search Fund Primer: https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/centers-initiatives/ces/research/search-funds/primer

The SEARCH FUND is an investment strategy popularly used by top MBAs and investment professionals to buy small businesses and become CEO. In a SEARCH FUND, you raise money from investors to acquire a single company and then manage it! It's one of the only ways to get meaningful equity in an already successful company.

The search fund is one of the most effective ways to mix one's finance and entrepreneurial skills. In this video, I discuss the typical SEARCH FUND process, how much you can expect to make, and explain why the strategy works.

0:00 - Intro
0:30 - What is a Search Fund?
1:19 - The Search Fund Process
3:02 - Search Fund Returns
3:49 - Why Search Funds Work
4:50 - Cons of a Search Fund

Peak Frameworks is a business career prep service started by Matt Ting and Patrick Fong, who have each spent several years working in investment banking and private equity in New York and Silicon Valley. Matt and Patrick met at Evercore, a top tier investment bank, and over the years have tutored and coached dozens of candidates to land their dream business job.

Matt Ting: https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthewting/
Patrick Fong (HBS 2021): https://www.linkedin.com/in/patrick-fong-0b773041/

metadata.title: Self-Funded Search vs. Traditional Search Funds
metadata.author: Acquiring Minds
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch a debate about the merits of two distinct models of search: self-funded search on one side, traditional search funds on the other.

The two guests, Greg Geronemus and Robert Graham, have each been both searcher and investor in his preferred model of search. Each is a strong proponent of his preference, so this is a high-quality debate.

You will come away with a stronger sense of the pros & cons of each model — self-funded vs. traditional — and have a much clearer sense for which would suit your own search.

metadata.title: How search fund operators convince owners to sell their business with Steve Divitikos
metadata.author: Built to Sell
metadata.shortDescription:
In recent years, “Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition” courses at Ivy League MBA programs have surged in popularity, outshining traditional classes in marketing or corporate finance. This trend reflects a shift in aspirations among students, many of whom now prioritize acquiring a business over roles in consulting or banking. 

As a business owner, you’re likely to encounter increased interest from these eager MBA graduates keen on acquiring your company with the backing of people that specialize in funding these first-time entrepreneurs. 

For example, this week we interviewed Steve Divitikos, a Harvard MBA who decided to acquire and build a small business using money he raised from investors. 

Read the show notes at https://builttosell.com/radio/episode-432/

segments.text: [MUSIC]
My name's Coley Andrews, GSB class of 2009.
My partner and I started a firm called Pacific Leg Partners, and
all we do are invest in and support search fund entrepreneurs.
The search fund model has it's roots here at Stanford, and
fortunately it's a very fast growing part of the little entrepreneurial universe.
[MUSIC]
The search fund model is really entrepreneurship through acquisition.
It's an opportunity for individuals who want to be their own boss, but
aren't necessarily a start up person.
To raise a little bit of walking around money,
to conduct a thoughtful two year search, to find a small business to buy.
Usually it's from an owner or someone in their 60's or 70's who wants to retire,
and doesn't have a son or daughter that they either want to hand the business to,
or would like to take over the business.
And it provides an opportunity for a recent MBA graduate to step into
the leadership role, and become the CEO of a small, profitable and growing company.
[MUSIC]
We believe in backing smarts and hustle, not experience.
And the way we get around the experience is by focusing on buying a company
that has very strong characteristics, it's very healthy,
it's unlikely to be broken, unlikely to be run into the ground
by a 30 year old who's never run a business before.
And when you have those ingredients at the company level, and you layer in on top of
that, somebody who's inexperienced, but well educated, has a lot of hustle and
drive, has turned down attractive offers to go work at other big companies,
because she or he wants to be in business for themselves.
You really can create an environment where a lot of magical things can happen.
[MUSIC]
Some people just say, you know what, I have to be passionate about the idea and
a product that I want to create, and therefore I'm going to go start my own
business, and that's just a certain type of personality.
There are those out there though who'll say, I'm not really that concerned too
much about the product, the passion is I just love the idea of managing.
I want to be in charge, I want to make decisions,
I want disproportion of responsibility early in my career.
Those are the folks that end up going the search fund path not necessarily
the start up path.
There's also a risk difference the odds of success in the search fund world
are materially higher than starting your own business.
They come in two phases, one you raise money to go out and find a company, and
you have about a 75% chance during a two year period, of actually finding and
buying a company.
Thereafter, once you buy the company you have about a two-thirds chance,
67% chance, that you're actually going to be successful and make money.
And there are investors out there that have skewed the odds on both of those
situations farther out to the right, to the positive.
So when you walk it all through, you have a greater than a 50%
chance of being successful, becoming a CEO, building a company and
having a financial outcome, and a life experience outcome that you want.
That's very different that the startup risk where it's much more boom or bust.
[MUSIC]
What we're looking for when we find a new entrepreneur or
a new entrepreneur reaches out to us is really two things.
One, the strategy that they're going to employee to look for a company to buy, and
the type of company that they want to buy.
So that gets to my earlier point about hey, buying a good business and
a good industry increases your odds of success.
So if they're focused on that, that's great, check the box.
Then it gets to the harder stuff, which is the softer side of the individual.
Why do they want to do this?
Have they turned down other attractive offers?
Are they really demonstrating commitment to this path to being their own boss?
The search fund model is predicated on taking somebody with high potential, and
surrounding them with people that can help him or her succeed.
If they're willing to listen and
take advice from those who have gone down the path before them and
avoid mistakes they otherwise might make, that's a good sign.
[MUSIC]
We often get that question.
Oh my gosh, you put a 30 year old in charge of a company on day one.
Doesn't everybody flee for the exits?
And the answer is no.
These are small businesses.
The employees, it's important for them.
It's their job.
They want to stay there.
And obviously, you're trying to minimize as much change as possible.
Particularly in the first year.
So the transition is really, do nothing.
Just listen.
Learn.
Make sure you're buying a business that is going to continue to move
forward even though you have this management change going on.
Then what happens is you wake up 12 or 18 months later, and the entrepreneur knows
an enormous amount, if not more about the business and the industry.
And the board that's been working closely with the entrepreneur understands things
much better.
And you can begin to slowly start to make changes to build out a sales force and
begin to attack a different part of the market that you weren't doing before.
Bring in some senior leaders to hopefully grow and scale.
[MUSIC]
For the investor it's not a lot of money upfront,
to run risks in a high potential individual.
So we're investing 30, 40, $50,000 for that entrepreneur to have two
years of runway to go out there and find that business okay, and
I know that 75% of the time I'm going to have an option
to invest more money into the company that they actually find and that's why I exist.
Is to invest larger amounts into the business on behalf of our LPs.
So you skew the risk materially and have, on the small dollar amount, there's
some chance you're going to lose that, but 75 out of a 100 is still pretty good.
And then you have a chance to decide whether or not you want to invest a lot
more money once you have something known, which is a known business.
A known history of profits and growth, a known industry, and
an entrepreneur that you've been working with for 18-24 months,
that you've gotten to know a lot better than you did back at the beginning.
[MUSIC]
Every day, you're waking up, and it's a new battle everyday,
to find somebody who will actually talk to you.
Search fund entrepreneurs over the life of their two year search,
will reach out to thousands of companies.
They'll have hundreds of conversations,
hopefully hundreds of in-person meetings but maybe not even that,
tens of in person meetings to have a chance to buy one company.
So it takes an enormous amount of inner strength and conviction to wake up every
morning knowing that 90% of your day is going to be rejection, to have a chance
at the end to achieve your goal which is to become a CEO when you're 30 or
31 years old.
[MUSIC]
1995 there were two or three search funds raised roughly that year, plus or
minus a year or two, in 2005 it was more like ten or 12.
And in 2015, there'll be over 50 search funds that have come out and raised.
So it is clearly now gotten to a place where
entrepreneurs who want to be their own boss, but they're not a startup person,
know that it's a viable path to achieving their goal.
And so therefore,
it's a super exciting time to be involved in the search fund community.
And if you just think about the number of businesses out there that are owned by
individuals in their 60's and 70's, the baby boomer generation,
they have to find something to do with their primary asset.
And a lot of them love the idea of selling their business to a younger version of
themself, which is the search fund entrepreneur.
[MUSIC]

How to Start a Search Fund from Nothing

segments.text: - Are you struggling to find a fulfilling career?
Maybe you're tired of the 9 to 5
and you've heard about private equity,
you think it's really interesting
but don't really know where to start?
Well, one of the places a lot of people start
is through search funds.
And now a search fund has been around
since probably sometime in the 1980s
it was really developed, at Stanford.
And the idea was there was a professor
that had a couple students that wanted to buy a business
and so he gave them some money to go
and find a company, buy it and run it.
And then ultimately they sold it
and he generated this great return.
And they also generated a great return
because they got a big piece of the equity.
This evolved quite a bit until today,
you've got lots of firms and accelerators
and other groups that are out there
all supporting and investing in searchers,
as they're called, or search funds.
Now what is a search fund, how does it work?
Well, it's kind of like a very, very mini
private equity fund of one to two people.
A good friend of mine, Deb Tan, is one of those searchers.
After graduating from undergrad,
she went and worked on Wall Street
for one of the large investment banks.
And after being there for a few years
she went to Harvard to get her MBA.
At graduation, she was like, what do I want to do next?
And really fell in love with the idea of search funds.
So I sat down with her and just peppered her
with tons of questions on how are search funds structured
and what is the industry like and so forth.
And so I'm gonna share some of the things
that I learned as well as what I've seen
working with other searchers over the years.
Now first let's talk about what is a search fund.
Now like I said, a search fund is kind of like
a mini private equity fund.
Essentially what happens is a searcher,
or somebody that works in the search fund
or that's putting it together,
will go to investors and say,
Hey, I am an exceptional leader and operator
and I want to go buy a business and I want your help.
In exchange for giving me some capital up front
to cover my salary, living expenses, travel, et cetera,
I'm willing to give you first rights of refusal
and quite a bit of equity when I buy this company
that I'm gonna go out and find.
I'll also give you quarterly reports
so you know what's going on
and hopefully thereby reduce your risk.
Now the amount of money that they raise varies
but is typically somewhere between 400
and $700,000 depending on inflation
and market and expertise and what kind of business
they're gonna buy, et cetera, et cetera.
Sometimes it edges up a little bit higher
towards the like 800, $900,000
if you have two searchers working together.
But you know, median is somewhere
in the like 500, $550,000 range.
Now that money should buy you enough runway
to be a searcher for about two years.
So typically searchers are gonna pay themselves,
let's say they raise 500,000.
They're gonna pay themselves probably somewhere
between 100 and $200,000 that will leave them
with a little over $300,000 to spend on you know,
hiring interns maybe, paying legal bills, travel,
working with bankers, legal diligence,
all the things that they need to do
in order to find an investment opportunity
or a company to buy, do the due diligence
and follow through with raising the money
to complete the acquisition.
So what'll happen is over those two years,
they'll spend a lot of time trying to find a deal.
So over those two years, they'll work tirelessly
to try to find a deal because at the end of those two years
or when they've used up all the money, it's done.
And you know, if they haven't found something then,
you know it'll just be kind of a waste,
for their investors and also for them to a certain extent.
During that time period, they'll need to come up
with an engine to help find the company they want to buy.
I know some searchers, they build out an army of interns.
Where, you know, they'll go to a university
and they'll pay, you know, 10 to $15 an hour
and they'll have all these interns
that are literally smiling and dialing for deals.
They're just calling lots of companies,
hopefully within like a sector
that they're really excited about.
But generally they're just kind of canvassing a large area
and trying to find kind of that diamond in the rough.
Other searchers use a more strategic approach.
They might say, hey, I am really interested in,
you know, personal care and so I'm gonna go look
at personal care businesses.
Or you know, I think there's an opportunity
to buy a really good HVAC company
and roll it up with a few more
and build it into a much bigger business.
Similar to like what a private equity fund would do.
There could be a lot of different strategies.
And it also kind of depends
on what that person's background is.
So if they come with a lot of expertise
in a particular industry or sector, right,
then they're obviously gonna spend more time
hunting for deals in that sector.
Let's say they find their deal.
Well now they have to package it all up
and go back to their original investors
that gave them the money in the first place.
The thing that's interesting about that
is when they go back, they're doing two things.
One, they're selling the deal,
but two they're also selling their job in the deal.
Because once they acquire the business,
they're actually gonna typically take a CEO
or a COO position in the company.
They'll negotiate some sort of salary
somewhere in the you know, call it roughly $200,000 range
depending on where the business is located
and inflation and so forth.
But you can imagine somewhere in that range.
So you know, a healthy salary for sure.
And then over time they'll earn
their equity in the business.
Now in this case, the way that they are structured
is typically the investors that are coming into the deal
and providing the capital will take preferred shares
and a majority of the board.
They basically sit in control.
But the day-to-day operations are left to the searcher.
And they are working hard to earn their equity
which amounts to a total
of typically 25 to 30% of the business.
And they'll earn that over time.
So once they close the deal, they'll get a chunk of equity
usually about a third of it.
As they hit certain milestones,
they'll earn additional equity.
And then when they sell the business
and generate a meaningful return back to investors,
they'll get an additional chunk of equity in the business,
kind of that remaining one third.
And usually these investors are targeting IRRs,
internal rates of return on their investment,
and then you know, 20 to 30, maybe upwards of 40%.
So if you feel confident that you can go in,
buy a business, help it grow and then sell it
and generate a 20 to 30 to 40% return,
then that can be a really great investment for you
where you end up with 25% of a really great business
without having to put up any of your own capital
and getting paid all along the way,
just like a private equity investor would frankly.
Because you get paid to find the deal,
and once you find it you get paid to operate the deal
and once it exits, you take out a big chunk of equity
right alongside the investors.
The other piece to keep in mind too
is a lot of these businesses are funded with debt.
So when the searcher identifies the company
they're gonna use dollars from their investors as equity
but then they'll also typically borrow money from banks
as well to consummate the transaction.
So, just like a private equity fund
they also get some additional benefit
from the leverage that they're putting on the business.
This also means though, that a lot of these searchers
are gonna be looking for businesses
that are generating positive cash flow,
versus ones that are more focused on growth, let's say.
All right, so what does all this mean for you?
Well, I think if I were you
and I wanted to get into the search fund space
and become a searcher, first I would figure
out like what's my unique angle?
Is it that I went to a prestigious university
and can tell like, hey, I'm really smart and capable?
Is that I've been working in an industry for a long time
and I really understand these industries
and I have relationships and so on and so forth
that give me an edge?
Or is it that I'm just like really good at hustling?
I'd figure out kind of like what's my unique angle.
Then I'd decide like, hey, what's my investment thesis?
What types of businesses do I think
I could be successful at running
and operating and improving?
You might also decide that rather than raising money
from investors to finance your salary,
maybe you wanna take out an SBA loan
or work off of your own savings.
This can be especially useful if maybe you didn't go
to Harvard or Stanford or some other top tier university
and so you don't have that credential
that you can tout to investors to give them confidence.
That doesn't mean that you know, only people
from Harvard and Stanford are great entrepreneurs
and great private equity investors,
because that's definitely not the case.
But they oftentimes can have a bit of an advantage
when it comes to fundraising.
So in that case, maybe you self-fund.
You get an SBA loan, you use your savings,
whatever it takes, right?
Some of the top accelerators include firms like Broadtree
and MixGen Growth, where they will bring you in,
they will help train you, they will help you find a deal,
they will help invest or connect you to their investors
and really smooth out the whole process.
Of course, the downside of working with an accelerator
is that you kind of become a part of their investment team
rather than your own investment team, right?
They're gonna have a lot of say and push
in terms of the type of company that you invest in
and acquire and how you ultimately run it.
So you know, there are pros and cons, but you know,
especially if you don't come from a top tier university,
they can be interesting ways to get
into the search fund space.
You also, like once you've built out your thesis
and been able to identify kind of your unique angle,
you'll need to go pitch to investors.
There are actually quite a few investors out there
that love investing in search funds.
And the reason for that is because the data shows,
consistently over time, that search funders return
significantly above-market return.
And so there are great funds, like Peterson
for example here in Utah,
that loves to fund these types of companies.
And so if you can go to them and demonstrate
why you are a good bet to go find a great business,
they and others will be excited to back you.
Another great source of capital for search funders
are entrepreneurs that have been there and done it.

videos.full_text: - Are you struggling to find a fulfilling career? Maybe you're tired of the 9 to 5 and you've heard about private equity, you think it's really interesting but don't really know where to start? Well, one of the places a lot of people start is through search funds. And now a search fund has been around since probably sometime in the 1980s it was really developed, at Stanford. And the idea was there was a professor that had a couple students that wanted to buy a business and so he gave them some money to go and find a company, buy it and run it. And then ultimately they sold it and he generated this great return. And they also generated a great return because they got a big piece of the equity. This evolved quite a bit until today, you've got lots of firms and accelerators and other groups that are out there all supporting and investing in searchers, as they're called, or search funds. Now what is a search fund, how does it work? Well, it's kind of like a very, very mini private equity fund of one to two people. A good friend of mine, Deb Tan, is one of those searchers. After graduating from undergrad, she went and worked on Wall Street for one of the large investment banks. And after being there for a few years she went to Harvard to get her MBA. At graduation, she was like, what do I want to do next? And really fell in love with the idea of search funds. So I sat down with her and just peppered her with tons of questions on how are search funds structured and what is the industry like and so forth. And so I'm gonna share some of the things that I learned as well as what I've seen working with other searchers over the years. Now first let's talk about what is a search fund. Now like I said, a search fund is kind of like a mini private equity fund. Essentially what happens is a searcher, or somebody that works in the search fund or that's putting it together, will go to investors and say, Hey, I am an exceptional leader and operator and I want to go buy a business and I want your help. In exchange for giving me some capital up front to cover my salary, living expenses, travel, et cetera, I'm willing to give you first rights of refusal and quite a bit of equity when I buy this company that I'm gonna go out and find. I'll also give you quarterly reports so you know what's going on and hopefully thereby reduce your risk. Now the amount of money that they raise varies but is typically somewhere between 400 and $700,000 depending on inflation and market and expertise and what kind of business they're gonna buy, et cetera, et cetera. Sometimes it edges up a little bit higher towards the like 800, $900,000 if you have two searchers working together. But you know, median is somewhere in the like 500, $550,000 range. Now that money should buy you enough runway to be a searcher for about two years. So typically searchers are gonna pay themselves, let's say they raise 500,000. They're gonna pay themselves probably somewhere between 100 and $200,000 that will leave them with a little over $300,000 to spend on you know, hiring interns maybe, paying legal bills, travel, working with bankers, legal diligence, all the things that they need to do in order to find an investment opportunity or a company to buy, do the due diligence and follow through with raising the money to complete the acquisition. So what'll happen is over those two years, they'll spend a lot of time trying to find a deal. So over those two years, they'll work tirelessly to try to find a deal because at the end of those two years or when they've used up all the money, it's done. And you know, if they haven't found something then, you know it'll just be kind of a waste, for their investors and also for them to a certain extent. During that time period, they'll need to come up with an engine to help find the company they want to buy. I know some searchers, they build out an army of interns. Where, you know, they'll go to a university and they'll pay, you know, 10 to $15 an hour and they'll have all these interns that are literally smiling and dialing for deals. They're just calling lots of companies, hopefully within like a sector that they're really excited about. But generally they're just kind of canvassing a large area and trying to find kind of that diamond in the rough. Other searchers use a more strategic approach. They might say, hey, I am really interested in, you know, personal care and so I'm gonna go look at personal care businesses. Or you know, I think there's an opportunity to buy a really good HVAC company and roll it up with a few more and build it into a much bigger business. Similar to like what a private equity fund would do. There could be a lot of different strategies. And it also kind of depends on what that person's background is. So if they come with a lot of expertise in a particular industry or sector, right, then they're obviously gonna spend more time hunting for deals in that sector. Let's say they find their deal. Well now they have to package it all up and go back to their original investors that gave them the money in the first place. The thing that's interesting about that is when they go back, they're doing two things. One, they're selling the deal, but two they're also selling their job in the deal. Because once they acquire the business, they're actually gonna typically take a CEO or a COO position in the company. They'll negotiate some sort of salary somewhere in the you know, call it roughly $200,000 range depending on where the business is located and inflation and so forth. But you can imagine somewhere in that range. So you know, a healthy salary for sure. And then over time they'll earn their equity in the business. Now in this case, the way that they are structured is typically the investors that are coming into the deal and providing the capital will take preferred shares and a majority of the board. They basically sit in control. But the day-to-day operations are left to the searcher. And they are working hard to earn their equity which amounts to a total of typically 25 to 30% of the business. And they'll earn that over time. So once they close the deal, they'll get a chunk of equity usually about a third of it. As they hit certain milestones, they'll earn additional equity. And then when they sell the business and generate a meaningful return back to investors, they'll get an additional chunk of equity in the business, kind of that remaining one third. And usually these investors are targeting IRRs, internal rates of return on their investment, and then you know, 20 to 30, maybe upwards of 40%. So if you feel confident that you can go in, buy a business, help it grow and then sell it and generate a 20 to 30 to 40% return, then that can be a really great investment for you where you end up with 25% of a really great business without having to put up any of your own capital and getting paid all along the way, just like a private equity investor would frankly. Because you get paid to find the deal, and once you find it you get paid to operate the deal and once it exits, you take out a big chunk of equity right alongside the investors. The other piece to keep in mind too is a lot of these businesses are funded with debt. So when the searcher identifies the company they're gonna use dollars from their investors as equity but then they'll also typically borrow money from banks as well to consummate the transaction. So, just like a private equity fund they also get some additional benefit from the leverage that they're putting on the business. This also means though, that a lot of these searchers are gonna be looking for businesses that are generating positive cash flow, versus ones that are more focused on growth, let's say. All right, so what does all this mean for you? Well, I think if I were you and I wanted to get into the search fund space and become a searcher, first I would figure out like what's my unique angle? Is it that I went to a prestigious university and can tell like, hey, I'm really smart and capable? Is that I've been working in an industry for a long time and I really understand these industries and I have relationships and so on and so forth that give me an edge? Or is it that I'm just like really good at hustling? I'd figure out kind of like what's my unique angle. Then I'd decide like, hey, what's my investment thesis? What types of businesses do I think I could be successful at running and operating and improving? You might also decide that rather than raising money from investors to finance your salary, maybe you wanna take out an SBA loan or work off of your own savings. This can be especially useful if maybe you didn't go to Harvard or Stanford or some other top tier university and so you don't have that credential that you can tout to investors to give them confidence. That doesn't mean that you know, only people from Harvard and Stanford are great entrepreneurs and great private equity investors, because that's definitely not the case. But they oftentimes can have a bit of an advantage when it comes to fundraising. So in that case, maybe you self-fund. You get an SBA loan, you use your savings, whatever it takes, right? Some of the top accelerators include firms like Broadtree and MixGen Growth, where they will bring you in, they will help train you, they will help you find a deal, they will help invest or connect you to their investors and really smooth out the whole process. Of course, the downside of working with an accelerator is that you kind of become a part of their investment team rather than your own investment team, right? They're gonna have a lot of say and push in terms of the type of company that you invest in and acquire and how you ultimately run it. So you know, there are pros and cons, but you know, especially if you don't come from a top tier university, they can be interesting ways to get into the search fund space. You also, like once you've built out your thesis and been able to identify kind of your unique angle, you'll need to go pitch to investors. There are actually quite a few investors out there that love investing in search funds. And the reason for that is because the data shows, consistently over time, that search funders return significantly above-market return. And so there are great funds, like Peterson for example here in Utah, that loves to fund these types of companies. And so if you can go to them and demonstrate why you are a good bet to go find a great business, they and others will be excited to back you. Another great source of capital for search funders are entrepreneurs that have been there and done it. And they ultimately can also be great resources and advisors as you are finding the business, helping you negotiate the terms of the deal, and once you acquire it, hopefully help you make it a roaring success. Anyways, if you enjoyed this video and you're interested in more opportunities in private equity or venture capital and what jobs look like, check out my other video where I talk about how much money VCs make and whether or not all VCs are actually rich or not. metadata.title: Earnouts vs Seller Financing - How to Document Each
metadata.author: Escamilla Law Office
metadata.shortDescription:
A $10 million price can mean $7 million at closing, a $1 million note, and a $2 million earnout. M&A attorney Rick Escamilla explains how to document each one.

When a business is sold, the headline price does not always tell you how much the seller receives at closing. Rick Escamilla of Escamilla Law Office explains why seller financing and earnouts should be documented as two different parts of the deal. A seller note is money the buyer already owes, so the main concern is credit risk. An earnout is money the seller may earn later, so the main concern is performance risk. Those risks need different protections.

Rick covers how to pick and define an earnout metric, why revenue and EBITDA raise different questions, and why a formula example in the agreement can prevent surprises. He looks at who controls the business after closing and what information the seller gets. He also covers seller note terms, default provisions, guarantees, collateral, and set-off. Then he shows how a senior lender can change the deal, and breaks down one $10 million example piece by piece.

In this episode:
- Why a seller note creates repayment risk and an earnout creates performance risk.
- How to think about revenue, EBITDA, and other earnout metrics.
- Why EBITDA calculated under GAAP may not answer the real questions.
- Which buyer decisions can distort an earnout after closing.
- What process a seller needs to review an earnout calculation and object to it.
- What a seller note should say about interest, payments, balloons, and default.
- How guarantees, collateral, and set-off rights affect the seller's protection.
- How a senior lender can subordinate or restrict payments on a seller note.

Questions this episode answers:
What is the difference between an earnout and seller financing?
With seller financing, the buyer generally owes the money, and the main concern is whether the buyer can pay. With an earnout, the buyer may owe more only if something happens after closing. If the condition is not met, the buyer may owe nothing.

Who controls the business during an earnout?
The buyer usually does. Rick does not think the buyer should have to run it the way the seller did, or be free to do whatever it wants. He prefers to address decisions that can distort the earnout, like corporate overhead, moving customers, and accounting changes.

How can a senior lender affect a seller note?
The bank will usually want priority. The seller's debt may be subordinated, its collateral may be junior, and payments may be restricted. The bank may also want the note to stay in place longer than expected. Rick prefers getting the lender into these questions early.

What should a seller ask before agreeing to deferred payment?
First, what has to happen before I get paid? Second, what could prevent the payment? Third, what protection do I have if something changes? If the answer to the first question is not clear, Rick says the documents are not ready.

Watch this if a buyer or seller in your deal is proposing an earnout or a seller note, and you want to understand the risk before closing.

segments.text: How should earnout and seller financing be documented? The short answer, earnouts and seller
financing should be documented as two different parts of the deal because they create different
risks. A seller note is money the buyer already owes. The documents should focus on when it gets
paid, what happens if the buyer does not pay, and what protection the seller has. An earnout
is money the seller may earn later. The agreement needs to clearly explain what has to happen before
the payment becomes due. With an earnout, control matters. The buyer usually controls the business
after closing. So, the agreement should address a decisions that would affect whether the seller
reaches the earnout target. The calculation has to be clear. If the earnout is based on revenue,
Ibida or another metric, the party should agree in advance and how that number will
be calculated. If a lender is involved, all the documents need to work together. A seller note,
guarantee, collateral, earnout, and senior loan cannot be negotiated in isolation. The main
point is that these are not just ways to play part to pay part of the purchase price later.
They are different ways of allocating risk after closing and the document should all reflect that.
When a business is sold, the headline purchase price does not always tell you how much money
the seller will actually receive at closing. Take a simple example. Assume a buyer and a
seller agree on a potential purchase price of $10 million. The buyer pays
$7 million in cash at closing. The seller takes back a $1 million promisary note. The other $2
million can be earned over the next two years if the business reaches certain financial targets.
People may call that a $10 million transaction, but those three pieces of the purchase price are
very different. $7 million is cash in the seller's account at closing. $1 million is owed later,
and $2 million may never become payable at all. That difference matters. I do not like treating a
deferred consideration as a small detail that can be worked out after the parties agree on price.
It is part of the price. If I am representing a seller, I want to understand not only the
total number, but how much is being paid now, how much is being paid later, and what has to
happen before the seller receives the rest. If I'm representing a buyer, I want to know that those
future payment obligations fit the financing and cash flow of the business. That's where the legal
documents become important. Earnouts and seller financing are often discussed together because
both involve payments after closing, but they are not the same thing. With seller financing,
the buyer generally owes the money. For example, the buyer may pay $7 million at closing and give
the seller a promisary note for $1 million. But note may have interest, monthly payments,
a maturity date, and maybe a balloon payment. But the the basic point is simple. The buyer
owes the money. The seller's main concern is whether the buyer can actually pay it. An earnout
works differently. With an earnout, the buyer may owe additional purchase price only if something
happens after closing. Maybe the business reaches a revenue target. Maybe it reaches a certain level
of ibida. Maybe a major customer stays with the business. Maybe a project is completed. If the
condition is met, the payment becomes due. If it's not met, the buyer may owe nothing. So,
the risks are different. With the seller note, we are mainly dealing with credit risk. Can the buyer
pay? What happens if the buyer does not pay? What collateral or guarantee supports the obligation?
With an earnout, we are dealing with performance risk. What has to happen before the seller gets
paid? How is that measured? And who controls the decision that affect the result? Those are
different questions, so they need different protections. Seller financing and earnouts
usually solve different problems. Seller financing often helps solve a funding problem. The buyer
may have enough cash and bank financing to fund most of the purchase price, but not all of it.
So, the seller agrees to finance the difference. That can help the transaction close. But from the
seller's side, I think it's important to call it what it is. The seller is extending credit to the
buyer. The seller is giving up cash at closing in exchange for a promise to be paid later. The
promise has value, but that value depends heavily on who made the promise and how likely that person
or company is to pay. Earnouts usually solve a different problem. They come up when the buyer and
seller disagree about a value. Assume a company has historically generated $1 million of IBIDA.
The seller recently added several large customers and believes IBIDA will soon grow to $1.5 million.
The seller wants the purchase price to reflect that growth. The buyer may say, "I believe the
growth is possible, but I'm not going to pay for it today." That is where an earnout can work.

metadata.title: Seller Financing and Set-Off Rights: Recovery Mechanisms in M&A Deals
metadata.author: SMB Law Group LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Sam Rosati and Kevin Henderson continue their detailed examination of indemnification in small business acquisitions on Main Street Deals. This episode focuses on the practical challenge of actually getting paid when an indemnification claim arises. The conversation addresses the common misconception that having an indemnity provision in a purchase agreement guarantees recovery, when in reality the structure of recovery mechanisms determines whether a buyer can survive a loss. Kevin explains why escrows, holdbacks, and set-off rights function differently in terms of liquidity, and why seller financing has become the predominant recovery tool in SMB deals despite being nearly absent in middle market transactions.

They discuss:
- Why indemnification against an empty corporate shell leaves buyers with no practical recourse
- How escrows differ from holdbacks and when offset rights against seller notes actually provide liquidity
- Why market data from lower middle market deals misleads small business buyers on caps, baskets, and escrow percentages
- The critical difference between having a right to recover and having immediate access to cash when a claim occurs
- Why reps and warranties insurance is emerging as a more viable option for small business deals

This episode offers essential guidance for anyone structuring or negotiating a small business acquisition where financial protection depends on more than just contractual language.

Topics:
00:00 - Intro
01:06 - Summer check-in and firm update
02:48 - Recap and continuing indemnification discussion
03:56 - How to actually get paid on indemnity claims
06:09 - Recovery mechanisms overview
07:52 - Escrows explained

How you structure a deal is just as important as the price you pay. Should you go all cash, seller financing, or an earnout? The right structure can help you reduce risk, improve cash flow, and get your deal across the finish line. In this video, Andrew Gazdecki breaks down the three most common deal structures to help you make the right choice.

We walk you through the key financing options:
► Cash Up Front: The simplest but most expensive option. You pay the full purchase price at closing.
► Seller Financing: Pay over time with seller-backed financing.
► Earnouts: Tie a portion of the sale to future performance.

At Acquire.com, we help buyers navigate deal structuring to minimize risk and maximize success. Tune in to learn:
► The best deal structure for your acquisition.
► How to negotiate seller financing or earnouts.
► How Acquire.com helps buyers secure the right terms.

metadata.author: Neo Expertise
metadata.shortDescription:
Post-acquisition finance integration  is where most M&A deals quietly lose value. In this guide we cover the first 100 days after an acquisition a step-by-step finance integration checklist to make inherited data audit-ready.

This video shows Group Controllers, CFOs and finance teams how to reconcile balances, map the chart of accounts, and pass a first group close after a merger or acquisition.

🔎 In this video:
• Post-acquisition data check: the 7 things to verify first
• Trial balance, AR/AP aging, intercompany reconciliation, bank access
• Statutory vs. management accounts & chart of accounts mapping
• Day 31–100 finance integration roadmap
• Solving the Group Controller capacity problem

.

📅 Free consultation with NEO Expertise → https://neoexpertise.net/contact/

#PostAcquisitionIntegration #MandA #FinanceIntegration #GroupFinance #DueDiligence

Now,

In this conversation with McGuireWoods partner and host Greg Hawver, e2E founder and CEO Nancy McCullough pulls back the curtain on this work. metadata.title: The First 100 Days After a Private Equity Deal: What LPs Should Check
metadata.author: Lighthouse Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Signing the deal is not the finish line. Most value is won or lost in the first 100 days after close. This explainer walks through the operational risks that show up right after a private equity acquisition: people, systems, cash and reporting. It also covers what LPs and allocators should ask a GP to prove.

Read the full article: https://lighthousecapital.io/insights/post-close-operational-risk-private-equity/
Get the free First 100 Days LP Toolkit: https://lighthousecapital.io/first-100-days-lp-toolkit/

Sources: Bain & Company 2026, AlixPartners 2026, Grant Thornton and PitchBook.

Lighthouse Capital is currently raising Fund I. This video is for information only and is not an offer to invest.

#PrivateEquity #LimitedPartners #ValueCreation

segments.text: Signing a deal? It's definitely not the finish line.
In private equity, the riskiest stretch starts the very day after closing.
those crucial first 100 days.
Bain & Company's 2026 report points out that a buyout that once needed about 5%
yearly earnings growth now needs around 10% to 12%.
Basically, 12 is the new 5.
AlixPartners found that 65% of private equity firms actually see their CEO
leave during the holding period.
So how can an investor tell a manager with a real solid 100 day plan?
from one who just has a really nice slide deck.
In this explainer, we're going to map that out by looking at four key areas.
Oh, and make sure you stick around, because at the end, you can download a free
first 100 days LP toolkit. First up, post-close operational risk, people,
systems, cash, and reporting.
Second, a three-stage plan. Third, day one governance rules. And finally,
essential investor questions.
Let's start with what post-close operational risk actually is.
Section one, defining post-close operational risk.
That's everything that can go wrong in running the business from that day
forward. That execution typically breaks down across four main risk
tiles. First up is people. Operations might depend entirely on a single founder
who's holding all the relationships.
Second is systems. Legacy IT setups simply can't produce the data a new board
requires. Third, cash. Nobody is actually watching working capital, so cash just
leaks quietly. And finally, reporting.
accounts arrive late, which ends up forcing you to make decisions based on
untrustworthy numbers.
Moving on to section 2, why early mistakes cost more.
According to the Global Private Equity Report 2026 by Bain & Company, the math
has fundamentally changed. In the 2010s, a typical buyout needed about 5%
yearly growth in EBITDA. Today, Bain estimates that exact same deal requires
around 10-12% yearly EBITDA growth.
Furthermore, Bain also notes that buyout holding periods now average around 7
years. That's up from just five to six years between 2010 and 2021.
A slow or messy start costs significantly more nowadays.
and those early mistakes just have much, much longer to compound.
Let's look at section 3, the three-stage action plan.
Now, there is some old data from a 2013 Grant Thornton and PitchBook survey
showing almost 90% of private equity firms claim to use a 100-day plan.
But, honestly, having a theoretical plan just isn't enough.
A truly strong plan actually starts well before closing, right in the middle of
due diligence.
And crucially, it includes a named owner for every single task.
This 100-day road happens in three very distinct stages.
Days 0 to 30 are purely for stabilizing and listening.
doing things like getting two signatures on bank accounts and building a
13-week cash forecast. Then days 31 to 60 are to fix the basics, forcing
accounts to close on time and setting key performance indicators, or KPIs.
Days 61 to 100 are where you finally set up growth, but only once cash controls
are actually working. And the whole thing culminates on day 100, with a strict
review requiring hard proof for every completed item.
Section 4. Playbooks, governance and rules. To make all this work, we need
governance.
This is formally mapped out in a Delegation of Authority, or DOA.
A DOA is basically the written, tiered approval ladder, detailing exactly

metadata.title: The First 30 Days After an Acquisition: What IT Must Decide Before Migration
metadata.author: Bridgeyard
metadata.shortDescription:
The First 30 Days After an Acquisition: What IT Must Decide Before Migration

The acquisition is complete. On Monday morning, the acquired business still needs to take orders, pay people and serve customers. A new logo and a target migration date do not tell the IT team what must keep working. This is a practical guide to the first thirty days after an acquisition: seven decisions that create a workable integration plan before you start moving systems. We will use a fictional company with one hundred employees across three sites. The sequence is a planning example, not a promise that every acquisition can be ready in thirty days.

Explore the Bridgeyard demo: https://demo.bridgeyard.io/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=first30days_20261113&utm_content=f01
Current Pilot scope and onboarding: https://bridgeyard.io/pricing?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=first30days_20261113&utm_content=f01

Illustrative acquisition planning, not a fixed migration schedule. Fictional examples and figures. Technical delivery and decisions remain with your team.
AI-assisted narration: Florence, generated with ElevenLabs.
#Bridgeyard #ITIntegration #MandA

CHAPTERS
0:00 The deal closed. What happens Monday?
0:38 1. Define Day One.
1:19 2. Trace one business service.
2:02 3. Give temporary access an expiry.
2:45 4. Put a date on the service dependency.
3:24 5. Compare the cost of the options.
4:13 Make the assumption visible beside the cost.
4:47 6. Pilot a useful business outcome.
5:29 7. Plan the day after cutover.
6:04 Turn seven decisions into one working plan.
6:46 Try it against your integration.

segments.text: The acquisition is complete.
On Monday morning, the acquired business still needs
to take orders, pay people and serve customers.
A new logo and a target migration date do
not tell the IT team what must keep working.
This is a practical guide to the
first 30 days after an acquisition.
Seven decisions that create a workable integration
plan before you start moving systems.
We will use a fictional company
with 100 employees across three sites.
The sequence is a planning example, not a promise
that every acquisition can be ready in 30 days.
First, separate day one continuity from the later integration.
In our example, the acquired team needs email, access
to its order system and a working support route.
That does not automatically mean moving the whole
company into the buyer's Microsoft tenant immediately.
Write down the business outcome, the people
affected and the minimum service needed.
Then put the later changes into a separate plan.
This distinction protects the team from treating
every integration wish as an urgent requirement.
The decision to make today is simple.
What must work now and what can safely wait?
Second, start with an important business
service and follow its dependencies.
Take order processing.
Who signs in?
Which application do they use?
Where is its data?
Who supports it?
What happens if the internet connection
or an external supplier is unavailable?
Follow one real transaction through the
chain with the business owner.
A long application inventory will not necessarily
expose the dependency that can stop trading.
Record what is confirmed, what is
uncertain, and who will investigate.
This is a focused conversation with the people
doing the work, not a request to collect
every possible detail before anything can move.
Third, decide how temporary access will
work and how it will end.
An acquisition often needs a transitional arrangement
while the future design is being agreed.
Name the people who need access, the approving owner,
the intended scope, and a review or expiry date.
Include a removal action in
the plan from the start.
The IT and security teams still need
to configure and validate the technical controls.
A planning record does not enforce those controls.
The useful management question is whether the temporary
arrangement has a responsible owner and a clear exit, so
temporary does not quietly become permanent.
Fourth, connect supplier support and transitional
services to the delivery plan.
Suppose the acquired business relies on a service that
will only be supported for another eight weeks.
The integration team needs more than that end date.
It needs to understand the service coverage,
the replacement work, the acceptance checks, and
the person responsible for the handover.
If the replacement slips, who must review the consequence?
Keep the commercial and technical
owners in the same discussion.
Review the actual agreement with the responsible team.
A calendar reminder cannot extend a
service or change a contract.
Fifth, make the cost of the
transition visible before choosing the pace.
A fast migration and a staged migration
can create different combinations of delivery effort,
supplier charges, duplicate subscriptions, and support demand.
In a fictional example, one option needs
20,000 pounds of one-time delivery work.
Another needs 12,000 pounds of delivery
work plus three months of parallel service
at 4,000 pounds a month.
That second option totals 24,000
pounds within this limited comparison.
It may still be the right choice for continuity.
These are invented planning figures, not supplier quotes, and
the team must include every relevant cost before deciding.
Show the assumption behind the amount.
Does parallel service really last three months?
Who can confirm the support effort?
Is a cost one-time or recurring?
Record the currency, the estimate owner,
and the next review date.
Do not present a provisional
comparison as a guaranteed saving.
If extending the transition by a month changes the
decision, make that sensitivity visible to the sponsor.
This turns the cost discussion into a
delivery choice with consequences rather than a
number disconnected from the plan.
Sixth, choose a small migration wave
that can teach you something relevant.
The easiest users may not represent the
business process you need to protect.
Choose a bounded group with an agreed reason for
inclusion, a business owner, and a clear acceptance question.
For order processing, success might mean an authorised user
can create an order, find the correct customer details,
and pass the order into the next operational step.
Record the result and the unresolved exceptions.
The team decides whether that
evidence supports the next wave.
A successful sign-in alone is
not the whole business outcome.
Seventh, design the support handover before the migration finishes.
Who receives a problem on the first morning?
Who can diagnose it?
What information must accompany an escalation?
Agree the route with the team
that will actually operate the service.
Give the transition a clear exit criterion.
The support owner accepts the handover, known issues
have owners, and the agreed evidence is available.
A project completion message is not
a substitute for operational acceptance.
Keep a route back to the delivery
team for the exceptions that remain.
Now turn those decisions into a first-month rhythm.
In the opening days, confirm the services that
must keep working and assign the unknowns.
Then agree the transitional access, the supplier dependencies,
and the options that need a cost comparison.
Use the next planning cycle to prepare
the representative pilot and the support handover.
At each review, ask three questions.
What changed, who owns the next
action, and what decision is required?
The timing should follow the acquisition,
its obligations, and the evidence.
30 days is a useful review
horizon, not a universal migration deadline.
Bridgeyard migration control brings delivery actions, dependencies, readiness evidence,
and the financial picture into a shared programme view.
Your technical teams carry out the migration,
and your accountable people make the decisions.
Use the fictional example in this
video as a starting point.
Then test the approach against one
real service in your own programme.
Explore the Bridgeyard demo through
the link in the description.
If the structure fits the way you
need to work, review the current pilot
scope and onboarding options on the website.
Start with one programme and a clear
question you want it to answer.

metadata.title: Post-Acquisition Financial Controls: The First 30 Days
metadata.author: Lighthouse Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
If you can't see the cash, you can't protect the investment. 66% of companies have no CFO successor in place (AlixPartners, 2026). This explainer covers the four financial controls a GP should have in place in the first 30 days after a deal: a 13-week cash forecast, two-signature bank mandates, a monthly close inside 10 days, and a Day-30 control memo.

Read the full article: https://lighthousecapital.io/post-acquisition-financial-controls-private-equity/
Get the free First 100 Days LP Toolkit: https://lighthousecapital.io/first-100-days-lp-toolkit/
Pillar guide: https://lighthousecapital.io/insights/post-close-operational-risk-private-equity/

Lighthouse Capital is currently raising Fund I. This video is for information only and is not an offer to invest.

#PrivateEquity #FinancialControls #LimitedPartners

segments.text: If you can't see the cash, you simply can't tell whether the business you just
bought is actually getting better or worse.
In this explainer, we're looking at the post-acquisition financial controls that fix
this exact blind spot.
The core problem is that on closing day, the owner changes,
but those daily habits, they usually don't.
To put that into perspective,
66% of private equity firms report having no chief financial officer,
or CFO, successor ready to go.
How can an investor, like a limited partner or LP,
actually verify that a fund manager has absolute control of the cash from Day 1?
We're going to walk through three essential controls:
a 13 week cash flow forecast, requiring two signatures on every bank account,
and completing a monthly close within 10 business days.
Then we'll look at the Day 30 Control Memo, which is the single document that proves
it all to investors.
Let's jump right into the forecast.
First up is the 13 week cash flow forecast.
Every single week, it gets updated and compared against what actually happened.
Any large gap has to be explained in writing.
And this needs to be live within just two weeks of closing.
When you're reviewing this forecast, look out for a major red flag:
an unexplained gap of more than 10% between the forecast and the actual cash,
for two weeks in a row.
Next, you absolutely need to verify the bank mandate.
This is the bank's official record of who is actually allowed to use an account.
In a lot of founder run companies, you'll find a single person who approves payments
and holds all the bank logins.
You must list every single account on one unified register,
check each mandate, and require two signatures before any money leaves the building.
Crucially, and this is to prevent fraud, the person who approves a payment should
never, ever be the same person who sends it.
A clear, immediate red flag here: any bank account still operating on a single
signature after Day 15.
The third control is the monthly close.
A 10 day close means this whole process is fully completed within 10 business days
of the month's end.
Your standard target here is to hit this 10 day mark for three consecutive months by Day 100.
And the red flag to watch for? A close that drags on for longer than 15 business days.
If the data is that stale, management is essentially flying blind.
By Day 30, everything we've just discussed gets packaged into one short,
dated document: the Day 30 Control Memo.
This is the definitive first proof that an investor can,
and should, ask to see.

You can download the free First 100 Days LP Toolkit
and read the full article.
This is strictly educational content, not investment advice.

metadata.title: How to Navigate the First 90 Days Post-Acquisition - The Intentional Owner #15
metadata.author: The Intentional Owner
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Intentional Owner, Sam Rosati and Kaustubh Deo dive deep into the critical first 90 days following a business acquisition. Drawing from their own operating experience, they discuss tactical items like transition checklists and asset conversion, while also exploring the softer—but equally important—aspects of communication with employees and customers. They examine the nuances of announcing a deal, managing early team dynamics, and the risk of misaligned retention strategies. Along the way, they share candid reflections on the evolving identity of a business owner and the long road to earning trust and building cultural buy-in.

They discuss:
- Practical challenges and checklists for the first week of an asset deal transition
- Strategic communication approaches for customers and employees post-close
- Why retention bonuses can backfire and what to consider instead
- The long timeline and emotional complexity of "owning" a business culturally
- How to assess operator readiness in self-funded search deals
- A valuable episode for anyone navigating the early stages of ownership or evaluating what it really means to lead a small business.

Links:
Kaustubh on Substack - https://bigdealsmallbusiness.substack.com/p/read-me-first
Sam on X - https://x.com/Sam_Rosati
Follow along with the guys' fitness tracker! - https://bit.ly/3T4EpHw

00:00 - Intro
01:02 - Catching up
06:06 - First 90 days post-acquisition
16:19 - Communication with the team 
23:32 - Retention bonuses
33:03 - The moment an acquirer feels like the business has become their own

metadata.title: Post-Deal Finance Integration: Why Acquisitions Underperform in the First 100 Days
metadata.author: Byron Thomas Recruitment
metadata.shortDescription:
Deals are won on strategy, but value is routinely lost in the first 100 days when reporting, cash visibility, ERP systems and finance team capability do not match the deal model.

Across Australian corporate acquisitions and private equity buy-and-build platforms, due diligence examines historical earnings thoroughly while spending far less time testing whether the acquired finance team can operate at the buyer's pace and reporting standard.

This episode examines what happens after completion, why bolt-on rollups stretch holding periods when finance and systems remain fragmented, when to back the existing Financial Controller versus introducing integration capability, and a practical first-100-day finance integration framework for boards, CEOs and CFOs.

TOPICS COVERED
- Why financial due diligence is not the same as finance capability diligence
- What PitchBook, PwC, Deloitte and McKinsey data show about post-deal value erosion
- Why buy-and-build and bolt-on acquisitions strain mid-market finance teams
- First-100-day pressure points: cash visibility, month-end close, ERP systems and payroll
- Auditable synergy tracking versus deal-model forecasts
- When to support the incumbent finance leader, add interim resources or upgrade the role
- A practical pre-close and first-100-day checklist for boards, CFOs and finance leaders

LINKS
Full article: https://www.byronthomas.com.au/blog/post-deal-finance-integration-australia-acquisitions/
Executive search: https://www.byronthomas.com.au/executive-search/
Accounting and finance recruitment: https://www.byronthomas.com.au/accounting-recruitment-australia/
Our methodology: https://www.byronthomas.com.au/our-methodology/
Contact Byron Thomas Recruitment: https://www.byronthomas.com.au/contact/

ABOUT
Produced by Byron Thomas Recruitment, executive search and accounting and finance recruitment specialists serving Australia and New Zealand.

This episode is an AI-narrated discussion based on published market insight.
