There's a 31 percentage point execution gap between successful and unsuccessful acquirers based on this pre-close discipline alone. >> 31%? >> Huge. >> That's massive. >> Huge. The top-tier buyers, the 59% who actually capture their intended synergies, are translating their value drivers into fully funded executable initiatives with assigned owners long before the integration phase begins. >> Meanwhile, the Deloitte Heads of M&A Survey 2026 frames this perfectly for the Australian landscape. Post-close, 68% of deal leaders report severe tension between their pre-deal assumptions and the operational reality regarding people and culture. >> 68%? >> And 62% experience massive friction across technology and systems. Both of those immense pressure points land squarely on the group CFO's desk at the exact same time. >> Because if you think about it, the financial due diligence providers essentially acted as a translation layer during the deal. >> Oh, that's an interesting way to put it. >> Well, the investigating accountants used sophisticated data analytics tools to extract the target's raw data, right? And they built these beautiful interactive dashboards for the buyer. >> Right, so the buyer sees this polished output. >> Exactly. And the buyer naturally assumes the target's internal finance team has the capability to produce those same dashboards. >> Ah, I see where this is going. >> The moment the big four advisors pack up and leave, the buyer asks the incumbent financial controller for the same dashboard, and they receive a broken PDF. >> Or a spreadsheet with hard-coded numbers that don't tie out. >> [snorts] >> Let's avoid the usual clichés here. This isn't just about, you know, changing the engine while flying the plane. >> No, it's far worse. >> It is much closer to organ rejection in a medical transplant. You can graft a highly profitable $20 million revenue stream onto your platform business, but if the legacy ERP system doesn't share the same data architecture, the parent company's operational body will literally treat it as a foreign object. >> Spot on. It just rejects it. >> Right. Rejecting the reporting data month after month until the integration team is forced to intervene with manual temporary solutions. >> The physiological analogy holds up really well, actually, because organ rejection requires immediate, highly expensive immunosuppressants. >> Right. >> Which, in the M&A world, translates to incredibly expensive interim consultants and totally diverted management focus. >> It's a massive distraction. >> It is. And this failure to assess operational finance capability, it transcends internal annoyance. It aggressively degrades investment timelines and exit strategies. >> Which brings us to the PitchBook data. >> Yes. The Byron Thomas recruitment report highlights PitchBook's 2026 data on Australian and New Zealand private capital. We're looking at a market that recorded $51.3 billion in deal value for 2025. >> $5.3 billion. And the composition of those deals is the critical variable here. 70% of PE-backed transactions in Australia right now are add-ons and buyouts. >> It's a classic consolidation play. >> Exactly. In a market environment defined by elevated financing costs, rolling up smaller businesses is the most mathematically reliable way to build scale. >> You acquire a smaller, founder-led add-on at say six times EBITDA. >> Right. >> You integrate it into a larger institutional platform valued at 12 times EBITDA, and you capture that multiple arbitrage. >> The thesis is bulletproof on paper. >> Yeah, on paper, yes. But the execution timeline tells a vastly different story. PitchBook's analysis reveals that portfolio companies executing these add-on acquisitions take roughly 12 months longer to exit on median than stand-alone buyouts. >> Wait, 12 months longer? Adding an entire year to a holding period absolutely destroys the internal rate of return. >> It wipes it out. >> If a sponsor modeled a five-year exit to clear their funds hurdle rate, and the asset is held for six years because the back office is a mess, the mathematical compounding turns a top quartile fund into a mediocre one. >> And that delay is entirely driven by the friction of integration. Think about it. If a sponsor aggressively bolts four or five businesses together without executing genuine foundational back office integration, they haven't built a cohesive platform. >> No, they've built a Frankenstein monster. >> Exactly. They have built a fragmented holding company masquerading as a unified brand. >> And buyers aren't stupid. >> No. When it comes time to exit, large strategic buyers or secondary private equity sponsors will conduct their own due diligence. And they'll look under the hood, they see three different payroll systems, totally unmapped charts of accounts, and manual consolidation processes, >> and they heavily discount the valuation to account for the operational risk. >> Instantly. >> So, the mandate is completely clear. Integration planning must happen pre-close. >> Yes. >> But, and this is a massive butt for Australian boards and corporate development teams, there is a serious regulatory barrier to early integration. >> The new ACCC rules. >> Yes. The Australian Institute of Company Directors has been aggressively broadcasting the implications of the new mandatory ACCC merger regime, which took effect on January 1, 2026. >> The shift from a voluntary notification system to a mandatory regime fundamentally altered deal pacing in Australia. >> It really did. Because if a transaction meets the notification thresholds, it legally cannot complete until the ACCC grants clearance. Crucially, directors face severe penalties for gun jumping, you know, exercising premature operational control or sharing sensitive competitive information before legal completion. >> Which terrifies most boards. >> Of course it does. If I am advising a board, I am naturally going to enforce a strict hands-off policy. The regulatory environment strongly suggests that early aggressive integration planning is legally perilous. >> Well, um, that is a very common misinterpretation. And it is a shockingly costly one. >> Really? How so? >> The regulatory clock, even under the new ACCC mandatory regime, does not mandate operational paralysis. Guidance from major advisors like McKinsey and EY Australia emphasizes that disciplined acquirers heavily utilize the period between signing and closing. >> But how do they do that without breaching the gun jumping rules? >> They do this through highly regulated clean rooms and clean teams. >> Okay, let's break down the actual mechanics of a clean room because the term gets thrown around in strategy meetings a lot without much understanding of the legal firewall involved. >> Yeah. A clean room is a secure, heavily restricted data environment. The crucial mechanism is that the personnel operating within the clean room, the clean team, must be entirely independent from the commercial decision-makers of the acquiring business. >> So it's not the CEO and the deal team looking at the stuff. >> Absolutely not. They are typically third-party consultants or strictly ring-fenced internal staff, like integration specialists, who have zero role in pricing, sales, or strategic deal making. >> Right, so they cannot report granular competitive data back to the deal team. They can only report aggregated, sanitized operating models. >> Precisely. Inside that legal firewall, the clean team can map baseline operational costs, review the target's chart of accounts, design the day-one target operating model, and heavily scope out the transitional service agreements or TSAs. >> They are building the architectural blueprints. >> Exactly. No competitive sensitivities are breached, zero operational control is exercised, but the moment legal completion actually occurs, the buyer isn't sitting around figuring out where the plumbing goes. They're simply executing a pre-approved blueprint. >> Deloitte's 2026 research, I think it's called operating model first, integration second, validates this approach entirely. >> It does. >> Yes, they argue that post-merger failures are often locked in permanently before the deal even closes, simply because leadership defers foundational governance choices. >> Which is such a common trap. >> It is. If you wait until day one to decide whose accounting policies apply, which ERP system will hold the single source of truth, or what the capital expenditure approval matrix looks like, your integration team will just spend the critical first 90 days escalating basic administrative disputes instead of capturing synergy value. >> And that failure to utilize the pre-close window catapults the acquiring business directly into the 100-day operational nightmare outlined in the Byron and Thomas Recruitment Insight. >> cooker. >> Exactly. They identify five specific structural pressure points where the financial machinery breaks down during those 100 days. >> Let's dissect these mechanically, starting with the most immediate existential threat, which is cash visibility and working capital management. The shift in cadence here is violent, isn't it? >> Oh, it's a massive shock to the system. The baseline state in a founder-led target is often highly informal treasury management. >> Right. >> The founder possesses an encyclopedic, almost intuitive knowledge of the working capital cycle. They know precisely which major client pays 45 days late, but is ultimately reliable. And they know which key supplier requires immediate payment to prevent a supply chain halt. >> But upon completion, that founder typically steps back or at least steps away from the daily accounts payable function. >> Yes. >> So that informal intuitive knowledge vanishes overnight. But the acquiring board, they demand immediate institutional grade visibility over every bank facility, every covenant limit, and every weekly cash movement. >> Because the acquiring platform is invariably carrying acquisition debt. >> Right, they have to service the debt. >> Private credit funds or syndicated lenders, they require a highly disciplined 13-week rolling cash flow forecast, usually with strict variance analysis attached. >> And when you ask a legacy financial controller who has only ever monitored a static bank balance to suddenly model working capital seasonality in an accrual framework over a 13-week horizon, the forecast inevitably fails. >> the mark entirely. >> Which instantly triggers a crisis of confidence at the board level. Then the private equity sponsor has to parachute their own deal team in just to manage basic treasury functions. >> Which bleeds directly into the second pressure point. The friction of the month-end close. >> The cultural shock here cannot be overstated. >> It is a fundamental re-wiring of the accounting function. Think about it. A private target historically closes its books 20 days after month-end, often strictly on a cash or tax basis. >> Very relaxed. >> Very. Post-acquisition, the new parent company mandates IFRS or AASB compliant accrual accounting, deep variance commentary, complex KPI dashboards, and debt covenant certificates to be delivered by working day five. >> Working day five? It forces a local administrative team to execute an enterprise-grade process without upgrading their tools. >> Exactly. >> Without additional resourcing or a complete process redesign, the first three month end closes post completion just devolve into an exhausting scramble. The friction of identifying unrecorded liabilities and forcing accruals through legacy systems means the finance team is working past midnight. >> Every single night. >> Yeah. Consequently, they have zero cognitive bandwidth left to support the actual commercial integration of the business. >> And what exact systems are they fighting with at midnight? >> Right, which brings us to the third pressure point, the ERP and spreadsheet bridge. We touched on organ rejection earlier, but let's look at the actual data mapping involved here. >> In bolt-on acquisitions, the target almost never operates on the identical ERP, payroll, or billing configuration as the platform business. >> It's always a mismatch. >> Always. Full ERP migration is notoriously complex. Takes months and frequently years to map the data architecture correctly. However, the acquiring board demands consolidated group reporting immediately on day one. >> And so the default solution is always an interim manual bridge. >> The dreaded spreadsheet. >> Exactly. An overworked management accountant extracts CSV files from the target's legacy system, dumps them into a massive Excel workbook, runs a series of incredibly complex macros, and maps it to the parent company's chart of accounts. >> And the danger really compounds when a sponsor executes a rapid roll-up strategy, completing three or four bolt-ons in 18-month window. >> Which is very common right now. >> Extremely common. If they refuse to invest in dedicated systems architecture, that temporary manual Excel bridge becomes a permanent load-bearing pillar of the group's financial reporting. >> That is terrifying. >> It introduces catastrophic operational risk. A single broken macro, a corrupted data lake, or heaven forbid, the resignation of the one accountant who actually understands how the spreadsheet links together, and the entire board reporting pack is completely compromised. >> If you are a corporate development leader modeling these acquisitions, the reality is that your sophisticated investment thesis doesn't fail during the strategic review. It fails in an unmapped spreadsheet cell at 11:00 p.m. on a Tuesday. >> Which perfectly leads us to an area where spreadsheet errors have severe legal and reputational consequences. The fourth pressure point, encompassing payroll, superannuation, and tax governance. >> The Australian compliance environment is just a total minefield for rapid integration. >> It's incredibly unforgiving. >> When you acquire a mid-market business, you often inherit highly bespoke legacy employee allowances. You inherit informal interpretations of complex modern awards. >> Oh, the holiday pay miscalculations alone. >> Exactly. You uncover creative independent contractor arrangements that likely fail the ATO's employee versus contractor tests. And you inherit incredibly complex payroll tax state groupings. >> These are compliance vectors where the we will figure it out later approach is absolutely lethal. >> just delay it. >> No. A payroll error in the first post-close pay cycle is the absolute fastest way to destroy employee trust and trigger union intervention. Furthermore, integrating single touch payroll reporting, and verifying superannuation guarantee obligations requires immediate forensic specialist attention. >> You cannot casually hand over forensic payroll tax remediation to an inherited financial controller who is already drowning in their first day five month end close. >> They will break under the pressure. >> The friction there guarantees compliance breaches. >> And the final pressure point in the 100-day window is where the CFO's authority is truly tested. Auditable synergy tracking. >> Ah, the synergies. >> Yes. This is where the theoretical deal model spectacularly collides with operational reality. >> Let's elevate this beyond the basic definition of gross versus net synergies. We know that gross savings are the theoretical head count or procurement reductions. And net synergies are what remains after subtracting the one-off integration costs, you know, the severance packages, the IT migration fees, the lease break penalties. >> Right. >> But the real friction lies in how those numbers are tracked and manipulated. >> The Byron Thomas recruitment insight heavily references McKinsey and BCG methodologies here, insisting that the CFO absolutely must own the cost baseline. >> Why is that mechanism so critical? >> Well, in many integrations, deal teams or integration consultants will artificially inflate the appearance of net synergies by aggressively pushing ongoing operating expenses into the one-off integration cost bucket during EBITDA normalization. >> Ah, so they manipulate the adjustments to make the core business look more profitable than it actually is. >> Precisely. It's a classic trick. And a weak inherited finance team simply lacks the commercial sophistication to spot this manipulation or to challenge the integration consultants. >> They just accept the numbers. >> Yeah. To genuinely capture value, those net synergies must be iteratively pressure tested, hardcoded into the financial planning and analysis process, and rigorously tracked through monthly departmental variance reporting for the next 3 years. >> And if the inherited finance function has only ever produced historical look-back profit and loss statements, they completely lack the forward-looking FP&A toolkit required to police that synergy discipline. >> Spot on. >> Which brings us to a deeply uncomfortable human element in all of this. >> The incumbent. >> Right. All of these systemic pressure points, the complex 13-week cash modeling, the aggressive day five close, the fragile ERP bridges, the forensic tax remediation, the synergy tracking, they eventually compress onto the shoulders of one individual, the incumbent financial controller or head of finance. >> The individual who, let's be honest, was managing the business perfectly well before the acquisition. >> Exactly. I really have to challenge the fairness of this expectation. We routinely see acquiring boards lay the blame for integration failure directly on the inherited financial controller. >> It happens all the time. >> But this is someone who likely ran a $40 million private enterprise brilliantly for 8 years. They were hired, praised, and incentivized for extreme cost consciousness and reliable stewardship. >> Yes. >> They were never hired to be a transformational M&A integration expert. Expecting them to just naturally absorb day one group reporting, complex purchase price allocation accounting, and debt covenant modeling without dedicated resources is literally engineering their failure. >> I completely agree with your assessment of the friction, but the market reality is unforgiving. It is unfair, yes. >> Very unfair. >> However, as the market insight details, buyers create immense operational risk when they avoid making an objective capability assessment out of misplaced politeness or out of a fear of losing historical knowledge. >> You can't just be nice about it. >> You must assess the capability objectively, regardless of how unfair the new demands are. The demands are the demands. >> So, we established that the friction is inevitable, and the assessment must be objective. What are the actual mechanical solutions here? The Byron Thomas recruitment report outlines three distinct operational choices for boards and group CFOs once that assessment is complete. >> Yes. The first option is to back and reinforce the incumbent. >> Meaning you keep them in the seat, but you alter their environment. >> Yes. If the capability assessment reveals that the inherited financial controller possesses strong commercial instincts, high adaptability, and align seamlessly with the acquiring culture, retaining them is strategically optimal. >> Because they hold all the institutional memory. >> Exactly. They hold the memory and the relationships with key suppliers. However, the mechanism for success here is scaffolding. >> Scaffolding? >> You cannot just leave them to manage the transition alone. The acquiring business must surround them with interim support, deploying a robust systems accountant to handle the data mapping, or an interim FP&A specialist to build the synergy tracking models. >> Right. So, the incumbent manages the business as usual operations while the scaffolding absorbs the one-off transition shock. >> Spot on. That is the most stable path if the talent allows for it. >> But, what if the transition requires structural surgery rather than just scaffolding? What is option two? >> Option two is deploying a dedicated ring-fenced integration finance specialist. >> You parachute an operator in. >> Precisely. This is mechanically necessary for complex transactions, corporate carve-outs requiring stand-alone financial infrastructure, multi-site bolt-ons, or when a complete ERP platform migration is mandated on day one. >> So, the board parachutes in an experienced interim integration finance manager for a defined, say, 6- to 9-month term. >> Yes, and their sole mandate is the transition. They unify the disparate charts of accounts, they map the internal controls to the parent company standards, they navigate the transitional service agreements, and they execute the systems migration. >> Which creates a firewall protecting the incumbent team. >> Exactly. The inherited finance function keeps the lights on and manages the day-to-day cash, while the specialist builds the new institutional house around them. >> And once the infrastructure is stable, the specialist hands over the keys and exits. >> Job done. That leaves the third option, which involves upgrading the permanent leadership seat. This is often the hardest conversation to have, but frequently the most necessary for long-term value creation, isn't it? It is necessary because the acquired business has fundamentally stepped into a new weight class. >> Right. >> The operational friction we discussed, managing complex leverage facilities, reporting to institutional private equity shareholders, navigating cross-border tax jurisdictions, or preparing the asset for a strict 3-year exit horizon, it requires a very specific pedigree. >> You need a leader who has seen the institutional movie before. >> Exactly. The business genuinely requires a divisional CFO or a sophisticated group financial controller who has operated at that elevated scale. >> And crucially, when this decision is made early during the due diligence phase or immediately at close, the transition can be executed professionally. >> Yes, you don't want to be doing this in a panic at month six. >> Exactly. The acquiring business can often retain the key operational and transactional accountants beneath that new leader, thereby preserving the daily operational knowledge while aggressively upgrading the strategic capability at the helm. >> It's all about timing. >> It really is. So, if we synthesize this entire landscape from the dangerous blind spots of financial due diligence through the regulatory realities of the ACC mandatory regime into the brutal operational friction of the 100-day pressure cooker, and finally to the tactical management of the inherited finance leader, the directive for the C-suite is absolutely undeniable. >> It couldn't be clearer. >> Moving finance leadership capability assessment forward, dragging it out of the post-close crisis phase and integrating it deeply into the due diligence and sign to close window is arguably the highest return operational decision an acquiring board or PE sponsor can make. >> Absolutely. >> You must protect the valuation premium you just paid by guaranteeing that the operational machinery actually possesses the elasticity to deliver your deal thesis. >> Because the alternative is spending the first 12 months of your holding period forensically searching for where your deal value leaked out while your investment timeline rapidly degrades. >> Which leaves us with a necessary and somewhat provocative paradigm shift for the market. We have spent this entire deep dive treating the operational plumbing, the ERP bridges, the manual data mapping, the month-end accrual friction as the ultimate barrier to M&A success. >> Right. >> But consider the trajectory of automation. As AI models increasingly automate complex data ingestion, chart of account mapping, and initial variance commentary, the friction of this technical plumbing might vanish entirely within the next 5 years. >> Oh, that's a fascinating thought. >> Right? If AI solves the data bridge, does that render the human financial controller obsolete during integration? Or does it mean their purely strategic commercial instincts, their ability to challenge synergy assumptions and align capital with strategy, becomes the only variable actually worth evaluating during due diligence? >> That is the big question. >> If the plumbing manages itself, the only failure point left is the human strategy. Something for you to mull over before your next board meeting.

metadata.title: The First 100 Days: How to Succeed After a Business Acquisition
metadata.author: Patrick O'Connell - M&A Transaction Services
metadata.shortDescription:
This Live discussion features Kjael Skaalerud of @skalingventures  an exceptional 2X entrepreneur discussing what life is like 100 days after buying a business.

What You’ll Learn in This Video:
How to stabilize your business in the first 30 days

What systems to clean up immediately after closing

How to build trust with legacy customers and employees

Why onboarding yourself and your team is crucial

Which metrics matter most during the first quarter

How to avoid post-acquisition burnout or misalignment

Why This Strategy Works for Any Business:
This approach isn’t just for tech or SaaS—it's for any buyer who plans to operate the business. By focusing on data cleanup, trust-building, and systemic improvements, you avoid chaos and set a foundation for long-term growth.

Whether you bought a plumbing company, a local agency, or a vertical SaaS platform, these lessons apply across industries.

⏱️ Timestamps:
0:00 – What to Expect After Buying a Business
1:03 – Choosing the Right Business (Quantitative Filters)
9:37 – Hardest Part of the First 90 Days
20:01 – Data Cleanup & Mapping the Business
25:01 – Building Trust with Customers & Team
35:00 – Structuring a Lean, High-Performance Team
44:57 – Finding & Prioritizing Constraints
52:01 – Pricing Strategy & Cash Flow Optimization
53:06 – Final Lessons & Resources

Step-by-Step Breakdown:
Step 1: Stabilize and Observe
Resist the urge to overhaul everything

Focus on keeping the business running smoothly

Document key processes and avoid breaking customer trust

Step 2: Clean the Data & Tech Stack
Fix CRM, financials, and onboarding systems

Use 60 days of clean data to identify real bottlenecks

Avoid assumptions from flawed diligence

Step 3: Rebuild with Focus
Identify high-leverage team roles and eliminate busywork

Map core revenue mechanics (ARR waterfall, churn, onboarding gaps)

Set benchmarks and reverse-engineer KPIs with clarity

Final Thoughts & Call-to-Action:
The first 100 days can make or break your acquisition.
Be humble, simplify, clean data, build trust—and don’t try to “add” your way to growth.

metadata.title: Everything you need to know about Post Acquisition and Execution
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch Walker Deibel, Author of the best-selling book "Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game" featured at VR Business Brokers – Charlotte hosted by Adam Petricoff and shared his wisdom and experience in business acquisition.

Their discussion covered the issues buyers must contemplate when buying a business to be successful. Walker provided his insights, guidance, and war stories. This discussion is great for individuals looking to buy a business now or in the future.

Watch the full video here: https://youtu.be/HtKpXgh9IaA

Join us and accelerate your acquisition with our “do-it-with-you” buy-side advisory service. Our collaborative approach blends graduate-level instruction with hands-on buy-side consulting. Together we will master the skills needed to identify, evaluate, and acquire the right business for you.

Don't forget to like and subscribe to be updated with new vlogs and learn more about business acquisition!

VISIT OUR WEBSITE: http://acquisitionlab.com

LEARN FROM OUR BLOGS: https://acquisitionlab.com/blog/
MORE BLOGS AT BUY THEN BUILD: https://buythenbuild.com/blog/
CLIENTS' TESTIMONIALS: https://acquisitionlab.com/testimonials/
JOIN THE LAB: https://acquisitionlab.com/application/
SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/buythenbuild
 

*********

Walker is a serial acquisition entrepreneur, bestselling author, and M&A advisor. He acquired seven companies over ten years and co-founded several startups. His bestselling book, Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game, released to critical acclaim including being recognized by Forbes as “one of the top 7 books all entrepreneurs must read,” and is currently being used in many universities. The Acquisition Lab, offers buy-side M&A services for first-time financial buyers in a do-it-with-you service, providing information, coaching, tools, and community. Read more here: https://acquisitionlab.com/meet-the-team/

metadata.title: Middle Market Smart – Episode 3 (Part 2 of 2) The M&A Playbook for Middle Market Leaders
metadata.author: Middle Market Smart
metadata.shortDescription:
The deal is closed. Now what?

Most acquisitions look strong on paper. Very few are executed well after closing. The first 100 days post-acquisition are where value is either created or quietly destroyed, and most organizations are not prepared for what that actually requires.

In Part 2 of this conversation on Middle Market Smart, Patrick Goulet and the team continue their discussion with Mark Ianni and Mark Beliczky of CXO Partners, two operators who have led integrations across private equity, strategic acquisitions, and family business transitions of every size and complexity.

In this episode, they walk through what experienced operators do differently from day one, how to align leadership and build cultural clarity without losing what made the acquired company valuable, and the three integration mistakes organizations repeat most often. They also share candid perspectives on AI in M&A, technology consolidation, financial transparency with employees, and why integration should begin before the deal ever closes.

If you are a founder, CEO, or operator on either side of a transaction, this is the execution playbook for what happens after the handshake.

What You'll Learn:

- Why value is created after closing, not at signing 
- What the first 100 days actually determine for the whole transaction 
- How experienced operators build cultural alignment without dismantling existing culture 
- Why integration is a leadership responsibility, not a project to delegate
- How to establish a communication cadence with employees and customers from day one 
- When and how to open the books to your team 
- The three most common integration mistakes and how to avoid them 
- Where technology and systems decisions tend to break down 
- How AI is and is not changing the M&A integration process 
- Why retention bonuses and loyalty-building should start before the deal closes 
- What a failed deal still teaches you about your own business

Timestamps:

[00:00] – Intro: Where success is actually determined in M&A
[00:18] – Reintroducing the guests: Mark Ianni and Mark Beliczky
[01:23] – Where experienced operators create the most value post-acquisition
[02:10] – Why the first 100 days set momentum for the entire transaction
[03:45] – The trap of trying to integrate everything at once
[05:00] – Why culture shows up in daily execution, not mission statements
[07:28] – Who leads culture after an acquisition: acquirer, acquired, or both
[08:39] – Integration in practice: how Mark Ianni approaches day one
[10:30] – Listening first: round tables, customer calls, and building trust early
[12:15] – Establishing a cadence with sales, operations, and the broader team
[14:30] – Technology as an integration challenge: CRMs, ERPs, and readiness
[16:09] – Cost cutting versus operational improvement: what is actually required
[17:30] – KPIs, lead indicators, and why lagging metrics mislead operators
[20:31] – People, purpose, and performance: a framework for post-deal leadership
[22:30] – Why family-owned businesses often keep financials hidden and why that changes
[24:48] – Technology and AI in the middle market: where it helps and where it does not
[27:05] – AI as a tool, not a strategy: what it can and cannot solve for in integration
[29:03] – What AI appetite signals about cultural fit between organizations
[31:04] – Systems sub-optimization: the opportunity most acquirers miss
[33:26] – Flexibility versus hard stances: what actually drives value through change
[35:37] – What a failed deal still teaches you about your business
[36:11] – The three integration mistakes organizations repeat most often
[38:09] – Why integration should start before the deal closes
[39:38] – Retention bonuses and building loyalty during the sale process
[41:10] – Buyer's remorse, seller cooperation, and letting go of control
[42:41] – Closing thoughts: the integration process never waits for the closing date

And the one thing most CEOs don't come out and say, but I know I hear it in their voices, I don't want you to disrupt my culture. >> Mhm. >> And so, my goal is to always enable a culture, but I will tell you that my playbook, the way I integrate, will eventually potentially shift the culture day by day. So, I walk into a situation where a PE firm just bought a company. I'm transitioning with the former leadership. And then I start implementing my cadence. If If If it If it exists, great. There's nothing much more that I could do or want to do. But the biggest thing I do on day one is communication. Is I sit down with every employee. I have round tables with num- numerous employees. I ask them what they think is going well. I ask them what they think they can improve on as a company. I get very candid with them, very transparent with them. And in conjunction with that, I start calling customers and introducing myself. And letting them know that I'm the new leader here. And I want to get your feedback on how we're doing things. What could we do better? So, those for me are two critical integration things that I do immediately. And when I use the word playbook, I will tell you my playbook evolves depending on the situation. So, I don't want to say that I always use the same playbook. Once those things are done and I get feedback from everybody, then I I'm armed with uh an understanding of where I can take this culture. Whether I embrace it or I or slowly evolve it or I enable it to get even better. And with that, I start establishing a cadence. You know, I sit down, call it every Monday with my sales team. I look at forecast. I look at pipeline. I look at who the top customers are and what they're ordering and how we're doing on those orders. Whatever those orders may be, whatever product we're selling. Then I establish a cadence with my operating team. People that are behind the scenes delivering whatever they need to deliver. It's a manufacturing process. I make sure that I visit the manufacturing facility. If it's a If it's a services business, I jump in a truck with with one of the guys and I go and spend a day with them. I do everything I can. But most of the time, I listen and I hear and I try to understand how I can improve things. How I can get the team to improve in what they do. So, establish a cadence of communication with the entire organization. Establish a cadence of communication with your customers. You know, and if if technology is an issue, start looking at different ways putting in technology that can help the business scale better. If somebody's using QuickBooks, it's not a bad thing, but there are better things out there. If there's no ERP system or MRP system, we got to start thinking about evolving towards that process. And I will say that, you know, talking about technology, I've seen businesses purchase millions of dollars of technology and it just stay on the shelf because the organization was not culturally ready for those massive changes that technology can bring. So, that process in itself is is a sub-integration process. We're trying to understand how people work today, how you can improve the process of how they work together, and how can technology enable that. So, I just want to emphasize integration is situational to what what the actual situation is. If you're being called in to be a new leader of a company post-acquisition, it's one form of integration. If you're being in to come in um as a strategic buyer component of the integration, that may look totally different. There might be a lot of change management going on. You might have to look at teams and say, "Well, this person is not the ideal individual for this role. Let's see if we can improve the role by finding somebody else to do it." There's a lot that involves integration, and and it could be disruptive. I mean, you know, like we I think Mark said it well earlier. It's disruptive when you're selling a business or when you're buying a business. It could be very disruptive to both parties. That process hopefully runs smoothly and the the transaction closes within a very reasonable period of time. And then the the transaction goes through, like Mark said, everybody's happy, we're finally here. And then the other work begins. And that work could be just as disruptive as the whole process that you just went through. So, having a playbook, having a plan that has worked, that works consistently is the way I approach these situations. >> I think it feels like the elephant in the room is we have to assume there's some redundancies. There's some cost savings to be had, there's some efficiency efficiencies to be had. So, in the context of that first 100 days is cost cutting and ringing out, you know, redundancies. Is the pressure really strong to do that? Or maybe that's for enterprise companies, they have earnings calls and, you know, they want to see some investors and the street wants to see some some efficiencies and there's a little longer ramp for middle market companies or no, let's it's the first 100 days, we're going to move decisively, that includes redundancies and finding efficiencies. >> Bill, that's I mean, that's a good question. Not all Not all situations require you know, operational efficiency does not necessarily mean cost cutting. It just means doing things better, to have an improvement mindset. One of the things that I found in in a lot of these specifically family-owned businesses is that the the incentivizing of the right behavior is not present. In some cases, the owner, as we said earlier, decides who gets the yearly bonus, how they get it. There's no real in in many cases, you know, the key performance indicators are either misaligned or don't even exist. And and I will tell you that, you know, we talk about culture a lot. You know, I come from a world having spent 50 years at GE Capital, where performance and performance culture was the way we did things. You perform. And and it was a very different time, a very different environment, not one that I would necessarily, you know, want to push on an organization immediately. But, you know, you raise a good point about cost-cutting. Um not all businesses need to cost-cut. Businesses just need to improve how they do things. And and having a mindset of constant improvement, you know, the days of Six Sigma are still upon us. We still have to be lean when we do things. We have to do things efficiently. And as an organization, the communication process, not only leadership to to to employees, but within employee groups. Making sure that, you know, that everyone's rowing in the same direction. Sorry for the, you know, but that's the reality of these things. And integration involves people. Again, people, process, and technology. Integration is about people. You integrate successfully if people that you're working with establish a cadence to improve and do things better, and to be incentivized. You know, I talk about wildly important goals when I go into an organization. What's What are we? What's wildly important? What does the strategy say we're going to do in the future? And and and then how are you as as employee generating those lead, you know, those lead factors, lead indicators to get us to being better. And I will tell you, a lot of businesses when it within the specific sphere that we're discussing today all they look at is what do we do this month, what's our revenue this month, what's our EBITDA this month, and they do the same thing the next month. I'm sorry, folks. That's a lagging indicator. It's a result of everything else you got to do to get to that point. It's like you don't get on a scale every 30 days and say, "Damn, I gained a pound." or "Damn, I lost a pound." If you're not exercising and eating well, that scale's going to look exactly the same month after month after month. And sometimes it's not going to be what you want it to be. So, you got to do things as I call them lead indicators to be successful in an organization. And integration integration is so critical the first as Mark said, the first 30 days, 60 days, 1 year into the post acquisition, post transaction. Integration is something that happens that has to happen successfully. Otherwise, your business will will will will show some performance shortfalls. >> Yep. I I think Mark and I think pretty similarly. You know, I have my three P's. So, people, purpose, and performance. It starts with people. And that's the first thing I do. I like similar to Mark, I spend time when I took over as a CEO of a firm that was acquired by a PE firm, first thing I did is you know, the the exiting CEO said, "What do you want to do first?" I said, "Would you please schedule me to meet every single team member here." I like that meeting so with them. And then I had meetings with every single leadership group and had meetings with them and listened. And then, you know, so it's being able to understand where you you are with your people. Uh and then purpose, you know, what's the why of the organization? I mean, what I found is that most people lack the alignment in an organization. So, is the organization aligned? Do they have a clear purpose? Do they have a mission? Do they have a vision? Do people live it or is it just window dressing? Because that is not going to be helpful. In most organizations it's window dressing, you know, it's not real. But when you have a compelling purpose, mission, and vision, you drive alignment, then you drive empowerment, and you drive freedom within the organization. People make decisions. That may be new for a lot of people, very frankly. They may not be ready to make decisions. But if you want a culture where, you know, you need fewer managers, where people can make decisions, or, you know, where you push decision making to all levels of the organization, then it gets really exciting. And then performance. One of the things I, you know, it takes time to understand what performance is, but you know, you want to mark as be a world-class operator, you know, one of the things that we look at is performance variability. Where is it? Is it Where is it this month? Where is it that month? You have leading indicators. You have lagging indicators. It you know, it takes time to pull all that data together and then you kind of level set where we are and say, "Fine. From this it makes sense that we can move in this sort of direction." So, you spend a lot of time understanding, asking questions, and then driving alignment within the organization. And then that has to happen really quick. >> You know, I like what you just said, Mark, and I want to give you guys a couple of examples that are very typical of if I go back to the situation where a family generational business is sold, let's say sold to a financial buyer like a private equity firm. The one thing that I've seen over and over again, and I and and and it happens very very often, is a family-run business, say they're a 100 million revenue or 50 million revenue, middle, you know, mid-market business. Typically, the owners um don't really share a whole lot of financial information with the team, right? It it lends itself, they think, to to the employees saying, "Wow, he's making all these millions and he's paying us $80,000 a year. It's just not fair." It creates a little bit of a a little bit of a uh a situation where you don't have to have that situation. So, what I've done is I've gone in and I remember in in two specific situations where I opened up my books to the organization. I said, "This is what we did last last month in revenue. This is what This is what our costs look like. And and and this is where I think we can get better." And I remember walking out of those meetings with a vast group of employees and they're all saying, "Wow, you you actually shared how what kind of money we're making?" And for that specific organization, that was a culture change beyond reason. Like, they couldn't believe that you're sharing this information with us. That you're telling us how much money you're making. How much money we are making? And I said, "Why why would I why would I not share that with you? The more you know about your own business, the more driven you're going to be to make it successful." And I will tell you, it happens in every situation I've been involved with where owners of businesses, especially family-run businesses, they like to keep certain things, especially financials, very close to their vest. Only very few people know how much money the company is making. And I think that's a mistake. >> How do you guys deal with um from a technology standpoint? Maybe there's two s- Both sales organizations are using different CRMs, or maybe more pertinent is um we're nowhere on AI adoption and we're almost, you know, we're we've got some level of maturity and implementation for agentic AI. How do you with systems and technology, how do you deal with that? >> I would, you know, I'll take that real quick. I will say that um there are organizations that are in the middle of you know, either selling or buying, mostly selling, let's say. Or there are organizations that need to go through some leadership change to prepare for potential liquidity event. And this AI stuff scares them to death. Scares them to death. There's a lot of reasons for that. Some of it is um confidentiality of data and data being out there. And then just just people are in most cases businesses of a certain level, certain size are not exactly embracing anything right now that involves AI. But to your point, Bill, I mean integrating business a business or say just a strategic buyer and there are two different CRMs. Uh that in itself is a very vast integration process of picking the one you're going to go with. You can't go with two. Data gets lost if you have two systems. And whatever you embrace, you better make sure that the other half of the organization is trained on it and learns it and uses it effectively. You know, you've heard this before, guys, garbage in, garbage out. You could have the best system in the world if you're not putting the right data in that system you're not going to get the right data coming out. So, I think it's critical. But AI, Bill, I think AI is is still a little place in these mid-market companies, organizations where it is an unknown and people are kind of afraid of the unknown. But I I you know, Mark's Mark's a big AI guy and I'm sure he has a different opinion. >> Well, now, you'll be surprised to say that I'm going to hold back in AI. Um I mean it's one of the things that you know I I do want to talk about and we'll kind of get ahead of the curve a little bit. AI is really helping mergers and acquisitions, but it it's not going to help make really good decisions and that's where leadership comes in and people still come in. It's great as a data you know accumulator and an assessment tool and there are good ways. It's mostly effective right now in assessing deals, right? Because it takes big bodies of data and helps you manipulate that data and look at it, but it's stopping not helping so much right now in the integration phase of where we are and it it's still an evolving area for businesses. So there are risks and a lot of uncertainty. You know, there are really great ways to do this and driving efficiency, but it still comes down to people and making decisions and in people's intuition and insights and that AI can't solve for you right now. Tell you about culture, right? AI is not going to do your interviews for all of your key personnel and say, "How are they thinking and feeling? What should I be doing?" You know, it's not going to probably give you a sense of what are the leading indicators that I should be looking at in this business. You mean So those are some of the things that it it's still not capable of doing. It has its limitations, but it still comes down to judgment and human factor. >> Yeah, we we you guys are hitting a similar note to one of your colleagues who's a CIO who says assume AI is baked into things. Focus on building capabilities and improving those and AI will is a tool and a function and a catalyst for automation or efficiency or whatever, but focus on increasing capabilities, not AI for AI's sake. So, and I think >> Yeah, AI is not a strategy, by the way. Because I've heard, you know, CEOs say, "Well, what's to be my AI strategy?" You know, that's that's the wrong question. What is your strategy? AI is a tool. Let's figure out how to use the tool that supports the strategy that you'd like to implement within your organization. >> I think when it comes to, you know, a culture maybe mismatch or culture fit, it's less about, you know, the the actual AI strategy and more about the approach towards AI and maybe the the overall curiosity, knowledge, and and their approach towards AI. Less like, "Hey, we're using this specific AI tool and you're not." More about like, "Hey, what's the um what's the appetite for it?" Might be a good way to put it. >> Yeah, and you know, AI has its limitations cuz AI reflects the body of current knowledge in the world. It doesn't help you project Oh, how about innovation? How about what's the possibility space for this business? What are we not capturing here to drive innovation that we might be able to capture? That is a human function where you're going to drive customer intimacy and and understand what the customer wants. AI is not going to help you with solve that right now. That's going to be our intuition, the sense of where we want to take the business. >> I think, you know, not to sound that I wouldn't embrace it. I would just say that there are places within an organization where AI, to what Bill said earlier, AI can can improve efficiencies, right? I hate to say this in front of Bill, but if you have three marketing people, and you could use AI, and you only need one of them, then so be it. Sorry, Bill. That's a bit of a >> I'm actually a robot. I'm a cyborg, anyways. >> There you go. There you go. But but there are places where I think, especially we're talking about integration, where you could use the AI tools available to you, where you can make things better for the organization, for sure. >> Yeah, I wanted to go back to a point that, you know, Mark was talking about systems and systems being used and build a question you asked. You know, first of all, when you look at systems and where people and the systems people are using right now, people may not be optimizing the systems that are in the organization, so it may So, that's a question. Going back to Mark's point about you have to ask questions. Well, how well are we using this? Oh, well, you're using 1/10 of it. Well, it's not the system, it's the fact that we're not up to speed and we're we're sub-optimizing it. So, I think that's an opportunity. So, leveraging the system effectively and then, frankly, there may be a highly efficient system that maybe a acquiring company maybe having that is a 10x driver of performance that they may not know about. So, you may want to say, "Oh, that's great, but we have a thing it can 10x and let me show you how to do it." And here's the magic question, which is, "What's in it for me?" So, one of the things that oftentimes never gets asked with team members is, "Here's what's Here's what's in it for you. We can do the following. This will make your situation go x times faster for you this and this is why we chose to do it. If you take time to explain it, then people say, "Oh, that's cool. Let's sign up for that. That That's a change we'll need to make." >> It It's a interesting also that when a merger happens and when there's, you know, a mix of different systems, different cultures, and different leadership teams, it's an opportunity to bring to light a lot of inefficiencies, a lot of complacencies, a lot of systems that are not being used at their maximum. So, it is kind of that uh that catalyst, that inflection point where hey, like, let's take another look at everything that's going on, and where can we make those improvements? So, it's good to see it as an opportunity as well. >> Mhm. Yeah, and I and I think people shouldn't assume just because, you know, you're now part of an a lot larger organization that everything's going to change. There will be some change, but you have to a first understand what's going on and say what's in the best interest of the teams, what's in the best interest of the the investment thesis, and what's in the best interest of driving value creation. And when you understand that, then things happen. >> No. Going back to it to an earlier point as well, disruption is inevitable, and like change management is difficult. In terms of on the buyer side and on the seller side as well, what are specific things that um lead to value in terms of being flexible about certain things versus kind of taking a hard stance when it comes to change? You know, you know, >> I'll answer your question and and cuz I know that we we were going to talk about this at some point or we we try I think we talked about a little bit earlier. Let's say a family-owned business decides to go down the path of selling their business. And they go through the process, they're 6 months in, the deal dies. The deal falls apart. During those 6 months of due diligence, they're getting information from outside party about things that they like about their business and potentially things they don't like about their business, which leads that organization, the buyer, to walk away. If if I'm a family-run business and I go through that process, it's not all lost because you've gained some very valuable information about how you can create value, how you can optimize EBITDA, by the feedback you're getting from the acquiring company and and and by the questions they're asking you and by the due diligence process in itself and the things they look at under the hood. And and it's remarkable to me that even going through that process and and and having let's call it a failure of transacting they're still valuable valuable insight you gain from that. And and and that insight should should should push the organization to get better. So that the next time there's a transaction on the table they're able to speak to those elements that may have may have made their company and look less attractive than they thought it was. >> It's got nothing lost going through the process. However Absolutely. What might be >> Experienced executives often say the real work begins after closing. Those 100 days we talked about. In terms of integration, what mistakes do organizations repeat most often? Are there any that you've seen come up quite a bit? >> Yeah. I think there are three mistakes, three key mistakes put in three key buckets. You know, that I've been able to experience. So treating integration as a project. This is not a project. So you don't give it to a project team. You don't delegate it to a team. It's managed as a work stream. Now, it's important that you know, it's tackled this way. And what you want to be careful about that senior management needs to be highly involved. They need to be visible. So I think that's mistake number one. Mistake number two is unclear decision-making. Who has the decisions? Who can make decisions? Do I do things the way I did on Friday and we got and the deal was signed on Saturday and now it's Monday. Like what should we be doing? So, unclear decision-making is probably mistake number two if you don't have that. And when when it's unclear or roles are not identified, here's what you get. You get hesitation, you get slower decisions, and you get confusion around authority. That is death in in these sort of deals. So, what you want to do is address that right up front. And the third mistake is delaying hard decisions. How about people? You know, or whatever it might be or you don't you know, you have to deal with a disruption issue or something like that. So, understanding what those hard decisions and you know, West Point trains you something is called making the right hard decision. You know, rip the band-aid off, understand it, make sure there's clarity, and make sure everyone's aware of it. Those are the three key things that I've seen in my experience. >> The other thing I personally want to emphasize is that there's this concept that integration starts you know, the second the transaction goes through. If you're running a good business and you're in a process and you're 99% sure or more that this deal will happen, integration should start before the deal actually closes. Integration is not time-bound by the day the deal closes. Integration should begin before. As I said earlier, if you're a family-owned business and you're learning during the due diligence process the things that are being pointed out are the things that you should be doing better or improve on, you should take the opportunity to start doing those things even before the deal closes. Um you know, you should start the integration process, whether it's communicating to key employees at at right time that this is going on. This is what this means. Preparing them, communicating with them, uh you see things unfold. There's an element of developing loyalty at the right time. And the right time is while you're going through the sell process or while you're going through the buying process. Even buyers that are good at what they do will ask ownership to start thinking about certain things. Um you know, in some cases, like I've been involved with this when I was in the process of selling a company, the buyer asked me to write up a 120-day bonus that the individual will get if they remain with the company post transaction. See, that's an integration thing. >> Yeah. >> You want to make sure you don't lose your key employees because in some of these businesses, those employees are like I said earlier, people, process, and technology. Those employees are key to the business moving forward. So, I've had to I've had to write retention bonuses for for my key employees. So, I've had to bring them into my office and say, "Hey, here's where we are. We're in the middle of a process. Chances are we're going to sell the company. But we love you. We like you. The people that have been here have seen the work you've done. Here's a retention bonus. 6 months, a year down the line, if you stay with this company, you get that bonus regardless." >> It's a fun you're talking I was thinking in my mind as you were talking about that. I wonder if there's seller's remorse ever or are they generally cooperative? You know, they know the terms you've been through the deal specifics. They've They've aired all of their concerns and so they're generally cooperative or they're like or maybe the control gene is so strong, you know, it's hard to let go. >> You know, Bill, so I know that we try to focus mostly on the people side of things here and the human side of transactions and the importance of everything around that. We haven't spent a lot of time talking about financials. >> Mhm. >> But if you're a private equity firm and you're saying, "I want to keep your best employees and we're going to write half a million dollars of checks a year down the line if these people stay here." And not everybody stays, by the way. So, you're trying to keep them and you think that's going to incentivize them? But that's, you know, that's an acquisition cost. It's below the EBITDA line, right? So, if you spend it, it's part of the acquisition cost. Which, you know, we can talk about valuations and how different firms do different things with valuations and and what valuations look like post-transaction. But there should not be buyer's remorse if if the key employees are rightfully identified. And I'm just giving you an example of retention bonuses. There's other things that you do prior to closing a deal that I think are part of the integration process. And and that's just one example. But no, if you go into the deal thinking you're doing the right thing and it's not the right thing at the end of the day, that one employee is the worst decision you've ever made. You turn around, you give them their bonus and you say, "Thank you, but we're going to voluntarily let you go." And and it There's no harm, no foul. >> Yeah. That to your point, that's it's all the integration process has begun before the deal closes, right? >> Doesn't it? Right. >> Ironed out all those things and dealt with objections and etc. So, that's good. That's really good. That it's not like now all these issues crop up, you've dealt with it in the course of the transaction. Well, that sounds like a great place to to stop here, guys. You have really armed us with amazing questions and perspectives and thoughts to work through, process stuff, the little intangibles we didn't think of. So, I really thank you both. This has been wonderful.

metadata.title: HubSpot + Apollo + Clay + Smartlead: The Outbound Stack Boundary
metadata.author: ToolColumn
metadata.shortDescription:
This stack brief walks through STK-A001, the SMB Outbound Velocity Stack from AIAutomationStacks: HubSpot as CRM truth, Apollo as source/list access, Clay as selective enrichment, n8n as handoff control, and Smartlead as outbound execution.
The $950-$3,200/month range is a directional planning model for a 2-8 person SMB outbound team, not an official bundle price. Pricing and access pages checked May 23, 2026. Always verify current official pricing, plan limits, sender rules, and CRM integration behavior before buying.

segments.text: If your outbound stack breaks, it
usually does not break because one tool
is weak. It breaks because every tool
thinks it owns the same record.
SDKa00001
is the SMB outbound velocity stack. It
is built for two to eight person teams
that need outbound volume without buying
an enterprise GTM suite. The operating
idea is simple. move faster but write
down which layer owns the truth before
records start moving between tools.
HubSpot is the CRM boundary. It owns
contact, company, life cycle, deal,
owner and suppression state. Everything
else has to respect that line. Apollo is
the broad source and list access layer.
It should help you find accounts and
contacts before deeper enrichment
becomes worth operating. Clay is
selective enrichment and research. It is
valuable when Apollo data is not enough,
but it should not quietly become the
sender or the CRM.
N8N is the handoff and exception layer.
It connects reviewed steps, records
failures, and keeps workflow logic
visible instead of hiding it in
spreadsheets.
Smartle is outbound execution. It sends
approved audiences, manages sender
controls and should not become the
source of customer truth. The big
boundary is Apollo versus Clay. Apollo
can source the list. Clay can enrich
selected fields. Both should not own the
same field without a written rule. The
second boundary is HubSpot versus
Smartle. HubSpot keeps CRM truth.
Smartle handles active sending,
suppression, reply ownership, and roll
back rules must be explicit. The
directional monthly planning range is
for a small SMB outbound team. Treat
that as a planning model, not official
pricing evidence. The setup model is 10
days. Name the Rev Ops owner Lockhubspot
Fields. Create the Apollo source list.
Set clay rules. Prepare smart lead
controls and build N8N handoffs before
increasing volume. QA a sample batch.
Look for duplicate domains, weak fit,
bad owners, suppression misses,
enrichment credit burn, and unclear roll
back paths. Weekly maintenance is the
real cost. Budget about six hours for
enrichment QA, suppression checks,
sequence health, HubSpot hygiene, N8N
exceptions, and budget monitoring. Use
the full stack when outbound speed
matters more than bespoke GTM
engineering. And one rev ops owner can
keep field ownership and launch review
disciplined. Use the budget variant when
Apollo, HubSpot, and Smartle are enough.
Add clay and deeper N8 in logic only
when enrichment depth becomes a
repeatable constraint. Do not use this
stack when nobody owns rev ops. The ICP
changes every week or Apollo only
prospecting already solves the job. The
rule is boring which is why it works.
Apollo sources Clay enriches
selectively. Hubspot stays the record.
N8 handles handoffs and smart lead
sends.

How do you build GTM efficiency in SMB sales? The CRO at Owner, Kyle Norton, shares his learnings and strategies for building better efficiency into your GTM motion at Workshop Wednesday, held every Wednesday at 10 a.m. PST.

metadata.title: The Pros and Cons of the SBA 7(a) Loan [2026 Update]
metadata.author: SBA Ray
metadata.shortDescription:
The Pros and Cons of the SBA 7(a) Loan [2026 Update]

Most bankers will sell you on the benefits of the SBA 7(a) loan and hide the negatives until you're sitting at the closing table. That's not how I operate. In this video I give you the full picture — the good, the bad, and the ugly — so you can decide for yourself if this program is right for you.

📌 What's covered:
- Why comparing SBA loans to COVID-era EIDL loans is the wrong move
- What conventional banks and online lenders actually offer — and why the SBA wins
- Con #1 — personal collateral and the lien on your house explained
- Con #2 — variable interest rates and what that actually means for your payment
- Con #3 — the personal guarantee and why it's becoming a bigger conversation
- Pro #1 — low or no equity injection requirements
- Pro #2 — longer terms and lower monthly payments
- Pro #3 — prepayment flexibility that doesn't exist anywhere else in the market
- Pro #4 — no loan covenants
- Pro #5 — bundling multiple uses into one loan
- Pro #6 — looser underwriting guidelines and why that matters

After watching this video you'll know exactly where you stand on the SBA 7(a) — and whether it's the right move for your business.

📲 Get in touch: https://www.sbaray.com/contact

🔔 Subscribe for weekly insider tips from an *actual* SBA lender.

metadata.title: Easy Breakdown of Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition.
metadata.author: Kristina M. Wynne
metadata.shortDescription:
A lot of people say they want to be entrepreneurs…

Here’s the truth:
You don’t have to build a business from the ground up to become a successful entrepreneur. You can acquire one that’s already operating, already profitable, and already positioned for growth.

That’s the power of Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA)—a lesser-known but incredibly strategic path to ownership.

As a Business Broker with Transworld Prospere, I help my clients:
🔹 Identify businesses with real cash flow and value
🔹 Navigate the due diligence process
🔹 Understand financing and deal structure
🔹 Close confidently with a clear path forward

Whether you’re a corporate professional ready to exit the 9–5, an investor looking for a turnkey opportunity, or someone who’s just tired of building from scratch—ETA might be the path you’ve been overlooking.

metadata.title: What is Entrepreneurship through Acquisition?
metadata.author: Kevin Henderson
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know you can become an entrepreneur without building a business? Entrepreneurship is gaining in popularity, so here is what you should know:

Most people think of startup companies when they hear “entrepreneur.” A lesser-known version is entrepreneurship through acquisition or ETA. In simple terms, it means buying an existing business or company.

Entrepreneurship through acquisition (ETA) differs from startup entrepreneurship in several ways. First, ETA reduces common financial burdens one might expect to see with startups. That is not to say there is no financial risk - the definition of an entrepreneur is one who assumes the financial risk in running a business.
When you buy an existing business, you also buy years of historical operation. That means your business is likely already profitable, has a proven market fit, and comes with existing customers. The day you incur your first penny to fund an acquisition, you earn revenue on the same day.

To hear more tips on small business and corporate law, subscribe and follow.
Where to connect with Kevin:
Twitter: @KHendersonCo
LinkedIn: Henderson
Website: Henderson.Co

So that's like the exact reason that you'd have us put together this ETA certification program that’s starting. So really excited to get all of you in there. And it's a pretty cool way to see if it's a fit for you. The search can also be a great test run because you're effectively running a small, very, very small business as a searcher. Really keeping yourself disciplined around actually running a process, following through on kind of your plan to either explore new industry or something like that. It's indicative of if you're the kind of person that's going to survive or thrive in an environment where there's not a lot of direction necessarily, other than what you're putting forward in front of yourself day-to-day. So it can be a great chance to sort of experience that. And love it, or you may feel like, hey, no, I actually would rather do this in a much bigger setting or a much more kind of structured way, etc., etc.. That's great. There's a question specifically for you, Aaron, and your small business acquisition understanding that the below two are not mutually exclusive, EBITDA versus revenue multiple. What is your perspective on the weight, quote unquote, or focus quote unquote between them? Oh, I love it so much. I'm like, I'd love to just chat about this for, you know, 30 minutes. I, really depends on the kind of business. I mean, the easiest way to understand it is that, from our perspective, is we're really looking at EBITDA multiples with a probably a minimum EBITDA margin, right? So we'd really say, I should have said this when we talked about the kind of qualifications of business. We really want to look at like a 15 to 20% plus EBITDA margin and just showing how much of the cash flow of the business is actually available for growth. And if you're down, you know, below 10 or 15% an EBITDA margin, it just means you're not getting a lot of leverage out of new revenue into that business. So the main case where we focus on a revenue multiple is with software as a service businesses, or SaaS businesses. And the reason would just be that, in theory, were you to stop new product development in a SaaS business, substantially all of the incremental SaaS subscription dollar drops to the bottom line and is so like EBITDA. So it's sort of like you're saying in SaaS businesses, a revenue multiple is sort of like an EBITDA multiple. It's not really that simple. It's just an over generalization. There are other cases and other particular industries that tend to get valued on a revenue multiple, but honestly, at our, the size of things that we're talking about today, you know, EBITDA is really what we're focused on. When you buy a business, you do not buy
a job. You are buying a business that
someone else is going to run and manage
for you. You are going to be the owner
of that business. Which is why people
are wrong when they say that buying a
business puts a lot more onto your
plate. It only does that if you are
working in the business. So you need to
be setting this up so that you work on
the business while other people work in

of businesses are listed for sale. Now,
you can do those things, but if you want
the very best deal on the very best

seller of businesses, especially if you
are a beginner. So your very best chance
of success is to negotiate with the

that we need to go off market. We need
to go to owners of businesses that
haven't yet advertised their business

deciding that you know what this is
enough. I've had enough of this. We've

that you are looking for and there are a

people. But let me tell you the things
that you do not do. You never cold call.

thousands of businesses and say to the
person on the end of the phone, do you
want to sell your business? I mean I
guess it might work occasionally, but
that feels like an awful lot of hard
work to me. You also don't spam people
with thousands and thousands of emails.
There are smarter ways of doing it. But
the most important thing to remember at
this stage is you need to be speaking to
lots of business owners in the sector
that you have chosen. You can't just
speak to one and expect that to be the
business that you buy. You need to be
speaking to lots and lots for several
reasons. The first reason is you'll find

think that you need to be looking at at

look at lots of businesses is that so

bad business? Is it an average business?

start to realize that the business you

four more. So that's the next very
important stage. Having conversations
with business owners in the sector that
you are interested in. Let me give you a
very important tip. When you're speaking

because you've bought a house before and

very smart way of buying a business. Let

you want for the company? And the seller

believe that that's what I need to do.
Go away, look at the numbers, try and
work out what the business is worth.

eventually I very nervously send my
email offer over to the seller. Now the

I've been rejected, but it's okay

send back my revised offer. And the

are buying the shares in the company,
which means that you're going to buy
everything. You're going to buy the

liabilities, you're going to buy the
good stuff, the bad stuff, and the
downright ugly stuff. So you get
absolutely everything. the contract is

you're also buying liabilities, and

focus. However, if you buy the assets of
the business, and I'd recommend anyone

of the business, what happens is that

So understanding the difference between
buying assets and buying shares is
absolutely critical. It's really
important to have a plan when you're
buying a business. The people who take
the longest time buying a business,
sometimes running into 6 months or more,
are typically the people who don't
really know what they are doing. They

Always takes a little bit longer with a

pointing towards that completion date

board. You need to have the right

pointing and aiming towards that
completion date. We're going to get
closer and closer. There are going to be
some bumps in the road. So, you've got
to be a determined individual. You have
to be resilient because some days it
will feel like the deal is off. But if

So, congratulations,
you've bought your first business. Now,
you might think that now you've bought
the business, all the work has been

we've got to take over the business. I
