metadata.title: Structuring the Acquisition Deal - Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition Event Series
metadata.author: The University of Chicago Booth School of Business
metadata.shortDescription:
Presented by the Chicago Booth Alumni Club of Chicago.


Joe Cortese, '10, Chicago Booth Alumni Club Co-President, Brian O'Connor, '08, Adjunct Assistant Professor of Entrepreneurship at Booth and Founder – Managing Partner of NextGen Growth Partners, and Josh Dennis, '16, Principal at NexGen, present the fifth webinar in the Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) series. In this edition, they discuss the process of structuring the acquisition, working through the transaction, and common pitfalls that can torpedo deals.

segments.text: - Appreciate everyone joining this evening.
Thank you for joining us on our "Entrepreneurship
Through Acquisition" webinar, focused on structuring deals.
I'm Joe Cortese, Co-President
of the Chicago Booth Alumni Club
and a Principal and Senior Consultant
with DiMeo Schneider and Associates here in Chicago.
With me again this evening is Brian O'Connor,
adjunct associate professor of entrepreneurship
at Booth and founder and Managing Principal
of NextGen Growth Partners.
Brian, nice to see you again, thanks for joining us.
We also have a special guest with us again this evening
and I'll ask him to introduce himself in just a moment
once we get through a few opening considerations.
So this is our fifth webinar focused on ETA.
We do have the links to the previous webinars available
on the Chicago Booth Alumni Club
of Chicago's website, so you can join there.
Tim State is with us, as well, has been kind enough
to put the link in the chat box in previous sessions.
So he may be able to do that as well, this evening.
As I mentioned, we will focus on structuring the deal
this evening and how you actually complete
the purchasing transaction of a small business.
And we'll spend some time learning about the various types
of deal structures, how the process plays out.
We'll walk through a couple of common pitfalls
that torpedo deals and hopefully hear a little bit
about some live examples as well.
As we've done in previous sessions,
we will take questions along the way.
So if you would like to submit a question
please go ahead and do that via
the question and answer box and we'll deal
with those as we go through the meeting here.
We do welcome any and all questions.
We'll do our best to get to all of them as we go.
Also mention quickly, we will have another webinar
focused on ETA in December and in this final one for 2020
we'll focus on actual day in the life of an entrepreneur
running a small private equity backed company
and learn a little bit more about that.
So with that, I'd like to turn to our special guest,
very pleased to have Josh Dennis with us here tonight.
Thank you for joining Josh.
If you wouldn't mind, please give us
a brief introduction and background of yourself
and then we'll dive into the content.
- That sounds great.
Well, I appreciate you having me on here.
I've watched several episodes, so it's great to be here.
Josh Dennis, I'm a Principal at NextGen Growth Partners.
Quick background, I started my career
in investment banking and then middle market private equity,
kind of a typical finance track before going
to business school at Booth, where I graduated in 2016.
And it was while I was at Booth that I learned about ETA,
or the search fund model as we called it,
everyone's familiar with the search fund model,
but in 2000, I think it was early 2015,
was the first year that they taught the ETA class
and Brian and Mark Agnew taught class.
And that's where I learned much more about it,
became extremely interested in it,
and also developed a relationship with Brian, Mark,
and a lot of others in the ETA community.
And from there I came back for my second year,
was trying to figure out if I wanted to raise a search fund
or go back in the investing role.
And that's when Brian told me
about this idea that he'd had, and it was a great fit
or mixed between kind of the benefits you get
from a traditional private equity fund, community capital,
we can get into all of that, but also taking the benefits
of the traditional search fund model.
And I thought it made a ton of sense
and it was a perfect combination of my experience
and interest in investing, but also in the entry
and real opportunity that I saw in the search fund model.
And so it was right then that I joined
NextGen Growth Partners and have been here since 2016.
And my role is really leading the investment team
and working alongside our entrepreneurs and residents
to help with the valuation of opportunities
or industry theses and then the valuation structuring
and negotiating and deal execution to get to close.
And then we'll work with portfolio companies
kind of on an as needed basis
for M&A or other strategic initiatives.
- Fantastic, appreciate that.
And I really appreciate you, again,
being here with us this evening.
Let's start at the top.
Walk us through kind of the steps of the acquisition process
from your seat and kind of the main points there.
And then we'll, we'll dive into the details as we go along.
- Yeah, so the first part of it is just sourcing.
So how are we finding these opportunities?
And we use two primary methods.
I think everyone uses these primary two,
it's is the deal intermediated,
meaning may have an investment banker
or business broker helping with the marketing
and negotiating to try to find a high price
and they're willing sellers, or is it more proprietary?
And that's when you reach out directly to a business owner,
they're not necessarily looking to sell
or at least they're not hiring
someone to help sell their business,
but they're interested in what you have to say
and you start a conversation from that point of view.
They're are similar processes.
I'll walk through the kind of typical bank process first.
I mean, you started by receiving some information
on the company and the industry.
It's usually in the form of a CIM
or a confidential information memorandum.
You take a look at that, see if you're interested.
And if you are maybe you have a follow-up call,
request some data from the intermediary
and then submit an indication of interest or an IOI.
It's kind of a high level valuation range
that is used to see if you're in the ballpark
of the other potential buyers.
Or, if it's proprietary, kind of, it could be even verbal,
but see if you're in the same ballpark as the seller
and what they're expecting for this transaction.
If that's somewhat in line then you move on
and then typically you go meet them in person,
continue to request data.
That's a theme that kind of never stops
throughout the process and also build rapport
and build the relationship with the seller.
I think that's, that's critical through this process.
I mean valuation, cash at closed, structure
is all very important but a lot of that can be figured out
if you have that rapport and foundation built
with the seller throughout the entire process.
And that trust starts to develop,
and that can go a long way.
So from there you have enough to come
to a pinpointed valuation structure.
If the seller decides that that's acceptable
then you sign a letter of intent
or an LOI and go into full due diligence.
Happy to walk through those phases,
but basically you are inspecting everything
you can about the company itself,
the team, the seller, the industry.
You're doing legal diligence, financial diligence,
and so the list goes on, but the full kind of inspection
until you finally negotiate legal docs and get to close.
- Got it, great.
- I think this will be one thing,
the one thing that I'd just sort of mention, Josh,
and we we've talked about Joe, we've talked about some
of this in prior sessions, but the diligence effort
in an ETA transaction, it looks a lot like it does
in a traditional private equity buyout situation
but for the fact that these are small businesses
and typically you're not operating
out of a huge budget that is able to sustain
what we at our at our firm and what in private equity
sort of called dead deal costs, which is,
you know, diligence fees and expenses
that you might rack up in a quality of earnings engagement
with an accounting service provider
or legal diligence fees with high priced lawyers
or documentation fees that you might
incur when you get further on.
So there's this balance in ETA deal-making
around what can you accomplish in diligence
that is your own kind of blood, sweat, and tears,
and just rolling up your sleeves and figuring out
the industry and getting to the core economics
of the business and how they make money
and how they contract or not with their client base
and what that, so there's a tremendous amount
of what we call at the firm business diligence
that goes into these things pre-LOI and then post-LOI.
Before you start engaging some of the
third-party service providers that
would be customary to engage post-LOI
as you're working an opportunity toward
to the closing and funding table.
We can talk a little bit about that.
I mean, I think like search funds historically
don't have a tremendous amount of operating budget
to sustain those types of dead deal costs.
A firm like NGP, we do have a little bit more,
but at the same time you know, again,
this is small part of the market.
These aren't billion dollar transactions
that can sustain dead deal costs or extraneous expenses
when, ultimately you don't effectuate a transaction.
- So how do you factor in those type deal costs?
That's interesting, I didn't know a lot about that.
You know, are you looking to kind of keep those
to a percentage of the transaction,
the overall transaction size,
or does that just factor into that model
that you put together to complete the transaction?
A little bit more information on that would be interesting.
- Yeah, I'll let Josh talked about it a little bit,
but we we liked 0% of the transaction! (laughing)
It can be detrimental to returns, right?
And it could almost be catastrophic.
I mean, in one of our earlier sessions
we talked about the three models that you can embark upon
to pursue ETA there's sort of the self-funded model.
And I suppose that the self, in the self-funded model
you can sustain shocks from dead deal costs to the extent
that your bank account can support them, right?
So that's sort of self fund, and in the search fund path,
I would argue there's not a ton of room
for dead deal expenses before you get to a position
where you're short on budget
to ultimately consummate a transaction.
We've talked about in that path, you're typically funded
for a two, two and a half, maybe three year period,
but that budget can't sustain a tremendous amount
in the way of billable hours from a high priced attorney.
So you gotta be really careful about that.
At our firm, again, we try to manage it down.
I think it's an inevitability in any private equity model
that you're going to spend time
and ultimately money with third-party service providers
on things that don't end up transacting.
But, you know, we, like any other private equity firm
try to keep those to a bare minimum
because they are they are a drag on returns.
- Yeah, and it helps to develop relationships
that with service attorneys or accountants
and so on that you work with on multiple transactions.
And so then when we do have a deal that falls apart
after spending some money on diligence,
they are a lot more willing to do a discount
and even defer until the next transaction closes.
So those types of things help a lot.
And I guess the last thing I would add is
it's, regardless of deal size,
you still have to go through similar steps.
It gets much more complex, the larger the company
and all the systems and team and all of that,
but we still have to dig in almost as much
as we would, if we're doing a $10 million deal
as we would a a hundred million dollar deal.
And so the cost of the service providers scale down
as you go down market to an extent, but they still do
cost money and it's something we're conscious of, for sure.
- Yeah, and I know we talked about this
a little bit in the past but just to orient folks,
so we've got a question from Nathan
that asks what's the typical deal size for ETA
and then maybe we'll stick to kind
of what you guys are looking
for in terms of the typical sizes
just to give some folks the perspective
that we're talking about here.
- It tends to be you know, call it
10 to 50 million in enterprise value.
So the typical transaction that I talk about
in a search fund setting is like
a $2 million EBITDA business bought
at five or six times trailing 12 months EBITDAS,
so, 10 to $12 million in enterprise value.
You're probably going to have some third party debt
versus seller financing as part of that capital structure
to the tune of maybe half of the capital structure.
So call it somewhere in the neighborhood
of five to $6 million in equity, I think, is sort of
a good zone to think about in a search fund setting.
Self-funded transactions, on average,
there are some larger, some smaller than that,
but they tend to be slightly smaller.
You know, at our firm, they tend
to be a little bit bigger than that.
Maybe, 4 million in EBITDAB, bought it somewhere
in the neighborhood of four and a half or five times,
getting you to a higher enterprise value.
But that's sort of the zone that we're talking about,
10 to $50 million annual, I mean, in enterprise value.
- That's great.
A couple of other interesting questions here.
Ramiro asks what are the core activities
that a funded searcher should really do themselves
prior to, or in parallel to hiring third-party providers?
Or said differently, what do you guys
look to do yourselves, your firm?
What does your firm look to do within your firm?
And then what are you typically looking to outsource?
- Yeah, so we, I mean, at a high level,
we do as much as we can internally and myself,
the rest of our investment team, my colleague Parker,
as well as the entrepreneur in residence
are digging into the data that we receive
immediately and continuing to do so until we have a level
of comfort that it shouldn't be very far off.
And I'm talking financial diligence right now,
EBITDA or revenue, there shouldn't be any huge differences
with what the queue of the providers will will find.
And what that means is a lot of customer data analysis,
really understanding the trends, what is driving the growth
of the business and how much concentration is there
and then kind of levels and levels deeper,
and putting that together in kind of a package.
And then we'll go to the rest of the group
and our investment committee to discuss some
of the findings, but all of that's done,
and I would say that it's quite a bit
of work upfront before we decide to,
usually the first step is to hire
a quality of earnings provider.

And from those lenders we've seen
a continued desire to deploy capital.
It's similar to terms that we were seeing
prior to the COVID environment.
- Yeah, there's a white paper that my teaching partner
and I, Mark Agnew and I, collaborated
with our friend at the Yale School of Management
that teaches a similar course
to the one that we do at Booth,
and the white papers called "On the Nature of Debt."
And it gets into some of the nuances of debt,
not necessarily amid COVID,
but on sort of the cost of that paper
vis-a-vis all of the other considerations
that we would argue are equally, if not more
important when evaluating what type of debt,
how much and how to use it in your capital structure.
So I'd encourage people to check out
the piece called "On the Nature of Debt",
if you're interested in this type of stuff.
- Thank you for that, appreciate it.
Just looking at a few more questions here.
Can you talk a little bit about,
I've got a couple more minutes here.
Can you talk a little bit about escrow accounts
and purchase price hold backs and sort of,
are there typical guidelines there
and instructions that you're looking for?
How do you think about that
and incorporate that into the transaction?
- Yeah, another thing to talk about upfront
with the seller, like at LOI stage
because that can be a shock if five to 10%
of the purchase price is held back in an escrow account.
And that's, I think that's a good general range,
roughly 8%, five to 10, and typically
that that's released after 12 months,
maybe half at 12 months, half at 18 or 24 months,
as long as basically everything checks out,
you didn't find any fraudulent activity
or things in the reps and warranties.
With all of that said, we started to see
a lot more providers of reps and warranties insurance.
It's lower in the market, meaning a lower transaction value.
This is then has become almost standard,
extremely common when you get to very large deals.
But what it does is you find an insurance provider
and the escrow goes from 10% of the purchase price
to 150,000, so you have, the seller has some skin
in the game, but then they cover any damages
from breaches of reps and warranties.
And so that gives the seller a lot more cash at close
and you don't have to worry as much
about dealing with those dynamics.
Do you draw it from the escrow or not?
if something technically happens, there's a lot of kind
of nuanced things that can happen that cause complications.
But I would say RNW insurance is something to look into,
even at sub 10 million transaction value.
- And along those lines, do you typically
see breakup fees in this area of the market?
Is that something that you guys have used in the past?
- No, and just to clarify by that, you mean, if we walk away
for whatever reason, do we owe a fee,
- Yes. - or vice versa?
Yeah, no, we don't come across that.
And if we do, we wouldn't agree to it right now or at all.
- Got it, that's helpful.
Well, we're coming up on the top of the hour here.
I really appreciate this.
We've got a few questions that we didn't get to,
but most of which we dealt with in previous session.
So if you did ask a question
that we didn't answer live on the in the meeting
this evening, I've encouraged you to go
to the Chicago Booth Alumni, Chicago webpage
and check out the previous webinars that we posted.
Most of the questions that we didn't get
to tonight have been answered there
but really appreciate everyone joining this evening.
We've got a lot of great questions.
So thank you all for the questions
that we did receive tonight.
Certainly want to thank Brian,
really appreciate you joining us again.
And Josh, it was really great having you on the meeting
tonight, really appreciate your participation here.
And as I said we will have another installment
in December where we'll talk with one of the folks
living the entrepreneur in residence,
ETA life and practice and working
with one of the companies on a daily basis.
So we'll look forward to that again.
Thank you all very much, Ryan and Josh, thank you.
And hope everyone has a wonderful evening.
- Thank you. - Thanks, Joe,
thanks everybody.
- Take care. - bye.

videos.full_text: - Appreciate everyone joining this evening. Thank you for joining us on our "Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition" webinar, focused on structuring deals. I'm Joe Cortese, Co-President of the Chicago Booth Alumni Club and a Principal and Senior Consultant with DiMeo Schneider and Associates here in Chicago. With me again this evening is Brian O'Connor, adjunct associate professor of entrepreneurship at Booth and founder and Managing Principal of NextGen Growth Partners. Brian, nice to see you again, thanks for joining us. We also have a special guest with us again this evening and I'll ask him to introduce himself in just a moment once we get through a few opening considerations. So this is our fifth webinar focused on ETA. We do have the links to the previous webinars available on the Chicago Booth Alumni Club of Chicago's website, so you can join there. Tim State is with us, as well, has been kind enough to put the link in the chat box in previous sessions. So he may be able to do that as well, this evening. As I mentioned, we will focus on structuring the deal this evening and how you actually complete the purchasing transaction of a small business. And we'll spend some time learning about the various types of deal structures, how the process plays out. We'll walk through a couple of common pitfalls that torpedo deals and hopefully hear a little bit about some live examples as well. As we've done in previous sessions, we will take questions along the way. So if you would like to submit a question please go ahead and do that via the question and answer box and we'll deal with those as we go through the meeting here. We do welcome any and all questions. We'll do our best to get to all of them as we go. Also mention quickly, we will have another webinar focused on ETA in December and in this final one for 2020 we'll focus on actual day in the life of an entrepreneur running a small private equity backed company and learn a little bit more about that. So with that, I'd like to turn to our special guest, very pleased to have Josh Dennis with us here tonight. Thank you for joining Josh. If you wouldn't mind, please give us a brief introduction and background of yourself and then we'll dive into the content. - That sounds great. Well, I appreciate you having me on here. I've watched several episodes, so it's great to be here. Josh Dennis, I'm a Principal at NextGen Growth Partners. Quick background, I started my career in investment banking and then middle market private equity, kind of a typical finance track before going to business school at Booth, where I graduated in 2016. And it was while I was at Booth that I learned about ETA, or the search fund model as we called it, everyone's familiar with the search fund model, but in 2000, I think it was early 2015, was the first year that they taught the ETA class and Brian and Mark Agnew taught class. And that's where I learned much more about it, became extremely interested in it, and also developed a relationship with Brian, Mark, and a lot of others in the ETA community. And from there I came back for my second year, was trying to figure out if I wanted to raise a search fund or go back in the investing role. And that's when Brian told me about this idea that he'd had, and it was a great fit or mixed between kind of the benefits you get from a traditional private equity fund, community capital, we can get into all of that, but also taking the benefits of the traditional search fund model. And I thought it made a ton of sense and it was a perfect combination of my experience and interest in investing, but also in the entry and real opportunity that I saw in the search fund model. And so it was right then that I joined NextGen Growth Partners and have been here since 2016. And my role is really leading the investment team and working alongside our entrepreneurs and residents to help with the valuation of opportunities or industry theses and then the valuation structuring and negotiating and deal execution to get to close. And then we'll work with portfolio companies kind of on an as needed basis for M&A or other strategic initiatives. - Fantastic, appreciate that. And I really appreciate you, again, being here with us this evening. Let's start at the top. Walk us through kind of the steps of the acquisition process from your seat and kind of the main points there. And then we'll, we'll dive into the details as we go along. - Yeah, so the first part of it is just sourcing. So how are we finding these opportunities? And we use two primary methods. I think everyone uses these primary two, it's is the deal intermediated, meaning may have an investment banker or business broker helping with the marketing and negotiating to try to find a high price and they're willing sellers, or is it more proprietary? And that's when you reach out directly to a business owner, they're not necessarily looking to sell or at least they're not hiring someone to help sell their business, but they're interested in what you have to say and you start a conversation from that point of view. They're are similar processes. I'll walk through the kind of typical bank process first. I mean, you started by receiving some information on the company and the industry. It's usually in the form of a CIM or a confidential information memorandum. You take a look at that, see if you're interested. And if you are maybe you have a follow-up call, request some data from the intermediary and then submit an indication of interest or an IOI. It's kind of a high level valuation range that is used to see if you're in the ballpark of the other potential buyers. Or, if it's proprietary, kind of, it could be even verbal, but see if you're in the same ballpark as the seller and what they're expecting for this transaction. If that's somewhat in line then you move on and then typically you go meet them in person, continue to request data. That's a theme that kind of never stops throughout the process and also build rapport and build the relationship with the seller. I think that's, that's critical through this process. I mean valuation, cash at closed, structure is all very important but a lot of that can be figured out if you have that rapport and foundation built with the seller throughout the entire process. And that trust starts to develop, and that can go a long way. So from there you have enough to come to a pinpointed valuation structure. If the seller decides that that's acceptable then you sign a letter of intent or an LOI and go into full due diligence. Happy to walk through those phases, but basically you are inspecting everything you can about the company itself, the team, the seller, the industry. You're doing legal diligence, financial diligence, and so the list goes on, but the full kind of inspection until you finally negotiate legal docs and get to close. - Got it, great. - I think this will be one thing, the one thing that I'd just sort of mention, Josh, and we we've talked about Joe, we've talked about some of this in prior sessions, but the diligence effort in an ETA transaction, it looks a lot like it does in a traditional private equity buyout situation but for the fact that these are small businesses and typically you're not operating out of a huge budget that is able to sustain what we at our at our firm and what in private equity sort of called dead deal costs, which is, you know, diligence fees and expenses that you might rack up in a quality of earnings engagement with an accounting service provider or legal diligence fees with high priced lawyers or documentation fees that you might incur when you get further on. So there's this balance in ETA deal-making around what can you accomplish in diligence that is your own kind of blood, sweat, and tears, and just rolling up your sleeves and figuring out the industry and getting to the core economics of the business and how they make money and how they contract or not with their client base and what that, so there's a tremendous amount of what we call at the firm business diligence that goes into these things pre-LOI and then post-LOI. Before you start engaging some of the third-party service providers that would be customary to engage post-LOI as you're working an opportunity toward to the closing and funding table. We can talk a little bit about that. I mean, I think like search funds historically don't have a tremendous amount of operating budget to sustain those types of dead deal costs. A firm like NGP, we do have a little bit more, but at the same time you know, again, this is small part of the market. These aren't billion dollar transactions that can sustain dead deal costs or extraneous expenses when, ultimately you don't effectuate a transaction. - So how do you factor in those type deal costs? That's interesting, I didn't know a lot about that. You know, are you looking to kind of keep those to a percentage of the transaction, the overall transaction size, or does that just factor into that model that you put together to complete the transaction? A little bit more information on that would be interesting. - Yeah, I'll let Josh talked about it a little bit, but we we liked 0% of the transaction! (laughing) It can be detrimental to returns, right? And it could almost be catastrophic. I mean, in one of our earlier sessions we talked about the three models that you can embark upon to pursue ETA there's sort of the self-funded model. And I suppose that the self, in the self-funded model you can sustain shocks from dead deal costs to the extent that your bank account can support them, right? So that's sort of self fund, and in the search fund path, I would argue there's not a ton of room for dead deal expenses before you get to a position where you're short on budget to ultimately consummate a transaction. We've talked about in that path, you're typically funded for a two, two and a half, maybe three year period, but that budget can't sustain a tremendous amount in the way of billable hours from a high priced attorney. So you gotta be really careful about that. At our firm, again, we try to manage it down. I think it's an inevitability in any private equity model that you're going to spend time and ultimately money with third-party service providers on things that don't end up transacting. But, you know, we, like any other private equity firm try to keep those to a bare minimum because they are they are a drag on returns. - Yeah, and it helps to develop relationships that with service attorneys or accountants and so on that you work with on multiple transactions. And so then when we do have a deal that falls apart after spending some money on diligence, they are a lot more willing to do a discount and even defer until the next transaction closes. So those types of things help a lot. And I guess the last thing I would add is it's, regardless of deal size, you still have to go through similar steps. It gets much more complex, the larger the company and all the systems and team and all of that, but we still have to dig in almost as much as we would, if we're doing a $10 million deal as we would a a hundred million dollar deal. And so the cost of the service providers scale down as you go down market to an extent, but they still do cost money and it's something we're conscious of, for sure. - Yeah, and I know we talked about this a little bit in the past but just to orient folks, so we've got a question from Nathan that asks what's the typical deal size for ETA and then maybe we'll stick to kind of what you guys are looking for in terms of the typical sizes just to give some folks the perspective that we're talking about here. - It tends to be you know, call it 10 to 50 million in enterprise value. So the typical transaction that I talk about in a search fund setting is like a $2 million EBITDA business bought at five or six times trailing 12 months EBITDAS, so, 10 to $12 million in enterprise value. You're probably going to have some third party debt versus seller financing as part of that capital structure to the tune of maybe half of the capital structure. So call it somewhere in the neighborhood of five to $6 million in equity, I think, is sort of a good zone to think about in a search fund setting. Self-funded transactions, on average, there are some larger, some smaller than that, but they tend to be slightly smaller. You know, at our firm, they tend to be a little bit bigger than that. Maybe, 4 million in EBITDAB, bought it somewhere in the neighborhood of four and a half or five times, getting you to a higher enterprise value. But that's sort of the zone that we're talking about, 10 to $50 million annual, I mean, in enterprise value. - That's great. A couple of other interesting questions here. Ramiro asks what are the core activities that a funded searcher should really do themselves prior to, or in parallel to hiring third-party providers? Or said differently, what do you guys look to do yourselves, your firm? What does your firm look to do within your firm? And then what are you typically looking to outsource? - Yeah, so we, I mean, at a high level, we do as much as we can internally and myself, the rest of our investment team, my colleague Parker, as well as the entrepreneur in residence are digging into the data that we receive immediately and continuing to do so until we have a level of comfort that it shouldn't be very far off. And I'm talking financial diligence right now, EBITDA or revenue, there shouldn't be any huge differences with what the queue of the providers will will find. And what that means is a lot of customer data analysis, really understanding the trends, what is driving the growth of the business and how much concentration is there and then kind of levels and levels deeper, and putting that together in kind of a package. And then we'll go to the rest of the group and our investment committee to discuss some of the findings, but all of that's done, and I would say that it's quite a bit of work upfront before we decide to, usually the first step is to hire a quality of earnings provider. And so I think we do a lot of the work internally to avoid those dead deal costs that we were talking about. - And Joe, as, I think we've talked about in a previous session, it's generally not the case that you're looking at a business that has an annual audit done. I mean, these are businesses that you're kind of lucky if their financials are housed within a system, as pretty bare bones as like a QuickBooks kind of thing. I mean, it's not uncommon that Josh and the investments team gets a neatly stacked pile of napkins that contain historically or historical financial statements. It's like, there is a tremendous amount of work that you all, as Booth MBAs given your training and your experience can do, but there definitely is some third-party work that needs to get down to validate the work that you've done in the data and the information that's been shared with you from the sellers. You start in the hope that no one is being deceitful in the information that they're sharing with you but, trust, but verify, and you need to, often you'll need, at some point later in the diligence process, a third-party expert to do some of that. - Yeah, seems to be a popular topic with the audience here. We're getting a few more questions. This is an interesting one from Dave. Do you often see self-funded searchers dealing with service providers on a contingent basis in order to offset the risk? Is that something that takes place from time to time in the industry or from your perspective? - Yeah, it happens, I would say there are certain service providers that are willing to work on a contingent basis. I think that Josh alluded to some of this earlier, some of them are willing to not forgo expenses in the event that the deal doesn't close but potentially defer them and roll them into a transaction that does get consummated if they have a high level of belief that that entrepreneur, self-funded or otherwise, is, at some point, going to consummate a transaction. So you might have some flexibility for deferral of some of that. Josh, I don't know if you have a perspective but, I think it's tricky. You'll find some that are willing to work a little bit on a contingent basis, but it's typically more sort of discount and deferral of incurred expenses as opposed to a complete sort of like, "I will only send you a bill for my services in the event that you consummate transaction." - Yeah, totally agree, some will defer until it closes and charge a little bit if nothing closes but full contingency is, I haven't seen it but maybe it's out there. - Yeah, I was thinking, as you were speaking, maybe it's a little bit of adverse selection, too, right? Like those folks that would operate on a contingent basis may not be the folks you necessarily wanna hire, right? - And Joe, I sort of had that adverse selection thought come through my mind as I was talking about it. So yeah, there may be some of that, but I know it does exist. It's worth exploring because service providers that do serve this kind of small part of the market understand and appreciate the constraints associated with a search funder or a self funded searcher's limited budget. - Yeah, that's an important point. Maybe something to note is is ask them how familiar they are with this type of model before going into any type of agreement. And there are some high quality service providers that are maybe starting a new firm on their own with a smaller team and looking to build that list of clients. And maybe that's an opportunity to get a fully contingent type of agreement in place, but you just gotta be careful. - Good point, Josh, talk a little bit about just the negotiation process as you're getting the deal started. I mean, how contentious is it? I know it's different for every transaction but just some general sense of how contentious is it? How much kind of back and forth goes on before you kind of get the bones of the deal in place and then can move forward, and what do you do if it gets contentious? Those sorts of things, I'd be interested in your experience there along those lines. - Yeah, no, it's a really important topic. I think the first point of contention can be when you're negotiating the letter of intent. And so that's really when you're getting engaged and preparing to get married. And so that engagement I mean, that's where it leads to a lot of dead deals. If you just can't bridge the gap. I think where the real contention comes into play is during diligence you're constantly asking for data or follow up questions, you're harassing the seller, maybe their team, if they've let anyone kind of in the circle, you have all of these service providers that are also kind of bugging them and they're trying to run their business. And so it can be overwhelming pretty quickly. And that leads to a lot of deal fatigue and just exhaustion for the seller. And it's completely understandable. It's also exhausting for the buyer. And so what happens when a lot of fatigue comes into play, people start to get on edge. You start to forget why you signed that LOI in the first place. And so I think there's a few things that are important to do upfront. and then throughout the process. The first is as soon as that LOI is signed set expectations with the seller on exactly what your plan for the process is, what you expect the data request list to look like comprehensively, there's a balance. You may not want to send every single thing but showing them like this is going to be a tough process. And just getting that out, getting out in front of that. And that way you can point back to it and they're not caught off guard, or at least they shouldn't be. And then throughout the process, trying to remember why you're so excited about this opportunity and why the seller should be excited about you and focusing on the relationship building and having, sometimes, a kind of a good cop, bad cop mentality can be helpful, especially with the person kind of leading the deal. If it's a searcher or an EIR, you know, typically they're going to be working day in and day out with the seller post-close and their team. And so it's not fun when you've signed and finally close the deal and then the next day you're working together but there's a lot of resentment leftover. So we try to let the EIR focus on that part. We try to be the annoying people and also don't be afraid to blame your service providers. - (laughing) That's a good little point at the end, there, Josh, don't be afraid to blame the service providers! You know, that notion of good cop, bad cop is an interesting one. And, listen, whatever path you choose for ETA, I think there will be points in time where there needs to be some of that dynamic. And often you can use your investors. You can use Brian or Joe or a service provider as a bad cop, because one of the things that Josh mentioned that's just critically important is that you're building a relationship. Remember in one of the prior sessions, or probably many of them, we talked about that it's highly unlikely that you're going to be the highest bidder in a very competitively run auction process. And so we tend to avoid those types of situations but, you know, in all likelihood, this seller is choosing you as the buyer for some reasons that are non-economic, right? And those are probably relational. They like you, they think you're going to do well by their employees, their customers, all stakeholders of the business post-transaction. And therefore it's critically important during these contentious situations, and every deal has many of them, And Josh pointed out a couple of points in the process that are typically more likely to be contentious than others, but it's critically important that you rely on the relationship and the trust and the goodwill that you've built early on in sort of the stages leading up to LOI or around LOI execution because there will be very tough days and very tough conversations in the engagement period, as Josh sort of put it, that you're going to have to draw on some of that goodwill, trust, and relationship that you've built with the seller, again, with the analogy during the courtship process, that's super important. - Couple more questions here. Would you recommend that the searcher send out the first draft of the purchase agreement? Or do you want the other side to kind of submit their offer first, their information first? - That could be a quick one for me. You want the power of the pen. You want to control the draft of the purchase agreement. I'm having a hard time thinking of a situation where there'd be an exception to that, but I, as the buyer, as the searcher, I wanna control the first agreement. - Is there more, Josh? - No, I mean, yeah, you definitely want to do that. - Great, let's focus a little bit on structure. Can you talk through just some of the structures that you've seen thus far? Again, I know there's a lot of optionality here, but some of the things that you've seen work that have worked better or some of the things that haven't worked as well and some more information there I think would be useful. - Yeah, so I think in a typical private equity transaction, and larger is what I mean by that, it's usually kind of cash at close and there's equity and there's debt. And that can be split up a bunch of different ways. I think, as you go further down market and a lot of what we're doing with the proprietary sourcing model that we have is we're talking with sellers that may have a number in their mind but maybe if you could get there, if they grow a ton or if you can mitigate risk in other ways and so ways to bridge the gap in valuation expectations versus what you may be willing to pay at close is like an earn-out. And so what that means is you work with the seller and first you kind of get an understanding of what they expect growth to look like in the next one year, two years, three years and so on. And then you kind of say, "Okay, well, "I agree, if you can hit those targets "we will pay you X amount more to bridge that gap. "We'll pay you 10 million at close, "and then we'll pay you another 4 million "over the course of three years." I'm making numbers up, but that's a tool that we use quite a bit. There are some downsides to it that I'd be happy to get into, but quickly, I think other useful tools, I mean, rollover equity from the seller is very common and it helps just align incentives. And I think that's what we're everything comes down to aligning incentives post-close. And so rollover equity is huge. Another way as a seller note. So they would fund a piece of debt at close and you would pay some interest on it but it could be really attractive because typically there's no covenants, it's usually a lower interest rate and you're working with the seller directly instead of like a senior bank or something to that effect. - Yeah, two quick, I agree with everything that Josh said. Two quick points, maybe one layer deeper. You know, it's often the case that because you've built such a relationship with the business owner operator, perhaps the founder, they get excited about the vision that you have for taking their business to the next level. And so the notion that they can roll equity and take a second bite at the apple and getting them excited about the future value of that equity, to Josh's point, aligns interests really well. And if they've got sort of this number in mind, however they arrived at that number, it might be completely irrational, but it may help bridge a gap if they sort of say "Oh boy, well, if I have continued equity interest "in this business, and I can take a second bite "at the apple, that's really interesting. "And I can sort of remain somewhat involved "in the business kind of on a go-forward basis." So that's, that's a really interesting and powerful tool. It does have the ability to bridge a gap. It does have the ability to align interests pretty nicely. One thing I'd say on renounce and you, and you do see them in the part of the market that we're sort of talking about in this series, they often become contentious. You know, the best earn out is the one that gets paid, because that means that the business is growing and it's performing and it's hitting all the targets. And frankly, at that point, you're happy to pay the earn-out and the seller is happy to receive that earn out. Where a business is faltering and an earn-out comes into question, whether or not it should, or shouldn't be paid, it can get litigious, it can get combative. It presents other unique operational challenges. If the seller remains involved operationally in the business, then you have a situation where you've got someone that is doing something for the business and presumably creating value that you have an issue with the economics of the payments and the capital structure that can create a really tough dynamic. And I've seen that go, I've seen that go the wrong way. So you gotta be careful with the way that you use some of these tools, specifically the earn-out tool, but to Josh's point, they can absolutely be powerful in bridging a difference in valuation expectations between buyer and seller. - This notion of, I'm sorry Josh, did you wanna add something, please? - Kind of getting more into the weeds. I think that could be more valuable. And once we talked about it, they hit it, that's great, cool. If they don't, then it could get really contentious. I think another really difficult situation is when it's very close to the target number and you have to decide, do you want to pay it anyway or not, even though maybe by the letter of the law you don't need to, and how does that affect the relationship? And also, what is the target based on, is it revenue or is it all the way down to some adjusted EBITDA number? And as the investor or the buyer, it's easy to say you prefer lower on the P&L because you want profitable revenue, you don't just want any top line growth, but it'd be, it creates a lot more complexity, especially if you're hiring a team or investing in some type of infrastructure technology. And that all goes to op ex, well, how is that calculated in the adjusted EBITDA you're talking about now that you're in control? And so I think if you do want to use an earn-out, it's just important to define everything extremely clearly and as explicitly as possible in the legal docs so that you can point back to it and there's no real questions. They look great on paper, but it gets really tough when you're trying to define those things. - Sure, notion or not is garnering a lot of questions here. Just to clarify, can you have an earn out situation where the seller is no longer involved in the business? - You know, to Josh's point, a seller might raise their hand and say, "Well, listen, if I'm not operationally involved "in the business anymore and you're making decisions "that are impacting my ability to achieve "that future earn-out payment, "I'll, a decide to make an investment into a new division "or build out a sales marketing and BD function." That has a immediate term PNL negative impact, an EBITDA margin compressing event for future earnings growth. That has a real implication for a seller that during that immediate term period is reliant on nominal earnings growth to achieve their earn-out targets. So you get into a situation where a savvy seller sort of says, "Well, this doesn't feel right, "that I have an earn-out tied to something "that I don't have operational control over anymore." Which, again, it's all a negotiation, right? So, and when you do have an a seller that's critically important to the ongoing operation of the business and you arrive in a situation where to Josh's point, it's close or the earn out is technically not to be paid or to be paid in full, but a portion of your revenue generation of that business is dependent on them getting excited and being happy about coming into work every day. Now that can be, so again, there's these things, they're tricky and the devil is in the details on these things. But the short answer to the question is, yes, you can have an earn-out situation where a seller not operationally involved if the seller is willing to agree to that. - And what do you see in terms of typical equity roll over percentage? Is there something you guys target or shoot for, or is there some sort of just guideline that's helpful that makes sure that somebody's incentivized? What's your experience there? - As a general ballpark number, if I had to pick one, roughly 20%, I'd say 10 to 20% is enough incentive, along with, and these are typically founder owners, not always, but along with the personal investment they've already made and the attachment they have to the company when they sell, keeping at least 10%, I think is important to us usually, but that said, it's not always the case. We've been able to close on transactions where the founder legitimately wanted to stop running the business after a transition period and hang out with his family and just not worry about the business. And so we can make that happen. But in those situations, it just, you really have to dig in and get to know the seller and really develop that trust to make sure they're not trying to pull one over on you in some way. - Yeah. I mean, I think it goes back to something we've talked about in a prior session, but there's always asymmetric information. The seller always knows more about his or her business than you do as the buyer. And therefore if there's an unwillingness to roll equity or carry some paper or participate in an earn-out, that may be okay. You really got to understand if they're selling you a bill of goods that you're you're not fully aware of, kind of what it is that you're buying now? Just a real quick point on, at our firm, and I think in ETA broadly, these are typically change of control transactions. So the range that Josh shared with you I think this is right on, that's sort of the way we think about it. You wouldn't likely get into a scenario, or I haven't seen many I, can't really think of any off the top of my head, where a seller is rolling equity and maintaining a control equity position in the business that feels like a sort of a growth equity type situation where there's a minority investor and the searcher coming in, I'm sure there are unique structures that exist where you might sort of think about doing that but typically it would not be that the seller would maintain a majority equity position in the business post-transaction. - Let's transition over and talk about some of the pitfalls that you tend to see. I'm interested to hear in your experience. Maybe you've got a couple of live, or, examples you could talk through about you've started the process, and then for whatever reason, it's fallen apart. I'd love to hear more about some of the things that can typically torpedo a deal. - Oh, man, where do we start? - [Joe] I'm sure there's a lot there. - I'll start kind of high level and then we can happy to talk as much as you guys want about specific examples but, can we just go with post-LOI? I think before then-- - Sure. - It's kind of too early. So I think one is something I mentioned, but deal fatigue and resentment starting to build on both sides and a lack of clear communication that just makes the relationship that used to be in a good spot in such a bad spot that both sides are ready to kind of toss in the towel. A couple of more specific examples, though, would be legal documentation. So these legal docs are not simple. They, I mean a purchase agreement, 90, 100 pages, whatever it is, and it's not in plain English. And especially for someone that's not an attorney or maybe they have hired their friend that's an attorney, but not necessarily experienced in M&A, that can lead to some real confusion. And like, "Why are you speaking in this crazy language? "Why can't we just do a handshake deal "or have it like on a one-page agreement?" That has caused contention in the past. We've had to try to explain it and work through it, but that can be a shocker to a lot of sellers. And on the notion of the service providers that the seller hires, whether that's an attorney or some other kind of advisor, it depends on how experienced they are and how well they know the typical process or what to expect, and then help communicate to the seller if this is kind of normal, or if they start saying things that are normal course are way kind of overboard or out of line and so on, they kind of poison the well to an extent with the seller and then they start to mistrust you. And so again, happy to dig into any of those things but those are a few topics that come to mind. - Yeah. I mean, and Josh said, I think that's right on. I think that there, we could go on and on, honestly, Joe, for like hours on sort of the ways that these things can fall apart. I mean, I'll give you one sort of nuanced example, and it's sort of inline, I think, with like this technical purchase agreement can be very intimidating and feel like, "Oh my gosh, this searcher or this buyer's trying to pull the wool over my eyes," sort of thing. I mean, things that may be as as second nature to Booth alum is like networking capital. Like you're establishing, when you find one of these businesses, you're buying it on a cash free, debt-free basis but it needs to be delivered with a certain level of working capital to be able to perform, right? The analogy that I use is like when you buy a car, you can't drive it off the lot without at least a workable level of oil and fuel in the gas tank. And so working capital tends to be sort of like the oil and the fuel of the car. And so we got into a situation where we were getting really close on a deal and it came time to negotiate the working capital tag and the seller just had a fundamental sort of disagreement about, he thought that receivables were his, and I can't even remember if the situation was that he wanted to leave the payables or what it was, or that all payables would be exhausted, and then the receivables were his at time of close, but it's like, I think, Josh correct me if I'm wrong, I don't know if you even know the example that I'm referring to, but I think it was like a $2 million networking capital type of need for this business. And, someone may take some of these things for granted, but a business owner and operator who's built a really great business might not necessarily think about some of these nuanced components of deal-making that are pretty customary that when you buy a small privately held business that it does need to be delivered with a normalized and agreeable level of networking capital. - [Joe] Sure. - Yeah, and it's understandable. And I'm glad you brought that up. This is a topic that comes up a lot and comes back to setting expectations up front. I think it can be helpful even pre-LOI, just because the words in the LOI say a normalized amount of working capital left on the balance sheet at close, or whatever the language is. And that doesn't necessarily mean you're on the same page with the seller. So explaining them to them how it works because it's like, "Well, I generated that revenue, "of course, I'm going to keep the cash "that comes in after that revenue is generated." And so there's other examples like that. I think, again, comes back to just being clear upfront and making sure you don't miss these big things. - What sort of a, just a, I know this, again general question, but just a sense, you know, you decided to, you found a business that you want to purchase, so sort of like when that process begins to when you can actually consummate the deal and sign the docs and the transactions complete, what are some ranges of time that it takes to do that? - Anywhere from, when you initiate the conversation or when you sign the LOI? - No, let's say, let's say, yeah not including all of that, 'cause again, that can vary widely, as well, but when you said, "Okay, we're gonna do this deal." Maybe you've agreed to the terms of an LOI or something. And so the real sort of transaction process begins. - Typically 75 days on average, if I had to pick a number. I think 60 to 90 is kind of the the general range we provide. But with that said, if there is some need to close extremely quickly and the seller and their advisors are providing data and very responsive and so on, we can close the deal in 30 to 45 days if that was on the line and everyone was working hard. And then there's also times where it's the opposite and it drags on 120 plus days. So yeah, I'll, I'll stop there. - On that topic, I think you're typically negotiating a letter of intent that stipulates an exclusivity period that is usually, that should be in line with the amount of time that you expect. Hopefully you can negotiate as the buyer a little bit of buffer, a little bit of wiggle room. So if you think you can close the deal in 60 days, you might try to negotiate a 90 day exclusivity period to work in earnest to get the deal consummated. But I think I need Josh's ranges are spot on. The pre-LOI stuff, and I know we're not focusing on that, Matt, Joe can vary widely. I mean, that's anywhere from a couple of days to several years, right? You know, we've been working opportunities for years and years and years in hopes that someday we'd get them to the finish line. But varies extremely widely. But post-LOI, that's a pretty good kind of general sense. - So, and kind of along those lines we're living in a COVID world these days and hopefully there's some light at the end of the tunnel but it seems like we've got a ways to go here. How has the COVID environment impacted getting deals done? Has it changed timelines lengthened them, and what impacts have you seen as a result of dealing with COVID? - Yeah, it's been challenging and there were some sellers and companies that we were negotiating with, they're like getting closer, further down the process and COVID hit and like a lot of businesses, they took a drop, especially in Q2 of this year. And so then, just because maybe their earnings of the revenue were declining among this economic environment, that doesn't mean that the number of the had in their head for the valuation of their business changed at all, but as the investor, as the buyer, it was really hard. And it still is, frankly, to know if this like a trough and it's about to bounce back, or if this is a longer term kind of more sustainable trend in the business. And therefore, well, I guess in either case, that does change the valuation, at least the structure, from our perspective and that led to, "Okay, well, let's put it on hold. Let's keep in touch and see kind of how this plays out." But that's been a difficult challenge with some deals that were already in the hopper. And then now in Q4, we're seeing volume pick back up as people have a little bit more visibility into the next year and kind of their customers and P&L and all of that, but you still have that question and there's still uncertainty of what happens in the next three, six, 12 months, for sure. So with all that said, I think there's a couple of points. One we've continued to reach out and try to use this as a way to add value if possible to business owners that are trying to navigate this difficult time like a lot of other business owners, like we are at NextGen and pretty much everyone in the world. So how can we be a value added partner to them during this time and build that rapport that we've talked about and during, and when things do, when the time does become right, then we are in a good spot. And I guess the second thing is the businesses that we've seen that had some kind of tailwind from COVID, and I mean picture a manufacturer of masks or something like that, we've seen premiums on those types of businesses because there are a lot of buyers out there, there's a lot of dry powder and people are putting out for companies that are growing and maybe accelerating growth during this time. - The good news is for all the uncertainty that COVID has brought, at least our political landscape in the US had a lot of clarity right now, so been a counterbalance. - So, no, I, I think that's, that's right. It's uncertain, buyers and sellers are uncertain. It's harder to form relationships like normally, Joe, you know, you and I will be doing this in person and we'd invite people like, it's just top of the funnel stuff, pre-LOI building the relationships that are required to get you to LOI execution and again, build that trust and goodwill that is going to need be needed to take you through the deal process. It's just harder to do in this environment. We're figuring out new ways to do it that, yeah, I mean, it's challenging. Josh focused on one of the kind of post-LOI and how is the company performing amid all that's going on. The other component to it, right, is like there's a big piece of this that's about building trust and building relationships and fostering those relationships. And I think that that's been certainly more challenging in this environment that we're all living in. And it was in November of last year where it would have been easier for us to hop on a plane and take a meeting in Omaha, Nebraska with a business owner that was inclined to engage with us. How do you do that in a way that makes everybody comfortable? Is it Zoom or, how do you? So there've been definite implications across the whole timeline and spectrum of activities. - And a question specific to that is how has the ability to obtain external financing been impacted, bank debt and otherwise, is that, ar those spigots starting to come open again, are some of the government programs that have been enacted available to use here at all, and how does that look in the current environment? - Yeah, the government programs have been options that we've considered and looked into and that's definitely helpful. From a senior banking, a senior bank lender perspective, they are typically, not always at all, but typically, a little bit more conservative and the lack of visibility and uncertainty in this environment has led them to be a little bit more particular or maybe a little bit more conservative in terms of covenants and things like that. Really, in our transactions we typically like to use very flexible debt options. And so it may be a little bit more expensive on a cash interest basis but with that comes no amortization, for example, so we can preserve that cash flow, very much looser covenants, and that helps a lot. And from those lenders we've seen a continued desire to deploy capital. It's similar to terms that we were seeing prior to the COVID environment. - Yeah, there's a white paper that my teaching partner and I, Mark Agnew and I, collaborated with our friend at the Yale School of Management that teaches a similar course to the one that we do at Booth, and the white papers called "On the Nature of Debt." And it gets into some of the nuances of debt, not necessarily amid COVID, but on sort of the cost of that paper vis-a-vis all of the other considerations that we would argue are equally, if not more important when evaluating what type of debt, how much and how to use it in your capital structure. So I'd encourage people to check out the piece called "On the Nature of Debt", if you're interested in this type of stuff. - Thank you for that, appreciate it. Just looking at a few more questions here. Can you talk a little bit about, I've got a couple more minutes here. Can you talk a little bit about escrow accounts and purchase price hold backs and sort of, are there typical guidelines there and instructions that you're looking for? How do you think about that and incorporate that into the transaction? - Yeah, another thing to talk about upfront with the seller, like at LOI stage because that can be a shock if five to 10% of the purchase price is held back in an escrow account. And that's, I think that's a good general range, roughly 8%, five to 10, and typically that that's released after 12 months, maybe half at 12 months, half at 18 or 24 months, as long as basically everything checks out, you didn't find any fraudulent activity or things in the reps and warranties. With all of that said, we started to see a lot more providers of reps and warranties insurance. It's lower in the market, meaning a lower transaction value. This is then has become almost standard, extremely common when you get to very large deals. But what it does is you find an insurance provider and the escrow goes from 10% of the purchase price to 150,000, so you have, the seller has some skin in the game, but then they cover any damages from breaches of reps and warranties. And so that gives the seller a lot more cash at close and you don't have to worry as much about dealing with those dynamics. Do you draw it from the escrow or not? if something technically happens, there's a lot of kind of nuanced things that can happen that cause complications. But I would say RNW insurance is something to look into, even at sub 10 million transaction value. - And along those lines, do you typically see breakup fees in this area of the market? Is that something that you guys have used in the past? - No, and just to clarify by that, you mean, if we walk away for whatever reason, do we owe a fee, - Yes. - or vice versa? Yeah, no, we don't come across that. And if we do, we wouldn't agree to it right now or at all. - Got it, that's helpful. Well, we're coming up on the top of the hour here. I really appreciate this. We've got a few questions that we didn't get to, but most of which we dealt with in previous session. So if you did ask a question that we didn't answer live on the in the meeting this evening, I've encouraged you to go to the Chicago Booth Alumni, Chicago webpage and check out the previous webinars that we posted. Most of the questions that we didn't get to tonight have been answered there but really appreciate everyone joining this evening. We've got a lot of great questions. So thank you all for the questions that we did receive tonight. Certainly want to thank Brian, really appreciate you joining us again. And Josh, it was really great having you on the meeting tonight, really appreciate your participation here. And as I said we will have another installment in December where we'll talk with one of the folks living the entrepreneur in residence, ETA life and practice and working with one of the companies on a daily basis. So we'll look forward to that again. Thank you all very much, Ryan and Josh, thank you. And hope everyone has a wonderful evening. - Thank you. - Thanks, Joe, thanks everybody. - Take care. - bye.

metadata.shortDescription:
I spent months figuring out how to find cash-flowing businesses to buy—so you don’t have to.
Subscribe for more Smart Money Moves!

In this video, I’ll show you how I actually find businesses to buy—whether it’s a $100K laundromat, $1M home services company, or a $500K HVAC business. We’ll cover the exact deal sourcing strategies I use, from BizBuySell and Flippa, to cold outreach, search funds, and off-market private listings.

This isn’t some make-money-online gimmick. It’s how real entrepreneurs—like Codie Sanchez, Alex Hormozi, and small private equity firms—build wealth through boring, profitable small businesses.
We’ll break down entrepreneurship through acquisition, how to create off-market deal flow, and how to tell if you’re looking at a hidden gem… or a bad investment. Whether you’re chasing your first boring business or scaling your acquisitions, this is your step-by-step blueprint for building real wealth through small business ownership—no MBA required. Let’s get to it.

2:10 Business Listings

Kenny Finance is an investor, entrepreneur, and personal finance creator with nearly a decade of experience on Wall Street at firms like Morgan Stanley, Blackstone, and KKR. His channel is dedicated to breaking down wealth-building strategies, smart investing principles, and the financial playbook used by the world’s most successful investors. With a focus on making complex financial topics simple and actionable, Kenny helps viewers take control of their money, grow their net worth, and make informed financial decisions. Whether it’s navigating the stock market, buying businesses, or optimizing personal finances, his content delivers expert insights designed for long-term success.

metadata.title: $60m Roll-Up That Started With an SBA Acquisition | Brian Boland and Onu Okebie Interview
metadata.author: Acquiring Minds
metadata.shortDescription:
Onu Okebie and Brian Boland started small—with an SBA loan to acquire a business doing just $500k in SDE. Today, they’ve grown HTL Freight to $60 million in revenue. Their story shows the power of bootstrapping: keeping 100% ownership early, proving themselves before raising equity, and then negotiating far better terms later. Brian estimates their cost of equity was just a tenth of what it would have been at the start. This episode is about how two entrepreneurs turned one SBA-backed deal into a major freight roll-up.

❤️ Enjoy this interview? SUBSCRIBE for more: https://shorturl.at/zaP1m

00:00 Introduction to HTL Freight founders
13:44 Understanding the freight brokerage business model
19:55 First acquisition strategy and platform building
31:43 Working capital optimization as growth driver
42:56 Scaling through multiple acquisitions
01:00:00 Strategic approach to raising capital
01:15:08 Future growth strategy and vision

ABOUT Acquiring Minds
Acquiring Minds is a podcast about buying businesses. Acquiring an existing business is an awesome opportunity for many entrepreneurs, and host Will Smith talks to the people who do it. New episodes 2x per week.

metadata.title: The Acquisition Search Process - Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition Event Series
metadata.author: The University of Chicago Booth School of Business
metadata.shortDescription: Join Joe Cortese, '10, Chicago Booth Alumni Club co-president, and Brian O'Connor, '08, adjunct assistant professor of entrepreneurship at Booth and founder – managing partner of NextGen Growth Partners, for this second webinar in our Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) series. We focus on the mechanics of the search process including how to identify suitable acquisition targets and how to measure the effectiveness of the search process. This discussion will be of interest to anyone contemplating a search.
