And again, back, you know, four months ago when it was okay to attend trade shows, meet business owners. (mumbles) Like sort of like, you know, flashback a little bit. You know, it really is those folks that had a hard time getting out of their comfort zone and executing and taking a bias to action approach and showing up to the trade show when that maybe was uncomfortable or they didn't feel like they were prepared to do so or taking the call with a business owner before doing all of the requisite, you know, research and analysis on their industry. And maybe if you stumble and maybe you'll learn, you'll learn a thing or two about something you did or somebody who might wanna change in your next approach. I found that the folks that ended up sit on their hands and not get out in front of business owners and have conversations get out in the market, building their pipeline early, they find that later in their search, because these opportunities tend to have long gestation periods between initial point of contact and when you ultimately transact with a business owner. So those folks that sat on their hands, you know, for months in the beginning, tend to struggle toward the latter stages of their search. The other thing I would mention is that it's critically important because there is so much there is unfortunately some luck in what we're talking about doing here and at any time a deal can fall apart. I've found that some folks can get tunnel vision on a particular target once they maybe get it under LOI. A letter of intent is basically a nonbinding agreement between a buyer and seller under which the terms are that you're gonna ultimately purchase their business hopefully, you know, 60 or 90 days later as you perform diligence. The folks that while they're doing that and while they're getting an opportunity under letter of intent and advancing and diligencing on that opportunity, they take their eye off the ball, as it relates to continued pursuit of their theses, that they've been pursuing, and continued outreach in dialogue with other potential targets in their pipeline. And listen, if it happens, then these transactions fall apart as you're working them in an exclusivity period in an LOI, they fall apart. And those folks that haven't been mindful of continuing to keep their pipeline full of opportunities, find themselves 30, 60, 90, potentially more days down the road flat-footed in the event that that deal falls apart. So the second piece is the folks that maybe take their eye off the ball on keeping their pipeline full. - Got it very helpful, thank you. You, mentioned, you know, your preference for higher growth industries. We did get a question about, you know, I'm sure folks prefer higher growth industries, but have you seen this model be successful in industries that aren't growing as fast or maybe languishing, can that work? - I think it can work. I just, you know, I would, there are some industries that I avoid that I believe to be sort of languishing or overly cyclical or troubled for one reason or another. And I would encourage you all to sort of have their do not touch list. And that's probably different for everyone. You know, businesses, I'm sorry, industries that are steady Eddy they've, you know, kind of been growing at GDP over the years. Listen, I think you can find interesting opportunities in those industries and perhaps they're less competitive, therefore you're gonna be able to structure yourself a better deal for the purchase of the business that you ultimately find in that industry. So I think that's a fine and fair approach, I just like to talk about stacking the deck in your favor. And one of those ways you can stack the deck in your favor is to, you know, buy a ship in a sea that has rising tides. You know, everybody's gonna be lifted a little bit. So yeah, it would be, you know, not crazy to think about finding a business and just a stable industry that you buy it and it's attractive price and you do things to that business. I would encourage you not to be naive about the assumptions that you make around taking an industry and a business that's been growing in line with that GDP industry and sort of immediately being able to turn that into a GDP times two or GDP times three growth, I think that's a little bit of a naive view on it. But yeah, you certainly, it's not crazy to think that you might find a good business in an industry that hasn't been growing as much as some others. - Maybe the way to think about it is businesses and industries that aren't growing as fast, just have less margin for error, potentially. - Yeah, I think that's well said, Joe. - One of the other questions that we got here just on the international market, do you see this model internationally? Do you see an interest in this type of model overseas? - Yes, absolutely. Mark and I have students every time we teach that come from international locations and bring these concepts and these tools back to their home countries and have been very, very effective. You've seen quite a bit of it from Booth alumni and otherwise in Latin America, there are several Booth alumni that have pursued it in Mexico, in Brazil and some other Latin American countries. There's a developed kind of ecosystem for this in Western Europe. And I would say it's starting we've seen a little bit in Asia, but probably not as much as what we've seen. Historically the concentration has been in the US but you have seen some in Canada, some in (mumbles), some in Western Europe. And I think it's continuing to grow in awareness and popularity. - Got it. I want to switch gears a little bit. And we talked about, you know, how do you sort of get the thesis going and get the process started? Let's say, you've got your thesis, you've got your industry, you know, one or two sort of targeted. How do you then begin to build your target list of prospective acquisitions? - Yeah, if anybody has like the silver bullet answer for this question, like, please call me after this cause that's a very valuable answer. So what I'll say, Joe is you gotta use the tools and resources that are available to you and you gotta get scrappy about it. So one of the things we talked about in class, I'll just give you a couple of anecdotes. Like, you know, you find the industry trade organization for the particular niche that you're chasing down and you try to attend the trade show or if you can't make it to the trade show or if COVID happens and there is no trade show, you get to the trade show exhibitor list and you research all thousand companies that last year exhibited at that trade show because very likely, those are probably pretty appropriately sized businesses for what you might be looking for. And they're obviously exhibiting their products or services at the trade show, so they're gonna be a very likely relevant target. So, you know, there are online databases and subscriptions and things that you could sign up for. But frankly, at the end of the day, it's a lot of hustle, it's being scrappy, it's being resourceful, it's developing lists. It's, you know, often you'll find people that pursue the ETA path are leveraging the help from interns because interns tend to do a lot of research and help the ETA practitioner, you know, develop target lists and go through those lists and identify whether or not a target is gonna be worth pursuing sort of thing. So at the end of the day, I think it is a numbers game in this path. And so you gotta develop that list of two, three, 400 targets that you think might be in the size range and in the business model type that you're looking for. And then you go out and you campaign them and you try to, in whatever way you can get a conversation going and develop a relationship with the business owner. - So that's great. And the question always comes up when we start to talk about thesis, do intermediaries work? Is that part of this process that can be affected? So talk a little bit about you know, the intermediaries, how you think about that and you know, do you see a lot of transactions that take place involving intermediaries? - Yeah, I figured that was gonna be the next question here, it's a natural next question. I mean, the answer is yes. I mean, I think that, you know, the approach that we've been talking about thus far is one that is often described as proprietary, right? So there's this proprietary path toward sourcing, which is develop a thesis, go out and campaign form a relationship directly with a business owner and avoid participating in a competitive process, that's run by an investment bank or a broker, right? There's this whole other path that is intermediated and a banker or broker driven. And to answer your question directly, Joe, yes, transactions in ETA happen all the time with a broker involved. I mean, I think that the trade off right, is that you're probably not the only person looking at that opportunity. So you've got the opportunity to just sort of get into a winner's curse scenario. And you know often when there's competition that drives up price. And so, you know, I often encourage ETA people that follow the ETA path to not necessarily be inclined to be the highest bidder in an auction process to win a business. You need to appeal to a seller for sometimes reasons that are non-economic. You know, you're going to be the long lost son or daughter of that business to carry the torch forward and preserve their legacy. That's a meaningful component of why a business owner might be compelled to sell to you versus someone else that might be willing to offer them more cash at close or more enterprise value for their business. So, yes, there absolutely is a universe of bankers and brokers and wealth advisors and accountants and attorneys and people that have access to these deals. And listen, the reality is all bankers and brokers are not created equally. So there is a component of finding that business that is misrepresented or under marketed, let's put it by a broker and frankly that might present an opportunity to buy a business that otherwise should have been valued at something much higher than where you purchase it. So the nice thing, frankly, about the intermediated channel versus proprietary channel is you know that you've got a willing seller on the other end of the telephone, right? They've engaged a broker not to sit around and do nothing, they've engaged a broker to try to find them a universe of buyers that will ultimately be the right buyer and the right fit and the right price and the right structure and all those sorts of things, you know, for their business. So yes, it happens often and I encourage searchers to not be exclusive in one path or the other. I think a well managed pipeline, well-managed deal flow comes from various different sources, both in proprietary thesis-driven as well as intermediate. - And so as you're forming this perspective list of companies to acquire, are there characteristics that make prospective businesses super attractive? And on the flip side of that, are there, you know, a few characteristics that make them really unattractive so that you can kind of get a quick sense of, okay, this is something I really should spend some time on, or I need to run away, this is a dumpster fire. - Yeah, for sure. I mean, some of it is gonna be easy for me to talk about generically, but then some of it is very much company specific and you need to get a look at the financials and the team that's incumbent and you know, all that, some of the nuances associated with that particular business, but some of the things that are more generic, right? Like I tend to favor businesses that have recurring revenue streams. So we talked a little bit about recurring revenue on the last call. But you know, when you have a relationship with a customer that month in and month out, unless they take action to stop their subscription to your service, it's gonna predictably and reliably produce the same amount of revenue the following month, the following year, unless you, as the service provider, screw something up. Those are fantastic businesses because you don't have to wake up every morning and think about where your first dollar of revenue for that particular day is going to come from. I, you know, I tend to favor and encourage people following this path to favor, you know, mission critical, low share of customer wallet business services, right? So let's take the environment that we're in right now. If you provide on behalf of a fortune 1,000 company, if you are a component of their compliance function and they need you and your subject matter expertise to exist and times get tough and they need to think about cutting expenses, you know, is it the compliance service provider that they pay a 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 dollars a month to have this nuanced little thing humming within their organization? That's probably not the thing that's gonna get up, right? So that check that you continue to receive is very likely to remain intact in good times and in bad. So I think about these mission critical asset light recurring revenue, B2B service models as kind of the "darlings" of the ETA path for good reasons. Those are really good companies. And then once you get a peak under the hood of the business, you know, you're obviously looking at things like historical growth, you wanna buy a business that's growing, not languishing. And you know, you wanna buy a business with enough breathing room in the P and L so healthy, EBITDA and free cashflow margins. And, you know, ideally you've gotta have a business that generate, you know, has a scenario whereby it's a negative networking capital business. So as you grow, you can use working capital to fund your growth. That's a really cool element of businesses, right? So there's a lot of nuances to what does or doesn't make a business attractive. But the last thing I'll sort of say on this, unless we've got questions you wanna get deeper into it is no business is perfect. Okay, especially a business that generates two, three, $4 million of annual EBITDA, right? These are small businesses. None of the businesses are gonna, be completely without, you know, customer concentration or completely without a deficiency in a particular part of their organization. None of them are gonna have a particular, like a perfectly linear growth path and illustrate, you know, perfect operating leverage in the model, such that every year that they grow their EBITDA margins expand. These are all great things that look for, but just be mindful of not letting perfection get in the way of progress and momentum, because nothing is perfect in this world, but certainly not perfect in this micro part of the middle market. - If they were perfect, they probably wouldn't be for sale, right? It's along these lines an interesting question from Tucker, as you develop your thesis, how much do you bank on being able to create incremental value post acquisition? Or said differently like, is there a certain threshold of value add that you think is important before you would actually look at transacting? - Yeah, so pretty question. Yeah, you need to absolutely have a thesis around what you wanna do with this business. But what I'll say before I get into that a little bit is remember core to this model and the success that's existed in this model since the mid eighties and the successes has been a while in this asset class and model is you're buying fundamentally sound businesses in healthy markets. So first order of business, when you buy a business at four or five six times trailing 12 months EBITDA, which is a good value for these types of companies that we just talked about. Illustrate characteristics of recurring revenue and healthy margins and growth, and all these things. Don't try to fix what isn't broken. You've bought a business for a good reason at a really good price and there's a reason why you've been attracted to that business at the purchase price that you bought it for. Take a minute, it's so easy for all of us as Booth alumni to wanna get in there and flex our MBA muscles and start to make changes and use all the playbooks and the things that we learned at Booth. But honestly, there's so much value in taking a step back, observing, learning the business, getting super familiar with the cash inflows and outflows in the business, meeting the spending tremendous amount of amounts of time with your team, your frontline people that are out delivering the service or making the product, or, you know, caring for the organization and your customers, right? There's tremendous amounts of learning when you go and have customer concentrations, that sort of thing. So yes, absolutely, you're gonna have a value creation plan and, all the beautiful thing about these businesses is often they are under utilized and can benefit from a really talented, you know, Booth minted, highly trained professional coming in and bringing new ideas and institutionalization and systems and technology and additional talent and all these great things. But let's not try to fix what isn't broken early on. There's a learning period. - Good advice. So zooming out for a second back to sort of putting the fund or the syndicate together, John asks how many initial investors are optimum? And do you find it, is there a sort of a frequent minimum that people are interested in, in this type of model? - Yeah, yeah. So John, good question. It's path dependent, right? So search fund, you know, typically for your search capital, the initial tranche capital that you raised, you might raise that from, you know, 10 or 15 investors that take a ratable share of your search capital that you're raising and then have the pro-rata right to participate in the equity associated with the ultimate acquisition that you find. In a self-funded model, you don't raise any outside capital in the beginning, and then when you ultimately find the acquisition that requires five, $10 million in equity to get the deal done, you've hopefully develop the relationships that you go to a stable of investors that have expressed interest in wanting to know about the deals that you unearth and ultimately participating when you find them. And so there's no right answer there. I mean, if you were to, you know, require a $10 million equity check to get the deal done, and that came from, you know, 10 people and there's an institution in there, there's a family office in there, there's a few advisors that are high net worth or ultra high net worth that may form your board of directors, post ex you know, that feels kind of about right. Or, you know, you go down the sponsored search model and you have a smaller concentrated group of investors in a private equity fund and maybe some co-investors and some advisors that participate alongside it. So there's no right answer there, but hopefully that gives you a little bit of a sense for how it typically works. - Yeah, thank you. Interesting question from Chast. What if you already have a target in mind? So let's say you've got a business that you wanna buy. Do you think it's then worthwhile to go back and do the whole industry thesis work and sort of re underwrite your interest in this business or kind of, how would you think about that? - Yeah, no, I think it's a good idea to, I'll give you my phone number and you can give me a call. (laughs) Good businesses are hard to find, right? No, I think, listen, if you've got a target, you're gonna wanna tell the story about that target to whomever you're gonna bring into your opportunity and ultimately partner with, to the equity requirements. And part of that story is like the thesis, right? Why do we wanna buy this business in this particular industry with this growth rate at this price and this structure and this amount of equity and this amount of debt. And so it's all part of a package that is gonna help you as the entrepreneur, understand what getting yourself into and your investors that are probably gonna have a lot of questions around industry and specific to the company and, you know, what's the, you know, to the earlier question, like, what's the growth plan? How are we structuring this thing? What's the valuation? All these sorts of things form your investment package. And sometimes that's invade you an investor group in a, you know, an offering memorandum or whatever. But yeah, it's all, I would say important when evaluating the attractiveness or not of a deal that you might have in hand. - Yep, got it. So we've got just about five minutes left here. I thought maybe the last couple of minutes, if you wouldn't mind take us through a recent search that you've heard about or seen or something in your firm and kind of talk about maybe like, what was the industry, what made it attractive and is it, an acquisition? You know, that'd be great too, if you could talk about sort of a live example that you've seen recently. - Yeah, yeah, sure. Let's see. So I'll give you one that's near and dear to me, it's one that we did at our firm at NextGen Growth Partners. It started with an entrepreneur in residence that happened to be a Booth grad. He had a particularly interesting thesis that was related to his background. So he got some formal training as a consultant and had some really good early career experience and then got some industry operating experience in the beverage alcohol space. So he ran operations for a wine distribution and retailing outfit. And in his free time, he also happened to be a (indistinct), which was this sort of serious personally interested in this industry as well. He came to me and to our firm with the thought of putting together a thesis where by, we would target mission critical compliance regulatory and importation services on behalf of beverage alcohol producers. So as we all know, there's this age old sense of prohibition, highly complicated, highly bureaucratic three tiered alcohol distribution system here in the US, God bless it because it's creating the need for service providers that help producers globally navigate require those producers to have a partner that helps them navigate the complexities associated with getting your products across borders out on the shelves and into consumer's hands, right? So there's this whole complex system, right? And then there's an industry that serves the producers of every Jackal. So we developed a thesis and it's very specific and refined thesis. He leveraged some of his network connections did a lot of primary research, did a lot of the scrappy things we talked about a lot of the web searching, a lot of the attending a trade shows and just meeting a lot of people and ultimately found a really great business that in the mid nineties was born out of PepsiCo. Pepsi, in the mid nineties, was divesting non-core, non soft drink related assets. And the gentlemen who headed up that division led a small kind of carve out, a small MBO of that division of Pepsi that handled clients and regulatory and importation services for producers of beer, wine and spirits. And so effectively, that was the owner, the entrepreneur that we developed a relationship with. And frankly, this entrepreneur that we partnered with him and still partner in running the business is positioned himself as like the long lost partner for this business owner. That would be the next chapter and the succession plan, ultimately for the principal shareholder, as he died, you know, a little bit later in his career, it might be contemplating, you know, retirement, or frankly was just drawn to the notion that a relatively early career, super hungry hustler could come in and create all these, you know, exciting opportunities for the business then, you know, the seller was the first to admit like, hey, listen, I neglected some of these things and so to have some fresh energy and some fresh blood into the organization to focus on these things would be tremendous. So not in all cases, but in this case, it made sense for the selling shareholder to remain involved both economically and operationally. So they rolled some equity, they have a minority stake in the go forward business. And so there's nice alignment in the capital structure with this person. And they've got a really cool opportunity to take a second bite at the Apple. And the reason that we ultimately turned this individual into a seller, they weren't inclined to sell until we got them compelled about the entrepreneur that was gonna be joining the organization and that they could roll a portion of equity that would ultimately based on our plan, turned into more economic value for them than the, you know, sale price that we were buying the business for at time of acquisition. So really cool kind of marriage between, you know, this industry focus whereby it's, you know, growing mission critical large enough TAM, the business had a lot of the characteristics that we talked about, recurring revenue, super high margin, history of profitability and growth mission critical. And you had this really cool angle whereby the entrepreneur leveraged their strengths and some of their early career operating experience to create a compelling story that was very attractive to a business owner and ultimately it led to the transaction that was consummated. - That's fantastic. Well, it's just about seven o'clock on the dot, so a great job on getting us right to the top of the hour there. Once again, that hour went by very, very quickly. We got a few questions that we didn't get to, sorry, that we weren't able to get to all of them. But for those of you who had questions that we weren't able to answer, I would encourage you to reach out, reach out and you can connect with me on LinkedIn, connect with Brian on LinkedIn I think our contact information is available as well. So certainly be happy to make sure you get to Brian and his firm to get any additional questions answered that you might have. - So real quick, Joe. Yeah, just to verify that that is true. Yes, please reach out anytime I'd love to hear from folks that are interested or didn't get a question answered or might be compelled to pursue this path. I'd love to hear from you, happy to be a resource. My contact information is available on the Booth faculty portal and on our firm's website, nextgengp.com. So reach out, I'm happy to be a resource, and you've got a lot of resources available to you as Booth alumni, as you think about potentially pursuing the ETA path. So yeah, we'd love to hear from any and all. - That's fantastic. All right, thank you again so much, really appreciate you taking some time. For everybody that's on the call, remember we will be doing a couple more of these. So look for information on ETA 301, where we'll dive deeper into maybe some valuation metrics and actual transacting and some of the nitty gritty, which I know all Booth alumni will really love. So again, Brian, thank you so much. Great to see you again, really appreciate everyone that joined the meeting tonight, and we'll look forward to the next one here in about a month or so.

metadata.title: BIG Update: Seller Note Standby Rules When Buying a Business
metadata.author: Owner Actions | Buy a Business with Us
metadata.shortDescription:
The new SBA guidelines taking effect June 1, 2025, will impact how seller notes (seller financing) factor into your down payment when using an SBA 7(a) loan.

That means the 2.5% down payment is about to become a relic of the past. You'll need to have at least 5% ready to put down to buy a business through this loan program.

Hi, I’m Mark from Owner Actions. I team up with people throughout the US to buy established, successful businesses. If you’d like to partner and buy a business together, learn more at my website: www.owneractions.com

#buyabusiness #sbaloan #sba7a #howtobuyabusiness #sellerfinancing #sellernote
keywords: sba 7a loan to buy a business

metadata.title: How to Buy a Business Using an SBA Loan | SBDC Workshop
metadata.author: Lower Hudson Small Business Development Center
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about buying a business instead of starting one from scratch?

This workshop from the Lower Hudson Valley Small Business Development Center walks you through the full process of acquiring an existing business with SBA financing, from deciding what to buy to your first 100 days as the new owner.

Millions of business owners are approaching retirement, and most have no successor lined up. That creates a real opportunity for prepared buyers. Learn how to find the right business, figure out what it’s worth, verify the numbers, and use an SBA 7(a) loan to buy it with as little as 10% down.

In this video:

- Why buying beats building, and how to know if ownership is right for you
- Six ways to acquire a business, with real-number examples
- Where to find businesses for sale, including off-market deals
- How to value a small business using SDE and earnings multiples
- Due diligence checklists and red flags to watch for
- How SBA 7(a) loans work: eligibility, down payment, seller financing, and DSCR
- Legal considerations with guest speaker Jonathan Brown, Director of the Food and Farm Business Law Clinic at Pace University’s Elisabeth Haub School of Law
- Asset purchase vs. stock purchase, including New York specifics
- A full case study: funding and cash-flowing a $900,000 acquisition
- Common first-time buyer mistakes and how to avoid them
- A typical timeline from search to closing

Ideal for aspiring entrepreneurs, first-time buyers, veterans, and corporate professionals ready to own a business.

Get free, confidential business advising from the Lower Hudson Valley SBDC, serving Rockland, Westchester, and Putnam Counties.
Email: SBDC@stac.edu
Phone: (845) 356-6065
Web: www.lowerhvsbdc.org

This workshop is made possible by a portability grant from the U.S. Small Business Administration. Funded in part through a Cooperative Agreement with the SBA. Full funding disclosures at nysbdc.org/funding-disclosures/

Educational content only. SBA and lender requirements vary and change; nothing in this video guarantees loan approval.

#SBALoan #BuyABusiness #SmallBusiness #Entrepreneurship #BusinessAcquisition #SBDC

What is seller financing?

metadata.title: Corporate Finance Explained | Financial Due Diligence
metadata.author: Corporate Finance Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
🔷 In corporate development and finance, the excitement of an acquisition often masks the underlying risks. Financial Due Diligence (FDD) is the structured investigation into a company’s total financial health. It is the crucial "forensic" step that moves a deal from celebration to investigation, determining whether a transaction is a winning strategy or a multi-billion dollar mistake.

The 5 Pillars of Financial Due Diligence

To assess risk and validate value, finance teams focus on five critical areas in the financial data room:

1. Quality of Earnings (QoE)

This is the bedrock of FDD. It separates "accounting profits" from repeatable, sustainable core performance. Teams look for Normalization Adjustments, stripping away one-time legal settlements or non-market salaries to find the true Adjusted EBITDA.

2. Revenue and Customer Analysis

High revenue numbers can be deceiving. Analysts dig into:

🔷 Customer Concentration Risk: If one customer accounts for 40% of revenue, the valuation must be discounted due to instability.

🔷 Churn Rates: Understanding why customers leave and how long they stay.

🔷 Revenue Quality: Differentiating between recurring contracts and one-time projects.

3. Working Capital and Cash Flow Health

This pillar determines if paper profits convert to usable cash. Red flags include:

🔷 Accounts Receivable Aging: Customers paying slower and slower, masking potential bad debt.

🔷 Inventory Turnover: Massive buildups that suck cash out of the business without guaranteed future sales.

4. Debt and Off-Balance Sheet Items

Lurking "landmines" can blow up deal economics. Analysts search for:

🔷 Pending litigation or unknown tax exposures.

🔷 Underfunded pension liabilities.

🔷 Environmental cleanup costs.

5. Forecast Assessment

Every target company presents a "conservative" growth story. FDD stress-tests these assumptions by modeling the unit economics (e.g., Customer Acquisition Cost vs. Lifetime Value) and building conservative "downside" scenarios.

The Role of FP&A: The Bridge to Integration

If you are in FP&A, your role is pivotal. You are the bridge between historical numbers and the forward-looking plan. Your team must:

🔷 Tear apart growth claims: If a company claims 20% growth, what is the required hiring plan and CapEx?

🔷 Scrutinize Synergies: Cost synergies (office closures) are reliable; revenue synergies (cross-selling) are highly speculative and should be heavily discounted in models.

Final Strategic Thought

FDD is not a box-checking exercise; it is the firewall that protects shareholder value. Master it by prioritizing the Quality of Earnings and never letting deal enthusiasm override forensic investigation.

metadata.title: Part 1 of Acquiring a Business (Asset purchase vs Stock purchase)
metadata.author: Paper Rich
metadata.shortDescription:
Asset purchase vs stock purchase: how you buy a company decides whether its old debts become yours.

Example: your startup buys a competitor for $5,000,000. It owes $400,000 in old supplier bills.

1. Buy the shares, and you own the company itself. Its old debts and lawsuits are still its own, and it is now yours.
2. Buy the assets, and the general rule in most states is that the old debts stay behind with the seller.
3. Courts make exceptions: if you agreed to take the debts on, if the deal is really a merger, if your company is just the old one carrying on, or if the sale was a way to dodge the debts.
4. Some taxes can follow anyway. In New York, for example, the buyer must notify the tax department at least 10 days before paying, or can be held liable for the seller's unpaid sales tax.

Sources: Illinois, Missouri and New York court opinions; New York State Department of Taxation and Finance; IRS Form 8594 instructions.

Example numbers, not a real company. Education, not legal or financial advice: ask a business lawyer about a real deal.

Education, not financial advice.

metadata.title: What Exactly Are You Buying in an M&A Deal? Share Purchase vs Asset Purchase #mergersandacquisitions
metadata.author: Acquireman M&A
metadata.shortDescription:
When you buy a company, what exactly are you acquiring?

Are you buying its shares, or are you purchasing selected business assets?

In this combined lesson of Acquireman M&A Academy, we explain:

- What a buyer actually acquires in an M&A transaction.
- The difference between share purchases and asset purchases.
- What happens to existing debts, contracts, intellectual property, and employees.
- Why due diligence and transaction structure matter.
- How buyers and sellers evaluate different acquisition structures.

Understanding this distinction is fundamental to evaluating M&A opportunities and negotiating acquisition agreements.

Explore Acquireman: https://www.acquireman.com

Educational content only. Transaction outcomes and legal consequences depend on the applicable jurisdiction and deal terms.

#Acquireman #MAAcademy #SharePurchase #AssetPurchase #MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessAcquisition #DueDiligence #CorporateLaw #BusinessValuation #InvestmentBanking

If you’re looking for tutorials for other IRS Forms that you can file directly through the IRS website, check out our free fillable forms page:  https://www.teachmepersonalfinance.com/free-fillable-tax-forms/

Both the seller and purchaser of a group of assets that makes up a trade or business must use Form 8594 to report such a sale if goodwill or going concern value attaches, or could attach, to such assets and if the purchaser's basis in the assets is determined only by the amount paid for the assets.

Form 8594 must also be filed if the purchaser or seller is amending an original or a previously filed supplemental Form 8594 because of an increase or decrease in the purchaser's cost of the assets or the amount realized by the seller.

Who Must File
Generally, both the purchaser and seller must file Form 8594 and attach it to their income tax returns (Forms 1040, 1041, 1065, 1120, 1120-S, etc.) when there is a transfer of a group of assets that makes up a trade or business (defined below) and the purchaser's basis in such assets is determined wholly by the amount paid for the assets. This applies whether the group of assets constitutes a trade or business in the hands of the seller, the purchaser, or both.

If the purchaser or seller is a controlled foreign corporation (CFC), each U.S. shareholder should attach Form 8594 to its Form 5471.

Exceptions. You are not required to file Form 8594 if any of the following apply.
A group of assets that makes up a trade or business is exchanged for like-kind property in a transaction to which section 1031 applies. If section 1031 does not apply to all the assets transferred, however, Form 8594 is required for the part of the group of assets to which section 1031 does not apply. For information about such a transaction, see Regulations sections 1.1031(j)-1(b) and 1.1060-1(b)(8).
A partnership interest is transferred. See Regulations section 1.755-1(d) for special reporting requirements. However, the purchase of a partnership interest that is treated for federal income tax purposes as a purchase of partnership assets, which constitute a trade or business, is subject to section 1060. In this case, the purchaser must file Form 8594. See Rev. Rul. 99-6, 1999-6 I.R.B. 6, available at IRS.gov/pub/irs-irbs/irb99-06.pdf.

metadata.title: Asset Sale Allocation: What Can't a Seller Note Spread? (2026)
metadata.author: Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning
metadata.shortDescription:
Hypothetical case study.
Rules: https://bigsaletax.com/tools/purchase-price-allocation/

Free 2026 tax sheets: https://bigsaletax.com/

This hypothetical walks through the asset allocation classes under Treasury Regulation 1.338-6 and how they interact with Section 453 to permit or deny installment deferral, then applies them to a worked example. The takeaway is that a seller note only spreads the goodwill, so the purchase price allocation and the down payment have to be negotiated together.

Chapters:
0:00 The short answer
3:02 The numbers, year by year
3:15 Hans's takeaway
3:25 Free 2026 tax sheets

Reg. 1.338-6, asset classes (Cornell LII); About Form 8594 (IRS); Instructions for Form 8594 (IRS); IRC 197 (Cornell LII); IRC 453, including 453(i) (Cornell LII)

Education only. Not tax, legal or financial advice. Tax law changes; every rate and limit in this video is dated and sourced on screen and on the linked page, which is the current source. Narration is an AI audio overview (NotebookLM) generated from the page; every sentence was checked against the page and anything that did not match was cut.

In this video, we explore financial due diligence through a practical case study focusing on working capital analysis. You'll learn how hidden working capital issues can impact business transactions, what buyers need to know, and the critical factors for successful financial evaluation.
0:00 – A profitable company can still destroy a deal with one hidden working capital problem. Miss it, and

0:34 – The Working Capital Workflow
0:48 – What Buyers Need To Know
1:00 – Quality Of Earnings Versus Working Capital
1:13 – Working Capital Fundamentals
1:26 – Net Working Capital
1:38 – Operating Working Capital
1:51 – Balance Sheet Versus Deal Working Capital
2:03 – Build The Historical View
2:15 – Core Working Capital Accounts
2:29 – The Three-Lens Review
2:41 – A Day In The Analysis
2:54 – The Practical Case Study

4:03 – Calculate The Case

This video highlights the importance of understanding working capital in financial due diligence and how it can affect business transactions. segments.text: A profitable company can still destroy a
deal with one hidden working capital
problem.
Miss it and the buyer may pay millions
for cash that never arrives. Working
capital analysis is not just an
accounting exercise. The real question
is whether the business generates the
cash profile that a buyer is actually
paying for.
Financial due diligence tests whether
reported results reflect sustainable
economic performance. It looks beyond
the income statement to uncover unusual
trends, risks, and cash requirements.
The work starts by defining exactly
which accounts belong in working
capital.
From there, the team builds a monthly
history, identifies unusual movements,
establishes a normalized target, and
calculates the deal impact. A buyer
wants to know how much cash the business
normally needs to operate after closing.
That means separating ordinary funding
requirements from seasonal swings and
one-off balance movements.
Quality of earnings asks whether
reported profit is sustainable.
Working capital asks whether the
business is delivered with enough
operating assets and liabilities to
function normally on day one.
Before touching a case study, we need a
clean definition of working capital.
The most important distinction is
between broad accounting working capital
and operating working capital used in a
transaction.
Net working capital measures the
operating resources tied up in the
business.
Receivables and inventory use cash,
while supplier payables and operating
accruals provide funding.
Operating working capital deliberately
excludes items that do not reflect
normal operations, such as cash, debt,
and often tax balances.
The exact scope must be agreed before
analysis begins.
The balance sheet is the starting point,
not the final answer.
Deal working capital is a negotiated
operating definition designed to show
what the buyer should receive at
closing.
Start with the general ledger and map
each account into the agreed categories.
Monthly detail is especially valuable
because a year-end balance can hide the
actual pattern throughout the year.
Receivables and inventory usually
consume cash, while payables and
accruals usually fund the operation.
Deferred revenue can also provide cash
upfront, although its treatment depends
on the business model and transaction
agreement. A strong review uses three
lenses.
Trend shows direction, seasonality shows
timing, and normalization removes
unusual items that should not define the
ongoing requirement. Picture an analyst
moving from a spreadsheet balance to
customer invoices, purchase orders, and
payment records.
The best conclusions come from
connecting the number to the operational
story behind it.
Now, we will apply the framework to a
fictional distributor.
The numbers are simplified, but the
thinking mirrors what you would do in an
interview case or a live transaction.
Our company sells industrial parts and
has generally steady demand. However,
revenue jumps near year-end, which makes
a single December balance potentially
misleading.
Days sales outstanding estimates how
long customers take to pay.
If the metric rises while sales remain
stable, cash may be getting trapped in
slower collections. Days inventory
outstanding converts stock into an
approximate number of holding days.
A rising result can signal over buying,
obsolete products, or weaker demand.
Days payables outstanding shows how long
the company takes to pay suppliers.
A sudden increase may boost cash
temporarily, but it could also indicate
stretched vendors or overdue invoices.
Seasonal working capital can be
perfectly normal if it repeats and
reverses.
Structural movement is more serious
because it changes the underlying
economics or indicates a lasting
operational issue.
For the case, we begin with the reported
accounts and remove anything outside the
agreed scope. Then we use monthly
history, test unusual movements, set a
normalized target, and compare that
target with the closing balance.
The normalized operating balances are 18
million in receivables, 12 million in
inventory, 14 million in payables, and 4
million in accruals.
These figures represent the recurring
operating level after review.
The calculation is straightforward. Add
the operating assets and subtract the
operating liabilities.
In this case, normalized net working
capital equals $12 million.
Suppose the closing working capital
balance is $14.4 million.
Compared with the $12 million target,
the seller is delivering $2.4 million
more than normal, creating a potential
purchase price adjustment in the
seller's favor.
The final step is not simply reporting a
number. You must explain what caused the
difference, whether it is sustainable,
and how the transaction agreement should
treat it. The reported balance tells you
what existed on a specific date.
The normalized balance is the more
useful benchmark because it reflects
what the buyer should reasonably expect
the business to require.
These warning signs deserve follow-up
rather than automatic adjustment. Ask
for aging reports, inventory listings,
vendor statements, and monthly detail to
determine whether the movement is
temporary, structural, or simply a data
issue.
Once the target and closing balance are
known, calculate the difference and
determine who benefits.
The final bridge should clearly show the
amount, the operational reason, and the
treatment required under the purchase
agreement. The working capital peg is
the benchmark written into the deal.
If the seller delivers materially below
it, the buyer may receive a downward
adjustment. If delivery is above it, the
seller may receive credit, depending on
the agreement. In an interview, do not
jump straight into arithmetic. Start by
defining the operating accounts, explain
the historical trend, identify
normalization items, and then connect
the result to the purchase price
mechanism. That four-part structure
works in both interviews and real
assignments. It demonstrates technical
skill, commercial judgment, and the
ability to turn detailed analysis into a
clear transaction conclusion.
Once you can separate normal operating
cash needs from deal adjustments,
working capital analysis becomes one of
the clearest parts of due diligence.
Follow Candy Mentor for more practical
finance lessons that make interviews and
real deals easier.
Thank you for watching. Please like and
subscribe for more content.

The purchase price you agree at signing is almost never the price you pay at closing. The difference is the working capital peg — and getting it wrong hands the seller a seven-figure cheque nobody negotiated.
 
This video shows you exactly how the peg works, the four distortions you must normalise for, and the games sellers play to inflate it. The Summit Industrial Services case study reveals how a proposed peg of nine point two million becomes eight point three when the analysis is done properly — nine hundred thousand dollars of real cash, settled dollar for dollar at closing.

post-closing disputes originate than any
other deal mechanism.

serves a specific purpose. It ensures
the buyer receives a business with
enough operational liquidity to run from
day one. The mechanism works like this.
The parties agree a target level of net
working capital, the peg. At closing,
actual working capital is measured.
If actual exceeds the peg, the buyer

price adjustment.

acquisitions is not the textbook

current operating assets minus current
operating liabilities with specific
exclusions. Cash and cash equivalents
are excluded because they're handled

metadata.title: Working Capital Adjustments in the Indirect Method (Add or Subtract?)
metadata.author: Accounting Rescue with Lisa
metadata.shortDescription:
Why do you subtract an increase in accounts receivable but add an increase in accounts payable when calculating operating cash flows? This indirect-method walkthrough explains the reason behind working capital adjustments, rather than giving you another sign chart to memorize.

Using the Campus Cravings example, we examine changes in accounts receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses, and current operating liabilities. We connect each balance sheet change to the timing of cash receipts or payments, then work toward a complete operating cash flow calculation.

This is especially useful for homework and exams where you're given net income, comparative balance sheets, and additional information and have to decide which changes are added or subtracted.

Introductory U.S. GAAP / Principles of Financial Accounting.

Statement of Cash Flows Visual Companion: https://accountingrescue.thinkific.com/order?ct=b32cc51b-50b4-4b91-9caa-c3c56b5e0dc0

Full Statement of Cash Flows Masterclass: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DFfYB0qpe4U
Next related lesson: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rrhL8_6KbT8

Subscribe for more practical accounting walkthroughs from Lisa, CPA and adjunct accounting professor.

metadata.title: How to Structure a Winning LOI for a Small Business Acquisition
metadata.author: SMB Law Group LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
The LOI is where the deal really takes shape: purchase price, structure, what you're buying, what you're assuming, and the exclusivity that protects you before you spend a dollar on diligence. Every line does work, and the lines buyers gloss over are usually the ones that come back as a re-trade or a dispute down the road.

In this episode of Main Street Deals, Eric Pacifici and Sam Rosati go line by line through their own LOI template, drawing on real deals and common failures to explain the decisions you have to make before signing.

What they cover:
1. Why the LOI exists, and how exclusivity protects buyers before diligence spend
2. Structuring purchase price across cash, SBA debt, and seller notes
3. Why debt-free, cash-free language and buying assets free and clear matters
4. How to model seller notes thoughtfully to protect post-close cash flow
5. Why clarity on structure and assumed liabilities prevents future disputes

Chapters:
00:00 — Intro
04:06 — Why LOIs exist
08:02 — LOI vs. IOI, and what's actually binding
10:26 — How to introduce yourself in the LOI
15:37 — Who signs the LOI: entities, affiliates, and the liability shield
18:26 — Setting the closing date: 60 vs. 90 days
21:35 — Asset purchase language
24:04 — Asset list pitfalls
25:11 — Debt-free, cash-free deals explained
28:09 — Buying assets free and clear: liens, lenders, and immaterial encumbrances
31:32 — Assumed liabilities in asset purchases
33:28 — Purchase price: why deals die after QoE, and how LOIs foreshadow re-trades
36:00 — Sources and uses 101
38:44 — Seller notes deep dive
44:44 — Wrap-up and what's next

__________________________________________________________

SMB Law Group combines decades of experience with a modern approach to help small and medium business buyers, sellers, and searchers reach their legal and deal goals.

Learn more: https://smblaw.group/

Kevin Henderson — https://www.linkedin.com/in/khendersonco/
Sam Rosati — https://www.linkedin.com/in/sam-rosati-68787a8/
Evan Thomson — https://www.linkedin.com/in/evan-thomson-327a78216/

metadata.shortDescription:
In this comprehensive video, we dive deep into the Letter of Intent (LOI) in mergers and acquisitions (M&A). Whether you're a business buyer or a seller, understanding the nuances of an LOI is crucial for a successful transaction.

🔍 What You’ll Learn:

- What is an LOI? Explore its significance in M&A.
- How to Write an Effective LOI: Step-by-step guidance on crafting a compelling offer.
- Common Mistakes to Avoid: Don’t let simple errors derail your deal!
- Ideal Level of Detail: Find out how detailed your LOI should be.
- Best Practices for Success: Ensure your offer is presented correctly and mitigates disputes during the closing process.
- Key Deal Points to Address Upfront: Increase your chances of closing by understanding what to prioritize.

💼 Key Video Sections:

[2:21] LOI Common Mistakes to Avoid – Learn the pitfalls that can jeopardize your offer.
[12:48] LOI Best Practices for M&A Success – Proven strategies for presenting a strong LOI.
[23:48] Overview of Key LOI Sections & Terminology – Understand the essential components of an LOI.
[31:40] Detailed LOI Template Walkthrough – Get a real-life example that showcases the level of detail needed for a high-quality LOI.

Whether you’re new to M&A or looking to refine your skills, this video equips you with the tools you need to navigate the LOI process effectively. Don’t forget to like, subscribe, and hit the notification bell for more valuable insights!

If you are interested in taking a deeper dive into a company you are looking to buy, you can book a 1-hour session with me! On this call, I can provide a more detailed analysis on the target company and provide suggestions on valuation, purchase price structure and how to position your bid in an auction scenario where you are dealing with a sell-side M&A broker. Click the link below to learn more:

https://calendly.com/robert-bezede/60min_consulting_zoom

Interested in selling your Canadian business? Harmony Succession Partners (HSP) is an independent M&A advisory firm focused on selling Ontario-based companies valued between $3MM to $30MM. HSP has one of the largest databases of qualified family offices, private equity, strategic buyers and high net worth investors focused on acquiring lower middle market companies. In the last 5 years, our team has closed over 50 acquisitions totaling $250MM in value with a 95% closing rate. Our mission is to provide the highest client experience to business owners looking to sell their business. Please see our website below:

https://www.harmonysuccession.com/

🔔 Subscribe for more expert insights on mergers and acquisitions! 

#MergersAndAcquisitions #LetterOfIntent #LOI #BusinessStrategy #Finance #M&A #DealMaking #CorporateFinance #Investment

metadata.title: Deal-by-Deal: Ep. 12 - How to Craft an M&A Letter of Intent with Greg Hawver and Jeff Brooker (Pt 1)
metadata.author: McGuireWoods LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
October 4, 2022: When buyers and sellers are unclear on what to include in a Letter of Intent (“LOI”) -- what is binding and what is not, and how to leverage exclusivity -- deals can go sideways. Join hosts Greg Hawver and Jeff Brooker in the first episode of a two-part series as they discuss best practices for M&A deal letters of intent. Gain insight on how to balance desire for exclusivity and what key terms to address to avoid miscommunication.

For more about the series, please visit: https://www.mcguirewoods.com/deal-by-deal

For series playlist, please visit: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIhiURlywxrgIWT4mTKj6sQBu-7749nRx

Videos may include attorney advertising and aren’t legal advice/opinion. Prior successes ≠ future results.

metadata.title: SMB PE Experts: The Essential Guide To The Letter Of Intent ("LOI") in M&A – Advice from a Lawyer
metadata.author: Dennis Unrein / SMB PE LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Summary
In this conversation, Eli Albrecht, a partner at Albrecht Law, discusses the intricacies of M&A transactions, focusing on the importance of the Letter of Intent (LOI) and its role in establishing the foundation for deals. 

He explains the differences between an LOI and an Indication of Interest (IOI), the significance of exclusivity periods, and the key elements that should be included in an LOI. 

Albrecht also shares insights on structuring acquisitions, the importance of working capital, and the role of escrows in M&A transactions. 

In this conversation, Eli Albrecht and Dennis Unrein delve into the intricacies of M&A transactions, focusing on the importance of tax structuring, legal documentation, and the critical nature of non-compete agreements. 

They discuss the necessity of having robust closing conditions, the role of landlords, and the significance of transition services post-closing. 

The conversation emphasizes the need for seller accountability and the strategic use of Letters of Intent (LOIs) to ensure a smooth transaction process.

Takeaways
- Good M&A lawyers are rare and valuable.
- The LOI is crucial for setting deal foundations.
- Exclusivity is key to securing a deal.
- Understanding the difference between LOI and IOI is essential.
- Reputation matters in the M&A community.
- Structuring the deal correctly can save millions.
- Working capital negotiations are critical in M&A.
- Escrows are important for indemnifications and adjustments.
- Personal connections can influence seller decisions.
- A well-crafted LOI can differentiate buyers in competitive markets. 
- Tax - structuring can significantly impact M&A deals.
- Legal documentation must be carefully controlled by the buyer.
- Closing conditions are essential for successful transactions.
- Landlords can have a veto right in M&A deals.
- Non-compete agreements are critical to protect the buyer's interests.
- Sellers often underestimate their importance post-closing.
- Enforcement mechanisms are necessary to hold sellers accountable.
- Transition services are vital for a smooth handover
- The Letter of Intent should create urgency in negotiations
- Dishonest sellers can lead to disastrous outcomes for buyers

Chapters

02:51 Understanding the Letter of Intent (LOI)
05:55 Differences Between LOI and IOI
08:52 Navigating Exclusivity in M&A Transactions
12:01 Positive and Negative Aspects of LOIs
14:59 Key Elements of an LOI Template
18:08 Structuring the Acquisition: Asset vs. Equity
21:10 Working Capital and Escrow Considerations
34:22 Navigating Tax Issues in M&A Transactions
36:09 The Importance of Tax Structuring in Deals
37:30 Understanding Legal Documentation in M&A
39:51 Key Closing Conditions for Successful Transactions
43:48 The Role of Landlords in M&A Transactions
45:21 The Critical Nature of Non-Compete Agreements
50:13 Ensuring Seller Accountability Post-Closing
51:54 Transition Services: A Key Post-Closing Strategy
56:51 Finalizing the Letter of Intent (LOI)

metadata.title: Walker at Codie Sanchez Mastermind Event
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Walker is a guest speaker at the Codie Sanchez Mastermind Event, where he gives a presentation called "Growing Through Acquisition: The Secret Accelerator to Unlocking Growth, Impact, and Value in Your Business." He breaks down everything you need to know about becoming an acquisition entrepreneur through case studies, frameworks, examples, and achievable actions.

If you haven't read Walker's best-selling book Buy, Then Build, you can download a FREE chapter sample here: https://acquisitionlab.com/free-chapter

Interested in buying a business in the next 6 to 24 months? With over 500 members, we've surpassed $200 million in member acquisitions and boast an impressive member-to-acquisition rate.

What sets us apart? We offer world-class education, diamond method coaching, valuable tools, and resources—all designed to support your journey to a successful business acquisition.

Check out acquisitionlab.com and see you on the inside.

Remember to like, subscribe, and click the bell to be updated when we have a new video and learn more about business acquisition with Acquisition Lab. Do you have any questions, tips, or ideas about managing risk in business acquisition? Let us know in the comments section below!

VISIT OUR WEBSITE: http://acquisitionlab.com
DOWNLOAD BUY THEN BUILD SAMPLE CHAPTER DOWNLOAD: https://acquisitionlab.com/free-chapter
FREE 29MIN CRASH COURSE To Acquire 7-Figures In Revenue: https://buythenbuild.com/free-training
LEARN FROM OUR BLOGS: https://acquisitionlab.com/blog/
MORE BLOGS AT BUY THEN BUILD: https://buythenbuild.com/blog/
CLIENTS' TESTIMONIALS: https://acquisitionlab.com/testimonials/
JOIN THE LAB: https://acquisitionlab.com/application/
SUBSCRIBE: youtube.com/buythenbuild 

********

Walker Deibel has practiced acquisition entrepreneurship since 2006, amassing $16.5 million in revenue through acquisitions. He has co-founded three startups, acquired seven companies outright, and has consulted (or participated in) over $200,000,000 in business transactions.

Walker holds an MBA from the Olin School of Business at Washington University in St. Louis, where he was awarded the Declaration of Accomplishment in Entrepreneurship. 

He is a Certified M&A Advisor, Certified M&A Professional, M&A Master Intermediary, Certified Exit Planning Advisor, and former SEC-licensed stockbroker. He was awarded the Platinum Award from M&A Source and Thought Leader of the Year by The Alliance of M&A Advisors and Axial.com. Forbes, Entrepreneur, Fast Company, Inc, and the Harvard Business Review have featured his work.

Find out more about Walker and the Acquisition Lab team here https://acquisitionlab.com/meet-the-team/

metadata.title: Making Billions Buying Businesses: A Masterclass
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
This is the world's best masterclass on M&A. Everyone knows it.

In this episode of Making Billions, Ryan Miller and I go deep — not into what M&A is, but how it actually works when you're in the trenches. This is a masterclass for acquisition entrepreneurs, independent sponsors, and serious operators who want to scale intelligently, avoid common traps, and play the long game in private equity.

Forget the surface-level hype. This is what it really looks like to build wealth through small business acquisitions — from someone who’s done it eight times over, advised on 100+ deals, and trained thousands inside the Acquisition Lab.

We cover:
➡️ Why my holding company almost imploded — and what I’d do differently
➡️ A tactical breakdown of how the best deals get structured today (and why seller financing isn’t always smart)
➡️ How world-class operators think about focus, vertical integration, and building real infrastructure
➡️ What independent sponsors do now that used to be unthinkable without a $500M fund

This isn’t theory. It’s not for tourists. It’s for people who are already in the game — or ready to be.
If you’re serious about private equity at the ground level, this conversation is your cheat code.

*📌 Want to go deeper?*

💼 Learn how to buy a business in 6–12 months at https://bit.ly/3HbfqQf
📩 Get insights like this in your inbox: https://bit.ly/3ZwJDzq
📚 Grab the bestselling book: https://www.amazon.com/Buy-Then-Build-Acquisition-Entrepreneurs/dp/1544501137/
👍 Like this video? Drop a comment below with your biggest takeaway or question!

#BuyThenBuild #AcquisitionEntrepreneurship #SmallBusinessAcquisition #WalkerDeibel #MakingBillions #EntrepreneurshipThroughAcquisition #mergersandacquisitions #privateequity

metadata.title: Search Fund Case Study: 5–10 Qualified Seller Meetings Every Month
metadata.author: Marco Palmero
metadata.shortDescription:
Get Deal Flow: https://ulyssesholding.com/strategy-session

A deal origination case study for CGS Partners, a Chicago-based search fund buying in Illinois and Indiana. A multi-channel campaign across email, LinkedIn and phone went live after a 10-day build-out and delivered 5 to 10 qualified, thesis-matched seller meetings every month for over six months, building a platform and add-on pipeline in HVAC, specialty distribution and industrial services.

0:00 CGS Partners and a two-state market
0:44 The search thesis and target industries
1:24 Targeting, messaging, channels and process
2:47 5–10 seller meetings every month
3:56 Why searchers need an origination system

—

We help capital-backed private equity firms, family offices, independent sponsors, search funds, M&A advisors, and acquisition entrepreneurs build consistent, high-quality deal flow pipelines, so they can stay focused on evaluating and closing opportunities instead of finding them.

Generate consistent off-market acquisition opportunities in 90 days or less.

We specialize in sourcing proprietary M&A deal flow for $1M to $50M acquisitions using targeted origination strategies to bring more qualified deal flow to your door in less time.

Our DealFlow Engine identifies motivated business owners across 40+ industries in the US, UAE, Europe, and Africa who are open to a conversation about selling, before they ever list with a broker.

—

Who we work with: private equity firms, family offices, independent sponsors, search funds, M&A advisory firms, investment banks, strategic acquirers, and business brokers targeting lower middle market acquisitions.

Schedule Strategy Session: https://ulyssesholding.com/strategy-session

metadata.title: Representations and Warranties in Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A)
metadata.author: Brett Cenkus
metadata.shortDescription:
#mergersandacquisitions #corporatelaw #business

Representations and warranties (or reps & warranties) come up often in the world of mergers and acquisitions. Whether you're the seller or the buyer of a business, reps and warranties make up a significant portion of the final purchase agreement. 

"What are representations and warranties? Why are they so important?" you ask. Well, dear viewer, put simply, they are statements about the state of the business that serve as the basis for indemnification and an allocation of risk between the buyer and the seller.

That's the explanation put simply. If you want to know more (and you should), watch the video where Brett makes six main points about the role of representations and warranties from his perspective as a corporate lawyer.

Here's a quick rundown in case you want to jump ahead:
0:51 - Representations and warranties are statements about a business
2:00 - Reps and warranties as basis for indemnification
4:36 - Why reps and warranties are important when buying a business
5:39 - Representations and warranties aren't always facts
6:58 - Reps and warranties as allocations of risk
7:34 - They are almost always joint and several
10:21 - The two main qualifiers: knowledge & materiality

_____________________________________________


Have questions? Book a call, and talk to Brett today: 
https://rebrand.ly/clarity-brettcenkus76

_______________________________________________


You can reach Brett through:
 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/brettcenkus
https://twitter.com/BCenkus
https://cenkuslaw.com
https://braatenwoods.com
https://merger-resources.com


_______________________________________________



Brett A. Cenkus has 20+ years of experience in business law, finance, and entrepreneurship. Through Cenkus Law, PC, he provides advice and services for mergers & acquisitions (M&A), securities offerings, founders’ agreements, and other general business law issues.
 
Through Braaten Woods, LLC, Brett helps business owners in the lower middle market ($2MM - $25MM) position themselves for sale, find buyers, negotiate, and close M&A deals. 

Brett also maintains merger-resources.com, a site packed with free articles, videos, checklists, deal diagrams, template contracts, and other tools to help pass M&A knowledge to others. 

Brett regularly consults with entrepreneurs and invests his own capital as an angel investor. 

From 2010-2013, Brett served as Chief Legal Counsel of a publicly-traded international oilfield services company. From 2001 to 2006, he and a partner founded and built Paragon Residential Mortgage. Bridge Investments acquired Paragon in 2006. 

Brett holds a Juris Doctorate from Harvard Law School and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics from Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania.

Brett lives in Austin with his wife, Cathryn, and two children. He enjoys reading, squash, classic movies, great food and wine, and the New England Patriots.

metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to another episode of Hundred days and beyond with Liam McGreevy, who is a co-founder, director and CEO at Elite growth, holistic herb. Leading into 11 years in the Agritech industry with exceptional knowledge across all areas of the production and distribution, assisting in building global supply chain. He is a progressive business manager and am market developer with 15 years of experience in sales and marketing, technical and compliance manufacturing and distribution operations as well as finance and business development. 

 

Background 

Liam McGreevy started his career as a science graduate working with RMC in an in-house laboratory, testing in the construction sector for 6 years. Then worked as a sales representative for distribution of water cultural equipment. Then moved to another employer who was setting up his business and they grew it rapidly with a lot of learning in that period. After that, he ended up in the medical side with the science background. He has worked with a number of companies across retail medical ingredient development raising money and doing acquisition. 

Agritech – Agriculture Technology 

Liam McGreevy says, it is as broad scope covering cultivation of vegetables into livestock farming on the technological side. He says, people don’t value farmers and do not understand the complexity of the process. Having the elements of risk like climate change, pollution, and waste materials, we need to balance things with right measurements and think reasonably for long-term sustainability.  

Marketing strategy 

Been working as a distributor for many years, Liam McGreevy thinks that to market a brand/product, it has to be able to deliver the right message with right price and right margin structure and right relationship with the supplier. Understanding the product is key as well.



M & A Integration 

Liam thinks that whether you are on the Merger side or on the Acquisition side, there are two things. 

1.      You will look at the people and business teams, if they have similar end goals and right funding structure as you have. 

2.      And secondly, if the merged or acquired business has the ability to capture the growth. So he think on both sides, there has to be alignment of  goals of mind-set and ability to work together. Liam has always been a hard worker and competitive person, played a lot of sports growing up. He has got the competitive streak at him and has the hard work ethics. His approach is to try and be really productive and stay fit and healthy within a certain time frame. He thinks that success comes from repeated positive habits and building them in life. These were few summarised points discussed in the episode with Liam Mcgreevy. To know more, tune into the podcast.



Connect with Liam Mcgreevy 



LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/liam-mcgreevy-5a808724

Links: http://mergerintegration.co.uk

http://www.100daysandbeyond.com

http://www.skilfulpursuit.com

metadata.author: Strategy Leaders Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
Just closed an acquisition? The paperwork is done, but now the real work begins. In this workshop, Robyn Goldenberg — Fractional CMO, VP at Strategy Leaders, and founder of Bad B Marketing — breaks down exactly how to lead marketing after an acquisition, even if you’ve inherited a mess.

💥 Learn how to:
Audit the acquired business’s marketing
Decide whether to merge, rebrand, or separate
Communicate clearly with your team, customers, and vendors
Avoid the “post-acquisition blackout” that kills trust and leads
Build a high-impact 90-day marketing plan that works

This is built for serious operators — $2M to $15M businesses navigating growth moments, integrations, or prep for scale.

🔗 Need help leading your next 90 days? Book a call: https://bit.ly/BookwithRobyn

metadata.title: How A $3B Multinational Company Integrated 40+ Mergers and Acquisitions [M&A Integration Case Study]
metadata.author: Digital Transformation with Eric Kimberling
metadata.shortDescription:
Experts estimate that a majority of merger and acquisitions fail. M&A integration is one of the most common and most misunderstood challenges for high-growth companies.

This video provides a case study of a successful merger and acquisition integration - a $3B global manufacturing and distribution company that had grown through a number of large acquisitions over the years.  The company had disparate systems and business processes, so our team helped define a digital transformation strategy to help ingrate the various companies' people, processes, and technologies.

client we found that the company was operating essentially as six different regions even though they had 40 different locations there was some regionalization and some commonalities that we could distill down to six different models six different ways of operating so one of the first things we did is we went in to analyze the business processes at each of the six regions and the purpose of that activity was to identify where the commonalities were because not everything was broken there were things they were doing well and they were doing consistently across the organization and then we identified the gaps the things that were differences or variations in the way they were operating and ultimately what we wanted to help them do was define how that future state operating model would need to look to support their goals and objectives longer term so defining those high-level business processes analyzing the processes introducing best practices to the equation and ultimately identifying how technology could enable some of those process improvements or some of the things that we help them do during this business process exercise so during our work and during our analysis as i mentioned before we found that the client was using four different erp systems throughout the world they were using two tier one systems one of the bigger erp names that you've heard of and they're also using two different niche or industry focused solutions and they all served a purpose they were all working okay for each of the different parts of the businesses that were using it but they were highly inefficient in the way they use technology the technology did not integrate with one another data wasn't flowing they didn't have a common view of the customer so if a customer was multinational and was buying from this particular company in multiple parts of the world they didn't have that visibility to see what was happening across the entire enterprise so part of our analysis was looking at the systems they had understanding where the systems were strong where they were weak where there were commonalities and where there was opportunity to tie together more technology and what was interesting about this project and this client is they led with technology they at first wanted us to focus on identifying ways that they could leverage technology and create a standard platform but as we quickly found the business operations and the organizational structure were bigger problems that need to be addressed first but regardless we still went in we analyzed the systems and we wanted to define a plan for how they could leverage technology to enable some of these bigger picture goals that they've identified in addition to looking at business processes and technologies in the overall strategy we also went in to identify and analyze the organizational structure the organization in general we looked at things like the organizational design what were the roles and responsibilities happening within this organization where were the commonalities in the synergies and where were the broken siloed parts of the organization we also looked at the skill sets that they had in house versus the skill sets they knew they would need to compete in the future especially with new technologies and new business processes we looked largely at the culture in really understanding the culture of the different parts of the organization so that we could create a cultural transformation plan that allowed them to create more of an aligned culture and where appropriate than the cultures of some of the different parts of the organization so they were operating as one more cohesive culture we also looked at change impacts so as we had analyzed the business processes and identified business process improvements or potential process improvements we also looked at what the impact to the organization would be if they actually executed on those improvements so that change impact assessment was meant to be a key input into the overall organizational change strategy and plan and then finally we assessed the potential resistance to change every organization we work with including this one has some degree of resistance the question isn't if there's going to be resistance but where is the resistance going to come from how severe is that resistance and what are the root causes of the resistance so part of the organizational assessment was meant to dig underneath the covers and dive into the organization and the culture to understand what the likely causes of resistance would be so that we could create a change strategy that would enable the ultimate integration between the different acquisitions they had made over the years [Music] so once we had completed this analysis from the people the process the technology and the strategy sides of things we then defined what the overall integration strategy was going to be and ultimately and to summarize we came up with a three-year transformation strategy that aligned and focused on how the organization was going to drive some of these process changes how it was going to drive the new organizational structure in the future the new operating model the new systems and basically everything that needed to happen to be able to support the integration of all the acquisitions to be able to ultimately support the overall strategy of the organization one example of a recommendation and a key part of the roadmap was defining how they were going to move to the shared services strategy so i talked about earlier about how hr finance and i.t were all examples of areas that they wanted to consolidate so they didn't have multiple redundancies throughout the organization but instead would have more of a centralized common operating model and a common organization to support the entire organization we also identified a whole host of business process improvements there were a ton of business process improvements that some cases were dependent on new technologies but in some cases were dependent on just rolling out new standard operating procedures so while this client thought that technology was going to drive most of the change it turned out there's a lot of change on the process and people side of things that were enabled without technology so the roadmap accounted for
