metadata.author: Brett Cenkus
metadata.shortDescription:
So, what M&A deal structure is best for you? Great question! You'll find out more about the pros and cons of each structure in this video.

There are a lot of aspects to consider when buying or selling your business. Today we will talk about considerations for the 2 M&A primary structures you'll see in low to middle market deals - sale of stock and sale of assets.

Check out Brett's article:
https://www.businessattorneyinaustin.com/ways-structure-company-sales-purchases-ma-deal-structures/

_____________________________________________


Have questions? Book a call, and talk to Brett today: 
https://rebrand.ly/clarity-brettcenkus35

_______________________________________________


You can reach Brett through:
 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/brettcenkus
https://twitter.com/BCenkus
https://cenkuslaw.com
https://braatenwoods.com
https://merger-resources.com


_______________________________________________



Brett A. Cenkus has 20+ years of experience in business law, finance, and entrepreneurship. Through Cenkus Law, PC, he provides advice and services for mergers & acquisitions (M&A), securities offerings, founders’ agreements, and other general business law issues.
 
Through Braaten Woods, LLC, Brett helps business owners in the lower middle market ($2MM - $25MM) position themselves for sale, find buyers, negotiate, and close M&A deals. 

Brett also maintains merger-resources.com, a site packed with free articles, videos, checklists, deal diagrams, template contracts, and other tools to help pass M&A knowledge to others. 

Brett regularly consults with entrepreneurs and invests his own capital as an angel investor. 

From 2010-2013, Brett served as Chief Legal Counsel of a publicly-traded international oilfield services company. From 2001 to 2006, he and a partner founded and built Paragon Residential Mortgage. Bridge Investments acquired Paragon in 2006. 

Brett holds a Juris Doctorate from Harvard Law School and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics from Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania.

Brett lives in Austin with his wife, Cathryn, and two children. He enjoys reading, squash, classic movies, great food and wine, and the New England Patriots.

segments.text: Hi everyone, hope you're having a great week.
Today we're gonna talk about structuring M&A deals.
How to structure the sale of your business or the purchase of a business.
There are 3 primary ways to do it - we'll get into that in a second.
In my experience, it's something that is not covered or addressed well enough up front.
By the time I get involved, and we're putting together the documents, the structure's already
been put together without a whole lot of thought about the consequences.
Not always, but often.
So, you need to know all about it up front - we'll get into that.
First, a little bit about me.
I'm Brett Cenkus, I'm a business attorney.
I do that from my law firm, Cenkus Law, based in Austin.
I have an office based in Houston, and I have clients all over.
I'm also a startup consultant and business consultant.
I do that out of my brand, The Startup Shepherd.
The links to the websites are in the descriptions.
I've done M&A at a very high level - billion dollar deals.
In this life I do half a million to about 20 million dollar deals.
That's kind of the size of the market in which I play.
And, that's considered the main street part of the market, the lower-middle market.
Those are kind of terms of art, but just so you understand what's going on, these are
smaller deals and this content is aimed at someone buying or selling in that space.
So, deal structures - there's 3 primary ways to structure the sale of a business.
One is to sell the stock or equity interests.
Two is to sell the assets.
Third is a merger.
We're not gonna spend a whole lot of time on mergers even though that's half of the
term M&A or mergers and acquisitions.
Not a lot of the deals at this part of the market are done as mergers.
Mergers are driven by kinda high level tax issues often, and that kind of deal just doesn't
show up down here.
So, stock sales and asset sales are primarily what I see.
So, a stock sale, the seller actually takes their equity interest and sells it to the
buyer.
They don't touch the company.
Kinda like if you have a share of Microsoft, you could sell it to me, we didn't touch Microsoft.
Now someone else, I, own that tiny little piece of the company that you used to own.
An asset sale, you actually itemize all the assets of the business and you transfer those
to the buyer.
So those are two main ways deals get done in this part of the market.
Generally speaking, sellers want to sell stock, and buyers want to buy assets.
Two main reasons.
One is tax, one is liability.
On the tax side, sellers want to sell stock or equity interest because they can get favorable
capital gains treatment.
Sometimes they can get capital gains treatment depending on the assets, but stock is clearly
gonna be a capital gains item.
And, if they held the stock for longer than a year, they get long-term capital gains treatment.
And, if it's qualified small business stock, a special type of corporate stock, they potentially
can have no tax.
So, there's usually a reason sellers want to be selling stock.
Buyers, on the other hand, want to purchase assets, they want to buy the individual assets.
The main reason is because, if they buy the stock and step into the seller's shoes they
take over the assets at the book value that are on the books of the company at the time
of the sale.
Now, if the assets have been held for a long time and have been heavily depreciated, there
may not be a whole lot of depreciation left.
Depreciation is write-offs against income.
So, you want as much depreciation as you can get.
A buyer who purchases assets gets to mark the value of those assets up to their fair
market value and depreciate the assets again.
So, generally interests are not totally aligned.
Sellers want to sell stock, and buyers want to buy assets.
That's tax - the other reason is liability.
So, when the seller sells the stock, the whole company - all of it - goes over to the buyer,
including the liabilities.
There are ways to carve out certain liabilities or the seller could indemnify the buyer for
things that are particularly sensitive items, but, generally speaking, the buyer is taking
the whole thing - the good and the bad.
If the buyer purchases assets, they could cherry pick the assets and leave behind the
liabilities.
There are exceptions, like there always are in law.
It's called successor liability and sometimes buyers can be responsible for liabilities
even though they didn't want them.
But, generally speaking, if you're concerned about liabilities, purchasing assets is a
safer play.
So, couple other things to think about.
That's generally, if you're selling that's what you want, if you're buying that's what
you want.
In my experience, a lot of the business brokers market assets.
It's kind of an easier thing to market.
Some of them are concerned about licensing issues because they are not investment bankers,
they don't have broker dealer licenses to market securities.
They're more comfortable just marketing the sale of a business as the sale of assets.
So, sometimes that doesn't get covered over up front too much because brokers are used
to just kind of doing things a certain way.
Another thing to consider on both sides - interests are aligned, here - is that getting a deal
done as a stock sale is a little easier.
Assets, when you start looking at the individual assets, every contract - is it assignable,
can we transfer that to the buyer?
If the buyer steps into the shoes of the seller and just takes over the stock or equity interest,
nothing changed at the company level.
We didn't transfer a contract.
We just transferred the owner of the business.
And, so there's anti-assignment clauses is what they're called in a lot of commercial
contracts that say you can't assign this contract without the counterparty's consent, without
their approval.
And an asset sale is an assignment or transfer that would trigger that.
So, sometimes there's concerns around being able to tranfer individual assets that make
it more compelling to structure deals as stock sales.
Those are the main things to consider.
There's always a lot of other nuances and reasons and thoughts, but that hopefully gives
you something to go on.
So, buying a company or selling your company, spend time up front.
Figure out what are the consequences.
As a seller, get with your CPA early on.
Does it matter if I sell stock or I sell assets?
As a buyer, you won't really know much until you start to see the books of the seller,
but you know enough now to at least ask the question, and tackle the issue before the
documents come out and the deal's already put together.
So, hope you enjoyed that.
If you want to dive a little bit deeper I've got an article on my website that goes into
more detail about it.
If you want to talk about this or have any other questions about M&A or business generally,
visit me at cenkuslaw.com.
Hope you enjoyed that.
If you have a question, leave it in the comments.
If you're involved in M&A and agree with me or disagree with me, if you see a lot of mergers
at this part of the market, I would love to hear about your experience.
Different things happen differently in different parts of the country, so drop a comment in.
Hope you enjoyed the content.
Have a great week.

It's called successor liability and sometimes buyers can be responsible for liabilities even though they didn't want them. But, generally speaking, if you're concerned about liabilities, purchasing assets is a safer play. So, couple other things to think about. That's generally, if you're selling that's what you want, if you're buying that's what you want. In my experience, a lot of the business brokers market assets. It's kind of an easier thing to market. Some of them are concerned about licensing issues because they are not investment bankers, they don't have broker dealer licenses to market securities. They're more comfortable just marketing the sale of a business as the sale of assets. So, sometimes that doesn't get covered over up front too much because brokers are used to just kind of doing things a certain way. Another thing to consider on both sides - interests are aligned, here - is that getting a deal done as a stock sale is a little easier. Assets, when you start looking at the individual assets, every contract - is it assignable, can we transfer that to the buyer? If the buyer steps into the shoes of the seller and just takes over the stock or equity interest, nothing changed at the company level. We didn't transfer a contract. We just transferred the owner of the business. And, so there's anti-assignment clauses is what they're called in a lot of commercial contracts that say you can't assign this contract without the counterparty's consent, without their approval. And an asset sale is an assignment or transfer that would trigger that. So, sometimes there's concerns around being able to tranfer individual assets that make it more compelling to structure deals as stock sales. Those are the main things to consider. There's always a lot of other nuances and reasons and thoughts, but that hopefully gives you something to go on. So, buying a company or selling your company, spend time up front. Figure out what are the consequences. As a seller, get with your CPA early on. Does it matter if I sell stock or I sell assets? As a buyer, you won't really know much until you start to see the books of the seller, but you know enough now to at least ask the question, and tackle the issue before the documents come out and the deal's already put together. So, hope you enjoyed that. If you want to dive a little bit deeper I've got an article on my website that goes into more detail about it. If you want to talk about this or have any other questions about M&A or business generally, visit me at cenkuslaw.com. Hope you enjoyed that. If you have a question, leave it in the comments. If you're involved in M&A and agree with me or disagree with me, if you see a lot of mergers at this part of the market, I would love to hear about your experience. Different things happen differently in different parts of the country, so drop a comment in. Hope you enjoyed the content. Have a great week.

metadata.title: How I Study Closed Deals Before Calling Brokers | Commercial Real Estate Case Study Review
metadata.author: The Acquisition Manager
metadata.shortDescription:
Preparation is one of the biggest advantages you can have in commercial real estate.

In this video, I review several recently closed case studies from my acquisitions community and explain how I use them to prepare before speaking with brokers and listing agents. Studying real transactions helps me sharpen my market knowledge, understand what buyers are looking for, and communicate with more confidence during acquisition calls.

I also discuss why preparation matters, how brokers naturally qualify potential buyers, and why understanding recent deals can help you have more productive conversations. The goal isn't to impress people with jargon—it's to understand the market well enough to ask better questions and recognize opportunities.

In this video you'll learn:

Why reviewing closed deals improves your acquisition skills
How case studies prepare you for broker conversations
What to look for when analyzing commercial real estate deals
How to build confidence before making acquisition calls
Why market knowledge helps you communicate more effectively
How preparation can improve your deal sourcing process

If you're an acquisitions professional, commercial real estate investor, or aspiring deal finder, this video shows how studying successful transactions can improve your performance.

3. Independent Sponsorship

metadata.title: Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition: A Legal Guide to Buying a Small Business // Ep 32 of DWLD
metadata.author: Dean Street Law
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Dealmaking with Laura DiFrancesco, Laura discusses her new book, 'Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition: A Legal Guide to Buying a Small Business.' She shares her personal journey as a five-time entrepreneur and M&A attorney, emphasizing the importance of legal knowledge in the acquisition process. The episode outlines the book's structure, covering essential topics such as groundwork for acquisition, designing an acquisition strategy, deal economics, due diligence, and the closing process. Laura aims to provide valuable insights and resources for aspiring entrepreneurs looking to navigate the complexities of buying a small business.

What You’ll Learn

The Inspiration Behind the Book
  // Hear why Laura, a five-time entrepreneur and M&A attorney, wrote Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition: A Legal Guide to Buying a Small Business and how her background shaped the book’s vision.
What to Expect Inside the Book
  // Explore the entire ETA journey, from understanding models and responsibilities of ownership to designing your acquisition strategy and aligning it with personal goals. Learn how to build your deal team, source opportunities, and navigate preliminary due diligence. Gain insights into deal economics, negotiation strategies, and the full scope of due diligence — legal, financial, and operational. Dive deep into transaction documents such as purchase agreements, employment contracts, non-competes, escrow agreements, and closing documents. Finally, see how to prepare for closing day, handle post-closing legal wrap-up, and implement a 100-day integration plan for employees, customers, and suppliers.
How to Get Involved
  // Find out how to access the first chapter, share early reviews, and support the book launch across platforms like Amazon and Barnes & Noble, plus opportunities to connect with Laura at ETA events.

metadata.title: SBA Loan to Buy a Business: What Changed on October 1, 2026
metadata.author: The Money Rules
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying a business with an SBA 7(a) loan? The SBA's rulebook changed on October 1, 2026 (SOP 50 10 8.1, Appendix 15) for every application that gets an SBA loan number on or after that date. We cover the four deal types and why a first-time buyer is the strictest, the 10% down payment that can't be waived, what a seller note can and can't do (full standby, at most half), the tougher earnings test (1.25 instead of 1.15, no projections) with the real math on a $1,000,000 purchase (about $57,000 more cash), the valuation and quality of earnings rules, partial sales, the two-year-employee path, and the citizenship rule.

Sources (opened November 4, 2026):
SBA Information Notice 5000-880695, Issuance of SOP 50 10 8.1 (August 14, 2026): https://www.sba.gov/document/information-notice-5000-880695-issuance-sop-50-10-81
SBA SOP 50 10 8.1, Lender and Development Company Loan Programs (effective October 1, 2026), Appendix 15, 7(a) Changes of Ownership; prior SOP 50 10 8 on the same page: https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs
Federal Reserve H.15, Selected Interest Rates (prime rate 7.00%, November 4, 2026): https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/

The example uses the SBA's maximum variable rate for a loan over $350,000 (prime + 3%) at today's prime rate; your rate and terms come from your lender. Rules can change: check the current SOP with an SBA lender before you sign.

General information, not personalized advice.

How to Buy a Business with SBA 7a or Seller Finance

Dive into the world of business acquisition in this episode and learn insider tips and tricks to structure deals for high-leverage acquisitions with little to no money out of pocket.

🔍 Gain Unique Perspectives:
Uncover hidden opportunities by observing day-to-day operations, like the story of a worker adding value to a trucking company by innovating a middleman role between loading and warehousing.

🤝 The Power of Partnerships:
Explore the benefits of partnerships, emphasizing that shared journeys lead to greater success over the long term, diving into how shared wins and challenges make partnerships invaluable.

💡 Creative Aspects of Seller Financing:
Learn the creative flexibility of seller financing, understanding that sellers often prefer gradual payouts over lump sums, showcasing how this benefits both parties.

📈 Essential Margin Insights:
Delve into crucial margin insights across various industries, emphasizing the importance of understanding industry-specific margins while evaluating businesses for acquisition.

🔄 SBA Rule Changes & Flexibility:
Unravel the recent SBA rule changes, particularly the game-changing partial change of ownership, offering buyers and sellers increased flexibility in structuring deals.

Are you an entrepreneur or business owner looking to buy or expand a business? Book a discovery call with Beau to learn all the ways he can help you - http://bookwithbeau.com/
Join my new Business Ownership Academy community on Skool - http://businessownershipacademy.com/

(03:44 ) Challenges with SBA Rates
(04:35) Partial Change of Ownership and SBA Guidelines

metadata.title: EP. 1: Can a Seller Note Cover Your SBA Down Payment? Plus, What Business Should You Buy?
metadata.author: Evan DiLeonardi | Acquisitions
metadata.shortDescription:
Getting a seller to agree to a ten-year standby note can be a tough ask. I discuss negotiating seller financing for an SBA acquisition and what to check with your lender before making an offer. Plus, how your experience affects which business you should buy, and where to start if you’ve never run one.

Questions covered:
• Can a seller note cover part of your SBA down payment?
• What kind of business should you buy, and how does your experience affect that choice?

Submit a question for a future episode: https://forms.gle/6kSxMJdEEJqBwwpKA
Learn about Vyterro: https://vyterro.com
Read Inside the Deal Room: https://insidethedealroom.beehiiv.com
Apply to work with Vyterro: https://www.vyterro.com/apply/

And if it works out, you can make money that way. A lot of people want to buy a business cuz they want to take the shortcut of just getting money as quickly as possible. There's no get-rich-quick scheme, though. There's no quick path to wealth. But it might make sense to just go start a pressure washing company in your neighborhood, a landscaping company, something where you can just go start doing a small amount of ads, maybe hire a person or two, buy a lawnmower, pressure washing machine, go do some jobs, work with customers, get some good reviews, and then you kind of understand how business works if you've never run a business before. And once you have that, then it's a lot easier to go, "Okay, now I understand how this works. I have more experience I can talk about with the bank, with the seller, and now I can buy something that I actually understand a little bit better. It's less risk because I understand it better. And worst case is you just or maybe best case, you start a small pressure washing company and it takes off and you never have to buy a business and you don't have to take a personal guarantee or any risk or put down a bunch of money because you can just start it and grow it organically and bootstrap it. The best thing you can do if you have experience and you don't know what industry to be in is talk to people who understand this world and get feedback on how your specific skills align with industries you could go after, which is a big part of what I do at Vitaro is work with people on what they're good at and then find businesses that match what they're good at and what they'd be qualified for because that's how you can really get the best business that's the lowest risk effectively and easiest to close on it because the seller and the bank will both be more willing to work with you if you have experience in that industry or at least something you can talk to that is related to that industry. That'll be the last question for today, but thanks for tuning in to Acquisition Office Hours. If you have a question that you want answered, feel free to visit bytero.com and submit your question there and we can get it answered on a future episode. Thanks, everyone.

When assessing the value of a small business for sale or purchase, accurately determining its profitability is crucial. One of the key metrics used in this assessment is Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE). SDE provides a clearer picture of a business's financial health by adjusting its earnings to reflect its true earning power. This video explores what is SDE, what common EBITDA add backs are,  and how to calculate them using a typical SDE calculator template.

metadata.title: Behind the Numbers: Quality of Earnings in a Transaction
metadata.author: XPX - Exit Planning Exchange
metadata.shortDescription:
Program produced by XPX Philadelphia.

To view the full video: https://www.exitplanningexchange.com/kx/behind-the-numbers-quality-of-earnings-in-a-transaction/

Quality of Earnings Reports are becoming a key activity during the due diligence process. In this session we will take a deeper look at what a Q of E report is and why it is important.

Our Speaker:

Richard Izzi, Partner, Marcum

Richard Izzi is a partner in the New York Advisory Group of Marcum, where he leads transaction services for the tri-state (NY/NJ/CT) area. He specializes in transaction advisory services to buy- and sell-side clients including private equity funds, strategic investors and lenders.

Mr. Izzi’s experience includes quality of earnings analysis, profitability analysis, financial projections, cash flow modeling, and purchase agreement consultation. He is also experienced in dispute resolution and litigation matters.

This is a free YouTube preview of my full M and A Due Diligence: The Practitioner's Masterclass on Udemy — built on 30 years of live transactions.

The Udemy course covers the complete methodology: Quality of Earnings, EBITDA bridge, NWC peg, commercial DD, legal deal-killers, the three-bucket triage, the valuation waterfall, sign-to-close gap management, plus 21 AI role-plays and a complete practitioner toolkit.

---

Planning your investment banking career? Get the free IB Skills Roadmap — 30+ years of M&A experience distilled into one essential guide.
👉 jbdcolley.com/ibskills

EBITDA is an opinion. Cash flow is a fact. The gap between them is where M&A deals succeed or fail. This video walks through the EBITDA-to-free-cash-flow bridge — the single most important framework in financial due diligence — including the five things EBITDA ignores and the conversion ratio that tells you the truth about a target business.
 
The Summit Industrial Services case study reveals how twenty point seven million of normalised EBITDA becomes eight point one million of free cash flow — a thirty-nine percent conversion ratio that completely changes the deal thesis.
 
This is part 6 of an eight-part walkthrough of financial due diligence.

02:45 The EBITDA-to-FCF bridge

04:14 Diagnosing cash conversion problems

metadata.title: Fixed asset toolkit: Asset acquisitions
metadata.author: PwC US
metadata.shortDescription:
In our Toolkit podcast series, we are taking a deep dive into one accounting topic each month that goes beyond the basics and into areas that require judgment. This month, we are covering fixed assets – from acquisitions and capitalization to disposals.


In this episode, Heather Horn was joined by Beth Paul from PwC’s National Office to discuss the accounting guidance for asset acquisitions, including distinguishing an acquisition of an asset from the acquisition of a business, along with complexities that may be faced when accounting for asset acquisitions.


In this episode, you will hear:

  •  1:24 - An overview of the asset acquisition and business combination models
  •  4:17 - How to use the screen test to identify asset acquisitions 
  •  9:21 - How to record asset acquisitions, and related transactions recognized separately
  •  18:03 - Complexities faced by the buyer, including contingent consideration
  •  24:06 - Key reminders for a seller when accounting for the disposal of an asset
  •  26:01 - Final advice for those beginning the asset acquisition process

Want to learn more? Listen to our podcast discussing the complexities faced in business combinations and asset acquisitions (https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/podcasts/podcasts_US/Asset_vs_business_acquisition_The_differences_you_need_to_know.html) , and read our chapters on asset acquisitions (https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/property_plant_equip/property_plant_equip_US/Chapter-2--Asset-acquisitions-formerly-BCG-7/21-Asset-acquisitions--chapter-overview.html)  in our PP&E and other assets guide and how to identify a business using the screen test (https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/business_combination/business_combination__28_US/chapter_1_scope_US/12_definition_of_a_b_US.html)  in our Business combinations guide.


Beth Paul (https://www.linkedin.com/in/bethpaulpwc/)  is a Deputy Chief Accountant in PwC’s National Office responsible for a team of consultants that specialize in business combinations and related areas, such as consolidations, disposals, impairments, and segment reporting. Prior to this role, Beth was the Strategic Thought Leader in PwC’s National office, working closely with firm leadership to determine PwC’s position on emerging trends in auditing, accounting, and financial reporting matters.


Heather Horn (https://www.linkedin.com/in/heather-horn/)  is PwC’s National Office thought leader, responsible for developing our communications strategy and conveying firm positions on accounting and financial reporting matters. She is the engaging host of PwC’s accounting and reporting weekly podcast and quarterly webcast series. With over 30 years of experience, Heather’s accounting and auditing expertise includes financial instruments and rate-regulated accounting.


Transcripts available upon request for individuals who may need a disability-related accommodation. Please send requests to us_podcast@pwc.com (mailto:us_podcast@pwc.com) .


Did you enjoy this episode? Text us your thoughts and be sure to include the episode name. (https://www.buzzsprout.com/276516/fan_mail/new)

metadata.title: Investment Banking - How To Calculate Net Working Capital for an M&A Transaction - Transact Capital
metadata.author: Transact Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
In this informative presentation, we delve into the world of Net Working Capital, covering three crucial topics that will provide clarity for business owners contemplating a sale of their business. Whether you're a seller or just curious about the intricacies of Net Working Capital, this video is designed to shed light on the subject.

Topic 1: Calculating Net Working Capital
Learn the step-by-step process of calculating Net Working Capital. We break down the elements involved, including adjustments to internal financial statements, and discuss which line items are included in the calculation.

Topic 2: Establishing a Net Working Capital Target
Discover how the Net Working Capital Target is determined, a critical aspect of the seller's obligations at closing. Dive into negotiations around line items and the historical period used to set the target.

Topic 3: Impact on Closing Cash
Explore how Net Working Capital affects the cash received at the day of closing. Understand the concept of "estimated closing Net Working Capital" and how it compares to the established target. Learn how this comparison can affect the purchase price, either increasing or decreasing it.

Remember, Net Working Capital can be complex, and understanding it is crucial in ensuring a smooth business sale. Don't let misunderstandings or disagreements over Net Working Capital derail your deal. Educate yourself and seek expert advice early in the process.

For a digital copy of this presentation, please reach out to us at Ross@transactcapital.com. 

Subscribe and stay tuned for more valuable insights into the world of business transactions!

metadata.title: How to Sell Your Business: The 8-Stage M&A Process Explained
metadata.author: THE M&A DESK
metadata.shortDescription:
Selling your business is not "find a buyer, agree on a price, get a check." It is typically a six to twelve month process with eight distinct stages, and most first-time sellers are caught off guard by almost every one of them.

In this video we walk through exactly what happens when a business gets sold, stage by stage, and where deals most often fall apart or get repriced.

What you will learn:

• Why preparation is the stage owners skip, and the one that costs them the most money later: clean financials, a quality of earnings review and knowing what kind of exit you want.
• How valuation works for small and mid-sized businesses, and why a financial buyer and a strategic buyer will value your company differently.
• How a company goes to market anonymously, using a teaser, an NDA and a confidential information memorandum (CIM).
• What indications of interest tell you about who is serious and what range the market supports.
• How management meetings and the letter of intent (LOI) work, and why exclusivity means you lose leverage the moment you sign.
• Why due diligence is where most deals die, and how undisclosed problems cost you negotiating power.
• What is negotiated in the definitive agreement, including warranties, indemnification, escrow and earnouts.
• What closing and the transition period really look like.

Timestamps:
0:00 Introduction
0:58 Stage 1: Preparation
2:27 Stage 2: Valuation
3:43 Stage 3: Going to market
4:42 Stage 4: Indications of interest
5:15 Stage 5: Management meetings and the LOI
6:21 Stage 6: Due diligence
7:12 Stage 7: The definitive agreement
8:02 Stage 8: Closing and transition
8:37 Summary

This is the first video in our M&A for Business Owners series. Upcoming videos will go deeper into each stage, starting with how buyers actually calculate what your business is worth, followed by letters of intent and how earnouts get negotiated.

Subscribe so you do not miss the next video, and let us know in the comments which part of the M&A process you would like us to explain next.

How does M&A work?

stage when a business actually gets

Before a single buyer ever sees your
business, the real work starts with
preparation. And this is the stage most
owners skip or rush, and the one that
costs them the most money later.
Buyers pay for what they can verify, not
what you tell them. That means clean,
consistent financial statements, ideally
3 years of them, with personal expenses
already separated out of the business.
It means having a handle on customer
concentration, contracts, and any legal
or operational loose ends.
Larger deals often involve a formal
quality of earnings review, essentially
an independent audit of your financials
done before you ever go to market, so
there are no surprises later.
This stage also means getting honest
with yourself about what you actually
want.
A full exit, a pre-exit or partial sale
where you stay on, or a transition
period. That answer shapes everything
that comes after it. Owners who skip
this stage and go straight to finding a
buyer almost always end up renegotiating
more on the price downward later in the
process. Once diligence uncovers what
preparation would have caught first.
Preparation can reduce the amount of
negotiation later in the process
increasing the price paid for the
company. Once your numbers are in order,
the next question is, "What's this
actually worth?"
For most small and mid-size businesses,
valuation comes down to a multiple of
earnings, typically EBITDA, or for very
small businesses, seller's discretionary
earnings.
The multiple itself depends on your
industry, growth rate, customer
concentration, and how replaceable you
personally are in the business.
It's also important to understand there
are two different types of buyers who
will value you differently.
A financial buyer, think private equity,
is underwriting a return based on your
stand-alone cash flow.
A strategic buyer, a competitor or a
company in an adjacent space, might pay
a premium because your business is worth
more to them combined with what they
already have through cost savings or new
customer access.
Knowing which type of buyer you're
targeting changes what number is
realistic.
A strategic buyer is usually interested
in an acquisition of 100% of the shares,
whereas financial buyers often buy a
majority or minority of the shares.
Financial buyers prefer the directors of
the company to have skin in the game
leading the company they invest in. Once
you have a valuation range, the business
gets marketed, usually anonymously at
first. This starts with a teaser, a one
or two page anonymous summary of your
business that gives enough detail to
generate interest without revealing your
identity or tipping off employees,
competitors, or customers.
Interested parties who want more sign a
non-disclosure agreement and only then
receive the confidential information
memorandum, a much more detailed
document covering your financials,
operations, market position, and growth
story.
This is usually where an owner working
with an M&A advisor or business broker
sees the biggest advantage since they
run out reach to a curated list of
buyers instead of the owner having to do
it themselves quietly.
An M&A advisor or business broker will
prepare the anonymous teaser and
confidential information memorandum
prior to approaching potential buyers.
Buyers who are seriously interested
submit an indication of interest, a
non-binding preliminary offer that
includes a proposed price range, deal
structure, and key assumptions.
This is the first real filter. It tells
you who's serious, what range the market
actually supports, and which buyers you
want to move forward with.
Most sellers narrow the field here
inviting a handful of the strongest
indications into the next stage rather
than negotiating with just one buyer at
a time. Shortlisted buyers typically
meet with you and your management team
directly together with your M&A advisor
or business broker if you work with them
asking detailed questions about
operations, customers, and growth plans.
This is as much about the buyer
evaluating you as it is about you
evaluating them. You're about to
potentially work with this buyer through
a transition period, so fit matters.
From there, your top buyer submits a
letter of intent, a much more detailed
though still mostly non-binding
agreement on price and structure.
Signing an LOI usually comes with an
exclusivity period, meaning you agree to
stop talking to other buyers while this
one completes due diligence.
This is a real commitment, so the LOI
stage is where you want your key deal
terms, price, structure, working
capital, closing mechanism, escrow, your
post-close role locked down as tightly
as possible because you lose negotiating
leverage the moment exclusivity begins.
This is the stage where most deals die
or get repriced. Due diligence is the
buyer verifying everything you've told
them. Financial audits, legal review of
contracts and liabilities, customer and
employee interviews, IT and operational
assessments, sometimes environmental or
regulatory checks depending on your
industry.
It's invasive, it's slow, and it's the
stage where undisclosed problems
surface. An unhappy key customer, an
unclear contract, an inconsistency
between what management said and what
the books show. This is exactly why
stage one, preparation, matters so much.
Problems that surface here, after you've
already signed an exclusivity agreement,
cost you leverage.
Problems you catch and fix before you
ever go to market cost you nothing.
Assuming diligence goes well, lawyers
draft the definitive purchase agreement,
the actual binding contract. This is
where the real negotiation often
happens. Representations and warranties
about the state of the business,
indemnification if something turns out
to be wrong after closing, how much of
the purchase price sits in escrow, and
how any earnout, a portion of the price
paid later, contingent on the business
hitting performance targets actually
gets calculated and paid.
Earnouts, in particular, are where many
sellers get burned if they're not
careful because they shift risk back
onto you after you've technically
already sold.
If a deal includes one, exactly how it's
measured and who controls the business
during the earnout period deserves real
scrutiny. Once the agreement is signed,
closing itself can be almost
anti-climactic.
Funds move, ownership transfers, and the
paperwork is finalized, often within
days of signing.
What matters more is what happens right
after.
Most deals include a transition period
where the seller stays on for weeks,
months, or years to hand off
relationships and institutional
knowledge.
How that transition is structured is
usually negotiated well before this
point, not figured out afterward.
Every one of these eight stages is its
own topic that deserves a much deeper
dive, especially valuation, letters of
intent, and how earn-outs actually get
negotiated, since that's where most of
the money either gets protected or lost.
If you're a business owner thinking
about a future sale, subscribe. We're

in upcoming videos, starting with how
buyers actually calculate what your
business is worth.
Let us know in the comments what topic
of an M&A process you'd like to see an

timeline), exclusivity and how long it lasts, the due diligence window,
and the deal terms from the seller's side: earn-outs, seller financing,
support periods and non-competes. What sellers do when a buyer asks to
lower the price late. Worked through on InvoicePing, a made-up product.
General information, not legal advice.

Then the buyer's draft doesn't arrive for two weeks.
New questions start coming in, one at a time.
Meanwhile the other interested buyers, told the product was taken, have stopped
writing.
Three weeks later, there's still nothing signed, and the buyer would like a few
more months of numbers before going further.
Nobody did anything wrong.
Nobody wrote anything down.
This is Selling your SaaS, episode five.
The offer is on the table.
This episode is about the documents and terms that turn it into a deal, seen from
the seller's side.
The step that was missing is a letter of intent: one or two pages that write down
what was agreed, before the detailed work starts.
It's not the final contract, but it gives both sides the same picture.
The price, and how much of it is paid at closing.
What's included: the domain, the code, the customers, the content, and any support.
The timeline: how long due diligence lasts, and a target date for closing.
Exclusivity: how long the seller stops talking to other buyers.
The conditions that have to be true for the deal to close.
And which parts are binding, which is usually only exclusivity and
confidentiality, with everything else confirmed in the final agreement.
On MySaaSForSale, the platform's part ends with the introduction: it was built so
indie developers can trade directly, peer to peer, with no intermediaries and no
fees, so the letter, like the deal, is between buyer and seller.
Exclusivity is the one thing a seller gives up at this stage, so its length
matters.
A buyer asks for time to check the product without competition, which is fair.
For a small product, thirty days is common, and it works best with an end date
in writing.
Inside those days, due diligence runs on a list agreed up front, so new questions
don't keep arriving in week four.
The final agreement gets drafted while the checks finish.
Then the deal closes, ideally inside the window.
And if it doesn't, the end date does its job: the seller is free to talk to others
again, or to agree an extension, knowingly.
The pricing playlist described the other terms that can appear in an offer.
Here they are from the seller's side.
An earn-out needs a target that's measured somewhere both sides can see, and an
answer to what happens if the buyer changes the product so the target can't be
hit.
Seller financing needs a schedule, and a clause for a missed payment.
A support period is the term sellers most often regret leaving vague: how many
weeks, how many hours a week, and whether it's by email or calls.
Two weeks of answering questions can become two months of unpaid work without a
limit.
And a non-compete needs a length and a scope: not building another invoicing
reminder tool is reasonable; not building any software at all usually isn't.
Between the first offer and the letter, there's usually some negotiating, and the
habit that helps most is trading rather than conceding.
When a buyer asks for a lower price, a seller can ask for more of it at closing,
or a shorter support period, so the lower number buys something in return.
When the buyer wants part of the price as an earn-out, a higher total and read-only
access to the numbers are fair things to ask back, because the seller is taking on
risk.
When the buyer wants a longer exclusivity, a faster due diligence list, or a deposit
held in escrow, keeps both sides committed.
And when the buyer wants longer support, paid hours after the first few weeks keep
it from becoming open-ended.
Each trade keeps the deal moving, and keeps it balanced.
Here's InvoicePing's deal, rewound to the call and written down that evening.
Price: €88,000, all of it at closing, through an escrow service the two of them
choose together.
Included: the domain, the code, the customer list, the help pages and the
brand.
Support: two weeks after the handover, by email, ten hours a week at most.
Exclusivity: thirty days from signing, ending automatically.
Due diligence: twenty-one days, on a list attached to the letter.
Non-compete: two years, covering invoice reminder tools only.
And only the exclusivity and the confidentiality are binding.
It fits on one page, and both sides signed it the next day.
The same call, the same price, and three weeks of drift avoided.
The list attached to InvoicePing's letter is short, and that's the point: it's
agreed before the twenty-one days start, so it doesn't grow during them.
Revenue and churn, by screen share, then read-only access for the length of due
diligence.
Costs, from twelve months of business card statements.
The code and the hosting: read access to the repository once the letter is signed,
and a test deploy with the seller on a call.
Customers: counts, plans, and the biggest customers' shares, still without names.
And the accounts: the list of everything that moves, and whose name each one is in.
Almost all of it already exists, because it's the numbers pack from episode two.
Sometimes, late in due diligence, a buyer asks to lower the price.
The first question back is what exactly they found: a specific finding, or a
general feeling that came with cold feet.
Then whether it was new.
This is where the listing and the numbers pack pay off: if the churn, or the
dependence on one channel, was written down from the start, it was already priced
into the offer, and pricing it twice isn't reasonable.
If something genuinely new turned up, like a cost nobody knew about, it can be
measured, and the price can move by what it's worth, not by a round number.
And the walk-away number, decided calmly before this call, does the rest.
Exclusivity ends on a known date, and other buyers exist.
Before the detailed work starts, five things are worth having on paper.
The price and its structure.
A short exclusivity, with an end date.
The due diligence list, agreed up front.
What's included, spelled out.
And the support period, capped in weeks and hours.
This is general information, not legal advice: for a real deal, the letter and
the final agreement are worth having checked by a lawyer you choose.
Next, the last episode of this playlist: closing and handover.
How escrow works, and the order in which a product actually changes hands.
The guides are linked below.
